332.text: Unlike its more common literal sense of persons being 'idle/lazy' (e.g. idle in the marketplace, Mt 20:3,6), here the adjective is applied metaphorically to faith itself as an abstraction, describing its ineffectiveness rather than a person's laziness.

337.text: Idleness (G0692) directly predicates faith (M13) as inoperative apart from works; it relates to the wanting/knowing verbs (G2309, G1097) only as the content to be recognized, not as a party-sharing characteristic itself -- its core tight relation remains with M13, same party (the professed believer).

338.text: No operation/role-T3 word is present in Jas 2:20 alongside a party tag in direct relation to G0692; the verb 'is' (copula) carries no operational force.

452.text: This occurrence matches spoude's usual 'earnestness/zeal' sense as elsewhere in 2 Corinthians (7:11-12; 8:7); no divergence from that pattern appears here.

454.text: Earnest care (G4710), as this word's own vantage: it is the content God places into the heart (G2588), and its presence there is the ground of Paul's thanks (G5485) -- it is the causal center that both the heart's reception and the resulting thanksgiving depend on.

586.text: G0692 functions as the negative pole of the M67 cluster, spanning literal unemployment (Matt 20:3,6), habitual moral laziness (1 Tim 5:13; Titus 1:12), and metaphorical spiritual unfruitfulness (2 Pet 1:8; Jas 2:20) -- the broadest and most semantically flexible term in the cluster.

594.text: Within its own 8 occurrences, G0692 shows the same negative-pole 'not-working' core as G0691 and H8220, but uniquely spans the full range from wholly literal/circumstantial idleness (Matt.20.3,6 -- unemployed day-laborers awaiting hire, a neutral economic state) to morally-loaded habitual laziness (1Tim.5.13; Titus.1.12) to fully metaphorical spiritual unfruitfulness (2Pet.1.8; Jas.2.20) to careless/culpable speech (Matt.12.36) -- making it the semantic bridge connecting the concrete physical sense shared with H8220 and the abstract personification sense shared with G0691.

606.text: G4709 and G4710 share the same root and semantic arc; G4710 supplies the same relational-earnestness sense that G4709 exhibits, seen concretely in Luke 1:39 (haste to a kinswoman) and 2Cor 8:16 (earnest care placed in Titus's heart for the Corinthians) -- both members thus converge on urgency/zeal directed toward persons, not only tasks.

608.text: G4710 is exclusively nominal across all twelve of its occurrences (N-ASF, N-GSF, N-DSF forms), meaning the subgroup's noun-member consistently names diligence/zeal/haste as a possessable, giveable, or measurable quality (something one 'shows', 'has produced in you', 'puts into a heart', or is measured 'by') -- structurally opposite to G4709's pure manner-of-action adverbial function. This is the clearest grammatical-role divergence between the two subgroup members: G4710 names the THING, G4709 describes the HOW.

667.text: The evidence does not establish a consistent precede/follow pattern relative to judgement or belief. In Matt.20.6 idleness precedes a challenge/question (which functions as address, not judgement per se); in Jas.2.20 'useless' functions as a conclusion about faith reached through argument (following an implied judgement); in 2Pet.2.3 'not idle' asserts the ongoing operation of a prior judgement (condemnation) rather than preceding or following a discrete belief-act. Signal: this may resolve further with adjacent-verse context on the argument structures in James and 2 Peter.

672.text: Yes, the mechanism differs sharply by context: in Eccl.10.18 idleness operates through bodily/instrumental neglect (slack hands failing to maintain a structure, producing physical decay); in Matt.20.3,6 it operates as an economic/circumstantial state (lack of an employer/opportunity) reversed by verbal address and assignment; in 1Tim.5.13/Titus.1.12 it operates as a habitual moral-social vice generating further vices (gossip, meddling); in 2Pet.1.8/Jas.2.20 it operates metaphorically as spiritual unfruitfulness/uselessness of qualities or faith; in 2Pet.2.3 it operates as personified negation describing the unceasing operation of divine judgement.

675.text: Yes -- mode varies: literal/physical (Matt.20.3,6 -- standing unemployed; Eccl.10.18 -- slack hands causing structural decay), social-habitual (1Tim.5.13; Titus.1.12 -- persons characterized as idlers/gluttons), verbal-moral (Matt.12.36 -- careless words), spiritual-metaphorical (2Pet.1.8 -- ineffective in knowledge; Jas.2.20 -- useless faith), and abstract-personified (2Pet.2.3 -- condemnation not idle). Constitutional level ranges from bodily/hand-instrumental (H8220) to purely predicated-abstract (G0691).

677.text: Idleness/uselessness takes hold rightly (i.e. is rightly named/exposed) under conditions of neglect: slack hands (Eccl.10.18), lack of assigned work/opportunity (Matt.20.3,6), habitual house-to-house wandering without occupation (1Tim.5.13), and absence of works accompanying professed faith (Jas.2.20). Inwardly, its 'proper' operation (as a negative diagnostic) requires an underlying absence of diligence, zeal, or productive engagement.

682.text: The relational scope is universal in principle -- idleness/uselessness is applied to Jewish day-laborers, Gentile Cretans, Christian widows, and abstract qualities (faith, condemnation) alike, with no ethnic, gender, or covenantal exclusion visible in the evidence; the only consistent exclusion is from those actively engaged in productive labor, virtue, or works.

684.text: None -- the subgroup's evidence does not depict a human-to-God movement associated with idleness/indolence; the characteristic is descriptive of human or abstract states, not itself a movement toward God.

688.text: Where idleness is present in a person (1Tim.5.13; Titus.1.12) or where useless faith lacks works (Jas.2.20), it indicates diminished or unrealized expression of the divine image's active/relational capacities; where it is absent and replaced by increasing virtue (2Pet.1.8), the image's fruitful function is evidenced as intact and growing.

699.text: The origin is multiple and context-dependent: circumstantial/economic (lack of a hiring employer, Matt.20.3,6), habitual/social (learned through idle house-to-house wandering, 1Tim.5.13), cultural-ethnic stereotype (Titus.1.12), spiritual deficiency (absence of increasing virtue, 2Pet.1.8), evidential absence of works (Jas.2.20), physical neglect (slack hands, Eccl.10.18), and rhetorical personification (2Pet.2.3). No single origin is uniform.

700.text: The faculties most engaged are the will/behavior (standing idle, going about, engaging or not in work) and speech (careless words, Matt.12.36; direct address, Matt.20.6), with the intellect/faith-conviction faculty engaged metaphorically in Jas.2.20 (faith without works). The affections/emotions are never engaged -- no occurrence attaches feeling-language to idleness, indicating the characteristic's nature is behavioral/volitional and evidentiary (visible in outward act or its absence) rather than affective.

704.text: At its edge, the characteristic excludes/resists productive labor, fruitful spiritual growth, and useful/effective works -- it is defined precisely by the negation and absence of these things (2Pet.1.8's 'ineffective or unfruitful'; Jas.2.20's 'useless...apart from works').

706.text: Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside idleness: sloth/H6103 (Eccl.10.18, synonymous parallelism); hand/body-instrument language (H3027-related, Eccl.10.18); gossip and busybodiness (1Tim.5.13); lying and evil-beast character (Titus.1.12, tricolon of vices); knowledge/virtue-list qualities (2Pet.1.8); faith and works (Jas.2.20); condemnation and destruction/'not asleep' (2Pet.2.3, synonymous parallel negation). These co-occurrences are frequent and consistently pair idleness with either vice-clusters or growth/virtue-clusters as its counterpoint.

708.text: Yes -- idleness precedes and generates further vice in 1Tim.5.13 (idleness -> gossip/busybodiness) and in Eccl.10.18 (indolent hands -> house decay); it is diagnostically dependent on/follows the absence of works in Jas.2.20 (faith without works -> shown to be useless). In Matt.20.3,6 idleness precedes and is resolved by being hired into work.

709.text: The sequence is causal in Eccl.10.18 and 1Tim.5.13 (idleness mechanically/socially produces decay or further vice) and diagnostic/correlational in Jas.2.20 (absence of works correlates with and evidences dead faith, rather than causing it). In Matt.20.3-6 the sequence is developmental -- idleness resolved into productive engagement through the householder's initiative.

778.text: The characteristic reads as belonging to created design rather than the fallen condition: it is commended as a positive Christian virtue to be exercised (Rom 12:8, 12:11; Heb 6:11; 2Pet 1:5) and modeled even by God himself in placing it in Titus's heart (2Cor 8:16) -- there is no instance where earnestness itself is portrayed as a fallen distortion, only its absence (idleness/sloth) is negatively marked.

782.text: Yes. The mode varies by direction: God-to-person (2Cor 8:16, earnest care put into Titus's heart by God), person-to-person (Luke 7:4 pleading for another; Titus 3:13 provisioning for others; 2Tim 1:17 searching for Paul), and person-toward-God/spiritual-goal (Rom 12:11 zeal in serving the Lord; Heb 6:11 earnestness toward hope; 2Pet 1:5 effort in supplementing faith). It operates at the level of will/action throughout, never at a merely bodily-reflex level.

788.text: Yes. Within existing relational bonds (kinship, close ministry partnership) the characteristic appears as warm, sustained care -- Luke 1:39 (Mary to kinswoman Elizabeth), 2Cor 8:16 (Titus's earnest care for the Corinthians, put there by God), 2Tim 1:17 (Onesiphorus's earnest search for his friend Paul). Across relational distance or unfamiliarity it appears as urgent advocacy or provision on behalf of someone less close -- Luke 7:4 (Jewish elders pleading for a Gentile centurion), Titus 3:13 (provisioning traveling workers). The characteristic thus operates in both settings but with differing textures: relational bonds intensify it into personal devotion, while distance channels it into practical intercession or hospitality.

790.text: The relational scope is broad: it includes fellow believers (2Cor 8:16, Titus's care for Corinthians), ministry partners and traveling workers (Titus 3:13, 2Tim 1:17), kin (Luke 1:39), and even those outside the community of faith or covenant (Luke 7:4, elders for a Gentile centurion). No occurrence shows the characteristic explicitly excluding any category of person; where it is withheld, it is due to personal sloth/idleness rather than the exclusion of a class of people.

794.text: Where God himself is shown extending earnestness/earnest care (2Cor 8:16, placing it in Titus's heart), the aspect of divine likeness instantiated is God's own active, purposeful care for his people -- the person's earnestness toward others mirrors God's own earnest care extended toward them.

795.text: Shared between God and the person: 2Cor 8:16 shows God himself placing 'the same earnest care' in Titus that Paul has for the Corinthians -- the identical quality (spoudē) is attributed to both God's giving and the human recipient's possession, not merely an analogue.

797.text: The pattern of occurrence shows the characteristic seated primarily at the level of will/spirit engaged in directed action, paired explicitly with 'spirit' in Rom 12:11 ('fervent in spirit') and with 'heart' in 2Cor 8:16 (placed 'into the heart of Titus'). It never engages purely bodily/sensory levels in isolation, though physical motion (haste, Mark 6:25; Luke 1:39) is its outward expression. The heart/spirit link here is expressive -- the inner earnestness expresses itself outwardly through bodily action (hurrying) or verbal/practical deeds (pleading, providing), rather than the body generating the earnestness itself.

798.text: The body link runs from inner disposition (heart/spirit) outward to bodily action: the earnest care placed in Titus's heart (2Cor 8:16) and the zeal/fervency of spirit (Rom 12:11) express themselves through physical haste (Mark 6:25; Luke 1:39) and active service. There is no instance of bodily feedback generating or intensifying the inner disposition in the reverse direction within this evidence; the direction is consistently spirit/heart-to-body/action.

799.text: Yes, movement is evidenced onto the person from an external source in 2Cor 8:16 -- God places earnest care 'into the heart of Titus', an inward-then-outward sequence (God to heart, heart to action toward the Corinthians). Elsewhere the movement is internally generated (spirit/heart to bodily action) without an external divine source named, as in Rom 12:11's spirit-to-service sequence.

800.text: God's extension of the characteristic in 2Cor 8:16 is unconditional and responsive -- given freely by God ('who put into the heart of Titus') in response to Paul's own existing earnest care for the Corinthians, prompting thanksgiving rather than being earned or conditioned on prior merit by Titus.

801.text: God's giving of earnest care shows a disposition of active, personal involvement in the well-being of his people -- he is not distant but works through his servants' hearts to secure ongoing practical care for the church, evidencing a relational, providential disposition.

802.text: Genuine extension of the characteristic from one person to another accompanies love that is sincere rather than merely commanded (2Cor 8:8, 'not as a command, but to prove... that your love also is genuine') and a heart already shaped by God's own gift of care (2Cor 8:16) -- the giver's inward sincerity and divinely-worked disposition underlie true extension.

803.text: A person must first receive the quality from God (as Titus received earnest care placed in his heart, 2Cor 8:16) before extending it genuinely to others -- the giving is grounded in a prior reception, not self-generated.

807.text: No occurrence in this subgroup shows earnestness/diligence being communicated, strengthened, or mediated through angelic ministry; its extension is shown as coming directly from God to a human heart (2Cor 8:16) without an angelic intermediary.

808.text: The origin is multiple and context-dependent: sometimes internally generated within the person themselves as their own resolve/effort (Luke 7:4's elders, Titus 3:13's imperative, 2Pet 1:5's self-applied effort), and sometimes explicitly God-given (2Cor 8:16, placed by God into Titus's heart). The subgroup shows no single fixed origin -- it shifts between human self-motivation and divine impartation depending on context.

809.text: The characteristic consistently engages the will/volitional faculty (deciding to act with intensity) and frequently the affective faculty (spirit/heart, as in Rom 12:11's 'fervent in spirit' and 2Cor 8:16's 'heart') but never the purely cognitive/reasoning faculty in isolation -- it is not primarily a matter of understanding or belief-formation but of engaged will and feeling directed into action, indicating its nature as a motivational rather than cognitive characteristic.

1109.text: In Ps.138.2 'give thanks' sits squarely within the base Hiphil liturgical gloss with no distinguishing nuance -- straightforward thanksgiving toward God's name.

1112.text: In Ps.138.2, thanksgiving (H3034) is directed at the divine name and stands alongside steadfast love (M07/M50, H2617A), faithfulness (M13, H0571G), and exaltation (M22, H1431) -- thanksgiving here is the responsive verbal act that answers and publicly announces those other divine attributes; it is the vehicle by which love/faithfulness/exaltation become spoken acknowledgment.

1122.text: In Ps.138.2 the psalmist (first person) initiates the thanksgiving-operation directed toward 'your name' (the Lord), a first-person-to-divine-second-person direction.

1346.text: In Ps.138.2 the Hiphil form sits squarely within the standard 'give thanks' sense (1c1), directed at the divine name alongside love/faithfulness -- no notable divergence from the base gloss.

1356.text: Building on the prior finding that thanksgiving answers love/faithfulness/exaltation: from thanksgiving's own vantage, it is the SOLE verbal-response mechanism in the verse that converts three separate divine attributes (steadfast love M07/M50, faithfulness M13, exaltation M22) into one unified act of acknowledgment -- without H3034 these attributes would remain unspoken states; thanksgiving supplies the only verb of address directed at the divine name itself.

1366.text: H3034 ('give thanks,' HVhu1cs) is the operation-tagged verb of thanksgiving-relevance in this verse, though role-T3 is not itself marked on H3034 here; the clear role-T3 operation is H7812 'bow down' -- initiated by the psalmist (first person) and directed toward God's holy temple, establishing the posture that the following thanksgiving-act (H3034) then verbally performs toward God's name.

1476.text: In Ezra.10.1 and Neh.1.6, H3034 appears in Hithpael as 'confession' rather than the more common 'thanksgiving' sense -- a marked divergence from the base Hiphil gloss of praise/thanks. Here the impact is penitential: Ezra's confession is paired with weeping and prostration over the people's sin, and Nehemiah's confession covers Israel's national sin -- contrasting with the celebratory 'give thanks' occurrences (Ps.86.12, Ps.28.7) where the same root denotes joyful praise. This shows the lemma's bifurcated stem-based sense split.

1480.text: In Neh.1.6, confession (H3034) co-occurs with M41 (attentive/hear), M42 (prayer), M36 (servant), M56 (sin, twice). Confession functions as the specific content of the prayer being lifted, naming the sin for which attentive hearing is sought -- prayer is the vehicle, confession is the substantive act naming the wrong, and the servant-language frames the posture of the one confessing.

1578.text: H7183A functions purely as an adjectival qualifier of 'ear,' not as an independently-shifting term; no divergence beyond its modifying role.

1579.text: In Neh.1.6 'prayer' sits within the base gloss of formal address to God; no notable divergence.

1580.text: In Neh.1.6 'sinned' sits within the base Qal gloss of moral transgression; no notable divergence.

1581.text: In Neh.1.6 'servant/servants' sits within the base gloss of humble self-designation/status before God; no notable divergence.

1730.text: In Ps.138.2 the Hiphil 'give thanks' sits squarely within the base gloss of praising/thanking the divine name; no notable surface divergence from the general stepGloss is present here.

1740.text: Building on the prior chain: thanksgiving's role as sole verbal-response converting love/faithfulness/exaltation into acknowledgment is reinforced by noting the temple/name-word cluster (T2 tags) surrounding it -- thanksgiving is the one act among all attributes present that actually crosses from named divine quality into spoken human response toward the temple/name.

1750.text: H3034 ('give thanks') itself is the T2-tagged act (not role-T3 operation) in Ps.138.2; the only role-T3 operation word present is H7812 'bow down', initiated by the psalmist and directed toward the holy temple -- no role-T3 tag attaches to H3034 here, so D7.7.1 targets the bowing rather than the thanking.

1828.text: In Neh.1.6 'confessing' likewise renders the penitential sense (confession of the sins of Israel), aligning with Ezra.10.1 rather than the thanksgiving/praise occurrences -- confirming a real bifurcation in usage across this cluster's own verse set between praise-occurrences and confession-occurrences of the same root.

1833.text: Adding to the prior finding for Neh.1.6: from confession's own vantage, it functions here as embedded WITHIN prayer (M42) rather than alongside it as a separate act -- confession is the specific content-clause of the prayer being offered, making it subordinate in form but central in substance to what is prayed.

1837.text: In Neh.1.6 Nehemiah (the speaking 'I', party) initiates the confessing operation, directed toward God (addressed as 'you'), naming the sins of the people of Israel including himself and his father's house.

1931.text: Here 'I give thanks... churches... give thanks as well' sits squarely within the base gloss of grateful acknowledgment toward human benefactors who risked their lives — no notable divergence from the term's ordinary interpersonal-gratitude sense.

1932.text: G2168 co-occurs with 'life/soul' (M47, G5590H) and 'churches' (M44, G1577). Here thanksgiving is directed corporately (by Paul and 'all the churches') toward those who risked their own life/soul for another's sake — thanksgiving functions as the corporate, ongoing response owed to sacrificial risk-taking on behalf of the community.

1933.text: The role-T3 operation word 'risked' (G5294) is initiated by the unnamed persons (Prisca and Aquila) and directed toward saving 'my life' (Paul's) — the risking-act is the ground for the thanksgiving that follows, though G2168 itself carries no T3 tag in this verse.

2211.text: In Lev.16.21 'confess' renders the Hithpael sense (confession of sin transferred onto the scapegoat), a distinct nuance from the Hiphil 'give thanks/praise' sense seen elsewhere in this batch (e.g. Ps.7.17, Ps.18.49) -- here the impact is ritual/transferential rather than doxological, marking the negative/penitential pole of the same root.

2215.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs with H3034 in Lev.16.21; the confession act stands alone amid role-only tags (M-codes present belong to non-home strongs but none are flagged as sharing this cluster's relational chain in prior context, and no prior pass exists for this verse).

2272.text: In Ps.142.7 the infinitive construct 'give thanks to' following deliverance from prison matches the base gloss of thanksgiving for rescue; no divergence.

2296.text: H3034 in Ps.142.7 carries only M49; the verse's role-T3 words (H3318H 'Bring', H3803 'surround', H1580 'deal bountifully') are separate strongs -- 'Bring me out' is God's operation directed toward the psalmist, but not H3034's own tag.

2307.text: H3034 co-occurs with M47 (soul/self, 'me') and M12 (righteous). First pass: the psalmist's own selfhood (M47) is the site from which thanksgiving arises upon deliverance, while the righteous (M12) are the community that will gather around him -- thanksgiving here bridges personal rescue and communal righteousness.

2606.text: Other M-codes are present in this verse (M52 built up, M62 established, M13 faith, M15 taught) but thanksgiving here functions as a summarizing capstone term ('abounding in thanksgiving') rather than in direct operational relation to any one of them individually -- it characterizes the overall state described by the other terms together.

2615.text: Role-T3 tags fall on 'rooted', 'built up' (implicit T3-type participles) and 'abounding', all initiated by the believers (party, 'you') and directed toward their own establishment in Christ and faith; G2169 (thanksgiving) itself carries M49 not T3, naming the overflow-state rather than an operation.

2773.text: In Neh.12.38 as in 12.31, todah functions as the name/designation of the second thanksgiving choir ('the other choir of those who gave thanks'), a concrete institutional-group sense rather than abstract praise, consistent with the divergence already noted at Neh.12.31.

2774.text: Other M-codes present are M08 (broad/wide, H7342G, qualifying 'Wall' as a place-name element); this is a purely toponymic co-occurrence with no relational bearing on the thanksgiving-choir's own function.

2775.text: Operation words (role-T3) are H1980I 'went' (initiated by the thanksgiving-choir itself, directed toward the north along the wall) and implicitly the narrator's own following action; the thanksgiving-choir (H8426) is here the initiating party of the movement operation, not merely its object, distinguishing this verse from Neh.12.31 where it was the object of 'appointed.'

2954.text: The large majority of G2168's occurrences (Rom.1.8; 1Cor.1.4; Eph.5.20; Col.1.3; 1Thess.5.18; Rev.11.17; 2Thess.2.13; Rom.16.4; 1Thess.2.13; 2Thess.1.3; 1Cor.1.14; 1Cor.14.18; Phil.1.3; 1Thess.1.2; Phlm.1.4; 1Cor.10.30; Col.1.12; 2Cor.1.11; Eph.1.16) share one core sense across the strong's own full occurrence list: an epistolary/liturgical, habitual first- or plural-person verb of thanking God, usually 'always'/'constantly' and grounded in some grace, faith, or benefit already received in the addressees or the speaker. This is the dominant register of the strong internally and forms the baseline against which the meal-blessing and single exceptional uses (below) stand out.

2956.text: Since G2168 is the subgroup's sole member strong, the cross-strong comparison this stage exists to perform collapses to a single-strong self-comparison: every occurrence -- whether epistolary-habitual, meal-blessing, exclamatory-nominal, negated, or personal/individual prayer-address -- shares the same root act (a verbal/enacted response of gratitude directed to God, occasionally to a human benefactor as in Rom.16.4) with no second lexeme to diverge from within this subgroup. The genuine internal variation is therefore register/context-driven (liturgical meal-formula vs. epistolary habit vs. individual prayer vs. negated failure) rather than lexical-sense divergence between two different words.

2963.text: G2169 is the sole member strong of this subgroup, so there is no cross-strong divergence to compare -- every occurrence uniformly names the noun-form state/act of thanksgiving (gratitude, the giving of thanks, or a liturgical category of thanks), never a different root sense; the subgroup is internally homogeneous at the lexical level, with variation occurring only in referent (God, a human patron) and rhetorical role (doxological list item, prayer accompaniment, virtue-marker, produced overflow).

2965.text: Across its full occurrence list, G2169 clusters into three recognizable functional groups sharing genuinely alike readings: (1) doxological/liturgical enumeration where thanksgiving is one item in a fixed list of praise-terms offered to God (Rev.7.12; Rev.4.9); (2) prayer-accompaniment usage where thanksgiving qualifies or accompanies the manner of praying/receiving (Phil.4.6; Col.4.2; 1Tim.2.1; 1Tim.4.3; 1Tim.4.4; Col.2.7); (3) thanksgiving as the relational/social outcome or debt produced by another's action -- generosity, grace, ministry, or joy (2Cor.9.11; 2Cor.9.12; 2Cor.4.15; 1Thess.3.9). Acts.24.3 and Eph.5.4 stand somewhat apart as non-liturgical, interpersonal/ethical uses (gratitude toward a civic patron; grateful speech replacing crude talk) and 1Cor.14.16 stands apart as a specifically public, intelligibility-conditioned liturgical speech-act.

2972.text: Across its full occurrence list H8426 clusters into three recurring realizations of one lexeme: (1) the concrete thank-offering sacrifice (Lev.7.12 x2, Lev.7.13, Lev.7.15, Lev.22.29, Ps.50.14, Ps.50.23, Ps.107.22, Ps.116.17, Amos.4.5, Jonah.2.9, 2Chr.29.31 x2, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11), (2) the vocal/manner accompaniment of praise, 'with/in thanksgiving' (Ps.69.30, Ps.26.7, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Isa.51.3), and (3) the institutional thanksgiving choir/procession/company (Neh.12.27, Neh.12.31, Neh.12.38, Neh.12.40, Ps.42.4). A fourth, rarer sense realizes it as verbal confession (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11). This is a single strong showing internally the full sense-range attributed to the subgroup label (hymn, choir, offering) without needing a second member strong to supply any of these senses.

2973.text: Since H8426 is the sole member strong of this subgroup, there is no second lexeme to compare it against directly; the meaningful cross-comparison available is internal -- between H8426's own sacrificial/cultic-object occurrences (e.g. Lev.7.12-15, Lev.22.29, 2Chr.29.31, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11, Amos.4.5) versus its choir/procession-as-institution occurrences (Neh.12.27-40, Ps.42.4) versus its purely adverbial/manner occurrences ('with thanksgiving', e.g. Ps.69.30, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Ps.26.7). These three groupings do not overlap grammatically: the sacrificial sense is always the head noun or a construct-genitive qualifier of an offering-word (zebach, shelamim), the choir sense functions as a collective-body noun (subject or object of appointment/movement verbs), and the manner sense is marked by a preposition (b-) modifying a separate main verb of praise. No morphological distinction (all occurrences are the same feminine noun stem, singular or plural absolute/construct) drives this three-way split -- it is purely syntactic/contextual, meaning the noun's referent is disambiguated entirely by its syntactic role in each verse rather than by any inflectional change.

2975.text: Within the choir/procession sense-group, Neh.12.31/12.40 use the plural morph (HNcfpa, 'gave thanks' referring to two choirs) while Neh.12.38 uses the singular (HNcfsa, referring to 'the other choir'); this plural/singular alternation tracks the narrative's own count of choirs (two choirs collectively vs. one choir individually) rather than any shift in the term's underlying sense -- a grammatical-number distinction driven by referential count, not by a change in meaning register.

2990.text: The mode of operation varies by context: liturgical/formulaic over food (Matt.26.27, Mark.14.23, John.6.11), individual spoken prayer address (John.11.41, Luke.18.11), corporate liturgical address by heavenly beings (Rev.11.17), and continuous mental/epistolary habit ('always,' 'without ceasing') in apostolic letters (Col.1.3, Eph.1.16) -- direction is consistently human/creature-to-God (or occasionally human-to-human, Rom.16.4), and no differing constitutional level (spirit/soul/body) is distinguished in the evidence beyond the embodied posture in Luke.17.16.

2995.text: Thanksgiving operates somewhat differently within existing bonds versus across distance: within covenantal/familial-in-Christ bonds it is habitual and relational ('I thank my God always for you,' addressed to known brothers/churches), while directed toward God as ultimate benefactor it is vertical/devotional regardless of any human relational distance; a rare instance crosses ordinary social distance entirely when directed toward human benefactors who risked their lives (Rom.16.4), showing the characteristic can also operate horizontally toward a non-divine party.

2996.text: The characteristic crosses covenantal boundaries: while most occurrences are within the believing/covenant community (thanks for brothers' faith, election, sanctification), the Samaritan leper (Luke.17.16, explicitly noted as an outsider) and the Pharisee's misuse (Luke.18.11) show thanksgiving extended to or attempted by persons outside the immediate believing-covenant circle, and the human-directed thanks of Rom.16.4 crosses into ordinary interpersonal (non-covenantal-strictly) gratitude.

2997.text: The relational scope is broad in principle (any person, believer or outsider, may give thanks, and thanks may be directed to God or to a human benefactor) but the evidence shows it functionally clustered among believers thanking God for one another and, in one negative case, withheld by those who knew God but refused to honor him -- excluding, by that refusal, themselves from the fitting response rather than the characteristic itself excluding any class of person.

3009.text: Where thanksgiving is extended toward a human benefactor (Rom.16.4), the inner condition accompanying it is recognition of costly sacrifice ('risked their necks for my life') -- genuine extension of thanksgiving toward another person requires acknowledging what was actually risked or given on one's behalf.

3010.text: The evidence shows a person must have received or perceived a benefit -- grace, deliverance, provision, an answered request, or a costly sacrifice made on their behalf -- before they extend thanksgiving; thanksgiving is consistently a response to prior reception, never a self-originating act.

3034.text: None recorded for the remaining occurrences (doxological, prayer-accompaniment, and outcome usages) -- these do not disclose a specific perception/belief/judgement content of the person expressing thanksgiving beyond the general recognition of a benefit received; the noun names the state/act rather than articulating a propositional judgement.

3039.text: Where the immediate response (D10.2) is a verbal act of thanks, the sustained effect shown in the evidence is an ongoing state -- 'abounding in thanksgiving' (Col.2.7), 'continue steadfastly... with thanksgiving' (Col.4.2) -- indicating thanksgiving moves from a discrete utterance into a durable habituated posture of life and prayer.

3040.text: The evidence does not directly address reversibility of a transformation caused by thanksgiving; thanksgiving is consistently portrayed as a response/accompaniment/outcome rather than as itself transforming the person in a traceable before/after sequence, so reversibility cannot be determined from this subgroup's own occurrences -- this could be resolvable with cross-cluster comparison to sanctification-type characteristics.

3044.text: In Col.2.7 and Col.4.2, thanksgiving is portrayed as a settled, sustained disposition ('abounding in thanksgiving,' 'continue steadfastly... with thanksgiving') rather than a fleeting emotional burst -- no bodily-feeling language accompanies it, only durative verbs of habituation.

3046.text: The felt quality varies by context: warm affective joy (1Thess.3.9), settled durative disposition (Col.2.7; Col.4.2), and unmarked formal/liturgical or civic register elsewhere (Rev.7.12, Acts.24.3) -- the subgroup does not present a single uniform emotional register.

3049.text: Thanksgiving takes hold rightly under conditions of belief and knowledge of truth (1Tim.4.3), rootedness and establishment in faith (Col.2.7), watchfulness in prayer (Col.4.2), and freedom from anxiety replaced by prayer/supplication (Phil.4.6) -- a settled, faith-grounded, non-anxious inner state.

3052.text: Thanksgiving operates differently within covenant/faith bonds versus across relational distance: toward God and fellow believers it is warm, joyful, faith-grounded (1Thess.3.9; Col.2.7), while toward a non-believing civic authority (Acts.24.3, Felix) it is formal, courteous gratitude without the theological content present elsewhere.

3060.text: Where thanksgiving is present and abounding (Col.2.7), it indicates a healthy condition of rootedness in faith reflecting the divine image rightly ordered toward God; where it is displaced by foolish/crude talk (Eph.5.4) or forbidden by false teaching (1Tim.4.3), its absence indicates a disordered or distorted condition of the image, though the evidence does not claim total effacement.

3073.text: The evidence shows thanksgiving consistently engaging the faculties of speech/mouth (public utterance, Amen-response, doxology) and belief/faith (knowledge of truth, rootedness in faith) but never sensory/bodily faculties directly, indicating its nature as a cognitively-and-verbally mediated response rather than a physical sensation or instinctive reflex.

3074.text: G2169 names a compound inner-being phenomenon: primarily a disposition/state (gratitude as settled attitude, e.g. Col.2.7's 'abounding'), also a concrete act (the giving of thanks, e.g. Rev.4.9's 'give... thanks'), and occasionally a countable event/category listed among prayer-types (1Tim.2.1's plural 'thanksgivings').

3079.text: Thanksgiving most frequently co-occurs with prayer/supplication (Phil.4.6; Col.4.2; 1Tim.2.1), and with glory/honor/power in doxological lists (Rev.4.9; Rev.7.12); also with faith/belief-of-truth (1Tim.4.3; Col.2.7), grace (2Cor.4.15), generosity (2Cor.9.11-12), and joy (1Thess.3.9).

3081.text: In the evidence, thanksgiving consistently follows a prior state or event: grace/generosity/ministry (2Cor.9.11-12), joy (1Thess.3.9), rootedness in faith (Col.2.7), or a good gift received (1Tim.4.3-4) -- it does not precede these but is their sequel/response.

3193.text: Across this pass's occurrences the surface form 'give thanks' overwhelmingly renders the Hiphil stem in liturgical/doxological contexts (e.g. Ps.138.2, Ps.106.1, Ps.111.1, Ps.44.8, Ps.86.12, Ps.28.7, 1Chr.16.35/8/41, Ps.54.6, Ps.75.1x2, Ps.92.1, Ps.106.47, Ps.122.4, Ps.140.13, 1Chr.16.34, Ps.107.1, Ps.118.1/28/29, Ps.30.4, Ps.97.12, Ps.30.12, Ps.9.1, Ps.79.13, Ps.145.10, Ps.118.19, Ps.57.9, Ps.108.3) -- a large, internally consistent block where the verb names a vocal, addressed act of gratitude toward the Lord's name, character, or acts, with no confession-of-sin sense present in any of these.

3200.text: Across this pass's occurrences the core Hiphil imperative/perfect/participle sense 'give thanks/praise' recurs as the dominant pattern in liturgical contexts: Isa.12.1, 2Chr.30.22, 2Chr.7.6, 2Chr.20.21, 2Chr.31.2, Ezra.3.11, Neh.12.24, Ps.109.30, Isa.12.4, Jer.33.11, Ps.7.17, 1Chr.16.4, 1Chr.29.13, Ps.35.18, Ps.118.21, Ps.52.9, Ps.107.8/15/21/31, Ps.100.4, Ps.136.1/2/3/26, Ps.33.2, 2Chr.5.13, 1Chr.16.7, Neh.12.46, Ps.138.4, Ps.138.1, 2Chr.7.3, 1Chr.23.30, 1Chr.25.3, Ps.142.7, Neh.11.17 -- all render the same basic act of vocal, often corporate/musical, thanksgiving directed at the Lord, frequently anchored by the refrain 'his steadfast love endures forever.'

3203.text: Within the confession-branch occurrences themselves, a further distinction is visible by stem/subject: Lev.16.21 (Qal-tq, Aaron confessing the people's sin OVER the scapegoat) and Num.5.7/Lev.26.40/Lev.5.5 (individual or corporate confession as a required legal/cultic act tied to restitution or covenant curse) represent a ritual-legal register, whereas Dan.9.20, Neh.1.6, Ezra.10.1, Neh.9.3, Dan.9.4 represent a personal/intercessory-prayer register (confession embedded within extended penitential prayer, weeping, and prostration) -- both are 'confession' but differ in whether the act is a discrete ritual requirement or an extended devotional/intercessory posture.

3215.text: Yes, the mechanism differs across contexts: in the cultic/temple context it operates through appointed liturgical office and musical instrumentation (1Chr.16.4, 2Chr.5.13, 1Chr.25.3 -- Levites appointed, with lyre/trumpets); in the personal-devotional context it operates through spontaneous individual speech-vow (Ps.9.1, Ps.86.12 'with my whole heart'); in the penitential context it operates through a required ritual or intercessory-prayer act (Lev.16.21's scapegoat confession, Dan.9.4's extended prayer of confession) -- three distinct mechanisms (institutional/musical, personal/vocal, ritual/legal) all realizing the same root verb.

3335.text: In Luke.2.48 the parents (father and mother, the party) initiate the searching-operation, directed toward the child Jesus (the other party) who had gone missing -- a relational, anxious seeking of a person.

3337.text: In Luke.2.48 M48 (astonished) and M24 (great distress/anguish) co-occur; the parents' searching (G2212) is the cause producing their distress (M24) upon finding him, while the astonishment (M48) belongs to the crowd's reaction to the child rather than to the search itself -- related in narrative sequence but not characteristics of the seeking-act itself.

3381.text: In 1Kgs.1.2 no other M-code characteristic is present in the verse's role tags apart from the seeking-act itself (M83); the surrounding vocabulary is untagged narrative detail.

3385.text: In 1Kgs.1.2, the seeking operation is initiated by the servants (party) directed toward finding a young woman for the king (party, the lord/king), i.e. an instrumental search on the king's behalf.

3476.text: In Esth.2.21, 1Sam.24.9, Num.35.23, and 1Kgs.20.7 the surface sense shifts from the base gloss 'seek/desire' toward a conspiratorial/hostile sense 'to plot against, seek to harm/kill' -- a marked negative-valence divergence from the neutral-to-positive base gloss. By contrast in 2Chr.15.4 the surface sense aligns with the base devotional gloss (seeking God). This shows the same lexeme's stepGloss splits sharply by direction of the object across these occurrences.

3479.text: Num.35.23: the operation word 'dropped' (H5307G, role-T3, tagged M02) is directed by the unwitting agent ('he') toward the victim ('him'), resulting in death; H1245's seeking (of harm) is explicitly negated in this verse ('did not seek his harm'), clarifying the dropping was accidental, not an intentional operation flowing from a hostile seeking.

3485.text: In Num.35.23, M02 ('dropped', tagged as an anger-related code) co-occurs with H1245's negated seeking ('did not seek his harm'); the verse explicitly denies hostile intent (H1245 negated) even though the fatal act (tagged M02) occurred, distinguishing accidental action from malicious pursuit.

3537.text: In Ps.40.14, Ps.70.2, Ps.71.13, and Ps.71.24 'seek' functions in the stock formulaic phrase 'those who seek my life/hurt' -- fully within the base gloss's hostile-pursuit sense, consistent across all four occurrences with no unique nuance.

3540.text: M07 (shame/disappointment, via H0954/H2659/H3637) is the fate wished upon those who 'seek' (H1245) the psalmist's life; the seeking (this cluster) is the malicious cause, and M07 is the desired consequence -- a cause-effect relational pairing across the verse.

3615.text: Col.3.1 uses zeteo as an imperative command to seek heavenly/spiritual realities -- this sits within the verb's attested 'seek, strive for' sense (cf. Mt.6.33) with no unusual surface divergence, though it carries elevated theological weight via its object 'things above'.

3618.text: No other M-code characteristic is present in Col.3.1 alongside seeking; the verse's other tagged words are T-role/party tags (Christ, God) not M-code characteristics.

3621.text: Col.3.1: zeteo is not itself role-T3 tagged (only M83); the verse's operation words are 'raised' and 'seated' (both T3), directed at the addressee/Christ respectively, but these are not the home strong -- no D7.7.1 relation recorded for zeteo itself.

3883.text: In John.1.38 Jesus (party) initiates the question 'What are you seeking?' addressed to the disciples following him, making them the target party whose zēteō-activity is being probed; the operation is verbal inquiry directed at the followers' own seeking.

3912.text: In John.1.38 'What are you seeking?' is a direct, literal use of zēteō asking about the disciples' immediate purpose -- within the base gloss, no shift.

3929.text: In John.1.38 M63 (hermēneuō, 'means/interpret') co-occurs with M83 (zēteō, 'seeking') but the two operate in separate clauses -- M83 governs Jesus' question to the followers, M63 explains the term 'Rabbi'; from M83's vantage the seeking-inquiry is unrelated to the interpretive gloss on the title.

3975.text: In John.1.38 hermēneuō is used in its standard translation-gloss sense ('which means Teacher'), matching the base gloss with no notable divergence.

4082.text: In 2 Kgs 1:3 darash names the illegitimate inquiry of Ahaziah's messengers to Baal-zebub, a pagan deity — the nuance here is negative/idolatrous consultation, contrasting sharply with the legitimate divine-inquiry sense (1 Kgs 14:5) and underscoring darash's capacity to name both true and false objects of seeking depending on context; the impact is rhetorical rebuke ('is there no God in Israel...') highlighting misdirected seeking.

4083.text: Other M-code tags present (M08/M74 arise, M37 meet) describe the messenger-angel's commissioning action and the encounter itself, not the inquiry-act; this cluster's vantage adds that darash here specifically names the illegitimate object of the seeking (Baal-zebub) which the arising/meeting sequence is sent to confront and correct.

4084.text: The operation 'inquire' is initiated by King Ahaziah (via his messengers, human party) and directed toward Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron (false-deity party) — a human-to-pagan-deity consultative movement that the Lord's angel is sent to rebuke.

4201.text: In 1Sam.16.16 ('seek out a man') and 1Sam.28.7 ('Seek out...a woman') and 2Sam.17.20 ('sought and could not find'), the surface sense of procurement/search sits squarely within the base gloss with no notable shift.

4203.text: In 1Sam.16.16, the seeking operation is initiated by the servants (at the lord's command) and directed toward finding 'a man skillful in playing the lyre' -- the party sought is the skilled musician, a benign procurement operation.

4209.text: In 1Sam.16.16, M36 (servants), M15 (skillful), M24/M58 (harmful), M47 (spirit), M05/M18 (well) all co-occur; baqash's own vantage is that the seeking-out act is the mechanism by which the household responds to Saul's affliction -- the procurement operation links the human agents to the remedy, distinct from the affliction/skill terms themselves.

4256.text: In 1Sam.16.16, 'harmful spirit from God' diverges from ruach's more common empowering/animating sense (e.g. Spirit of God imparting gifts) -- here the divergence is toward an afflicting, tormenting agency; the impact is to frame Saul's distress as divinely permitted affliction requiring music as remedy.

4270.text: In 1Sam.16.16 'harmful' sits within the base gloss's 'hurtful/evil' sense (1h), a standard, unremarkable application; no notable divergence.

4367.text: In 1Sam.9.3 'look' translates baqash in its plain concrete sense of searching for lost donkeys -- squarely within the base gloss 'seek' with no divergent nuance.

4368.text: In Prov.23.35 'must have' renders baqash in an appetitive/compulsive sense (craving another drink) rather than the more common searching or supplicating sense -- a shift toward addictive desire, distinct from its usual object-search or face-seeking uses elsewhere.

4373.text: In 1Sam.9.3 the operation 'look/seek' (role-T3) is initiated by the young man Saul is told to bring, directed toward the lost donkeys -- Kish's command sets Saul as initiator toward the object sought.

4377.text: 1Sam.9.3 contains no other M-code characteristic; H1245 (seek) stands alone in this verse's role annotations.

4382.text: Prov.23.35 contains no other M-code characteristic; H1245 (must have/seek) stands alone, describing the drunkard's compulsive craving.

4398.text: In Jer.30.14 'care' likewise renders darash in the interpersonal-neglect sense (lovers who 'care nothing' for the addressee) rather than the cultic-enquiry sense, matching Ps.142.4's usage and marking a consistent secondary nuance of relational abandonment across these occurrences.

4400.text: In Jer.30.14 H1875 ('care') is negated and not itself tagged role-T3 as an operation in the given role list; no operation-relation to record for this strong here.

4402.text: Jer.30.14 co-occurs H1875 (care nothing, negated) with M51 (lovers), M81 (forgotten), M06 (enemy), M16 (punishment), M10 (merciless foe), M56 (guilt/sins) -- the withdrawal of care by 'lovers' functions as the relational betrayal underlying the judicial blow described, paralleling forgetting (M81) as its companion failure.

4442.text: In Zech.11.16 H1245 ('seek the young') is used pastorally of a shepherd's duty of care toward vulnerable animals/people - the nuance shifts from literal search toward neglect-implying pastoral responsibility (here notably negated), contrasting with the more neutral seeking of Gen.37.16 and Prov.15.14's intellectual seeking.

4447.text: In Zech.11.16 no other M-code characteristic co-occurs with H1245 in this verse's tag set (the raising-up and destruction/binding words carry M-codes M08/M74/M20/M24 respectively, but these appear on different words, not co-tagged as home-cluster items here) - treating from H1245's own vantage, it stands as the sole M83 instance; other M-codes present (M08, M74, M20, M24, M16) belong to different characteristics but the question scope is restricted to what THIS characteristic's pass records, and since no prior context exists this begins the chain, noting M16 (folly/stupidity, via H1197B-type sense) and M24 (brokenness) surround the neglect motif but relation to seeking is thematic contrast (neglect of shepherding duty) rather than direct semantic overlap.

4452.text: In Zech.11.16 the (negated) seeking operation would be initiated by the shepherd toward the young/lost sheep, but the verse denies this action occurs, marking a failed shepherd-to-flock directional operation.

4533.text: In Prov.17.19 'seeks destruction' is a figurative/idiomatic extension of baqash's base gloss (seek to find/secure); rather than literal pursuit of an object, it describes the unintended but inevitable consequence courted by prideful behaviour -- a nuance of self-incurred ruin distinct from the term's more common sense of deliberately pursuing a desired good (e.g. Gen.25.22's seeking of the Lord, Ps.10.15's judicial demand).

4534.text: No prior context recorded. Other M-codes in Prov.17.19 -- M51 'loves' (twice), M56 'transgression', M10 'strife', M08 'high/pride' -- form a chain of causes (love of transgression/strife, pride) that baqash's 'seeks destruction' names as their outcome; the seeking-characteristic thus functions as the terminal consequence-marker for the preceding dispositional M-codes rather than being directly related to any single one of them.

4822.text: In Gen.42.22 the surface rendering 'reckoning' translates the Niphal participle of darash, diverging sharply from the base gloss 'inquire/seek' toward the idiomatic legal sense 'blood being required/demanded' — the impact is to frame guilt as something actively sought/exacted rather than a general search, distinct from the more literal 'inquire' senses in Exod.18.15/Deut.12.30.

4826.text: In Gen.42.22, M56 (sin) and M41 (listen) are present as other M-codes but are not directly tied to darash's own reckoning-action; from this characteristic's vantage, the 'reckoning'/required-blood sense stands as consequence-language responding to the sin named earlier in the verse, though no prior cluster pass exists yet to build on.

4943.text: In 2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord our God... he has given us peace' extends the devotional sense (1a3a) into a covenant-causation frame -- seeking is presented as the ground of national security/peace, a nuance beyond the punctual consultation sense seen elsewhere and matching 2Chr.14.4's devotional register.

4961.text: In 2Chr.14.7, 'we' (Judah, T8/T11 party) is the initiator of the seeking, directed toward the Lord our God (T7 party) -- the operation is presented as the cause of the peace subsequently given, a covenant-causal relation between party and party.

4971.text: In 2Chr.14.7, M83 (sought) co-occurs with M02/M50 (still ours, H6440G, land/presence) and M33 (given us peace, H5117) and M46 (prospered, H6743B); here the seeking-of-the-Lord is presented as the causal ground for the peace and prosperity that follow, making M83 the operative characteristic upon which the other outcomes depend within this verse.

4988.text: In Esth.2.2 'sought out' shifts H1245 toward administrative procurement/selection (gathering virgins for the king), a bureaucratic sense distinct from personal or religious seeking seen elsewhere -- the impact is depersonalized, institutional searching rather than individual pursuit.

4992.text: In Esth.2.2 the king's young men initiate the seeking-out operation directed toward beautiful young virgins, on behalf of the king.

4996.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs meaningfully with H1245 in Esth.2.2 as home-cluster interaction; the seeking-out operates alongside descriptive terms (beauty, youth) but no other M-code party characteristic is present.

5258.text: In Ezek.14.7 'consult' carries the nuance of hypocritical or corrupted inquiry -- the idolater comes to a prophet to consult God while harboring idols in his heart; the impact is that the surface act of seeking is emptied of sincerity, contrasting sharply with the sincere seeking of Isa.55.6 and 2Chr.1.5.

5263.text: Other M-codes in Ezek.14.7 (M01 sojourn, M64 separates, M47 heart, M15 putting, M77 stumbling block, M56 iniquity, M43 prophet, M22 answer) surround the consulting act but are not positively related to it: darash here is corrupted by co-present idolatry (M77/M56) rather than harmonizing with them -- the seeking is nullified by what accompanies it, a distinct vantage from any prior finding.

5268.text: In Ezek.14.7, H1875 is the role-T3 operation: the idolater ('any one', party) initiates consulting, directed toward God via a prophet (parties), though the act is compromised by the idolater's simultaneous devotion to idols.

5312.text: Deut.12.5 'seek the place' draws on the 'resort to, frequent' sense (1a1) combined with devotional pursuit of the divinely chosen worship-site; a standard extension within the base gloss, no notable divergence.

5313.text: 1Chr.22.19 'seek the Lord' is the classic devotional sense (1a3a), squarely within the base gloss.

5317.text: In Deut.12.5, M15 (choose, of God choosing the place) is present but functions as God's own prior action, not something darash (Israel's seeking) directly modifies; the two characteristics operate on different agents (God chooses; the people seek) within the same verse without direct interaction.

5318.text: In 1Chr.22.19, darash (seek the Lord) sits alongside M47 (heart/mind, 'set your mind and heart to seek') and M44 (covenant, the ark of the covenant) -- the seeking here is explicitly heart-directed, showing darash functions as the outward enactment of an inward disposition (heart/mind) toward covenant faithfulness.

5392.text: Mic 6:8 renders darash as 'require' (what does the Lord require) rather than the more common 'seek' — a divergence in surface form emphasizing God as the DEMANDING party rather than the seeker, shifting agency onto God's requirement of covenant ethics from man, distinct from the more typical human-seeking-God direction seen in Hos 10:12 and 1Chr 10:14.

5397.text: In Mic 6:8, darash ('require') co-occurs with M05/M18 (good), M12 (justice), M51 (love), M07/M50 (kindness), M09 (humbly). This characteristic's vantage: darash frames God as the REQUIRING party, making the other M-codes (justice, love-kindness, humility) the CONTENT of what is required — seeking/requiring here functions as the covenantal umbrella-verb under which the triad of ethical characteristics are named.

5401.text: In Mic 6:8, the requiring operation is initiated by the Lord (party, T7) and directed toward 'man' (party, T8) — God as the demanding party toward humanity.

5492.text: In 2 Chr 15:13 darash carries its well-attested devotional sense 'seek the Lord' -- this is within the base gloss's own listed sub-sense (1a3, seeking deity in prayer/worship), not a divergence from it; contrast with the necromantic-object occurrences shows the same verb pivoting entirely on its object rather than on any special contextual nuance of the verb form itself.

5495.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in 2 Chr 15:13 alongside the seeking of the Lord; the other tagged items are structural/role tags only.

5498.text: In 2 Chr 15:13 the operation 'put to death' (H4191, role-T3) is directed by the covenant community against whoever fails to seek the Lord; the seeking itself (H1875) is the required act of the individual party directed toward the Lord/God of Israel, and its absence triggers the death-operation against that same individual.

5527.text: In 1Kgs.10.24 'sought' extends the base sense to seeking royal audience/presence (a social-diplomatic seeking), a well-attested figurative use already within the tree's own range (1a3 'to seek the face'); no unusual shift beyond the term's normal coverage.

5528.text: In 2Chr.9.23 'sought' repeats the same audience-seeking sense as the parallel 1Kgs.10.24 occurrence; no additional divergence.

5532.text: In 1Kgs.10.24 the seeking operation is initiated by 'the whole earth' (collective party) and directed toward Solomon's presence, seeking access to his wisdom.

5533.text: In 2Chr.9.23 the seeking operation is initiated by 'all the kings of the earth' and directed toward Solomon's presence, identical relational structure to the 1Kgs.10.24 parallel.

5538.text: In 1Kgs.10.24, H1245 (sought) co-occurs with M02/M50 (presence), M16 (wisdom), M47 (mind); this characteristic's vantage: the seeking-operation is the vehicle by which the collective party accesses Solomon's presence (M02/M50) in order to hear the wisdom (M16) that God placed in his mind (M47) - H1245 functions as the connecting act, not itself the content sought.

5539.text: In 2Chr.9.23, H1245 (sought) co-occurs with M72 (kings), M02/M50 (presence), M16 (wisdom), M47 (mind); same relational role as the 1Kgs.10.24 parallel - the seeking-act is the connecting operation between the royal parties and Solomon's wisdom.

5556.text: In Ezek.20.40 'require' shifts to the base sense 'to seek (with a demand), demand, require' (1a4) applied to cultic contributions/gifts - a distinctly legal-cultic exaction nuance compared to the devotional-seeking sense dominant elsewhere in the arc (e.g. Ps.119.155, 2Chr.30.19); here the impact is to frame God's acceptance of Israel's worship as itself an act of formally demanding their offerings, intensifying the transactional-covenantal register of the verse.

5560.text: In Ezek.20.40, the operation 'require' (H1875) is initiated by the Lord God (T7-tagged party) and directed toward the house of Israel (T11-tagged party), demanding their contributions and offerings - a divine-to-covenant-people exaction operation.

5564.text: In Ezek.20.40, H1875 (require) co-occurs with M61 (holy/sacred offerings), M08 (height), M42 (declares), M36 (serve), M39 (accept); this characteristic's vantage: 'require' is the concluding transactional act that formally claims the sacred contributions (M61) after acceptance (M39) of the people's service (M36), closing the covenantal exchange sequence.

5576.text: In Ezek.20.40 'height' functions as a qualifier of 'mountain' (the mountain height of Israel), specifying the elevated topographical status of the sanctuary-mountain rather than naming an independent quality; a modifying rather than standalone use.

6171.text: In Luke.19.3 'was seeking to see who Jesus was' sits within the base gloss 'to seek, look for' -- an ordinary conative/intentional use (seeking-to-do-X), matching the well-attested infinitive-complement pattern.

6180.text: In Luke.19.3, M15 (seeing) co-occurs. Seeking here is the enabling desire behind the attempted act of seeing -- seeking-to-see names Zacchaeus's intent, while seeing (M15) names the not-yet-achieved perceptual goal; the two are linked as intent-and-object rather than independent themes.

6258.text: In Rom.2.7 zeteo (kath' hupomonen ergou agathou doxan... zetousin) sits within its base gloss of diligent pursuit/striving toward a good end -- no unusual nuance beyond the standard 'seek/strive for' sense used elsewhere for pursuing eschatological goods.

6259.text: The operation word zeteo ('seek') is directed by 'those who' (the subject party, believers described by patient well-doing) toward the object 'glory and honor and immortality' -- the seeking party initiates the action toward the divine reward, not toward another person.

6260.text: Seeking (G2212) here functions as the operative disposition that yields glory (M22), honor (M71), and immortality (M61) via well-doing (M05) and patience (M34) and eternal life (M25); seeking is the pursuit-verb binding these other characteristics together as the sought objects/means, giving the first relational read of this verse's M-code cluster.

6547.text: In Ps.37.25 'begging' renders baqash for a child seeking bread out of want, a specific nuance of desperate physical need rather than the more common senses of hostile pursuit or devotional seeking found elsewhere (e.g. Ps.27.4, Ps.35.4); the impact here is to underscore God's providence toward the righteous by contrast, since such begging is said never to be observed.

6548.text: In Esth.6.2, Job.10.6, Ps.24.6, Ps.27.4, Ps.34.14, Ps.35.4, and Ps.37.36 baqash is used in its standard senses (hostile pursuit, investigative search, devotional seeking, seeking peace) with no notable divergence from the base gloss.

6559.text: Other M-codes present in Ps.35.4: M07 (put to shame/dishonor/disappointed), M47 (life), M15/M64 (devise). Baqash (seek after my life) names the hostile pursuit that the psalmist prays will be met with shame (M07); it is the initiating act to which the shame-outcome responds, but does not modify the shame-terms themselves.

6560.text: Other M-codes present in Ps.37.25: M12 (righteous), M30/M59 (forsaken). Baqash (begging) describes the hypothetical desperate act of a righteous person's child; it stands in negated contrast to being forsaken (M30/M59), illustrating what does NOT happen to the righteous (M12), but does not itself modify those terms.

6571.text: In Ps.35.4, H1245 (seek) is an operation initiated by the psalmist's enemies, directed toward the psalmist's life ('my life') as the target — hostile pursuit.

6572.text: In Ps.37.25, H1245 (begging) is an operation hypothetically initiated by 'his children' (the righteous person's offspring), directed toward obtaining bread — but the verse denies this ever occurs, so the operation is negated rather than actually enacted.

6646.text: In Ezek.34.6 'seek' (paired with H1875 'search') describes shepherds' neglect of the sheep, sitting within the base sense of active caretaking-seeking without further divergence.

6661.text: In Ezek.34.6 'search' activates the pastoral-care/diligent-tending sense of darash (caring for lost sheep) rather than the cultic consult-God sense, a shepherding-specific nuance with the impact of framing the shepherds' negligence as a failure of basic pastoral duty, not merely a failure of religious devotion; this differs markedly from its use of seeking God in Jer.29.13.

6677.text: In Ezek.34.6 the seeking (paired with H1875) is negated -- 'none to search or seek' -- meaning the shepherds who should be the initiating party toward the scattered sheep (the target) are absent from performing the operation, itself the verse's core indictment.

6679.text: In Ezek.34.6 'search' (darash) is negated together with H1245 -- 'none to search or seek for them' -- the shepherds who should initiate the caring-search toward the scattered sheep are absent, the operation's non-performance is the point.

6689.text: M76 (wandering/straying) and M22 (height, 'high hill') co-occur alongside H1875 (also home cluster): the negated seeking (paired with H1875) is presented as the direct remedy that ought to have addressed the sheep's wandering (M76) but did not -- seeking's absence is causally tied to the wandering's continuation.

6691.text: Building on H1245's note for this verse: darash's own vantage adds the specifically pastoral-care dimension to the negated search -- it is not just general seeking (H1245) but the diligent shepherding-inquiry (H1875) that is absent, doubling the indictment of the shepherds' neglect toward the wandering (M76) sheep.

6768.text: In Ezek.33.6 'require' (of blood at the watchman's hand) matches the catalogued sense 1b3 ('to be required, of blood') precisely -- no notable divergence from the base gloss.

6776.text: In Ezek.33.6, H1875 ('require', of blood) co-occurs with M74 (watchman) and M56 (iniquity). First pass: darash here shifts from a seeking-verb to a judicial-demand sense -- it is God's requiring of accountability for the negligent watchman's failure, standing over against M74 (the watchman's duty) and M56 (the iniquity that occasions the death), naming the reckoning rather than the fault or the office.

6785.text: In Ezek.33.6, H1875 ('require') is tagged M83 only, not role-T3. The verse's own T3 operation words (blow, warned, comes, takes) are performed by/against the watchman (M74, a party role) and the people (T11 party) -- God's 'requiring' of blood stands as the covenantal consequence attached to, but grammatically outside, the T3-tagged action set.

6822.text: In Job.3.4 'may God ... not seek it' applies H1875 metaphorically to God's non-regard of a day, extending the 'seek/care for' sense (1a8, seek with care) to a poetic wish that the day be utterly disregarded -- a figurative extension within the base sense rather than a distinct nuance.

6832.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in Job.3.4 besides H1875 itself; the verse's other tagged words are role-T2/T3/T5 grammatical markers, not M-code characteristics.

6842.text: In Job.3.4, H1875 ('seek') is negated with God as the withheld initiator: God is asked not to direct seeking-regard toward 'that day', a wish that the day be excluded from divine attention.

6891.text: In Gen.9.5 darash is used three times in the specific legal-forensic sense 'require a reckoning/exact an accounting' for bloodshed, sharply narrower than the general 'seek/inquire' gloss; here it carries judicial, retributive force (God as avenger holding to account) rather than devotional or investigative seeking, distinguishing it from occurrences like Ps.34.10 or Heb.11.6 where the devotional sense dominates.

6897.text: Gen.9.5: no other M-code characteristic co-occurs in this verse alongside darash ('reckoning'/'require').

6902.text: Gen.9.5: God (implicit speaker/party) is the initiator of the require-operation, directed toward beast and man/fellow-man as the parties from whom bloodguilt is exacted.

7015.text: Ps.119.45's 'I have sought your precepts' fits the base gloss's sense of seeking/enquiring with application (1a7), consistent with its use in v.94; no distinguishing nuance beyond standard devotional seeking.

7020.text: Ps.119.45 also contains M08 (wide place, H7342H). The wide place is the resultant condition of walking freely, not something sought directly by darash; seeking precepts is the ground and cause of the freedom described, but the two M-codes describe distinct elements (act of seeking vs. resulting spaciousness).

7073.text: Across this pass's 'inquire' surface-form cluster (1Kgs.22.8, 2Chr.18.7, 2Kgs.22.13/2Chr.34.21, 2Kgs.3.11, 2Kgs.1.2/1.3/1.6/1.16, 2Kgs.8.8, 1Kgs.14.5, Ezek.20.3, 1Sam.28.7, Jer.10.21, Gen.25.22, Exod.18.15, Deut.12.30, 1Sam.9.9, 1Kgs.22.7/2Chr.18.6, 2Kgs.22.18/2Chr.34.26, Isa.8.19, Jer.37.7, 2Chr.32.31, Isa.19.3, Zeph.1.6, Isa.11.10, Ezek.20.1, 1Chr.21.30, Isa.9.13) the term consistently denotes formal consultation of a deity or authoritative source (the Lord, a prophet, an oracle, Baal-zebub, mediums/necromancers) for a verdict or answer -- the single largest and most cohesive sense-cluster in H1875's full occurrence set, matching this subgroup's core description of institutional/cultic resort to authority for guidance.

7075.text: The 'require' surface form (Deut.18.19, Ezek.34.10, Mic.6.8, Ezek.20.40, Ezek.33.6, Deut.23.21, Gen.9.5) diverges sharply from the consultation sense: here H1875 denotes a superior party (God) formally demanding an accounting, exacting a debt, or requiring conduct/contributions from an inferior party -- the direction of the inquiry is inverted (God is the one requiring, not the one consulted), showing this single root spans both 'humans formally consulting a superior' AND 'a superior formally demanding of an inferior,' unified by the notion of a binding, authoritative claim being pressed rather than a casual search.

7081.text: Ezek.34.6 and Ezek.34.11 both use 'search' of shepherding care for scattered sheep -- one negated (no shepherd searches) and one emphatic (God himself will search) -- forming a matched pair where the pastoral-care sense of darash is activated on both the human failure side and the divine remedy side of the same extended shepherd metaphor.

7088.text: Isa.31.1 and Ezek.14.7 both use 'consult' of illegitimate or compromised inquiry -- Isa.31.1 negates true consultation of the Lord in favor of trust in horses/chariots, while Ezek.14.7 depicts an idolater hypocritically approaching a prophet to consult God while harboring idols in his heart. Both instances show darash's consultation-sense corrupted or withheld by competing loyalties.

7090.text: Gen.42.22 and Gen.9.5 (x2) render darash as 'reckoning' via the Niphal/legal-demand sense -- 'there comes a reckoning for his blood' and 'I will require a reckoning...for the life of man' -- a specialized forensic-accountability nuance (blood-guilt exacted) sharply distinct from the consultative/devotional senses dominant elsewhere in this strong's occurrences.

7097.text: Jer.30.14's 'care' renders darash in the interpersonal-neglect sense (lovers who 'care nothing' for the addressee) -- the relational/compassionate-concern nuance of darash rather than its cultic-consultation or forensic-demand senses, paralleling the similar 'care' rendering elsewhere in this strong's fuller occurrence list (Ps.142.4, Jer.30.17).

7275.text: Across the verses both patterns occur: seeking/inquiring often precedes a resulting belief or outcome (e.g. 2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord... he has given us peace', Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord, and he answered me'), while elsewhere the failure or presence of seeking follows from an already-settled disposition (Ps.10.4's pride precedes and explains the non-seeking; 2Chr.12.14's evil is explained by not having set the heart to seek). The characteristic functions bidirectionally as both antecedent to and consequence of belief/judgement.

7276.text: Several occurrences orient the seeker toward a future promised fullness -- life (Amos.5.4,6,14 'Seek...and live'), finding/being found (Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'), and restored peace/prosperity (2Chr.14.7) -- showing darash is not only a present act but a movement toward an anticipated covenantal reward not yet possessed.

7277.text: The immediate response to seeking is varied across contexts: it produces answer/deliverance (Ps.34.4), peace (2Chr.14.7), prospering (2Chr.26.5), being found (Jer.29.13), but also, when directed at illegitimate objects, provokes divine anger (2Chr.25.15) or judgment ('come to nothing', Amos.5.5). The response is consistently proportionate to the legitimacy of the object sought, not uniform in kind.

7278.text: Where the immediate response to seeking is a discrete event (an answer, a deliverance, a single oracle), the sustained effect is a settled state of peace, prosperity, or ongoing relationship: 2Chr.14.7 moves from the single act of seeking to years of peace and building; 2Chr.26.5 links sustained seeking ('as long as he sought the Lord') to sustained prospering, showing the sustained effect is durative and conditional on continued seeking rather than a one-time reward.

7284.text: In 1Chr.22.19 and 2Chr.15.12 seeking is framed as a settled, wholehearted disposition ('set your mind and heart to seek', 'seek the Lord... with all their heart and with all their soul') rather than a transient emotional reaction -- the language of heart/soul signals an internalized, durable orientation.

7285.text: The felt quality of seeking varies by context: it is crisis-driven and emotionally anguished in Ps.77.2 and 2Chr.20.3 (trouble, fear), yet presented as a settled, wholehearted covenantal disposition in 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, and 2Chr.22.9 ('sought the Lord with all his heart') -- the same term covers both transient emotional response and durable devotional orientation depending on narrative occasion.

7288.text: Seeking takes hold rightly under conditions of wholeheartedness and sincerity: 'set your mind and heart to seek' (1Chr.22.19), 'with all their heart and with all their soul' (2Chr.15.12), and freedom from co-present idolatry -- in Ezek.14.7 the presence of idols in the heart is what disqualifies otherwise-outward consultation. Genuine seeking requires an undivided heart free from rival objects of devotion.

7289.text: Seeking is blocked or nullified when the heart harbors idols or a stumbling block of iniquity even while outwardly consulting God -- Ezek.14.3, 14.7 explicitly describe men who 'have taken their idols into their hearts' yet 'come to a prophet to consult me' -- God declares he will not let himself be consulted (or will answer in judgment) in such cases; similarly pride (Ps.10.4 'in the pride of his face') suppresses seeking altogether.

7290.text: The person whose outward act of inquiry does not take hold rightly is inwardly divided: Ezek.14.3-7 describes them as having 'taken their idols into their hearts' and 'put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face' -- the inner-being state is one of divided loyalty and self-deception, performing the religious gesture of consultation while the heart remains given to a rival object of devotion.

7293.text: Relational scope is broad in principle (any nation or person may seek any deity or authority) but narrow in legitimacy: the Lord invites 'a people... their God' (Isa.8.19) and even nations beyond Israel are said to inquire of the root of Jesse (Isa.11.10), showing an eschatological widening of inclusion; yet within Israel's own covenant, failure to seek excludes one from covenant blessing and even life (2Chr.15.13 'whoever would not seek the Lord... should be put to death'), showing exclusion is covenantal-moral rather than ethnic.

7298.text: The characteristic is an exclusively creaturely analogue rather than a shared attribute: only humans (and other creatures) 'seek/inquire' of God; God himself is never said to darash toward humanity in this evidence (his own use of the root is either refusing/allowing himself to be sought, Ezek.20.3/31, or, in the forensic sense, 'requiring' an account, Gen.9.5) -- the seeking-movement is one-directional, from creature to Creator.

7300.text: The evidence shows seeking engages the heart/soul level most deeply and consistently ('with all their heart and with all their soul', 2Chr.15.12; 'set your mind and heart', 1Chr.22.19), with the body's role limited to expressive gesture (Ps.77.2's stretched-out hand) rather than being the seat of the characteristic itself. The pattern indicates seeking's depth and seat is the heart/soul (volitional-affective center), while the body-link (where present) is expressive/indicative of the inner state rather than mediating or generative of it -- darash never engages purely bodily/instinctive levels without heart involvement in these texts.

7306.text: Uptake of a sought answer from another (a prophet, an oracle) is blocked when the inquirer's heart harbors rival loyalties -- Ezek.14.3-7 shows that idols hidden in the heart nullify the legitimacy of the consultation even though the outward act of inquiry is performed; genuine uptake requires the wholehearted disposition seen elsewhere (2Chr.15.12).

7307.text: The person who inquires but does not genuinely take up what is sought (as in Ezek.14.3-7) is inwardly divided, harboring 'idols... into their heart' and 'the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face' -- an inner-being state of duplicity, where the outward gesture of consultation masks an unyielded heart.

7311.text: The pattern of engagement shows heart/soul faculties (mind, will, affection) consistently engaged when seeking is genuine (1Chr.22.19 'set your mind and heart', 2Chr.15.12 'with all their heart and with all their soul'), while purely external/ritual engagement without heart involvement is exposed as illegitimate (Ezek.14.3-7) -- indicating the characteristic's nature is fundamentally a volitional-relational act requiring the engagement of the inner faculties, not a mechanical or merely verbal performance.

7315.text: At its edge, seeking excludes casual, passive, or half-hearted attention -- it resists mere outward performance without inner devotion (Ezek.14.3-7's idol-hearted consulters are the negative exemplar), and it excludes self-sufficiency/pride that renders inquiry unnecessary (Ps.10.4).

7317.text: Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside seeking include 'heart/mind' (M47, frequently paired as the seat/manner of seeking, e.g. 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, Ps.119.2/10), 'trust' (M19, Ps.9.10, Isa.31.1), and 'forsake' (M30/M59, as antithetical pairing, Ps.9.10, 1Chr.28.9) -- these co-occur with notable frequency, showing seeking is characteristically bound to heart-language and its antithesis, forsaking.

7321.text: Seeking produces peace and prosperity (2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord... he has given us peace on every side'; 2Chr.26.5 'as long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper') by the mechanism of covenantal blessing responsive to faithful devotion -- the mechanism is relational/covenantal reward rather than mechanical causation.

7323.text: Seeking is a constituent element of the larger characteristic of 'setting the heart' (2Chr.19.3, 2Chr.30.19, 1Chr.22.19 all pair 'set the heart/mind' with 'to seek') -- the heart-setting act supplies the internal disposition of which seeking is the outward-directed enactment, making seeking a component within the fuller act of wholehearted devotion.

7848.text: Building on prior network sketch: idleness (G0692) remains the terminal predicate of the network, directly qualifying faith (M13) as inoperative; the desire/knowing verbs (G2309, G1097) form the rhetorical approach to this predicate but do not alter its core two-node (M13-M67) structure.

7849.text: No operation word is paired with 'useless' as an M67 Operation here; it is a predicate adjective describing faith's state, not an initiated action.

8068.text: No angelic or adversarial spiritual beings are involved with this earnestness.

8308.text: No operation/movement word tagged for M67 is present in this verse; 'useless' is a predicate adjective, not an action word, so no initiator/target relation applies.

8312.text: Uselessness here states the effect of faith without works -- it names the null result/purpose failure of such faith for the person who holds it.

8313.text: No immediate inner response is described as following from this predicate; it states a diagnosis rather than triggering a response within the verse.

8314.text: No inner-being state or capacity is produced by uselessness itself; it names a deficiency, not a formative product.

8315.text: Depicts the condition of faith itself (its efficacy/validity) rather than a change process; faith apart from works is diagnosed as inoperative, a condition-level statement, not a described transition with duration.

8316.text: No sequence of inner states is shown; this is a static predicate about faith's uselessness.

8317.text: No mechanism of change in the person is described; uselessness is a predicated diagnosis, not a formation process.

8318.text: Operates as a predicate qualifier marking faith's inoperative/idle mode when disconnected from works.

8319.text: Located at the level of the professed heart-faith of the person, marking its inoperative condition when unaccompanied by works.

8320.text: Origin is not stated for this predicate; it is a diagnostic quality attached to faith apart from works, not something generated, received, or bestowed.

8321.text: Engages moral evaluation/cognition -- the reader is meant to judge that faith without works fails as genuine, active faith.

8322.text: Uselessness does not itself describe a movement toward God; it describes a deficiency in the faith that should express itself that way.

8323.text: No operation from God toward the person is depicted by this term; it is a diagnostic predicate about the person's own faith.

8324.text: Uselessness is not extended from one person to another; it characterizes the addressee's own faith-state.
