8325.text: Idle is not something taken up by a person from another; it is simply the found condition of the standing workers.

8326.text: No relation to angelic or adversarial spiritual beings is shown for this term in this verse.

8327.text: Not predicated of God; it is predicated of the human's faith, judged useless when apart from works.

8582.text: Earnest care (G4710) here leads Titus to act on the Corinthians' behalf just as Paul does -- it serves the purpose of mirroring Paul's own concern in Titus.

8583.text: The immediate response shown is Titus possessing the same earnest concern for the Corinthians that Paul himself holds, following directly from God's gift.

8584.text: Over time this earnest care establishes in Titus an ongoing orientation of active concern for the Corinthians, matching Paul's own.

8585.text: A change is shown in Titus's disposition -- he now bears the same earnest care Paul has, a change in his orientation toward the Corinthians; the verse presents this as a settled given quality rather than temporary.

8586.text: No before/during/after sequence is traced for earnest care itself; only its resulting presence in Titus is stated.

8587.text: The mechanism is direct divine bestowal -- God places this earnest care into Titus's heart, a sovereign act rather than gradual formation or discipline.

8588.text: Earnest care operates here as an implanted zealous concern for others' welfare, functioning as an active disposition directed outward toward the Corinthians.

8589.text: Earnest care is located at the level of the heart -- explicitly stated as being put into Titus's heart by God.

8590.text: Earnest care is explicitly bestowed by God -- stated directly as God's act of putting it into Titus's heart.

8591.text: Earnest care engages volition and affect -- it is the quality moving Titus to be zealously concerned for the Corinthians, paralleling Paul's own eagerness.

8592.text: Earnest care here is directed toward the Corinthians, not toward God as seeking or worship.

8593.text: Earnest care operates from God toward Titus -- God is the one who puts this earnest care into his heart, an act flowing from God to the human person.

8594.text: Earnest care is extended by Titus toward the Corinthians -- it operates as the same zealous concern Paul has, now given by God to Titus for their benefit.

8595.text: Earnest care is not depicted as taken up by Titus from another human; it is placed there directly by God.

8596.text: Earnest care is directly related to God as its giver -- God is the one who puts this same earnest care (that Paul has) into Titus's heart.

9124.text: Thanks (G5485) here serves as Paul's response to God, expressing the effect God's gift (earnest care in Titus) has had -- it leads Paul to gratitude, not a change in Paul's own being.

9125.text: Thanks engages Paul's affect and moral evaluation -- he recognizes and values God's act of placing earnest care in Titus, evidenced by his exclamatory gratitude.

9126.text: Thanks operates as Paul's movement toward God -- it is offered TO God as an act of worshipful acknowledgment of what God has done.

9127.text: Thanks here does not operate from God toward the person; it is the reverse direction, Paul's response directed to God.

9128.text: Thanks is not extended from one human to another in this verse -- it is directed from Paul to God, not person to person.

9129.text: Thanks is not depicted as taken up by Paul from another person; it originates as his own response to God's act.

9130.text: No angelic or adversarial spiritual being is in view in relation to thanks in this verse.

9131.text: Thanks is directly related to God here as its object -- God is the one thanked for having put earnest care into Titus's heart.

9132.text: The immediate response shown is Paul's spontaneous exclamation of gratitude toward God upon recognizing what God has done in Titus.

9133.text: The verse shows a single momentary act of thanksgiving, not a produced lasting inner state or capacity in Paul.

9134.text: No change in Paul's own state or disposition is depicted by this act of giving thanks; it is a response, not a transformation.

9135.text: No sequence of inner states is shown for thanks here -- it is a single expressed response, not a before/during/after progression.

9136.text: The mechanism is encounter/recognition -- Paul's thanks arises from perceiving God's act of placing earnest care into Titus's heart.

9137.text: Thanks here operates in the mode of verbal acknowledgment/praise directed at God, expressed as a discrete declarative outburst.

9138.text: No constitutional level (heart, spirit, mind) is explicitly named for Paul's own thanks in this verse; further cross-verse context on Paul's typical usage could clarify whether he locates it in a specific faculty.

9139.text: Thanks originates within Paul himself, generated as his response to observing God's action -- not bestowed or received from another.

9140.text: The heart here is the receptacle into which God places earnest care, serving the purpose of enabling Titus to feel and act on that care for the Corinthians.

9141.text: The heart engages affect and volition -- it is where God implants the earnest care that moves Titus to feel and act on Paul's behalf.

9142.text: The heart here is the location acted upon by God, not itself an act of seeking or worship toward God.

9143.text: The heart operates as the site of God's action toward the human person -- God puts earnest care into Titus's heart, God acting on the human from outside.

9144.text: The heart itself is not extended between two people here; it is the site where God places something, not a person-to-person exchange.

9145.text: The heart is not shown as taken up by Titus from another person; it is the receiving site of God's own action.

9146.text: No angelic or adversarial spiritual being interacts with the heart in this verse.

9147.text: The heart is directly related to God here as the object of his action -- God is the one who puts (acts into) Titus's heart.

9148.text: The immediate result following God's placing earnest care in the heart is Titus's own possession of that same earnest care for the Corinthians.

9149.text: Over time the heart, having received God's gift, establishes in Titus an ongoing disposition of earnest care matching Paul's own.

9150.text: A change is depicted in Titus's disposition -- God's placing of earnest care into his heart shifts his orientation to match Paul's concern; the verse implies this is a settled state, not merely temporary.

9151.text: No before/during/after sequence of states is traced for the heart itself; only the resulting state (bearing earnest care) is stated.

9152.text: The mechanism is divine bestowal -- God directly puts (didomi) earnest care into the heart, a sovereign act rather than gradual formation.

9153.text: The heart operates here as the inner seat receiving and holding the implanted quality of earnest care, functioning as a vessel/locus rather than an active agent.

9154.text: The heart itself is the constitutional level explicitly named -- it is engaged directly as the seat where God places earnest care.

9155.text: The heart's content (earnest care) originates as bestowed by God -- explicitly stated as God putting it into Titus's heart.

9230.text: Earnest care's own membership in the network is as its pivotal content: it is what God gives, what the heart receives, and what grounds the thanks -- the single element linking all three parties.

9231.text: The operation 'put' (G1325) is initiated by God and directed toward Titus, with earnest care (G4710) as the content transferred into his heart.

9269.text: The relative pronoun 'who' (G3588) is a grammatical linker introducing the clause about God's action; it names no distinct characteristic of its own.

9270.text: The verb 'put' (G1325) functions as the operation-word for God's giving action; it is a supporting verb, not itself a distinct inner-being characteristic.

9271.text: The preposition 'into' (G1722) is a purely structural connector marking the direction of the operation; it names no characteristic.

9272.text: Titus (G5103) is a proper name identifying the recipient; it carries no independent characteristic content of its own to analyze.

9273.text: The pronoun 'same' (G0846) functions as a qualifier linking Titus's earnest care to Paul's own, modifying G4710 rather than naming its own characteristic.

9274.text: The preposition 'for' (G5228) is a structural connector marking the object of the earnest care; it names no characteristic in its own right.

9275.text: The pronoun 'you' (G5216) simply identifies the Corinthians as the object of the earnest care; it names no characteristic of its own.

9979.text: The wanting/desiring here serves to press James's rhetorical challenge -- it leads the foolish person toward recognizing faith without works as useless, not toward any positive formation.

9980.text: The desiring engages cognition/volition -- the person's will to be shown/persuaded of the truth about faith and works.

9981.text: This desiring is directed at being shown a proof, not toward God in seeking, supplication, or worship.

9982.text: The desiring is the human interlocutor's own wanting, not an operation of God toward the person.

9983.text: The wanting is not something extended from one person to another; it is the addressee's own inner stance.

9984.text: This desiring is not taken up from another person; it is the interlocutor's own wanting to be shown.

9985.text: No relation to angelic or adversarial spiritual beings is shown; this is a purely human rhetorical desire.

9986.text: Not predicated of God here; it is the human addressee's own wanting to be shown proof about faith and works.

9987.text: The immediate response the wanting shows is an openness to being shown/persuaded, setting up the challenge that follows.

9988.text: No lasting inner state or capacity is depicted as produced by this desiring; it functions as a rhetorical device within the verse.

9989.text: No change of state or disposition is shown; the wanting simply frames the question posed to the foolish person.

9990.text: No before/during/after sequence of inner states is depicted for this desiring.

9991.text: No mechanism of change is shown; this is a rhetorical question posing a challenge, not a formation process.

9992.text: It operates as a volitional query mode -- the will to be persuaded/shown, driving the rhetorical challenge.

9993.text: Located at the level of the will/volition of the addressed person, engaging their capacity to be persuaded.

9994.text: Originates within the addressed person themselves -- their own wanting to be shown proof, not stated as coming from elsewhere.

9995.text: Being shown/coming to know here serves to lead the foolish person to recognize that faith without works is useless -- its purpose is corrective realization.

9996.text: Engages cognition/spiritual discernment -- the person is to come to know/perceive that faith apart from works is useless.

9997.text: This knowing is not itself an act of seeking or worship toward God; it is intellectual recognition of a truth about faith.

9998.text: No divine-to-human operation is depicted; this is James's rhetorical offer to demonstrate a truth to the reader.

9999.text: James (the writer) extends this knowledge to the reader by showing/demonstrating the point about faith and works.

10000.text: The foolish person is to take up this knowledge from James's demonstration -- being shown is precisely this uptake.

10001.text: No relation to angelic or adversarial spiritual beings is shown here.

10002.text: Not predicated of God directly; it is James demonstrating a truth about faith and works to a human interlocutor.

10003.text: The immediate response sought is recognition/realization that faith apart from works is useless.

10004.text: Over time this knowing is meant to establish a corrected understanding that faith must be joined to works.

10005.text: A change in the person's understanding/orientation is implied -- from not grasping to recognizing that faith without works is useless; the verse presents this as intended to be lasting correction.

10006.text: No explicit before/during/after sequence of inner states is laid out beyond the single act of being shown.

10007.text: The mechanism is rhetorical demonstration/argument -- James proposes to show the addressee the truth through reasoned confrontation.

10008.text: Operates in cognitive mode -- coming to perceive/recognize a truth through demonstration.

10009.text: Located at the level of the mind/understanding of the addressed person.

10010.text: Originates from another person (James) demonstrating/teaching the truth to the addressee.

10011.text: Faith here is stated as the very thing that must be joined to works or else it is rendered useless -- its purpose/effect is what is under scrutiny.

10012.text: Faith engages volition and moral evaluation -- it is presented as a professed conviction that must be paired with active moral response (works).

10013.text: Faith is the person's professed trust/belief oriented toward God, but the verse shows it as inert apart from works -- a deficient form of that movement.

10014.text: The verse does not depict faith here as an operation from God toward the person, but as the person's own held/professed state being evaluated.

10015.text: Faith is not depicted as extended from one person to another in this verse.

10016.text: Faith is not shown here as taken up from another person; it is the addressee's own possessed (but inert) faith.

10017.text: No relation to angelic or adversarial spiritual beings is shown for faith in this verse.

10018.text: Faith is related to God as its proper object/orientation, though the verse's focus is that such faith, apart from works, fails to be operative.

10019.text: No immediate inner response following from faith is described here; the verse instead states a negative condition (uselessness) about faith itself.

10020.text: No positive inner-being production is shown; the verse instead flags this faith's failure to be effective without accompanying works.

10021.text: The verse implies faith's condition (whether it is living/effective or dead/useless) depends on the presence of works, but does not itself narrate a change occurring -- it states a diagnostic condition.

10022.text: No sequence of inner states through faith is depicted here.

10023.text: No mechanism of change in the person is shown; the verse states a condition about faith's uselessness rather than a formation process.

10024.text: Faith operates here as a professed conviction/disposition mode, evaluated for whether it issues in action.

10025.text: Located at the level of heart/mind conviction -- the professed inner trust that this verse tests against outward works.

10026.text: The verse does not state faith's origin here; it is simply presupposed as possessed by the addressee.

10027.text: The interjection "you" (O, vocative particle) is purely a supporting exclamatory marker addressing the foolish person, not a candidate for its own inner-being characteristic.

10028.text: "Foolish" functions here as a vocative qualifier describing the addressee's lack of understanding, a supporting descriptor for the rhetorical rebuke rather than its own distinct characteristic.

10029.text: "Apart from" is a prepositional qualifier specifying the separation of faith from works, not itself a characteristic.

10030.text: "Works" here functions as the counterpart term faith is measured against; it names a concrete category of deeds, a supporting term rather than an inner-being characteristic in its own right in this verse's usage.

10031.text: The copula "is" is a linking verb joining faith and useless; purely grammatical, not a candidate characteristic.

11002.text: Surface 'thanks' (N-NSF) as subject of an implied verb of being names God as recipient of gratitude for stirring Titus's care -- the nominative form casts thanks as the response-offering itself, not merely a feeling.

11003.text: Here charis takes its 'grateful frame of mind / thanks' sense (per LSJ II.2, Mounce): Paul's grateful acknowledgment that God is the one who moved Titus's heart, not an abstract theological grace-gift.

11004.text: Directionally this thanks moves from Paul toward God, crediting God as the origin of Titus's earnest care -- it constitutes an acknowledgment of divine agency behind a human disposition.

11005.text: The root sense of favor/gratification operates here as gratitude returned to God for a favor received (Titus's care being put in his heart), matching LSJ II.2's 'sense of favour received, thankfulness.'

11006.text: This occurrence matches the term's common NT 'thanks/thanksgiving to God' sense (as in Rom 6:17, 1Cor 15:57); no divergence from that usual sense is shown here.

11007.text: As nominative singular feminine noun functioning as subject of an elided 'be' verb, the form casts thanks as a standalone declarative exclamation ('thanks [be] to God'), not a verbal action.

11008.text: Within charis's range from outward grace/beauty to divine favor to human gratitude, this occurrence sits at the 'thanks/gratitude' end (LSJ II.2), a doxological response rather than a gift bestowed.

11009.text: This occurrence expresses an act -- the act of giving thanks to God -- rather than a static disposition or condition.

11010.text: No structural opposite term for charis is identifiable as relevant to this occurrence's thanksgiving sense.

11011.text: No person-type term (one who habitually exercises charis) is relevant to this occurrence, which names an act of thanksgiving rather than a character trait.

11012.text: No supplication/seeking term is relevant here; the occurrence expresses offered thanks, not a request for favor.

11013.text: As an NT Greek term in a Pauline epistolary doxology, the Testament context matches the term's standard NT usage of thanksgiving toward God; no distinct interpretive shift arises from Testament context here.

11014.text: Charis is a classical Greek term (attested from Homer onward for grace/favor); this thanksgiving usage is a semantic extension of an already ancient word, not an NT coinage.

11015.text: Surface 'heart' (N-DSF, dative object of 'put into') names the inner seat where God implants disposition -- its essential nature here is as the locus receiving a God-given impulse toward care.

11016.text: Here kardia takes the sense 'seat of impulse, affection, desire' (per the meaning tree): the inner faculty into which God places earnest care for others.

11017.text: Constitutionally, the heart here is the receiving vessel of divine action -- God 'puts' care into it, implying the heart's disposition originates from outside itself, from God.

11018.text: The root sense of kardia as seat of feeling/impulse operates here as the internal location where God instills Titus's earnest care, showing the heart as the origin-point of that disposition.

11019.text: This occurrence matches kardia's usual sense as seat of feeling/impulse/affection (as in Mt 6:21, Phil 1:7); no divergence from that common usage appears here.

11020.text: As a dative singular feminine noun governed by 'into,' the form marks heart as the destination/recipient of God's placing action, not an agent acting on its own.

11021.text: Within kardia's range from seat of thought/intellect to seat of feeling/desire, this occurrence sits at the affective/volitional end -- the heart as recipient of implanted earnest care rather than intellectual seat.

11022.text: This occurrence expresses a condition -- the heart as the site into which a disposition (earnest care) has been given -- rather than depicting the heart's own act.

11023.text: No structural opposite term for kardia is relevant to this occurrence's use as recipient of God-given care.

11024.text: No person-type term relevant to this occurrence; kardia here names an inner location, not a personal habitual trait-bearer.

11025.text: No supplication/seeking term is relevant here; the verse depicts God's unprompted placing of care, not a request for it.

11026.text: As an NT Greek term used in its standard sense (seat of feeling/impulse), the Testament context makes no distinct interpretive difference to this occurrence.

11027.text: Kardia is attested in classical Greek from Homer onward as seat of feeling and passion; this NT usage continues that established pre-NT sense rather than coining a new one.

11028.text: Surface 'earnest care' (N-ASF, accusative object of implicit 'the same') names the very disposition God placed in Titus's heart -- its form as accusative direct-object-like complement shows it as a content, the thing given/possessed, not an action performed.

11029.text: Here spoude carries its 'earnestness, earnest application, zeal' sense (per the meaning tree citing this very verse), denoting Titus's zealous concern matching Paul's own for the Corinthians.

11030.text: Relationally, this earnest care (spoude) is directed toward the Corinthians ('for you') and is shared identically between Paul and Titus ('the same'), implying a constitutional bond of shared zeal placed in both by God.

11031.text: The root sense of spoude (from speudo, 'to hasten/exert oneself') operates here as zealous, active concern for the Corinthians rather than mere haste, matching LSJ's religious-zeal sense (II.b).

11032.text: As an accusative singular feminine noun, the form presents earnest care as a definite quality given/possessed ('the same care'), a concrete disposition rather than a verbal process.

11033.text: Within spoude's range from literal haste to zealous effort to goodwill/esteem for a person, this occurrence sits at the 'goodwill/zealous concern for a person' end (LSJ II.2, citing this very verse: sigma. huper tinos), showing devoted concern rather than mere urgency.

11034.text: This occurrence expresses a disposition (God-given inner earnestness/zeal for the Corinthians) rather than a specific act performed.

11035.text: As the M67 cluster's positive pole, spoude here names zealous, diligent care as opposed to negligence or indifference, though no specific opposite term is named in this verse itself.

11036.text: No person-type term (e.g. one who habitually exercises spoude) is named or relevant in this verse's own content.

11037.text: No supplication/seeking term is relevant here; the verse depicts spoude as divinely implanted, not sought after.

11038.text: As an NT Greek term used in its standard epistolary sense of zealous concern, the Testament context makes no distinct interpretive difference here.

11039.text: Spoude is attested in classical Greek from Homer onward (haste, zeal, effort); this NT occurrence continues that established pre-NT semantic range rather than coining a new sense.

11610.text: Surface 'want' (V-PAI-2S, present active) shows James addressing the reader directly, naming a present act of will/desire to be shown proof, not a settled disposition.

11611.text: Here it means to be willing/wish, introducing a rhetorical demand: the reader is asked whether he wishes to have it demonstrated that faith without works is useless.

11612.text: The willing here is directional: it points the addressee toward receiving proof/demonstration, setting up the argument that follows rather than expressing an independent desire of its own content.

11613.text: Root sense 'to exercise the will, be willing' operates here as the trigger verb introducing the rhetorical question that drives the passage's argument.

11614.text: The sense matches the term's usual 'wish/be willing' use with a following infinitive-type construction; no divergence from ordinary usage here.

11615.text: Present active indicative 2nd singular shows an ongoing, direct address to 'you' the foolish person, framing this as a live rhetorical challenge in the moment of speaking.

11616.text: Within its range (wish, be inclined, intend, choose), this occurrence sits at the basic 'wish/desire' sense governing a following demonstration, a common rhetorical usage.

11617.text: This occurrence expresses an act (a present wish/desire being voiced), not a fixed disposition or condition.

11618.text: No structural opposite among G2309's related terms is relevant to this occurrence's plain rhetorical use of 'want to be shown'.

11619.text: No person-type term (one who habitually wills/desires) is relevant to this occurrence, which is a simple verb of address, not a naming of character trait.

11620.text: No supplication/seeking term is relevant here; the verb simply expresses the addressee's own wish, not a request directed at another.

11621.text: As an NT Greek occurrence in a direct rhetorical address, Testament context (NT vs OT) makes no interpretive difference to this common volitional verb here.

11622.text: Thelo/ethelo is attested well before the NT period (Homer onward per LSJ); this occurrence is an ordinary classical-continuous use, not a NT coinage.

11623.text: Surface 'shown' (V-2AAN, aorist passive-form infinitive of ginosko) names the essential act of being made to know/perceive -- the reader is to be given knowledge, not simply told.

11624.text: Here it means to come to know/perceive by demonstration -- James wants the fool to be brought to a realized understanding that faith apart from works is useless.

11625.text: The term carries a directional force here: knowledge is to be brought TO the addressee via demonstration, moving him from ignorance to recognized understanding of the claim about faith and works.

11626.text: Root sense 'to know/come to know, perceive' operates here as the goal-verb of the rhetorical question -- the addressee is to be brought to perceive a truth by demonstration.

11627.text: This use matches the term's usual 'come to know/perceive' sense via demonstration; no divergence from its ordinary NT usage here.

11628.text: Aorist active infinitive form shows a single, completed act of coming-to-know being sought for the addressee, dependent on the governing verb 'want'.

11629.text: Within its range (perceive, ascertain, understand, acknowledge), this occurrence sits at 'to be shown/made to understand by demonstration,' a common evidential use.

11630.text: This occurrence expresses an act -- the act of coming to know/being shown -- rather than a fixed disposition or condition.

11631.text: No structural opposite among G1097's related terms is relevant to this occurrence's use as the verb of demonstrative knowing.

11632.text: No person-type term is relevant here; the verb names an act of being brought to knowledge, not a habitual character trait.

11633.text: No supplication/seeking term is relevant; the verb expresses coming-to-know, not petitioning another for it.

11634.text: As an NT Greek occurrence in ordinary demonstrative usage, Testament context makes no interpretive difference to this occurrence's plain sense.

11635.text: Ginosko/gignosko is attested from Homer onward per LSJ; this occurrence is an ordinary continuation of classical usage, not a NT coinage.

11636.text: Surface 'faith' (N-NSF, nominative singular feminine) names the subject of the clause -- faith itself is being characterized (as useless when apart from works), showing its essential nature as a state that must be paired with action to have effect.

11637.text: Here it means firm persuasion/belief -- specifically the professed trust in God that James contrasts with accompanying deeds; without works, this belief is declared useless.

11638.text: The term's relational implication here is that faith is constitutionally meant to be joined with works; named 'apart from works' it is shown as incomplete/inert on its own.

11639.text: Root sense 'trust, persuasion' (from peithomai) operates here as a disposition of the person which, when isolated from works, is declared ineffective/useless.

11640.text: This occurrence matches the term's usual NT theological sense (belief/trust in God), presented in its ordinary abstract-noun form; no divergence from that sense here.

11641.text: Nominative singular feminine noun form shows faith functioning as the grammatical subject being evaluated/qualified by the predicate 'useless apart from works'.

11642.text: Within its range (trust, faithfulness, ground of belief), this occurrence sits at the theological sense of professed belief/trust in God, evaluated for whether it produces action.

11643.text: This occurrence expresses a disposition/condition (a state of belief held) rather than an act, being evaluated for its lack of accompanying action.

11644.text: Works (ergon, T2 term 'works' in this verse) functions as the structural counterpart/opposite pole here -- faith is declared useless precisely 'apart from' works.

11645.text: No person-type term (one who habitually has faith) is directly relevant to this occurrence, which evaluates faith itself in the abstract, not a person's character.

11646.text: No supplication/seeking term is relevant here; the verse evaluates faith's effect rather than the act of seeking faith from another.

11647.text: The NT theological sense of pistis (belief/trust in God/Christ) governs this occurrence, distinct from the term's more general classical Greek senses of pledge or credit; that NT-specific sense is what is being tested against works here.

11648.text: Pistis is attested from Hesiod onward per LSJ, with classical senses of trust/pledge/proof predating the NT; this occurrence continues and narrows that established word to its NT theological use.

11649.text: Surface 'useless' (A-NSF, nominative singular feminine adjective) predicates faith itself, showing this occurrence's essential nature as marking faith-without-works as inert/unproductive -- the negative pole of the idle-vs-active cluster.

11650.text: Here it means unprofitable/ineffective -- faith apart from works produces nothing, per the lexicon's 'unprofitable, hollow, ineffective' sense applied specifically to this verse.

11651.text: The term's implication here is constitutional: faith without works fails to constitute genuine, functioning faith -- it lacks the productive outworking that would make it real/effective.

11652.text: Root sense 'not working, idle' (a-ergos, 'without work') operates literally here: faith lacking works is 'not-working,' unproductive faith.

11653.text: Nominative singular feminine adjective agrees with and predicates 'faith,' grammatically marking faith itself as the thing characterized as useless/inert.

11654.text: Within its range (inactive, idle, unprofitable, careless), this occurrence sits at the metaphorical 'unprofitable/ineffective' end, applied to faith rather than to a person's labor.

11655.text: This occurrence expresses a quality/condition attributed to faith (its uselessness) rather than an act.

11656.text: Works (ergon) is the structural opposite here -- 'useless' names exactly the state faith falls into when works are absent, making ergon its direct counterpart term.

11657.text: No person-type term (a habitually idle person) is relevant here since the adjective modifies faith, an abstraction, not a person's character.

11658.text: No supplication/seeking term applies; this occurrence describes a state of ineffectiveness, not an act of seeking something from another.

11659.text: As an NT Greek occurrence used in ordinary metaphorical extension of a classical adjective, Testament context makes no additional interpretive difference here beyond the metaphorical application itself.

11660.text: Argos is attested from at least the 5th century BC (Herodotus, Sophocles, etc. per LSJ) with established senses of idle/lazy/unproductive; this verse's metaphorical use of that established term is not a NT coinage.

12479.text: A person chooses a thing or place for oneself by sight or use: "the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose" (Gen 6:2); "Lot chose for himself all the Jordan Valley" (Gen 13:11), and they separated; David chose five smooth stones (1Sa 17:40); the bulls of the contest on Carmel are chosen (1Ki 18:23, 25).

12480.text: People select men for battle, leadership or a task, and the word marks fitness: "Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people" (Exo 18:25); "700 chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss" (Judg 20:16); "300,000 choice men, fit for war, able to handle spear and shield" (2Ch 25:5). The same word names the men "chosen from the assembly, well-known men" who rose up against Moses (Num 16:2).

12481.text: God chooses a person for a task or office: priests and Levites, the king, David, Solomon, the servant, witnesses. Choosing goes with bringing near: "The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him" (Num 16:5); "Blessed is the one you choose and bring near" (Psa 65:4). The choice is shown, not argued: "the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout" (Num 17:5). It is followed by a charge: "the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it" (1Ch 28:10). In the servant it is joined to God's soul and Spirit: "my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18).

12483.text: God chooses a place "to make his name dwell there" (Deu 12:11), and the choosing carries his own presence: "My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (2Ch 7:16). The people's offerings, eating, rejoicing, judgement, reading of the law and prayer are all directed to the place he chooses. The choice can be cast off, "I will cast off this city that I have chosen" (2Ki 23:27), and made again: "the Lord will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem" (Zec 1:17).

12487.text: Inner-being words stand beside choosing: God's heart in what he chooses, "My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (2Ch 7:16); his soul in his chosen servant, "my chosen, in whom my soul delights" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18); the people's heart and soul turned toward the chosen city in repentance (1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 6:38); the soul's delight in chosen ways (Isa 66:3); the soul choosing death (Job 7:15); the heart given a worth (Pro 10:20); the soul's appetite, "whenever you desire" (Deu 12:21; Deu 18:6); the self humbled in a fast God does not choose (Isa 58:5); "one deeply despised" whom the Lord has chosen (Isa 49:7).

12489.text: The word stands for a person's own decision, desire or accord: "whatever my lord the king decides" (2Sa 15:15); "all that you desire of me I will do for you" (2Sa 19:38); "For you must choose, and not I" (Job 34:33); "choosing my words with him" (Job 9:14); "I chose their way and sat as chief" (Job 29:25). The escaped slave dwells "in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him" (Deu 23:16). With G0830 the Macedonians gave "beyond their means, of their own accord" (2Cor 8:3), and Titus went "of his own accord" (2Cor 8:17).

12496.text: What God offered and was refused was good: the land, "Yet you would not go up, but rebelled" (Deu 1:26); rest, "This is rest; give rest to the weary," "yet they would not hear" (Isa 28:12); "In returning and rest you shall be saved" "But you were unwilling" (Isa 30:15), with their own plan, "We will flee upon horses" (30:16); "children unwilling to hear the instruction of the Lord" (Isa 30:9); "Israel would not submit to me" (Psa 81:11), "So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels" (81:12); "would have none of my reproof" (Pro 1:25), "would have none of my counsel" (Pro 1:30); "whose law they would not obey" (Isa 42:24); "will not listen to me" (Lev 26:21); "not willing to listen to me: because all the house of Israel have a hard forehead and a stubborn heart" (Eze 3:7); "they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me" (Eze 20:8). Once the will is invited with if: "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land" (Isa 1:19).

12499.text: A refusal that keeps faith: "the servants of the king would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the Lord" (1Sa 22:17); David, "I would not put out my hand against the Lord's anointed" (1Sa 26:23); David longed for the water of Bethlehem, "But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord" (2Sa 23:16), "Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?" (2Sa 23:17; 1Ch 11:18-19). The faithful refuse enticement and demand: "you shall not yield to him or listen to him" (Deu 13:8); "if sinners entice you, do not consent" (Pro 1:10); "Do not listen or consent" (1Ki 20:8).

12505.text: People value and regard: "Are we not regarded by him as foreigners?" (Gen 31:15); "Let not my lord hold me guilty" (2Sa 19:19); "who have no regard for silver" (Isa 13:17); "there is no regard for man" (Isa 33:8); "they were considered reliable" (Neh 13:13); God's laws "would be regarded as a strange thing" (Hos 8:12); "The precious sons of Zion" "how they are regarded as earthen pots" (Lam 4:2); "will be counted as cursing" (Pro 27:14). And a person is regarded: "we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psa 44:22); "I am counted among those who go down to the pit" (Psa 88:4); Israel "not counting itself among the nations" (Num 23:9).

12506.text: The same word names design as skill: "to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze" (Exo 31:4), given by God to Bezalel; Huram-abi, "trained" "to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him" (2Ch 2:14).

12508.text: A thing can be devised from one's own heart: Jeroboam's feast "in the month that he had devised from his own heart" (1Ki 12:33); "you are inventing them out of your own mind" (Neh 6:8). The purposes are hidden until the Lord comes, "who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart" (1Co 4:5).

12511.text: God also purposes and does not turn back: "I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back" (Jer 4:28); "so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not" (Zec 8:15); "the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath" (Heb 6:17).

12513.text: Plotting is also turned against God: "What do you plot against the Lord? He will make a complete end" (Nah 1:9); "From you came one who plotted evil against the Lord, a worthless counselor" (Nah 1:11); "Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me" (Hos 7:15).

12514.text: The looking-ahead words are used most often against another person. It is placed in the heart: "let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zec 7:10), "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zec 8:17). It is done together: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (Jer 18:18); "In Heshbon they planned disaster against her" (Jer 48:2); "they made plans to put him to death" (Joh 11:53), and Lazarus as well (Joh 12:10); "The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners" (Act 27:42). It is aimed at the righteous and the weak: "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psa 37:12); "who have planned to trip up my feet" (Psa 140:4). It hides behind a friendly word: "Come and let us meet together" "But they intended to do me harm" (Neh 6:2); Saul's bride-price, "Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (1Sa 18:25). It is pinned on the other side: "you and the Jews intend to rebel" (Neh 6:6). Another pleads against it: Esther "pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman" (Est 8:3; 9:24).

12515.text: The will resolves, intends and steers: Joseph, "unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly" (Mat 1:19), until the angel spoke as he considered; Herod "intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people" (Act 12:4), and the intention was not carried out; "I wanted to come to you first" (2Co 1:15); "the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan" (Act 27:43); "guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs" (Jam 3:4).

12518.text: Looking ahead weighs before it acts: a king "will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand" (Luk 14:31); "She considers a field and buys it" (Pro 31:16); "consider it, take counsel, and speak" (Judg 19:30). It plans without knowing: "on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix" (Act 27:12), "supposing that they had obtained their purpose" (Act 27:13), "they planned if possible to run the ship ashore" (Act 27:39). A plan carries a word: "Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say Yes, yes and No, no at the same time?" (2Co 1:17). Plans part people: "Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark" (Act 15:37); Joseph of Arimathea "had not consented to their decision and action" (Luk 23:51). And a plan can be for another's good: "because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom" (Dan 6:3).

12519.text: God's plan takes in what people do against him without excusing them: "this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Act 2:23); "to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place" (Act 4:28).

12521.text: The will word also carries wanting to know and stated wishes: "desiring to know the real reason" (Act 22:30; 23:28); "We wish to know therefore what these things mean" (Act 17:20); "I would like to hear the man myself" (Act 25:22); "I refuse to be a judge of these things" (Act 18:15). Paul's wishes in teaching each come with their reason: "I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1Ti 2:8); "So I would have younger widows marry" (1Ti 5:14); "I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works" (Tit 3:8); "I want you to know" (Phi 1:12); "so that our joy may be complete" (2Jo 12); "I want to remind you" (Jude 5).

12528.text: The same giving can be turned to an idol. Micah's mother: "I dedicate the silver to the Lord from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image" (Judg 17:3), in days when "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (17:6). Israel "came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the thing of shame, and became detestable like the thing they loved" (Hos 9:10), after "Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel". And one "who separates himself from me, taking his idols into his heart" (Eze 14:7), whose heart God means to "lay hold of" (14:5).

12537.text: Face B, felt before God's presence, act or word, or a spirit: dread, terrified, trembled and trembling, with God's presence, his voice in the thunder, his word read aloud, a vision or his act as the object; once a spirit in the night.

12540.text: Face F, what or who inspires dread: God named "the Fear of Isaac"; a person who is an object of dread; Ephraim's speech.

12541.text: Face G, dread laid on nations and peoples: laid by God, or fallen on peoples because of Israel, the Jews, Mordecai, a king.

12548.text: Face O, *rāgaz* stirred: one root rendered rage, anger, quarrel, grief and disturbance; the subjects include God, Sennacherib, David, Joseph's brothers, a fool, Samuel brought up and Sheol.

12553.text: Face T, trembling called for: a summons or decree to the earth, the peoples, the complacent and the heavens.

12554.text: Dread and trembling arise before God's presence, voice, word and act: "I am terrified at his presence; when I consider, I am in dread of him" (Job 23:15-16); "At this also my heart trembles" at the thunder (Job 37:1); "all the people in the camp trembled" at Sinai (Exo 19:16); at Daniel's vision "I stood up trembling" (Dan 10:7, 10-11); "they turned trembling to one another, saying, 'What is this that God has done to us?'" (Gen 42:28); "The sinners in Zion are afraid" (Isa 33:14); "I was in terror of calamity from God" (Job 31:23); "Will not his majesty terrify you" (Job 13:11).

12556.text: God lays dread on peoples, and the verses say what follows: "The Lord your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you on all the land" (Deu 11:25); "the Lord brought the fear of him upon all nations" (1Ch 14:17); "the fear of the Lord fell upon all the kingdoms" and "they made no war against Jehoshaphat" (2Ch 17:10); "Terror and dread fall upon them ... they are still as a stone" (Exo 15:14-16); "dread of them had fallen upon [Egypt]" (Psa 105:38); "Trembling took hold of them there" (Psa 48:5-6); "that the nations might tremble at your presence" (Isa 64:2).

12557.text: Making others afraid, as an act (the subject is the one who frightens): Ahithophel, "throw him into a panic" (2Sa 17:2); Gideon "threw all the army into a panic" (Jdg 8:12); to Babylon, "perhaps you may inspire terror" (Isa 47:12); "so that man who is of the earth may strike terror no more" (Psa 10:18); "those awake who will make you tremble" (Hab 2:7); "Will you frighten a driven leaf" (Job 13:25); "to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations" (Zec 1:21); "messengers ... to terrify the unsuspecting people of Cush" (Eze 30:9).

12561.text: Trembling is called for and decreed: "tremble before him, all the earth!" (Psa 96:9; 1Ch 16:30); "let the peoples tremble!" (Psa 99:1); "Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord" (Psa 114:7); "Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble" (Joe 2:1); "Tremble, you women who are at ease" (Isa 32:9-11); Darius, "people are to tremble and fear before the God of Daniel" (Dan 6:26); "Be appalled, O heavens" (Jer 2:12).

12563.text: One root, rāgaz, "to tremble", is rendered by the ESV as trembling and quaking (Exo 15:14; Psa 18:7; Hab 3:16), "Be angry" (Psa 4:4), "raging" and "raged" (2Ki 19:27-28; Isa 37:28-29), "enraged" (Eze 16:43), "provoke" (Job 12:6), "quarrel" (Gen 45:24), "rages" (Pro 29:9), "deeply moved" (2Sa 18:33), "disturbed" (1Sa 28:15), "stirred up" (Isa 14:9), "roused" (Isa 28:21), "unrest" (Jer 50:34).

12564.text: External parties in the rāgaz verses: God (enraged, roused); Samuel brought up from the dead (1Sa 28:15); Sheol (Isa 14:9).

12569.text: The trembling root rāgaz stands behind two verses the anger material already uses (Psa 4:4; 2Ki 19:27-28).

12572.text: Face B, fear felt before God's presence or act: afraid, feared, fear and awe, with God himself, his fire, his act or the place he is met as the object.

12574.text: Face D, fearing God as a way of life: fear, fears, feared, fearing, reverence, God-fearing and worship; not a passing state but a standing, commanded, learned, taught, given, lived, joined with walking, serving, keeping and turning from evil.

12577.text: Face G, nations and peoples made to fear: the fear is laid on others, by God or because of his people.

12580.text: Face J, other faces: fear rendered as a manner of acting (cautious, shuns, reveres, the word feared).

12581.text: "Do not fear" nearly always comes with a ground, introduced by "for": "for I am with you" (Gen 26:24; Isa 41:10; 43:5; Jer 1:8; Jer 42:11; Deu 20:1; Deu 31:8); "I have given him into your hand" (Num 21:34; Deu 3:2; Jos 8:1; 10:8; 11:6); "I have redeemed you" (Isa 43:1); "I am your shield" (Gen 15:1); "God has heard the voice of the boy" (Gen 21:17); "you have borne a son" (Gen 35:17; 1Sa 4:20); "I will show you kindness" (2Sa 9:7); "those who are with us are more than those who are with them" (2Ki 6:16); idols "cannot do evil" (Jer 10:5); "am I in the place of God? ... I will provide for you" (Gen 50:19, 21); "for God has come to test you" (Exo 20:20).

12582.text: "Do not fear" is paired with other commands: "be strong and courageous" (Deu 31:6; Jos 10:25; 1Ch 22:13; 28:20; 2Ch 32:7); "do not be dismayed" (Deu 1:21; 31:8; Jos 8:1; 2Ch 20:15, 17; Isa 41:10); "stand firm, and see the salvation of the Lord" (Exo 14:13); "Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome" (Neh 4:14); "remember what the Lord your God did" (Deu 7:18); "Be careful, be quiet" (Isa 7:4); "let your hands be strong" (Zec 8:13); "let not your hands grow weak" (Zep 3:16); "Peace be with you" (Dan 10:19); "Peace to you" (Gen 43:23; Judg 6:23).

12583.text: What God does toward those who fear him, one verse each: steadfast love (Psa 103:11, 17); compassion "as a father shows compassion" (Psa 103:13); "The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him" (Psa 25:14); he instructs (Psa 25:12); "the eye of the Lord is on those who fear him" (Psa 33:18); "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him" (Psa 34:7); no lack (Psa 34:9); food (Psa 111:5); "fulfills the desire ... hears their cry" (Psa 145:19); "takes pleasure in" (Psa 147:11); goodness stored up (Psa 31:19); salvation near (Psa 85:9); a banner (Psa 60:4); a heritage (Psa 61:5); the book of remembrance (Mal 3:16); "the sun of righteousness shall rise" (Mal 4:2).

12585.text: Turned onto what is feared, the root describes: God himself, "the great, the mighty, and the awesome God" (Deu 10:17; 7:21), the great and awesome God "who keeps covenant and steadfast love" in three prayers (Neh 1:5; 9:32; Dan 9:4); his name (Psa 99:3; 111:9; Deu 28:58); his deeds (Psa 66:3, 5; 145:6; 106:22; Exo 34:10; Isa 64:3); his day, "great and very awesome; who can endure it?" (Joe 2:11, 31; Mal 4:5); a place (Gen 28:17); an angel's appearance (Jdg 13:6); the wilderness, "great and terrifying" (Deu 1:19; 8:15); an invading nation, "dreaded and fearsome" (Hab 1:7); a people "feared near and far" (Isa 18:2, 7); the living creatures' rims and the crystal expanse (Eze 1:18, 22); the human frame, "I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14).

12587.text: The root is rendered as a manner of acting: "One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil, but a fool is reckless" (Pro 14:16); "he who shuns an oath" (Ecc 9:2); "he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded" (Pro 13:13); among Pharaoh's servants "whoever feared the word of the Lord ... hurried his slaves and his livestock into the houses" (Exo 9:20).

12589.text: Heart near or far: fear taught by men while "their hearts are far from me" set against fear put "in their hearts" (Isa 29:13; Jer 32:40).

12590.text: One verse carries both values of the word: "Do not fear ... that the fear of him may be before you" (Exo 20:20); "they feared the Lord but also served their own gods" beside "They do not fear the Lord" (2Ki 17:33-34).

12591.text: The woman of Tekoa's "the people have made me afraid" (2Sa 14:15) is part of a staged story (2Sa 14:2-3); the verse stays in face A as data only.

12597.text: As a standing toward God: commanded, learned, given: "what does the Lord your God require of you, but to fear the Lord your God"; "that they may hear and learn to fear the Lord your God"; "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me"

12598.text: The fear of God, named by what it is: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge"; "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil"; "a fountain of life"; "It was a covenant of fear, and he feared me"

12612.text: Face S. In age (2 / 2 hits and verses, units 2–3): | Ecc 12:3, 5

12624.text: Face D. Fearing God as a standing (177 / 170 hits and verses, units 1–4): Commanded, learned, given, owed, lived

12631.text: Face U. Made a horror, a desolation (43 / 41 hits and verses, units 3): A people or land as what others are horrified at

12634.text: Face G. Dread laid on nations, peoples, creatures (53 / 41 hits and verses, units 1–3): By God, or because of his people

12636.text: What it is turned toward: The same people, the same root: "they feared greatly" at Egypt; after the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed". In the boat: afraid in the storm, then "filled with great fear" and "Who then is this". "do not fear what they fear … Let him be your fear"

12640.text: Where the heart is: Fear "taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me"; fear put "in their hearts"

12644.text: What it leads to, before the same kind of act: "they were afraid, and they glorified God"; "asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear". Rahab's dread ends "for the Lord your God, he is God"; Moab's dread ends "Come now, curse this people for me"

12646.text: Pride: "So do not become proud, but fear"; "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart"

12649.text: One root, many renderings: rāgaz (to tremble) rendered "Be angry", "deeply moved", "quarrel"; paḥad (to dread) rendered "thrill"; phobos (fear) rendered "terror", "respect", "reverence", "awe"; ekthambeō (to be alarmed) rendered "greatly amazed", "troubled", "alarmed"; eulabeomai (to be reverent) rendered "afraid", "reverent fear"

12652.text: Being feared works on the one feared: "The horror you inspire has deceived you"; those "who spread terror in the land of the living"

12666.text: Fear leads to glory, confession: "they glorified God"; "Truly this was the Son of God!"; Rahab: "he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath"

12673.text: Fear and Inner seat (M47): Fear is felt in the heart; given in the heart; a trembling heart in the curse; the heart firm and not afraid (verses shared or near: 97 / 50).

12679.text: Fear and Worship and service (M36): Commanded together: "to fear the Lord your God … to serve the Lord" (verses shared or near: 56 / 24).

12684.text: Fear and Pride (M08): Set against: "do not become proud, but fear"; the pride of the heart deceived by the horror it inspired (verses shared or near: 40 / 23).

12687.text: Fear and Love (M51): Commanded together (fear, walk, love, serve); set against ("perfect love casts out fear") (verses shared or near: 10 / 5).

12688.text: Fear and Shame (M07): Horror listed with "a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse"; "horror covers them. Shame is on all faces" (verses shared or near: 27 / 16).

12697.text: Face G. Dread laid on nations, peoples and creatures (H4172A, môrāʾ; 2 / 2 hits and verses): the word rendered fear · dread.

12700.text: Face C. Spoken against (5 / 5 hits and verses; surfaces intimidated · afraid · fear · amazed): Each with a ground: the judgment is God's; the word did not come true; "Is there a God besides me?"; a higher watcher.

12702.text: Face F. What or who inspires dread (12 / 11 hits and verses; surfaces terrifying · dreadful · dreaded · awesome · inspire · terror · frightening): A king, the Chaldeans, God's power, beasts in a vision, the horse, Leviathan, the beloved.

12703.text: Face G. Dread laid on nations, peoples and creatures (8 / 8 hits and verses; surfaces terror · dread · fear · feared): Laid by God, on cities, peoples, beasts; once so that the nations may know they are men.

12712.text: Face S. In age (1 / 1 hits and verses; surfaces terrors): "terrors are in the way".

12714.text: Face U. Made a horror, a desolation, a waste (43 / 41 hits and verses; surfaces horror · desolation · waste · desolate · astonishment · terror): The word names the people or land as the thing others are horrified at. Reasons are given in the verses.

12716.text: Face W. A horrible thing done (5 / 4 hits and verses; surfaces horrible thing · appalling): What God sees in his people.

12718.text: Face Y. Terror on every side (8 / 8 hits and verses; surfaces Terror on Every Side · terror · terrors): One phrase in many mouths: a name given by the prophet; the whisper of friends against him; a battle cry; God's summons.

12719.text: Face Z. Pangs as of a woman in labor (7 / 7 hits and verses; surfaces pain · pangs · anguish · panic): At a report heard or a sight seen.

12721.text: Face AC. Waves and storm (9 / 9 hits and verses; surfaces waves · breakers · tempest · sweeps · rush · away): No fear in the English. "Your waves" over a person.

12731.text: What dread leads to: a confession of God (Rahab); hiring a curse (Moab); the cities not pursuing.

12732.text: Being feared works on the feared.

12735.text: Labor pain, and in Micah its end in rescue.

12741.text: Face E. Awe, respect or reverence toward people (7 / 6 hits and verses; surfaces respect · respectful · respects · feared): The fear root rendered "respect": to rulers, masters, husbands, any who ask; Herod toward John.

12758.text: G1568 ekthambeō (4): greatly amazed (Mar 9:15) · troubled (Mar 14:33, Jesus) · alarmed (Mar 16:5, 6). One root for a crowd, for Jesus in Gethsemane, and for the women at the tomb (FE-143).

12769.text: One root, three settings: a crowd "greatly amazed"; Jesus "troubled"; the women "alarmed".

12783.text: Ecc 12:1-7 is one figure of old age, framed by "Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come" (12:1) and ending "the dust returns to the earth ... and the spirit returns to God who gave it" (12:7).

12784.text: Inside the figure: "the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent" (Ecc 12:3); "one rises up at the sound of a bird" (12:4); then the fear of high places and of the road (12:5).

12786.text: Fear that comes as the body fails (Ecc 12:5): of high places and of the way out of doors, with the trembling of 12:3 and the startle at a bird in 12:4, set inside the call to remember the Creator before those days (12:1). It is not fear of a threat: the person is the one acted on, and the cause is age.

12787.text: Psa 103:8-18 says "those who fear him" three times: the love "as high as the heavens" (103:11), the Father's compassion (103:13), and the steadfast love "from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him" (103:17).

12789.text: The main operation in Psa 103:11 is God's steadfast love toward the one who fears him: the height word (M08) is a measure, and fear is the standing of the one loved.

12794.text: The root ḥûl, "to twist, whirl", is rendered as the body writhing in labour or pain: "Writhe and groan, O daughter of Zion, like a woman in labor" (Mic 4:10); Saul "badly wounded" (1Sa 31:3).

12795.text: The root ḥûl, "to twist, whirl", is rendered as trembling, of the earth and of people: "tremble before him, all the earth" (Psa 96:9); "who shall hear the report of you and shall tremble and be in anguish because of you" (Deu 2:25).

12800.text: The root ḥûl, "to twist, whirl", is rendered as waiting: "Be still before the Lord and wait patiently for him" (Psa 37:7); "wait anxiously for good" (Mic 1:12).

12803.text: Hands and heart go together: "all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt ... pangs and agony will seize them" (Isa 13:7-8); "Every heart will melt, and all hands will be feeble; every spirit will faint, and all knees will be weak as water" (Eze 21:7), heart, hands, spirit and knees in one breath; "All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water" (Eze 7:17).

12824.text: H3372H "to fear: revere" is rendered awe-inspiring: Eze 1:22.

12840.text: H7264 rāgaz "to tremble" is rendered raging / raged / enraged (5): 2Ki 19:27–28, Isa 37:28–29, Eze 16:43.

12844.text: H7264 rāgaz "to tremble" is rendered stirred up: Isa 14:9.

12862.text: H4867 is tagged M01 but the English renders another face: waves / breakers (2Sa 22:5, Psa 42:7, 88:7, 93:4).

12864.text: H2427A is tagged M01 but the English renders another face: pain / pangs (Jer 6:24, 22:23, 50:43, Mic 4:9).

12874.text: "Long of nostrils": slow to anger is understanding, glory, better than the mighty; ruling one's spirit is better than taking a city.

12882.text: Quick temper and evil devices, side by side.

12893.text: Face of aph (H0639), "Long of nostrils": patience: Said of God first, then of the wise; and of the one who is not angry but bears another's anger (Pro 25:15) (Exo 34:6; Pro 14:29; 16:32; 19:11; 25:15). A long nose takes time to heat. The virtue and the divine name share one idiom (S, lexical).

12896.text: Face of aph (H0639), A nose given a ring in love: Rebekah; God adorning his bride (Gen 24:47; Eze 16:12). A gift of love (S).

12897.text: Face of aph (H0639), A nose given a hook: "Because you have raged against me … I will put my hook in your nose" (2Ki 19:28 = Isa 37:29). The raging nose is led back the way it came (S).

12901.text: charah (H2734): anger kindled · "fret" = heat yourself (Gen 4:5; Jon 4:1, 4, 9; Psa 37:1, 7, 8; Pro 24:19). Turned on another, it burns outward. Turned inward at the wicked's success, it "tends only to evil" (S).

12902.text: ka'as (H3707/3708): provocation done (to God) · vexation borne (Hannah, Job) · sorrow that does good ("by sadness of face the heart is made glad") · the fool's vexation that kills him · God-induced vexation of the nations (Deu 32:16, 21; 1Sa 1:6–16; Job 6:2; 17:7; Ecc 7:3; Job 5:2; Eze 32:9). Done to another, it is provocation. Borne, it is suffering. Taken to heart, it can make the heart good (Ecc 7:3). The word follows the direction of the act (S/R).

12922.text: Factor Haste / pause: Confirmed strongly. quick in spirit / slow to anger (Ecc 7:9; Pro 14:29; Jam 1:19).

12923.text: Factor Brought before God: Confirmed strongly. be still and wait (Psa 37:7); leave it to God's wrath (Rom 12:19); Jonah's anger brought to God and met by a question (Jon 4:2–4).

12925.text: Factor New: whether it is seen truly: New factor. kindled by a lie (Gen 39:19); misreading (1Sa 17:28); the heavy hand misread from fear (Mat 25:24–25).

12933.text: It is set off by something heard or seen, for God and for people: "when the Lord heard it, his anger was kindled"; "As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him … his anger was kindled"; "When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath"; "when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate … he was filled with wrath".

12939.text: God's anger named with who God is: "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger"; "I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man"; "until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart"; "I have no wrath".

12952.text: Form of anger, "Slow to anger": the proclaimed name (9 / 9 hits and verses; faces F; units 1).

12958.text: Form of anger, People provoke God: what provokes, named each time (52 / 49 hits and verses; faces 3J, 4B, 5B; units 3–5).

12975.text: Form of anger, Governed in the sayings: slow, quick, turned, stirred (21 / 17 hits and verses; faces V, W, 2S; units 1, 2).

12976.text: Form of anger, Kindled by what is heard or seen (20 / 12 hits and verses; faces O, 3M, 5N; units 1, 3, 5).

12987.text: Form of anger, "Fret not yourself" (4 / 4 hits and verses; faces 3W; units 3).

12988.text: Form of anger, The fool's vexation (4 / 3 hits and verses; faces 3Z; units 3).

12998.text: What sets it off: God and people both: "when the Lord heard it, his anger was kindled"; "As soon as his master heard the words"; a sight: "when Haman saw Mordecai"; a refusal: "But Queen Vashti refused to come"; "Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me"; news and alarm: "news from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury".

12999.text: Whether what sets it off is true: Potiphar's anger rises on his wife's report, untested; the officials rage at Jeremiah's "It is a lie; I am not deserting"; the disciples' "Why this waste?" is answered "she has done a beautiful thing to me".

13001.text: What it is joined with in the verse: Jealousy (Deu 6:15); grief: Jonathan "was grieved for David", Jesus "looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart"; the Spirit (1Sa 11:6); "the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred" (Eze 35:11); fear: "he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged"; compassion set against it (Hos 11:8–9).

13003.text: The answer it meets: "A soft answer turns away wrath"; "A gift in secret averts anger"; Moses' plea; "when he humbled himself the wrath of the Lord turned from him"; Aaron's reason, "And when Moses heard that, he approved"; Naaman's servants; "His father came out and entreated him"; Jesus called the ten; Gamaliel's counsel. Or none: "I sought for a man … but I found none"; "I looked, but there was no one to help".

13005.text: Power: The ruler's anger is followed at once by a command: custody, a decree, destruction, killing. "A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion".

13009.text: Who speaks to it: God asks: "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?"; "Do you do well to be angry?"; Joseph: "do not be distressed or angry with yourselves"; "Fret not yourself"; "Be angry and do not sin".

13011.text: The same words in different settings: One storm sentence among the false prophets and among the promises (Jer 23:19 = 30:23); the Exodus "a mighty hand and an outstretched arm" with "wrath poured out" added, aimed at Israel; provocation as threat and as a question inside a lament ("Why have they provoked me to anger with their carved images"); kaʿas as what "kills the fool" and as the "Sorrow" that "is better than laughter".

13012.text: The same phrase, the speaker's purpose: "slow to anger": God's proclaimed name, Moses' plea, Joel's call to return, Nahum's warning, Jonah's complaint, the wise man's virtue.

13015.text: Correction with or without the anger: "I myself will discipline you sevenfold for your sins", "in fury"; against it: "rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath"; "Correct me, O Lord, but in justice; not in your anger".

13020.text: Prayer and anger meet (v2, U2 §65 points 5 and 7): "how long will you be angry with your people's prayers?"; "you have wrapped yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through"; "As for you, do not pray for this people"; "There is no one who calls upon your name"; "As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear"; "we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy".

13031.text: God's anger leads to borne in the body and in company: "There is no soundness in my flesh"; "I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink"; "You have caused my companions to shun me"; "I sat alone, because your hand was upon me".

13036.text: A person's anger leads to a command, where the angry one has power: "and he put them in custody"; "commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed"; Herod "sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem".

13040.text: A person's anger leads to folly, evil, a snare: "A man of quick temper acts foolishly"; "Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil"; "lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare".

13089.text: The anger that imprisons also places: "But the Lord was with Joseph" (Joseph in prison after Potiphar's anger; the officers Pharaoh imprisoned in anger later bring about his release, Gen 41:9–13).

13093.text: Sequence in Gen 27:41–45: the blessing lost → hatred → murder planned in his heart (ESV "said to himself"; Hebrew in his heart), comforting himself → flight → waiting until the anger "turns away" and he "forgets".

13095.text: Sequence in Gen 44:18–45:8: Judah's plea against anger → Joseph weeps → "dismayed" → "do not be … angry with yourselves" → reframing: "not you … but God".

13098.text: Sequence in 1Sa 11:5–13: hearing → Spirit → anger → act → dread spreads → victory → mercy: "not a man shall be put to death".

13104.text: Sequence in 1Ki 20:42–21:7: verdict on his life → sullen → refused → sullen, bed, face turned, no food → another names the spirit → the heart offered a crime as comfort.

13106.text: Sequence in 2Ch 16:9–12: diagnosis of a failed heart → rage at the seer → cruelty → disease → not seeking the Lord.

13108.text: Sequence in Neh 5:5–9: an outcry heard → anger → "I took counsel with myself" (Hebrew my heart took counsel) → charges → public assembly.

13109.text: Sequence in Est 1:10–2:1: merry heart → refusal → rage "within him" (Est 1:12) → counsel ("contempt and wrath in plenty", Est 1:18) → decree → anger abates → memory returns.

13110.text: Sequence in Est 5:9–13: glad of heart → seeing Mordecai → wrath → restraint → boasting of riches → "Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai" (5:13).

13111.text: Sequence in Job 32:1–20: the friends fall silent → anger ×3 → waiting from deference and fear → "the spirit in man" → belly like wine with no vent → "I must speak, that I may find relief".

13112.text: Sequence in Psa 37:1–9: seeing the wicked prosper → heating oneself (fret) + envy → "trust … commit … be still … wait" → "refrain from anger" → the wicked fade, the waiting inherit.

13113.text: Sequence in Psa 55:3–5: the enemy's noise → their anger bears a grudge → "my heart is in anguish within me" → terrors of death → fear and trembling.

13114.text: Sequence in Isa 7:2–9: news of alliance → hearts shake like trees → "do not fear … do not let your heart be faint … at the fierce anger" → the anger shrunk to smoking stubs → "if you are not firm in faith …".

13119.text: Sequence in Jon 3:10–4:11: God relents → Jonah angry → prayer quoting "slow to anger" → asks to die → "Do you do well to be angry?" → shade, plant, worm, wind → asks to die again → "angry enough to die" → God's comparison: pity for a plant, pity for Nineveh → (no answer).

13120.text: Sequence in Mar 3:4–6: a plain question → silence → Jesus looks with anger, grieved at hardness of heart → healing → the plot to destroy him.

13125.text: Sequence in Exo 32:10–14; Deu 9:7–22: provocation → anger → "let me alone" → intercession from fear, with fasting → relented → the memory made into a warning against self-righteousness.

13126.text: Sequence in Num 11:1–15, 33: complaint → fire → cry to Moses → prayer → craving → Moses asks to die → plague.

13128.text: Sequence in Deu 29:18–29: heart turning / blessing itself → anger smokes, no forgiveness → ruin → onlookers ask why → answer → secret and revealed things.

13129.text: Sequence in Jos 7; 22:10–34: one man takes → anger on all → defeat → offender removed → anger turns → the memory drives a later confrontation → answer "He knows".

13130.text: Sequence in Judg 2:10–23; 10:6–16: a generation not knowing → provocation → given over → distress → cry / confession → pity → deliverer → relapse, worse.

13131.text: Sequence in 2Sa 24:1–17 (+ 1Ch 27:24): anger → incitement → objection overruled → act → heart strikes → "fall into the hand of the Lord" → "let your hand be against me".

13137.text: Sequence in Psa 106:19–45: forgot God → Moses in the breach → despised the land → Peor → Phinehas, "counted to him as righteousness" → Meribah, Moses' loss → child sacrifice → given to nations → "he heard their cry … relented".

13140.text: Sequence in Isa 51:17–23: cup drunk to the dregs → "There is none to guide her" → sons fainted, "full of the wrath" → cup taken, given to the tormentors.

13141.text: Sequence in Isa 57:14–18: God dwells with the contrite spirit → "nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me" → struck, hid face → backsliding "in the way of his own heart" → "I will heal him".

13142.text: Sequence in Isa 63:1–64:12: no one to help → God's arm alone → "I will recount the steadfast love" → "you were angry, and we sinned" → no one who calls → "we are the clay … please look".

13143.text: Sequence in Jer 7:16–29: intercession forbidden → whole families provoke → "Is it I whom they provoke? … themselves" → wrath poured → "did not accept discipline" → "cut off your hair … lament".

13145.text: Sequence in Jer 42–44: "Pray for us … we will do it" → the word given → refused → flight to Egypt from fear of the sword → provocation continued → "Have you forgotten …?".

13147.text: Sequence in Eze 9:1–10: abominations → mark on those who sigh and groan → slaughter begins at the sanctuary → the prophet alone, face down: "Will you destroy all the remnant?" → "my eye will not spare".

13150.text: Sequence in Eze 22:17–31: dross → melted in the furnace → every rank has failed → "I sought for a man … and stand in the breach … but I found none" → indignation poured out.

13151.text: Sequence in Joe 2:11–14; Jon 3:5–10: the day, "who can endure it?" → return with the heart, fasting, sackcloth → the creed (Joel) or the preached word (Nineveh) → "Who knows?" → (Jonah) God relented.

13152.text: Sequence in Mic 7:7–20: "I will look to the Lord" → the enemy gloats → "I will bear the indignation … because I have sinned" → vindication → "Who is a God like you …? He does not retain his anger forever".

13153.text: Sequence in Rom 1:16–2:10: gospel, righteousness by faith → wrath revealed against suppression of the truth → without excuse → judging others → presuming on kindness → hard heart storing up wrath → to each by works.

13161.text: Anger and Wickedness (M58); sin (M56): The cause named before the anger: "because of the evil of your deeds"; "Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil"; "one given to anger causes much transgression".

13170.text: Anger and Wisdom and folly (M16): "Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding"; "A man of quick temper acts foolishly"; folly ruins a man's way and "his heart rages against the Lord"; "a heart of wisdom" asked under the anger.

13173.text: Anger and Grace and mercy (M50); kindness (M05): "being compassionate … he restrained his anger often"; "merciful and gracious, slow to anger"; "for I am merciful"; "But God, being rich in mercy"; "should not you have had mercy"; "Be kind to one another".

13179.text: Anger and Patience (M34): "With patience a ruler may be persuaded" (the same ʾaph); God "has endured with much patience vessels of wrath"; "Be still before the Lord and wait patiently for him" beside "Refrain from anger".

13182.text: Anger and Inner seat (M47), side by side with fear: fear side, fear felt in the heart; given in the heart; the heart firm and not afraid (1Sa 28:5; Jer 32:40; Psa 112:7); anger side, anger answers a heart turned; burns within; the heat of the spirit; a hard heart stores up wrath (1Ki 11:9; Est 1:12; Eze 3:14; Rom 2:5).

13186.text: Anger and Wisdom and folly (M16), side by side with fear: fear side, "the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom" (Job 28:28); anger side, "Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding" (Pro 14:29).

13190.text: Anger and Shame (M07), side by side with fear: fear side, horror listed with reproach (Jer 24:9); anger side, "They shall be ashamed of their harvests because of the fierce anger" (Jer 12:13).

13196.text: What sets God's anger off: broke the covenant → anger → given over (Judg 2:14, 20); heard → anger → fire (Num 11:1); hearts diamond-hard, lest they hear → therefore great anger (Zec 7:12); blood left uncovered → wrath roused (Eze 24:8); mocking the messengers → wrath rose → no remedy (2Ch 36:16); proud heart → wrath came (2Ch 32:25); suppress the truth → wrath revealed (Rom 1:18).

13198.text: What turns or ends God's anger: humbled → wrath turned (2Ch 12:12); Moses prayed → the Lord listened (Deu 9:19); stood in the breach → wrath turned (Psa 106:23); atonement → stood between → plague stopped (Num 16:46–48); jealous with my jealousy → wrath turned back (Num 25:11); wrath satisfied → calm, no more angry (Eze 16:42); with the last plagues → the wrath is finished (Rev 15:1).

13199.text: What restrains it, by the verse's reason: compassionate → did not stir up all his wrath (Psa 78:38); "I said I would pour out my wrath" → acted for my name (Eze 20:8–9); heart recoils → will not execute burning anger, for I am God and not a man (Hos 11:8–9); not always angry, for the spirit would grow faint (Isa 57:16); feared the enemy's provocation → not wiped out (Deu 32:26–27).

13202.text: What a person's anger leads to: heard → anger → broke the tablets (Exo 32:19); angry → put them in custody (Gen 40:2–3); company of the angry → learning his ways → a snare (Pro 22:24–25); fret → tends only to evil (Psa 37:8); angry → afraid (2Sa 6:8–9); angry → cried to the Lord all night (1Sa 15:11); Naboth's word → vexed and sullen → would eat no food (1Ki 21:4); provoke your children → lest they become discouraged (Col 3:21).

13206.text: God's heart is named with his anger three times: "My heart recoils within me" before "I will not execute my burning anger" (Hos 11:8–9); "the intents of his heart" (Jer 23:20); "the day of vengeance was in my heart, and my year of redemption had come" (Isa 63:4).

13207.text: "Slow to anger" is one phrase (Exo 34:6; Pro 14:29): God's proclaimed name, used by many speakers to different ends, and the wise man's virtue.

13211.text: The fierce anger is the anger that turns (ḥārôn with "turn" in 12 of 40 verses); Josiah's whole-hearted turning beside the burning not turned (2Ki 23:25–26); turning asked for without a guarantee ("It may be", Jer 36:7; "perhaps", Zep 2:3; "Who knows?", Jon 3:9); inner acts named as turning it (humbling, a resolve in the heart).

13227.text: U1 §37, Neh 5:5–9: the reading says I took counsel with my heart; the ESV says "I took counsel with myself" (Neh 5:7); the text carries H3820A lēḇ (heart), rendered "myself", tagged M47.

13230.text: U1 §37, Gen 27:41–45: the reading says murder planned in his heart; the ESV says "Esau said to himself" (Gen 27:41); the text carries H3820A lēḇ, rendered "himself", tagged M47.

13231.text: U1 §37, Est 1:10–2:1: the reading says fear for every household; the ESV says Est 1:18 speaks of "contempt and wrath"; the text carries no fear word in 1:18 (no M01 token): a true slip.

13233.text: U2 §65, 2Sa 24:1–17: the reading says heart strikes; the ESV says "David's heart struck him" (2Sa 24:10); the text carries the wording holds; the subject is David.

13234.text: U2 §65, Isa 51:17–23: the reading says no one to guide; the ESV says "There is none to guide her" (Isa 51:18); the text carries wording only.

13241.text: Where the angry person's own heart or spirit is named: in the narratives it is rare (2Ki 6:11; Est 5:9; Act 7:54; Act 17:16; Eze 3:14), and in the wisdom books frequent (Job 36:13; Pro 6:14; 14:29; 16:32; 19:3; Ecc 2:23; 7:3; 7:9; 11:10); the narratives show anger by what is done.
