13606.text: Face 5G. The cup, the winepress, the bowls: the wrath finished: Hits / verses: 10 / 7; Toward: the one who worships the beast; Babylon; the nations; Other parties named: angels; the four living creatures; the Lamb; the rider with the sword from his mouth; Example verses: Rev 14:10, 19; Rev 15:1, 7; Rev 16:1, 19; Rev 19:15.

13611.text: Face 5L. Anger in the lists of what is put away: Hits / verses: 11 / 6; Who, and at whom: people; no object named; Example verses: Gal 5:20; Eph 4:31; Col 3:8; 2Cor 12:20; Rom 1:29; Rom 13:13.

13626.text: Face 5AA. Hot and cold: Hits / verses: 3 / 2; What: the works of the church in Laodicea; Example verses: Rev 3:15–16.

13636.text: What meets it (new cases): a father who comes out (Luk 15:28); Jesus's teaching on serving (Mat 20:25–26); a question from their own practice (Luk 13:15; Joh 7:23); a Pharisee's counsel (Act 5:34–35); a chamberlain persuaded (Act 12:20); one another's daily exhortation (Heb 3:13): Verses: as listed.

13642.text: F.6: What emerged: What meets anger decides its end, in the Gospels: the father who comes out (Luk 15:28); the teaching on serving (Mat 20:25–26); a question from their own practice (Luk 13:15); Gamaliel's counsel (Act 5:34).; What it changes elsewhere: Extends unit 4 F.6. Overview part D.; Where: overview D.

13662.text: should have had mercy → in anger delivered to the jailers → so also my heavenly Father (Mat 18:33–35); killed his servants → the king angry → destroyed, burned (Mat 22:6–7); made excuses → angry → bring in the poor (Luk 14:18–21).

13666.text: heard → filled with wrath → drove him out (Luk 4:28–29); heard → enraged → wanted to kill → Gamaliel's counsel (Act 5:33–35); heard → enraged → stopped their ears, rushed → stoned (Act 7:54–58); heard → enraged → crying out → confusion (Act 19:28–29).

13671.text: healed on the Sabbath → indignant → Jesus's answer → adversaries put to shame (Luk 13:14–17); teaching the resurrection → greatly annoyed → arrested (Act 4:2–3).

13678.text: lukewarm → spit you out (Rev 3:16); those whom I love, I reprove → be zealous and repent (3:19).

13687.text: Samson: the Spirit's rushing goes with the striking at Ashkelon, and the "hot anger" comes at the end, with its ground given: his wife wept "You only hate me; you do not love me" (Judg 14:16), he told her "because she pressed him hard" (14:17), and his own word is "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle" (14:18); then "Samson's wife was given to his companion" (14:20).

13701.text: "Weeping and gnashing of teeth" stands seven times in the judgment sayings (Mat 8:12; 13:42; 13:50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30; Luk 13:28); Luke gives the moment: "when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out" (13:28).

13703.text: Links that do not count are non-inner-being senses of the M47 word: Pro 25:23, Eze 13:13, 19:12 and Psa 11:6 (wind); Num 11:33 (meat); Eze 16:26 (lustful "flesh"); Eze 7:19 (nephesh as hunger); Psa 124:5 ("us"); Est 8:11 (lives as targets); no M02 Strong's loses its implicit status through this.

13710.text: Indignation is carried by speech ("Why this waste?", Mat 26:8); in Mar 14:4, "said to themselves indignantly" (pros heautous), the inner place is given by a reflexive pronoun; the status rivalry between disciples (Mat 20:24; Mar 10:41) is relational.

13714.text: Luk 15:28: the elder brother "was angry and refused to go in"; his father came out and entreated him; the complaint that follows (15:29-30) exposes a hidden grievance, "these many years I have served you": the inner state was held behind service, and anger releases it (hidden-behind-act).

13724.text: 2Ch 16:10 (Asa "in a rage with" the seer) and Dan 2:12 (the king "angry and very furious"): anger issues in orders, imprisonment and execution.

13732.text: Job's vexation (ka'as H3708B): "Oh that my vexation were weighed" (6:2) and "my eye has grown dim from vexation" (17:7); the eye carries it, and the whole body, "all my members are like a shadow"; Job 5:2, "vexation kills the fool", shows the inner state as lethal.

13733.text: Rev 3:15-16, zestos: "Neither hot nor cold ... lukewarm ... I will spit you out of my mouth": the inner state is given as temperature, and the response as the body rejecting food.

13736.text: Whose seat the anger points to, The angry party's own seat: genuine links Human: Job 36:13 "the godless in heart cherish anger"; Job 18:4 "you who tear yourself in your anger"; Pro 14:29 / 16:32 (slow to anger with "rules his spirit"); Ecc 7:9 "anger lodges in the heart of fools"; Act 17:16 Paul's "spirit was provoked within him". Divine: Jer 23:20 / 30:24 "the intents of his heart / mind". What it implies for the no-seat verses: The human anger narratives (§2.1 below) and the wisdom sayings (§2.2).

13740.text: Jon 4:1-3: "it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry. And he prayed ... I knew that you are a gracious God ... slow to anger ... please take my life from me": Jonah quotes God's own "slow to anger" against him, so the anger comes from a creed he knows well; God's reply, "Do you do well to be angry?" (4:4, 9), leads to "angry enough to die".

13743.text: "Slow to anger" (Pro 14:29; 15:18; 16:32; 19:11) is literally "long of nostrils", the same idiom as God's self-description in Exo 34:6 (Num 14:18; Neh 9:17; Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Jon 4:2; Nah 1:3): a human virtue and a divine attribute share one body idiom.

13752.text: God hardens a human seat (19 verses): Pharaoh (Exo 4:21; 7:3; 9:12; 10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8) and the Egyptians (14:17); Sihon, "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deu 2:30); the Canaanites (Jos 11:20); "Make the heart of this people dull [heavy]" (Isa 6:10); "why do you ... harden our heart?" (Isa 63:17); Joh 12:40; Rom 9:18; "I gave them over to their stubborn hearts" (Psa 81:12).

13754.text: A human seat is hardened by the person, or with no agent named (68 verses): Pharaoh by himself (Exo 8:15, 32; 9:34); the stiff neck (Exo 32:9 ... Neh 9:29; Jer 7:26; 17:23; 19:15); sherirut, "the stubbornness of their evil heart" (Jer 3:17; 7:24; 9:14; 11:8; 13:10; 16:12; 18:12; 23:17; Deu 29:19); "diamond-hard" hearts (Zec 7:12); Nebuchadnezzar's "spirit was hardened" (Dan 5:20); the New Testament hardness of heart (Mat 19:8; Mar 3:5; 6:52; 8:17; 10:5; 16:14; Rom 2:5; Eph 4:18); Psa 95:8 and its New Testament reuse (Heb 3:8, 13, 15; 4:7).

13755.text: God's own seat in grief and compassion, none of it hardened: "it grieved him to his heart" (Gen 6:6); "My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender" (Hos 11:8); "he became impatient over the misery of Israel" (Judg 10:16, nephesh short); "my heart moans for Moab" (Jer 48:36); "he does not afflict from his heart" (Lam 3:33).

13756.text: God's own seat in resolve and purpose, none of it hardened: he "said in his heart, 'I will never again curse the ground'" (Gen 8:21); "what is in my heart" (1Sa 2:35); "a man after his own heart" (1Sa 13:14; Act 13:22); "my eyes and my heart will be there" (1Ki 9:3; 2Ch 7:16); 2Ki 10:30; 1Ch 17:19; Psa 33:11; "the day of vengeance was in my heart" (Isa 63:4); "the intents of his heart" (Jer 23:20; 30:24); "with all my heart and all my soul" (Jer 32:41); Job 7:17; 10:13; 34:14.

13758.text: God's own seat in delight and aversion, none of it hardened: "my soul delights" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18); "his soul hates the wicked" (Psa 11:5); "an abomination to his soul" (Pro 6:16); "my soul hates ... I am weary of bearing them" (Isa 1:14); "I abhor the pride of Jacob" (Amo 6:8, sworn "by himself"); "my soul has no pleasure in him" (Heb 10:38); "my soul will abhor you" (Lev 26:30; negated in 26:11); "the beloved of my soul" handed over (Jer 12:7); the human question "Does your soul loathe Zion?" (Jer 14:19).

13761.text: Hardness, heaviness and strength are said of God's hand, arm, sword and breath, not of his heart: "The hand of the Lord was heavy" (1Sa 5:6, 11); "his hand is hard against us" (1Sa 5:7); "your hand was heavy upon me" (Psa 32:4); the "strong hand" of the Exodus (Exo 6:1; 13:9; Deu 4:34); the "thick" rising smoke of his coming in anger (Isa 30:27); "his hard and great and strong sword" (Isa 27:1).

13768.text: Hardening runs one way: God hardens and humans harden, but God's own heart is never hardened; where it turns, it turns in compassion (Hos 11:8) or in refusal (Jer 15:1).

13769.text: The heavy or hard hand, chains, sword and breath (kaved, qashah, qasheh: 1Sa 5:6, 5:7, 5:11; Psa 32:4; Lam 3:7; Isa 27:1, 27:8; Isa 30:27; Jer 20:7; Mat 25:24; Mal 3:13) is spoken of by humans under it, or by the narrator describing them; in this set God never calls his own hand heavy or hard; it is framed as experience: terror, affliction, wasting, being walled in, fear.

13770.text: The "strong / mighty hand and outstretched arm" (chazaq) is the Exodus formula (Exo 6:1; 13:9; Deu 3:24; 4:34; 5:15; 6:21; 7:8; 7:19; 9:26; 11:2; 26:8; Jos 4:24; 1Ki 8:42; 2Ch 6:32; Neh 1:10; Psa 89:13; 136:12; Isa 40:10; Jer 21:5; 32:21; 50:34; Eze 20:33-34; Dan 9:15; Exo 32:11; Pro 23:11), spoken by God, Moses, the creed and prayers; it is framed as deliverance remembered, taught to children (Deu 6:21), and pleaded in prayer (Deu 9:26; Dan 9:15).

13779.text: The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Righteousness and justice, with steadfast love and faithfulness: "You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand … Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you" (Psa 89:13–14). "The Lord our God is righteous in all the works that he has done" (Dan 9:14), then "who brought your people out … with a mighty hand" (9:15), then "according to all your righteous acts, let your anger … turn away" (9:16)

13786.text: The context names as the source of the heavy hand, The shepherd's arm: "his arm rules for him … He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms" (Isa 40:10–11). The same arm rules and carries

13787.text: The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Anger (named, and set inside a purpose): Jer 21:5 ("in anger and in fury"); Isa 30:27 ("burning with his anger"). The purpose that follows: "the way of life and the way of death" (Jer 21:8); "when the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26)

13789.text: The heaviness has its source in God's character: the texts name righteousness and justice (Psa 89:14; Dan 9:14, 16) together with steadfast love, faithfulness, the oath, and the cause of the weak; anger is named too, but never as the last word, standing inside a purpose of covenant, atonement and healing.

13797.text: Jon 4:2 is Jonah's angry prayer quoting "slow to anger" back at God, one passage with Jon 4:1, 4 and 9, which are human.

13842.text: Eze 21:31 (4I God's wrath on the nations and enemies; the earth before it): wrath on Ammon; no life word in the verse.

13843.text: Eze 22:20 (A God angry with his people as a whole): parallel of 22:21,.

13844.text: Eze 22:21 (4A God's wrath comes upon, goes out against or uproots his people: the cause named): the breath that gives life named in his anger.

13853.text: Job 5:2 (3Z The fool's vexation, and anger lodging in the fool): vexation kills the fool.

13861.text: Psa 138:7 (U Enemies' anger, as the one attacked bears it): life preserved against the enemies' wrath.

13865.text: Psa 7:6 (4W Enemies' fury and rush, as the one attacked bears it): arise in your anger, awake for me.

13878.text: In Lam 2:22 the lament speaks to God about his anger, "Look, O Lord, and see! With whom have you dealt thus?" (2:20), "you have killed them in the day of your anger, slaughtering without pity" (2:21); the figure is a call to a feast, and a festival day gathers people to rejoice, but here what is gathered is "my terrors on every side".

13879.text: The speaker of Lam 2:22 does not turn away from God in the terror: he asks him to look, and names what his anger did to those "I held and raised".

13920.text: Ecc 11:9 "let your heart cheer you". Genuine.

13922.text: Outside the verse: no seat in Gen 45:2–9 or Job 18:1–7.

13936.text: Outside the verse: Pro 25:13 "he refreshes the soul of his masters" (a faithful messenger), two verses before 25:15. Genuine. The master's soul, as what is refreshed. The one who turns a ruler's anger by patience is the one who refreshes the ruler's soul. This is a neighbourhood observation, marked [Claude reading].

13937.text: Psa 58:2 and 140:2 "hearts … heart". Genuine. The enemy's own, where the wrong is devised.

13938.text: Psa 7:5 "let the enemy pursue my soul". Genuine / life.

13940.text: Outside the verse: Jer 48:29 "haughtiness of his heart". Genuine. The bearer's own. This is the same lifted heart as 2Ch 26:16 (§4) and D v2 §9.1.

13952.text: Seat. None in-verse. Neh 9:20 "your good Spirit to instruct them" is God's, given (divine; C v3 §1.6). Pointer: U1 §13 has Jonah using the same creed against God (Jon 4:2). With Moses and the Levites of Neh 9, one creed is used three ways: worship, plea, and complaint. Pilot §2.2 already notes the idiom shared between God and the wise (Pro 14:29 and others), and U1 §22 reads the human side of it.

13954.text: Seat (v2). Outside: Jer 17:5 "whose heart turns away". Genuine (C v3 §8.2; E v2 §5.6, §13). Nothing new.

13957.text: Seat. None in-verse. 2Ch 24:20 "Spirit of God clothed Zechariah". God's, given. Divine. Num 12:12 "flesh" is bodily.

13966.text: Outside: Job 6:7 "My appetite refuses to touch them" (nephesh). Appetite-sense, the bearer's own (C v3 §1.1, §9.4). Job 9:4 "wise in heart" is God's (#1890 findings §4.1). Job 14:13 is the verse G v3 §16 left for M20 or unit 2 (U1 §R-V). It is read here: its movement is hiding until the wrath passes, followed by being remembered. It is not a death-wish.

13969.text: Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Psa 76:5 "stouthearted". The warriors' heart, stripped. Genuine (G v3 §3.4: "might located in one's own heart fails").

13970.text: Outside: Psa 78:37 "heart" (E v2 §5.1, §7.1); 78:39 "flesh … wind"; Isa 57:15 (C v3 §8.4; D v2 §10.2; G v3 §2 and others). Nothing new.

13997.text: In Joseph's story the anger that imprisons also positions. "The Lord was with Joseph" in the prison (Gen 39:21), and the officers imprisoned by Pharaoh's anger bring about Joseph's release (41:9–13).

13998.text: Elihu burns with anger three times (Job 32:2, 3, 5). Then comes a long speech (32:6 onward).

14002.text: Public action: Nehemiah's "great assembly" and charge (Neh 5:7–9).

14004.text: being made "a byword of the peoples" (Job 17:6).

14011.text: A burden shared: Moses (H v1 §3.3, "Moses' burden, then the Spirit shared", Num 11:10–17).

14016.text: Betrayal (Judg 14:16–18: the riddle given away through his wife).

14034.text: What it leads to. Arrest (Act 4:3), the reframing (above), and in Joh 7:25, the people's question, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?". The indignation borders on the plan to kill. Compare Mar 3:6 (§32).

14044.text: "the haughtiness of his heart" (Jer 48:29) before Moab's insolence.

14052.text: What it leads to. Praise (Exo 15), or deliverance (2Sa 22:17 onward, not read here).

14055.text: The protected are the people the anger struck earlier: "the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26).

14059.text: The name is used at once, in the next breath, to ask: "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (Exo 34:9), with "for it is a stiff-necked people". The name and the people's stiff neck are put side by side by Moses himself. The same pairing returns in Neh 9:16–17.

14069.text: Deu 29:18–19 "whose heart is turning away" / "blesses himself in his heart … stubbornness of my heart". E v2 §4.1, §12; C v3 §9.1; F v4 §9.6. Pilot §1.6 reads 29:20 with it.

14081.text: Killed: after Jehoiada died, "the king listened to them [the princes]"; prophets "testified against them, but they would not pay attention"; Zechariah, whom "the Spirit of God clothed", was stoned "in the court of the house of the Lord" (2Ch 24:17–21).

14087.text: A song as witness. "write this song and teach it … that this song may be a witness for me against the people of Israel" (Deu 31:19). The explanation is given before the ruin, so that the ruin can be read when it comes.

14089.text: Where it comes from. From memory of shared punishment: "Have we not had enough of the sin at Peor from which even yet we have not cleansed ourselves" (Jos 22:17).

14095.text: The cry is answered while the relapse is foreseen. Nations are left "to test Israel by them" (Judg 2:22).

14109.text: Lightness: "as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam" (1Ki 16:31).

14134.text: From what God has done: "The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil … At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned" (Psa 76:5–6).

14141.text: "Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them … They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame" (Isa 13:7–8).

14147.text: Blindness: "I will bring distress on mankind, so that they shall walk like the blind" (Zep 1:17); "the mighty man cries aloud there" (1:14).

14169.text: Where it comes from. From a former way of life: "at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord" (Eph 5:8); "Christ who is your life" (Col 3:4).

14172.text: Daniel's confession resting on mercy, not righteousness (Dan 9:18).

14175.text: How it co-exists: Someone else reads it off the body and names it. God asks Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?" (Gen 4:6). Jezebel asks Ahab, "Why is your spirit so vexed that you eat no food?" (1Ki 21:5). The angry person names nothing. The inner state is put into words by the questioner; The questioner then offers a way forward, and the two ways are opposites; God: "If you do well, will you not be accepted? … sin is crouching at the door … you must rule over it" (Gen 4:7). This is mastery of the anger from within; Jezebel: "Arise and eat bread and let your heart be cheerful; I will give you the vineyard" (1Ki 21:7). This is removing the denial by a crime.

14177.text: Seat: In the verse: none of the four; Whose seat: in context, named by the other party. 1Ki 21:5 "spirit" is Ahab's own, but Jezebel names it, not the narrator. Genuine; Outside the verse:; Before: 1Ki 20:42 nephesh "your life shall be for his life". Life-sense only. It is the verdict on Ahab's life that sends him home sullen; After: 1Ki 21:7 "let your heart be cheerful". Genuine. The heart is offered as the place where the anger will be undone, and the price is Naboth; Gen 4: no seat word in Gen 4:2–9. God's question and the image of sin "crouching at the door" do the seat's work: the inner struggle is given as a scene at a door, not as an organ. This agrees with pilot §1.4 and does not change it.

14182.text: What it does: It runs a course and passes, with time and forgetting: "until your brother's fury turns away … until your brother's anger turns away from you, and he forgets what you have done to him" (Gen 27:44–45); It is held and fed: "The godless in heart cherish anger" (Job 36:13); It draws the bearer on: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (Job 36:18); It kills its bearer: "Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2).

14185.text: What it leads to: For Esau: the anger turns away over years, and there is no killing. When they meet, "Esau ran to meet him and embraced him … and they wept" (Gen 33:4). Rebekah's "until he forgets" comes true, beyond embrace; For the godless: "They die in youth" (Job 36:14); For the fool: death by his own vexation (Job 5:2); Eliphaz sets this beside "man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward" (Job 5:7). Trouble is universal, but dying of vexation is the fool's.

14191.text: (c) Rebuked by a holy person: Asa, told by the seer that he "relied on the king of Syria", "was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks … for he was in a rage with him" (2Ch 16:10). The rage spreads: "Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time" (16:10); Uzziah, withstood by the priests at the altar: "Uzziah was angry … and when he became angry with the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead" (2Ch 26:19); In both, the anger is against the messenger of a boundary, and the story ends with the angry king's own body struck: Asa "diseased in his feet … Yet even in his disease he did not seek the Lord" (16:12); Uzziah "a leper to the day of his death" (26:21).

14192.text: (d) Refused by a subordinate, or exposed: Vashti's refusal: "the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him" (Est 1:12). The counsellor at once generalises the fear to every household: "there will be contempt and wrath in plenty" (1:18). One refusal is read as a threat to the whole order of husbands, and answered by decree (1:19–20); The king of Syria, whose plans Elisha keeps disclosing: "the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled because of this thing" (2Ki 6:11). He suspects a traitor: "Will you not show me who of us is for the king of Israel?" (6:11). The servant's answer shows how completely he is exposed: Elisha "tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom" (6:12).

14193.text: How it co-exists: With a prior high state: Uzziah "when he was strong, he grew proud" (2Ch 26:16), and the king's "heart … merry with wine" (Est 1:10). Anger comes where a lifted state is checked. F v4 §7 already read Est 1:10 as "the merry heart as the threshold"; this adds Uzziah; With striking (Num 22:27; 24:10, hands; 2Ch 16:10), and with going away (2Ki 5:12; 2Ch 25:10).

14197.text: Seat . No in-verse seat in the six: Outside the verse: Dan 11:28 "his heart shall be set against the holy covenant". Genuine. The bearer's own, two verses before the rage. The heart was set before the thwarting. The anger only releases it; Dan 2:11 "not with flesh". Spurious as a seat: flesh as the human realm.

14198.text: What it does to the one who holds it. It turns at once into custody or death: Potiphar, hearing his wife's story, "his anger was kindled", and "Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison" (Gen 39:19–20); "Pharaoh was angry with his two officers … and he put them in custody" (Gen 40:2–3; recalled at 41:10); the king "arose in his wrath" and says "Hang him on that" (Est 7:7, 10).

14199.text: What it does to those beneath it: Pleading against it before it rises:; Judah: "let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself" (Gen 44:18). The plea is a long retelling of the father's love (44:19–21 onward); Rachel: "Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me" (Gen 31:35). The plea for no anger covers a concealment: she is sitting on the stolen gods (31:34); Reading it as a sign: "If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him" (1Sa 20:7). Saul's anger is to be read as the evidence of Saul's intent. Jonathan's knowledge follows the same path: after the spear, "Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death" (20:33); Anticipating it and scripting a reply: Joab to the messenger: "if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city?' … then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also'" (2Sa 11:20–21). The anger is foreseen, and so is the one sentence that will turn it. That sentence works because the king had wanted Uriah dead. The line manages the king's anger by exposing the king's own secret; Plotting against it from below: "Bigthan and Teresh … became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus" (Est 2:21). This is anger rising from the servants, discovered through Mordecai (2:22); Anger acting covertly: Zebul, "when [he] heard the words of Gaal … his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly" (Judg 9:30–31). Anger turned into an ambush plan, "set an ambush in the field" (9:32); A group overrules its king: "the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him … 'Send the man back … how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord?'" (1Sa 29:4). The king Achish yields: "Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you" (29:6). The anger comes from suspicion: they fear a loyalty they cannot see.

14200.text: Where it comes from. A report heard (Gen 39:19; Judg 9:30), an offence by servants (Gen 40:1–2), or suspicion (1Sa 29:4). In Gen 39 the anger is kindled by a lie, and the text lets the reader see that the anger is misdirected.

14202.text: What it leads to. Imprisonment (Joseph, the officers), hanging (the baker, Haman, the eunuchs), a friend sent away (David from the Philistines): In Joseph's story the anger that imprisons also positions. "The Lord was with Joseph" in the prison (Gen 39:21), and the officers imprisoned by Pharaoh's anger bring about Joseph's release (41:9–13).

14208.text: How it co-exists: With enforced silence first. "Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he" (32:4), and "I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion" (32:6). Fear and deference hold the anger in, until the others fall silent; Elihu describes the pressure in bodily terms: "I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:18–20). The held anger is felt as pressure in the belly, and speech is its release.

14215.text: What it leads to: Public action: Nehemiah's "great assembly" and charge (Neh 5:7–9); Vengeance with deceit: the brothers "answered Shechem … deceitfully" (Gen 34:13), and "Simeon and Levi … took their swords and came against the city while it felt secure and killed all the males" (34:25). This is the deed Jacob's curse names in §10; Self-conviction: David; Nothing: David at 13:21; Fasting: Jonathan.

14220.text: Where it comes from: A rival's provocation, "because the Lord had closed her womb" (1Sa 1:6); calamity and God's "arrows" (Job 6:2, 4); being made "a byword of the peoples" (Job 17:6); dreams with "no one to interpret them" (Gen 40:8).

14224.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. Three new strands: (a) The eye wasting, as in Job 17:7; "My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes" (Psa 6:7), after "every night I flood my bed with tears" (6:6); "My eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow" (Psa 31:9–10); The eye is where ka'as shows in the body, in all three texts (Job 17:7; Psa 6:7; 31:9); What turns Psa 6 round is being heard: "the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping. The Lord has heard my plea" (6:8–9). In Psa 10:14, "you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself". The vexation is seen by God, and the helpless hands it over; (b) Provocation from those closest; "A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him" (Pro 17:25); The reverse direction: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" (Eph 6:4), and "do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); Vexation passes both ways between parent and child. Col 3:21 names its outcome as losing heart. Hannah's rival (1Sa 1:6) was a co-wife. These are the family members; (c) Qoheleth's vexation: the vexation of the thinker and the worker; Knowing brings it: "in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow" (Ecc 1:18). This comes after "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (1:17); Work brings it, and it keeps the heart awake: "his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (2:23); "all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger" (5:17); Its answer is enjoyment received as God's gift: "There is nothing better … than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God" (2:24), and "this is the gift of God" (5:19); It is to be removed: "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10), after "Rejoice, O young man … let your heart cheer you" (11:9); It is sometimes better than laughter: "Sorrow [ka'as] is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). The one place where ka'as is valued. The face is sad and the heart made good. Face and heart go in opposite directions.

14229.text: What it leads to. Joseph: reconciliation, and a summons to the father (45:9). Job: Bildad goes on to the fate of the wicked (18:5–7).

14230.text: Seat: In the verse: Job 18:4 "yourself" (nephesh). The bearer's own. Genuine, as the self that anger harms; Gen 45:5 "with yourselves" is literally "in your eyes" [lexical, not in DB]. It is not tagged as a seat in the DB. [verify] if the researcher wants the Hebrew checked; Outside the verse: no seat in Gen 45:2–9 or Job 18:1–7.

14248.text: What it leads to: Withdrawal from what God struck: David will not take the ark home (2Sa 6:10). The anger ends in avoidance, and the ark's blessing goes to Obed-edom instead (6:11); A burden shared: Moses; Obedience with grief: Samuel goes to meet Saul the next morning (15:12).

14250.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The occasion widens from God striking to God's mercy, and to the consequences of one's own folly: Jonah: anger at God's mercy; The occasion: "When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster" (Jon 3:10). "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry" (4:1); He quotes God's own character against him: "I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster" (4:2). Pilot §2.1 read this. The anger is at the very attribute that is the opposite of anger; It asks to die: "please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (4:3). After the plant withers, "It is better for me to die than to live" (4:8), and "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die" (4:9); God asks a question, as he did with Cain: "Do you do well to be angry?" (4:4, 9). Compare "Why are you angry?" (Gen 4:6). Twice in Scripture God meets a man's anger by asking about it. Both times, the question comes before a decisive act or teaching, and both times the answer is left open; God reframes by comparison: "You pity the plant … And should not I pity Nineveh …?" (4:10–11). The anger is set beside the pity the angry man feels for a plant. The book ends on God's question. Jonah's answer is not given; The heart rages at God for one's own ruin: "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the Lord" (Pro 19:3). The anger is misdirected: the cause is his own folly, and the target is God; Deprivation turns to cursing God, then darkness: "when they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God, and turn their faces upward. And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness" (Isa 8:21–22). The face turns up in anger and finds nothing, then down and finds darkness. It is set after "should not a people inquire of their God?" (8:19).

14258.text: Where it comes from: Hearing (1Sa 11:5–6: "they told him the news of the men of Jabesh"); Betrayal (Judg 14:16–18: the riddle given away through his wife); Seeing: an Israelite brought a Midianite woman "in the sight of Moses and … the whole congregation … while they were weeping" (Num 25:6). "When Phinehas … saw it, he rose … and took a spear" (25:7), and killed them both (25:8); Victory in battle (2Ch 28:6–8).

14265.text: Where it comes from. Idolatry (32:16–21), and the enemy's lack of understanding: "a nation void of counsel, and there is no understanding in them" (32:28).

14273.text: How it co-exists: With surveillance: "Saul eyed David from that day on" (1Sa 18:9); With joy that flips. Haman "went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai … he was filled with wrath" (Est 5:9). Then he goes home and recounts "the splendor of his riches" (5:11). A v3 §4.4 read this ("Haman's swing"), and H v1 §2.1 read it as "wealth does not satisfy a heart set on a grievance". Both stand; With restraint that is only postponement: "Haman restrained himself and went home" (5:10); With plotting: "they all plotted together to come and fight" (Neh 4:8).

14277.text: Context (3:24–27) was read and gives no bearer. The wrath could be divine, Moabite, or a terror in Israel. The verse does not say, and this reading does not supply one.

14288.text: Where it comes from: The angry person: "A hot-tempered man stirs up strife" (15:18); "A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression" (29:22); The evil heart: "with perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord" (6:14); The tongue: a backbiting tongue (25:23), and the whisperer (26:20, 22); Wine: "Who has strife? Who has complaining? … Those who tarry long over wine" (23:29–30).

14291.text: Seat: In the verse: Pro 6:14 "heart". The sower's own. Genuine. The heart is where discord is devised before it is sown. Pro 25:23 "wind". Spurious; Outside the verse: Pro 26:23 "fervent lips with an evil heart". Genuine. The whisperer's.

14292.text: What it is. The governed form of anger: "long of nostrils", the human side of the idiom God uses of himself (Exo 34:6).

14294.text: Where it comes from. Understanding and good sense: "Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly" (Pro 14:29); "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (19:11); in 1Cor 13:5, love: "it is not irritable or resentful".

14295.text: How it co-exists: Its opposite is quickness, which acts foolishly: "A man of quick temper acts foolishly" (Pro 14:17). The overseer "must not be … quick-tempered" (Tit 1:7); In the next verses, with a tranquil heart: "A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot" (Pro 14:30).

14296.text: What it leads to: Understanding (14:29), glory (19:11), and the righteousness that human anger cannot produce: "for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God. Therefore put away all filthiness … and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:20–21). Slowness to anger opens the way to receiving the word; A "cool spirit" belongs to the "man of understanding" (Pro 17:27).

14297.text: Seat: In the verse:; Pro 16:32 "spirit" (ruach). The bearer's own, as what is ruled. Genuine; Pro 14:29 "temper" (ruach, "short of spirit"). The bearer's own. Genuine; Outside the verse:; Pro 14:30 "a tranquil heart gives life to the flesh". Genuine; Pro 17:27 "a cool spirit". Genuine; Jam 1:21 "save your souls". Genuine; Across §22 the seat is the ruach, as the thing ruled or kept cool. The anger word and the spirit word stand side by side, and "slow/long" and "short" describe both.

14301.text: Seat. None in-verse: Outside the verse: Pro 25:13 "he refreshes the soul of his masters" (a faithful messenger), two verses before 25:15. Genuine. The master's soul, as what is refreshed. The one who turns a ruler's anger by patience is the one who refreshes the ruler's soul. This is a neighbourhood observation, marked [Claude reading].

14302.text: What it does. It heats the self, and "it tends only to evil" (Psa 37:8). The anger turns inward on its bearer, and outward into wrongdoing.

14303.text: Where it comes from. Seeing others prosper: "fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way, over the man who carries out evil devices!" (37:7). Envy is paired with it: "be not envious of wrongdoers" (37:1; Pro 24:19).

14304.text: How it co-exists. Its remedy is given as a set of inner acts, each replacing the fretting: "Trust in the Lord, and do good" (37:3); "Commit your way to the Lord" (37:5); "Be still before the Lord and wait patiently for him" (37:7); "Refrain from anger, and forsake wrath!" (37:8).

14307.text: What it does. It stands among its companions: "envy, murder, strife, deceit" (Rom 1:29); "quarreling and jealousy" (Rom 13:13); "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Cor 12:20); "enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy" (Gal 5:20–21); "bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander … malice" (Eph 4:31); "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Col 3:8).

14314.text: What it leads to. Arrest (Act 4:3), the reframing (above), and in Joh 7:25, the people's question, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?". The indignation borders on the plan to kill. Compare Mar 3:6.

14322.text: Where it comes from. The enemy's heart: "in your hearts you devise wrongs" (Psa 58:2); "who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually" (140:2); they are "estranged from the womb" (58:3).

14323.text: How it co-exists: With the attacked one's inner state named next: "My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me. Fear and trembling come upon me" (Psa 55:4–5). The enemy's anger (55:3) is felt as anguish of heart (55:4); With an appeal to God's anger against it: "Arise, O Lord, in your anger; lift yourself up against the fury of my enemies" (Psa 7:6, B2). The human's answer to another's anger is to call on God's. Compare §24, where the answer to the wicked's success is waiting, not heating oneself.

14324.text: What it leads to. Deliverance, looked back on or asked for: "If it had not been the Lord who was on our side" (Psa 124:1–2); "you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me" (138:7); "all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame" (Isa 41:11), after "fear not, for I am with you" (41:10); "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2Cor 7:6).

14325.text: Seat: In the verse: 2Cor 7:5 "bodies" (sarx, flesh). The bearer's own, bodily: "no rest". Not in any batch: new. The inner state is carried by "fear within", not by the seat word; Outside the verse:; Psa 55:4 "My heart is in anguish within me". Genuine. The attacked one's own; Psa 58:2 and 140:2 "hearts … heart". Genuine. The enemy's own, where the wrong is devised; Psa 7:5 "let the enemy pursue my soul". Genuine / life; 2Cor 7:3 "you are in our hearts". Genuine. The bearer's own, holding others. Not in any batch; So the seat appears on both sides: the enemy's heart that devises, and the attacked one's heart that is in anguish.

14332.text: Where it comes from. The heart lifted up: "We have heard of the pride of Moab … of his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart" (Jer 48:29). Moab's pride is heaped up in word after word (Isa 16:6; Jer 48:29).

14334.text: Seat: In the verse: none; Outside the verse: Jer 48:29 "haughtiness of his heart". Genuine. The bearer's own. This is the same lifted heart as 2Ch 26:16 and D v2 §9.1; Hos 7:14 "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds". Genuine. The insolent tongue (7:16) comes from a heart that does not cry to God (7:14).

14336.text: Where it comes from. Mercy refused or invitation refused: "should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (Mat 18:33); "they paid no attention … the rest seized his servants … and killed them" (22:5–6); the excuses of oxen and a wife (Luk 14:19–20).

14345.text: What it does. Lukewarmness makes the church rejected: "Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm … I will spit you out of my mouth" (3:15–16). Either extreme is preferred to the middle.

14353.text: The anger is very often kindled by something perceived: Part 1: thirteen verses name "heard" or "saw" in the verse itself (Gen 34:7; 39:19; Exo 32:19; Judg 9:30; 1Sa 11:6; 17:28; 2Sa 13:21; Neh 4:1, 7; 5:6; Est 3:5; 5:9; Job 32:5); Part 2 adds Psa 112:10; Mat 2:16; 20:24; 21:15; 26:8; Mar 10:14; 10:41; Luk 4:28; Act 5:33; 7:54; 17:16; 19:28; These are counted from the texts cited. No wider count was made.

14370.text: Gen 27:41–45: Sequence the text gives: the blessing lost → hatred → murder planned in his heart (ESV "said to himself"; Hebrew in his heart), comforting himself → flight → waiting until the anger "turns away" and he "forgets".

14372.text: Gen 44:18–45:8: Sequence the text gives: Judah's plea against anger → Joseph weeps → "dismayed" → "do not be … angry with yourselves" → reframing: "not you … but God".

14375.text: 1Sa 11:5–13: Sequence the text gives: hearing → Spirit → anger → act → dread spreads → victory → mercy: "not a man shall be put to death".

14381.text: 1Ki 20:42–21:7: Sequence the text gives: verdict on his life → sullen → refused → sullen, bed, face turned, no food → another names the spirit → the heart offered a crime as comfort.

14383.text: 2Ch 16:9–12: Sequence the text gives: diagnosis of a failed heart → rage at the seer → cruelty → disease → not seeking the Lord.

14385.text: Neh 5:5–9: Sequence the text gives: an outcry heard → anger → "I took counsel with myself" (Hebrew my heart took counsel) → charges → public assembly.

14386.text: Est 1:10–2:1: Sequence the text gives: merry heart → refusal → rage "within him" (Est 1:12) → counsel ("contempt and wrath in plenty", Est 1:18) → decree → anger abates → memory returns.

14387.text: Est 5:9–13: Sequence the text gives: glad of heart → seeing Mordecai → wrath → restraint → boasting of riches → "Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai" (5:13).

14388.text: Job 32:1–20: Sequence the text gives: the friends fall silent → anger ×3 → waiting from deference and fear → "the spirit in man" → belly like wine with no vent → "I must speak, that I may find relief".

14389.text: (v2) Psa 37:1–9: Sequence the text gives: seeing the wicked prosper → heating oneself (fret) + envy → "trust … commit … be still … wait" → "refrain from anger" → the wicked fade, the waiting inherit.

14390.text: (v2) Psa 55:3–5: Sequence the text gives: the enemy's noise → their anger bears a grudge → "my heart is in anguish within me" → terrors of death → fear and trembling.

14391.text: (v2) Isa 7:2–9: Sequence the text gives: news of alliance → hearts shake like trees → "do not fear … do not let your heart be faint … at the fierce anger" → the anger shrunk to smoking stubs → "if you are not firm in faith …".

14396.text: (v2) Jon 3:10–4:11: Sequence the text gives: God relents → Jonah angry → prayer quoting "slow to anger" → asks to die → "Do you do well to be angry?" → shade, plant, worm, wind → asks to die again → "angry enough to die" → God's comparison: pity for a plant, pity for Nineveh → (no answer).

14397.text: (v2) Mar 3:4–6: Sequence the text gives: a plain question → silence → Jesus looks with anger, grieved at hardness of heart → healing → the plot to destroy him.

14414.text: (v2) Pro 6:14: Seat word (Strong's as tagged): "heart" lev (H3820A); Phenomenon: SK §21; Whose seat: the sower's own, where discord is devised; Seat-sense check: genuine; Already read in: D v2 §2.2.

14415.text: (v2) Pro 14:29: Seat word (Strong's as tagged): "temper" ruach (H7307J); Phenomenon: SL §22; Whose seat: the bearer's own, short of spirit; Seat-sense check: genuine; Already read in: A v3 §2.1 [T]; B v3 §1.6; pilot §2.2.

Psa 31:7 "distress of my soul": bearer's own · E v2 §10.1 · used. Ecc 1:16–17 heart · E v2 §1.3, B v3 §1.2 · used. Ecc 2:22 heart · new · used. Ecc 2:24 "find" [make his soul see good] · new · used (enjoyment as answer). Ecc 5:16 "wind" · spurious. Ecc 7:2, 7:4 heart · A v3 §3.3 · used. Ecc 11:9 heart · F v4 §7, H v1 §4.1 · used. Eph 6:5–6, Col 3:22–23 "heart … heartily" (bondservants) · E v2 §6, H v1 §3.1 · not used (next household rule).

Pro 19:18 heart ("do not set your heart on putting him to death") · G v3 §16.5 et al. · not used. Pro 19:21 "plans in the mind" · B v3 §2.6 · not used. Jam 1:21 souls · B v3 §4.4 · used.
