14494.text: What it does. Two different occasions: At the call: "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else." "Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against Moses" (Exo 4:13–14). The anger is answered at once by provision: Aaron "is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart" (4:14); "I will be with your mouth and with his mouth" (4:15); At the end: "Even with me the Lord was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there'" (Deu 1:37); "the Lord was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me … 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again'" (3:26); "I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan" (4:21–22).

14502.text: Part B: Psa 7:11; 18:7; 21:9; 78:49; 78:50; 110:5; Isa 30:27; 30:30; 66:14; 66:15: Psa 18:7 is the psalm text of 2Sa 22:8: "In my distress I called upon the Lord … because he was angry" (Psa 18:6–7); The upright in heart, and the call to repent. "God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day" (Psa 7:11). This follows "you who test the minds and hearts … who saves the upright in heart" (7:9–10), and is followed by "If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword" (7:12). The protection is for the upright in heart, and the indignation waits on repentance; The king who trusts: "the king trusts in the Lord … Your hand will find out all your enemies" (Psa 21:7–9). The king at God's right hand: "Your people will offer themselves freely" (110:3, 5); The Exodus retold: "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death" (Psa 78:50). "Then he led out his people like sheep" (78:52); The protected rejoice in the heart; "You shall have a song … and gladness of heart" (Isa 30:29), while "the Assyrians will be terror-stricken" (30:31); "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you … You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass" (66:13–14); The protected are the people the anger struck earlier: "the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26); Seat ; In the verse: Isa 66:14 "your heart shall rejoice". The comforted people's own. Genuine. Psa 78:50 "them" (nephesh) is the Egyptians' life. Life-sense; Outside: Psa 7:9–10 "hearts" / "upright in heart". Isa 30:29 "gladness of heart"; What part B adds. Part A had only praise (Exo 15). Part B places the joy of the protected in the heart.

14510.text: Part C: Eze 9:8; Dan 9:16; Zec 1:12: The prophet refused. "while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, 'Ah, Lord God! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel …?'" (Eze 9:8). The answer is no: "The guilt … is exceedingly great … For they say, 'The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see.' As for me, my eye will not spare" (9:9–10). Some are spared: the mark is put "on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations" (9:4, context read). Those who grieve over the sin are marked. The one who pleads for the rest is not answered; Daniel's confession-intercession:; "O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem … because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem … [has] become a byword" (Dan 9:16); "the Lord our God is righteous in all the works that he has done" (9:14); "for your own sake" (9:17); "we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy" (9:18); An angel intercedes: "O Lord of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem …, against which you have been angry these seventy years?" This is answered with "gracious and comforting words" (Zec 1:12–13).

14511.text: What it does. Three moments: Proclaimed and received: "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger" (Exo 34:6). Moses "quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped" (34:8); Pleaded back: Moses quotes it to God word for word as his argument: "'The Lord is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love …' Please pardon the iniquity of this people" (Num 14:18–19). It is answered: "I have pardoned, according to your word" (14:20); Recited in confession, as history: "they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger" (Neh 9:17). The name is now told as what God has shown himself to be through Israel's whole story.

14512.text: Where it comes from. From God's own mouth first (Exo 34:6). Every human use goes back to that proclamation.

14513.text: How it co-exists: The name is used at once, in the next breath, to ask: "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (Exo 34:9), with "for it is a stiff-necked people". The name and the people's stiff neck are put side by side by Moses himself. The same pairing returns in Neh 9:16–17; The name includes its limit: "but who will by no means clear the guilty" (Exo 34:7; Num 14:18). Moses quotes the limit too, and still pleads.

14514.text: Seat. None in-verse. Neh 9:20 "your good Spirit to instruct them" is God's, given. Pointer: U1 §13 has Jonah using the same creed against God (Jon 4:2). With Moses and the Levites of Neh 9, one creed is used three ways: worship, plea, and complaint. Pilot §2.2 already notes the idiom shared between God and the wise (Pro 14:29 and others), and U1 §22 reads the human side of it.

14515.text: Part B: Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8. Three more uses of the name. Pilot §2.2 already lists all three as uses of the idiom: An individual's plea against "insolent men": "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger … Turn to me and be gracious to me" (Psa 86:14–16); A recital with its reasoning: "He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins" (103:9–10). This comes straight after "He made known his ways to Moses" (103:7). The psalm names Moses as the one to whom the name was made known; Praise: "The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made" (145:9); The one creed is now used five ways: worship (Exo 34:8), plea (Num 14; Psa 86), confession (Neh 9), complaint and praise (Psa 145); Seat . Outside: Psa 86:13 "you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol". The pleader's own. Genuine.

14516.text: Part C: Mic 7:18; Nah 1:3: "Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression …? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love" (Mic 7:18); "you will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea" (7:19). (#1892 pointer: read.) This is the creed turned into a question of wonder; Used against an enemy: "The Lord is slow to anger and great in power, and the Lord will by no means clear the guilty" (Nah 1:3), against Nineveh. The same words that Jonah complained were used to spare Nineveh are here used to announce its end; The creed is now used eight ways: worship, plea, confession, complaint, praise, wonder (Micah), the announcement of judgment (Nahum), and the ground for returning.

14521.text: What it does. It is warned of in advance (Lev 26; Deu 4–32; Jos 23) and narrated afterwards (Judg 2; 1Ki 11; 2Ki 17; 2Ch 28). The same act appears as prediction and as history.

14522.text: Where it comes from. This is where the texts give most. The roots named in the context of these verses: Forgetting. "take care lest you forget the Lord" (Deu 6:12); "You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you, and you forgot the God who gave you birth" (Deu 32:18); Fullness. "Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him" (Deu 32:15); "when … they have eaten and are full and grown fat, they will turn to other gods" (Deu 31:20). Plenty comes before the turn; A deceived or turning heart. "Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside" (Deu 11:16); "a man or woman … whose heart is turning away today" (Deu 29:18); Solomon's "heart had turned away" (1Ki 11:9), because "his wives turned away his heart" (1Ki 11:4); False security in the heart. The man who "blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'" (Deu 29:19). Here the anger is said to refuse forgiveness to one man, singled out: "The Lord will not be willing to forgive him … the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will smoke against that man" (29:20); Intermarriage. "they would turn away your sons from following me" (Deu 7:4); Distress. "In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the Lord — this same King Ahaz. For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him" (2Ch 28:22–23). Distress drives Ahaz further from God, not back. Contrast §16, where distress leads to crying out; Stubbornness, and not believing. "they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the Lord their God" (2Ki 17:14); "I know how rebellious and stubborn you are" (Deu 31:27).

14523.text: How it co-exists: You become what you follow. "They went after false idols and became false" (2Ki 17:15). In exile "you will serve gods of wood and stone … that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell" (Deu 4:28); Walking contrary meets walking contrary. "if … you will not listen to me, but walk contrary to me, then I will walk contrary to you in fury" (Lev 26:27–28). The anger answers in the form of the provocation. The next verses are the famine ("eat the flesh of your sons", 26:29) and "my soul will abhor you" (26:30). F v4 §4 reads this as mutual abhorrence; What is known in the heart. Joshua ties the threat to what the people already know: "you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things … so the Lord will bring upon you all the evil things" (Jos 23:14–15). The heart's own knowledge of God's faithfulness is made the ground for believing the warning; The generation that did not know. "there arose another generation after them who did not know the Lord or the work that he had done" (Judg 2:10), and they "provoked the Lord to anger" (2:12).

14525.text: Seat: In the verse: 1Ki 11:9 "his heart had turned away". Solomon's own. Genuine, the cause. Already read in A v3 §2.2 and pilot §2 ("the heart that provokes the anger"); Outside the verse (all genuine unless noted):; Deu 11:16 "lest your heart be deceived" (before) and 11:18 "lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul" (after). The deceived heart is the cause; the heart filled with the words is the guard. B v3 §4.1; C v3 §8.2; E v2 §4.1; G v3 §10; H v1 §5.1; Deu 29:18–19 "whose heart is turning away" / "blesses himself in his heart … stubbornness of my heart". E v2 §4.1, §12; C v3 §9.1; F v4 §9.6. Pilot §1.6 reads 29:20 with it; 1Ki 11:4 "his wives turned away his heart … his heart was not wholly true"; Jos 23:14 "you know in your hearts and souls". B v3 §1.1 ("the heart as the knower"); Lev 26:29–30 "flesh" (bodily) and "my soul will abhor you"; Nothing new in the seat itself. What part A adds is how regularly the heart is named in the verses around the anger verse, and not in the anger verse itself. Pilot §2 had said that the "anger was kindled" series carries "the human inner cause by narrative". Part A confirms this, and finds that the seat is named nearby, in warnings and explanations.

14526.text: Part B: Psa 78:58, 78:59, 78:62; Isa 65:3; Jer 7:18, 7:19, 7:20; 11:17; 15:14; 17:4; 25:6, 25:7; 32:29, 32:30, 32:31, 32:32 (16 verses): More roots; Treachery like the fathers': "turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow" (Psa 78:57); Self-holiness: "who say, 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you'" (Isa 65:5). This is said to a God who says "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2); Trust in man: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the Lord" (Jer 17:5); From youth, turning the back: "done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth" (Jer 32:30); "They have turned to me their back and not their face … they have not listened to receive instruction" (32:33); Whole households, all ranks: "The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough … to provoke me to anger" (Jer 7:18); "their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets" (32:32); The provocation turns on the provoker. "Is it I whom they provoke? declares the Lord. Is it not themselves, to their own shame?" (Jer 7:19); "that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm" (25:7); Pilot §2 lists Jer 7 in the ka'as series; What part B adds is the text's own statement that the provoking harms the provoker. Part A had "they … became false" (2Ki 17:15). Jeremiah adds "to their own shame" and "to your own harm"; Seat . Outside: Jer 17:5 "whose heart turns away". Genuine. Nothing new.

14527.text: Part C: Eze 8:17; 8:18; 20:28; Hos 8:5; 12:14: "Is it too light a thing …? … they put the branch to their nose" (Eze 8:17), with "their backs to the temple of the Lord, and their faces toward the east, worshiping the sun" (8:16); Prayer refused: "And though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them" (8:18); God's own "how long?": "How long will they be incapable of innocence?" (Hos 8:5). The question the laments ask of God is asked by God of the people; "Will you defile yourselves after the manner of your fathers …?" (Eze 20:30); "Ephraim has given bitter provocation" (Hos 12:14).

14530.text: How it co-exists: The provocation is inherited. "you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the Lord" (Num 32:14). The sons are warned that they are repeating the fathers. They answer by offering to go armed before their brothers (32:16–17); Remembering is commanded against self-righteousness. "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (Deu 9:4); "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath in the wilderness" (9:7). Memory of provoking God is the cure for the heart's claim to righteousness; Moses caught between. In Num 11:10–15 Moses hears the weeping, is "displeased", and says: "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? … kill me at once … that I may not see my wretchedness" (11:11, 15). The leader between God's anger and the people's complaint asks to die.

14535.text: What it does: Spoken against: "Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" And the anger of the Lord was kindled against them (Num 12:8–9). The charge is a lack of fear; Silenced: Amaziah to the prophet: "Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! Why should you be struck down?" (2Ch 25:16). The prophet stops, but says: "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel."; Killed: after Jehoiada died, "the king listened to them [the princes]"; prophets "testified against them, but they would not pay attention"; Zechariah, whom "the Spirit of God clothed", was stoned "in the court of the house of the Lord" (2Ch 24:17–21).

14538.text: What it does: Atonement carried into the plague: "Take your censer … carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the Lord" (Num 16:46). Aaron "ran into the midst … And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped" (16:47–48). The priest's body stands on the line; Execution of the leaders: "hang them in the sun before the Lord, that the fierce anger of the Lord may turn away from Israel" (Num 25:4). Then Phinehas's spear (25:7), read in U1 §15 (SP, 25:11); Nothing of the devoted thing kept: "None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand, that the Lord may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you" (Deu 13:17).

14547.text: How it co-exists: A limit on reading. "The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law" (Deu 29:29). Read straight after the explanation of the ruin, this sets the reading of God's anger inside what is revealed, and turns it to doing; A song as witness. "write this song and teach it … that this song may be a witness for me against the people of Israel" (Deu 31:19). The explanation is given before the ruin, so that the ruin can be read when it comes.

14553.text: What it leads to. Teaching and priesthood: "They shall teach Jacob your rules … they shall put incense before you" (33:10).

14564.text: How it co-exists: God's pity answers the groaning, not a repentance: "the Lord was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them" (Judg 2:18). In Judg 10:16 they put away the foreign gods, and "he became impatient over the misery of Israel" (the Hebrew has God's nephesh; God's, not the object here); The cry is answered while the relapse is foreseen. Nations are left "to test Israel by them" (Judg 2:22).

14580.text: Where it comes from: Contempt: "you … have cast me behind your back" (1Ki 14:9); Ingratitude for elevation: "Because I exalted you from among the people" (1Ki 14:7); "Since I exalted you out of the dust" (16:2); Self-sale: "you have sold yourself to do what is evil" (1Ki 21:20). "There was none who sold himself … like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife incited" (21:25); Lightness: "as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam" (1Ki 16:31); The measure given is David's heart: "you have not been like my servant David, who … followed me with all his heart" (1Ki 14:8).

14584.text: What it does: "my wrath will be kindled against this place, and it will not be quenched" (2Ki 22:17; 2Ch 34:25); Even after the fullest turning: "Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the Lord with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might … Still the Lord did not turn from the burning of his great wrath … because of all the provocations with which Manasseh had provoked him" (2Ki 23:25–26); "it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence" (2Ki 24:20); "they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the Lord rose against his people, until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16).

14587.text: Seat. None in-verse. Outside: 2Ki 23:25 "all his heart and … all his soul" (Josiah's own). Genuine; 2Ch 36:13 "hardened his heart against turning" (Zedekiah's own). Genuine; 2Ki 22:19 / 2Ch 34:27; Correction. v1 said 2Ki 23:25 was not found in the batch files. It is in E v2 §6 (Torah and obedience). It is not new. Read from the M02 side, it stands as the fullest turning of heart and soul, named next to wrath that did not turn.

14602.text: Part B: Psa 56:7; 59:13; 69:24; 79:6; Jer 10:25; 18:23; Lam 3:66 (seven verses). The imprecation is a recurring form in part B, as part A's pointer expected: The grounds given:; enemies who "injure my cause … have waited for my life" (Psa 56:5–6); "the sin of their mouths … the cursing and lies" (59:12); "they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded" (69:26): they add to God's striking; "the nations that do not know you … have devoured Jacob" (79:6–7; Jer 10:25 in the same words); Restraint inside the imprecation: "Kill them not, lest my people forget … consume them in wrath … that they may know that God rules over Jacob" (Psa 59:11, 13). The purpose given is knowledge; Tears and trust beside it: "put my tears in your bottle … This I know, that God is for me" (56:8–9); Paired with the speaker's own plea against anger:; Psa 79:6 is followed by "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8); Jer 10:25 is preceded by "Correct me, O Lord … not in your anger"; The one who asks for wrath on the nations asks to be corrected without it; The intercessor turned imprecator; "Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them" (Jer 18:20); Three verses later: "Forgive not their iniquity … deal with them in the time of your anger" (18:23); The one who turned the anger away now asks for it, because good was repaid with evil: "they have dug a pit for my life" (18:20). See §45; Lam 3:66 comes with "You will give them dullness of heart" (3:65); Seat ; In the verse: none; Outside: Lam 3:65 "dullness of heart". The enemies'. Genuine. Psa 56:6 "my life" (nephesh). Life-sense.

14610.text: How it co-exists: Isolation. "He has put my brothers far from me … My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me" (19:13–14). "Men have gaped at me with their mouth" (16:10); Not being able to see God. "Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not" (9:11). "If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice" (9:16); A wish not to have been born. "Why did you bring me out from the womb?" (10:18). "leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer" (10:20); Hope beyond the anger, in the same breath. "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me! … You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands" (14:13, 15). Job asks for a hiding place from God's anger in God's own keeping, and expects God to long for him afterwards.

14612.text: Seat: In the verse: Job 6:4 "my spirit drinks their poison". Job's own, as receiver. Genuine. A v3 §1; pilot §2 ("the spirit that receives the anger"); U1 §8 and §39; Outside: Job 6:7 "My appetite refuses to touch them" (nephesh). Appetite-sense, the bearer's own. Job 9:4 "wise in heart" is God's. Job 14:13 is the verse G v3 §16 left for M20 or unit 2. It is read here: its movement is hiding until the wrath passes, followed by being remembered. It is not a death-wish; Nothing new in the seat. Part A has Job 6:4 as its single verse where God's anger is located inside the human seat by the bearer himself. Parts B and C are expected to add the laments.

14613.text: Part B: Psa 88:7; 88:16; 102:10: Psalm 88, like Job, gives no cause. "Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves" (88:7); "Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me" (88:16); "Afflicted and close to death from my youth up" (88:15); Isolation: "You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them" (88:8); "my companions have become darkness" (88:18); Not seeing God: "O Lord, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?" (88:14); Calling continues: "Every day I call upon you, O Lord; I spread out my hands to you" (88:9); Unlike Job, Psalm 88 has no turn. Its last verse (88:18) ends in darkness; Psa 102:10: "For I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink, because of your indignation and anger; for you have taken me up and thrown me down" (102:9–10). His enemies "use my name for a curse" (102:8). Then "But you, O Lord, are enthroned forever" (102:12); Seat . Outside: Psa 88:14 "cast my soul away". The bearer's own. Genuine. Pilot §2 (second row) cites Psa 88:7, 16.

14635.text: How it co-exists: Past mercy as the ground: "You forgave the iniquity of your people … You withdrew all your wrath … Restore us again" (Psa 85:2–4); "Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?" (85:6); Relationship as the ground:; "the sheep of your pasture" (74:1); "Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old" (74:2); "you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand … please look, we are all your people" (Isa 64:8–9); Confession, or none; Isa 64 confesses: "you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved? … all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment" (64:5–6); Psa 79 asks: "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8); Psa 89 does not confess. It holds God to his covenant (89:38–39); The anger reaches even prayer:; "angry with your people's prayers" (Psa 80:4); "There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities" (Isa 64:7).

14638.text: Where it comes from: From what God has done: "The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil … At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned" (Psa 76:5–6); From the living God set against idols: "the instruction of idols is but wood!" (Jer 10:8).

14641.text: Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Psa 76:5 "stouthearted". The warriors' heart, stripped. Genuine.

14646.text: What it leads to: Healing: "I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will lead him and restore comfort to him and his mourners" (Isa 57:18); God dwelling with the contrite: "I dwell … with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (57:15).

14647.text: Seat: In the verse:; Isa 57:16 "spirit". The human spirit, as what would faint. Genuine; Isa 57:17 "his own heart". The backslider's. Genuine; Outside: Psa 78:37 "heart"; 78:39 "flesh … wind"; Isa 57:15. Nothing new.

14648.text: Part C: Eze 20:8; 20:13; 20:21; Hos 11:9: Three times in one chapter: "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them … But I acted for the sake of my name" (Eze 20:8–9, 13–14, 21–22: "I withheld my hand"). The chapter ends: "you shall remember your ways … and you shall loathe yourselves … when I deal with you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways" (20:43–44); Hosea gives another reason: "How can I give you up, O Ephraim? … My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hos 11:8–9). The people were "bent on turning away from me" (11:7). They will return "trembling like birds from Egypt" (11:11); The reasons given for restraint now include God's own nature ("God and not a man"), beside human frailty and the name; What the restrained do:; they remember and loathe themselves (Eze 20:43; also 16:63: "that you may remember and be confounded … when I atone for you"); they come trembling (Hos 11:10–11); Seat . Outside: Hos 11:8 "My heart recoils". God's. Divine.

14662.text: Part C: Zep 3:8; Zec 7:12; Mal 1:4: Correction refused: "I said, 'Surely you will fear me; you will accept correction' … But all the more they were eager to make all their deeds corrupt" (Zep 3:7). The next verse (3:8) is wrath on the nations, followed by "a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the Lord" (3:9); The heart made hard against hearing: "they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears … They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came" (Zec 7:11–12); Refusal returned in kind: "As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear" (7:13); Rebuilding against the blow, again: "If Edom says, 'We are shattered but we will rebuild the ruins,' the Lord of hosts says, 'They may build, but I will tear down … the people with whom the Lord is angry forever'" (Mal 1:4). This is Isa 9:10's "we will build with dressed stones" said by another nation; Seat . In the verse: Zec 7:12 "hearts diamond-hard". The people's own. Genuine. The same verse has "his Spirit" (God's; divine). Outside: Zec 7:10 "devise evil against another in your heart"; What part C adds. Part B's "heart that does not take it in" was a failure to understand. Zec 7:12 names an act: the heart made hard so as not to hear.

14670.text: What it does: "Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger" (Isa 13:9); "the Lord is enraged against all the nations" (34:2); "the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the Lord" (Jer 25:37); The human side:; "Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them … They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame" (Isa 13:7–8); "like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land" (13:14); "No refuge will remain for the shepherds … the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock!" (Jer 25:35–36); "I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life" (49:37); Onlookers: "everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds" (50:13).

14674.text: Part C: Eze 7:12; 7:14; 7:19; 21:17; 21:31; 30:15; 38:18; 38:19; Mic 5:15; Zep 1:15; 1:18; Luk 21:23: Ordinary life suspended: "Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn, for wrath is upon all their multitude" (Eze 7:12); Paralysis: "They have blown the trumpet and made everything ready, but none goes to battle" (7:14); The body: "All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water. They put on sackcloth, and horror covers them. Shame is on all faces" (7:17–18); Survivors "moaning, each one over his iniquity" (7:16); Wealth useless: "Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the Lord. They cannot satisfy their hunger … For it was the stumbling block of their iniquity" (7:19); "Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the Lord" (Zep 1:18). The wisdom saying of Pro 11:4 appears in prophecy twice; Blindness: "I will bring distress on mankind, so that they shall walk like the blind" (Zep 1:17); "the mighty man cries aloud there" (1:14); Hearts melting: "that their hearts may melt" (Eze 21:15); Every man against his brother: "Every man's sword will be against his brother" (Eze 38:21), as in Isa 9:19–21; In the Gospel: "Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people" (Luk 21:23), with "let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains" (21:21); Seat ; In the verse: Eze 7:19 "hunger" (nephesh). The people's appetite. Appetite-sense; Outside: Eze 21:15 "that their hearts may melt". Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat.

14677.text: How it co-exists: Fear addressed: "Let not your heart faint, and be not fearful at the report heard in the land" (Jer 51:46); Hope: "Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise" (Isa 26:19).

14682.text: How it co-exists: No one left to help: "There is none to guide her among all the sons she has borne" (Isa 51:18); "who will console you? … who will comfort you?" (51:19); "drunk, but not with wine" (51:21); Humiliation: "you have made your back like the ground and like the street for them to pass over" (51:23); The community lament uses the same image: "you have given us wine to drink that made us stagger".

14683.text: What it leads to. The cup is taken away and given to the tormentors: "Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering; the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more; and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors" (Isa 51:22–23). It is done by "your God who pleads the cause of his people" (51:22).

14684.text: Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Isa 51:23 "to you" (nephesh). Zion's self. Self-sense. Not found in the batches.

14685.text: Revisit of U1 §34 and its pointer. U1 §34 is "anger and passion as a drink given to others" (Hab 2:15; Rev 14:8; 18:3). Its pointer was "the cup that comes round" (Hab 2:16; Rev 14:10): Isa 51:22–23 is the cup coming round: taken from the one who drank and given to the tormentors; Part C (Hab 2:16; Rev 14:10) will be read against it.

14688.text: Where it comes from. The human side here is an absence: Part A §4 had Moses standing before the anger, and Psa 106:23 says "had not Moses … stood in the breach"; Isa 64:7 gives the people's side of the same absence: "There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you".

14697.text: Revisit of part A §7. Deu 29:19 has one man blessing himself: "I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart". Jeremiah shows the same false peace spoken by prophets to a whole people, in almost the same words ("stubbornly follows his own heart"). F v4 §9.6 ("Peace — true and false") already holds both.

14704.text: What it does: "For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the Lord has not turned back from us" (Jer 4:8); "Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the Lord has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath" (7:29); The land itself: "I looked, and behold, there was no man … the fruitful land was a desert … before his fierce anger" (4:25–26); "For this the earth shall mourn" (4:28).

14708.text: Part C: Eze 19:12. "And you, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel" (19:1, context read). "But the vine was plucked up in fury … This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation" (19:12, 14). Also Eze 6:11: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas". The lament is commanded of the prophet himself: Seat . Eze 19:12 "east wind". Spurious.

14724.text: What it does: "Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow, which was brought upon me, which the Lord inflicted on the day of his fierce anger" (Lam 1:12); "The Lord has become like an enemy" (2:5). "He has bent his bow like an enemy … and he has killed all who were delightful in our eyes" (2:4). "The Lord has made Zion forget festival and Sabbath" (2:6); "you have killed them in the day of your anger, slaughtering without pity" (2:21); "on the day of the anger of the Lord no one escaped or survived" (2:22); "I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath" (3:1); "You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us, killing without pity; you have wrapped yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through" (3:43–44); "The Lord gave full vent to his wrath" (4:11).

14726.text: How it co-exists: The body of the one speaking: "From on high he sent fire; into my bones he made it descend … he has left me stunned, faint all the day long" (1:13); "He has made my flesh and my skin waste away; he has broken my bones" (3:4); "He has walled me about so that I cannot escape; he has made my chains heavy; though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer" (3:7–8); Hunger at its worst: "The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children" (4:10); "Should women eat the fruit of their womb …?" (2:20); Pouring out the heart: "Arise, cry out in the night … Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord! Lift your hands to him for the lives of your children" (2:19); "Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven" (3:41); Hope inside the lament (context of Lam 3:1, read this session):; "My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me. But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases" (3:20–22); "For the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion … for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men" (3:31–33); "Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the Lord!" (3:40); Outsiders' disbelief: "The kings of the earth did not believe … that foe or enemy could enter the gates of Jerusalem" (4:12).

14728.text: Seat: In the verse: none; Outside:; Lam 2:19 "pour out your heart like water"; 3:20 "My soul … is bowed down"; 3:41 "lift up our hearts"; 3:33 "from his heart": God's, divine; Lam 1:11 "revive their strength" (nephesh): appetite/life-sense, not found in the batches.

14748.text: What it does: "the house of Israel has become dross to me … As one gathers silver and bronze and iron and lead and tin into a furnace, to blow the fire on it in order to melt it, so I will gather you in my anger and in my wrath, and I will put you in and melt you" (Eze 22:18, 20); "you shall know that I am the Lord; I have poured out my wrath upon you" (22:22); The pot: "Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose corrosion is in it, and whose corrosion has not gone out of it!" (24:6). "To rouse my wrath, to take vengeance, I have set on the bare rock the blood she has shed, that it may not be covered" (24:8).

14749.text: Where it comes from: Refused cleansing: "because I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed from your uncleanness, you shall not be cleansed anymore till I have satisfied my fury upon you" (24:13); Effort without change: "She has wearied herself with toil; its abundant corrosion does not go out of it" (24:12); Blood left uncovered (24:7).

14758.text: What it does. "Behold, I will make known to you what shall be at the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end" (Dan 8:19). "He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done" (11:36).

14759.text: How it co-exists: The seer's fear and collapse: "I was frightened and fell on my face … I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground. But he touched me and made me stand up" (8:17–18); The proud king prospers within the time: "the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god" (11:36); The wise are refined within it: "some of the wise shall stumble, so that they may be refined, purified, and made white, until the time of the end" (11:35).

14762.text: How it co-exists. What is required instead: "He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Mic 6:8); "it is sound wisdom to fear your name" (6:9).

14765.text: What it does: "'Yet even now,' declares the Lord, 'return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments.' Return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger … Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him …?" (Joe 2:12–14); The king of Nineveh: "Let neither man nor beast … taste anything … let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish" (Jon 3:7–9).

14766.text: How it co-exists: Fasting and the body, and the heart: "rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joe 2:13). Outward signs are not refused; the heart is named as what must be torn; Awe: "the day of the Lord is great and very awesome; who can endure it?" (Joe 2:11).

14768.text: Seat: In the verse: Joe 2:13 "rend your hearts". The hearers' own. Genuine; Outside: Joe 2:12 "with all your heart".

14774.text: Compared with earlier sections: Part B §28 asked "correct me, but not in anger".
