14966.text: The passage. The Rabshakeh's speech has been heard (2Ki 18). Hezekiah "tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the Lord" (19:1). His message: "This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace" (19:3). Isaiah answers: "Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me" (19:6). A letter comes; Hezekiah "spread it before the Lord" and prays (19:14–19). The Lord answers with an oracle against Sennacherib (19:21–28), and the camp is struck (19:35). 2Ch 32 tells the same campaign with the purpose of the shouting stated (32:18) and the end: "he returned with shame of face to his own land" (32:21).

14975.text: Sennacherib as a passage. Mockery of God sent through servants, letters and shouting; its stated aim is to make the hearers afraid (2Ch 32:18). Hezekiah's response: sackcloth, the house of the Lord, the letter spread before God, prayer (2Ki 19:1, 14–19). God's word to the people: "Do not be afraid" (19:6). God names himself as the one mocked (19:22), knows the mocker's raging (19:27), turns the scorn back (19:21), and the mocker goes home with shame of face (2Ch 32:21). Hezekiah calls the day one "of disgrace" (2Ki 19:3, a contempt word, M06).

14981.text: What it does (1:4): "As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven." Then a confession: "we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned" (1:6–7).

14982.text: Face: reproach as something to be ended by work. What follows: "they jeered at us and despised us" (2:19), and Nehemiah's answer: "The God of heaven will make us prosper ... but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem" (2:20).

14984.text: Relational observation: the prayer asks for a return: "Turn back ... on their own heads". I read this beside 10.4 What is devised comes back (the same "on his own head" in Psa 7:16 and Est 9:25), as a prayer that what was aimed at them come back. The verses state their own returns; the comparison is mine.

14998.text: The passage: Gideon and his 300, "exhausted yet pursuing" (8:4), ask Succoth for bread (8:5). The officials answer with the question of 8:6. Gideon promises to "flail your flesh with the thorns" (8:7). After the victory he "took the elders of the city ... and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson" (8:16), literally "made the men of Succoth know" (yāḏaʿ, Hiphil).

15000.text: The passage: the generation born in the wilderness is circumcised (5:2–7), after "the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of the Lord" (5:6). They stay in camp "until they were healed" (5:8).

15001.text: What "the reproach of Egypt" is: the verse does not say. The passage gives two things beside it: the uncircumcised state of the new generation (5:5, 7) and the fathers who died in the wilderness for disobedience (5:6). I read it as left open by the verse; I do not choose between them.

15004.text: mocking carried by a boast from a lifted-up stance (2Ki 19:22–23).

15005.text: the mockery laid before God in prayer (2Ki 19:14–16), and the taunt asked to return on the taunters (Neh 4:4).

15009.text: the taunt verb turned on one's own life and praised (Judg 5:18).

15010.text: reproach as a people's condition, wept over and confessed by one outside it (Neh 1:3–7), and to be ended by work (Neh 2:17).

15011.text: reproach earned by conduct among brothers, preventable by the fear of God (Neh 5:9).

15014.text: reproach foreseen as a burden with nowhere to go, then borne for life (2Sa 13:13, 19–20).

15019.text: Responses to taunt and reproach in these passages (as the verses state them): fear (2Ch 32:18 aim; 1Sa 17:11 in the trial), weeping (1Sa 11:4; Neh 1:4), anger with the Spirit (1Sa 11:6), sackcloth and the house of the Lord (2Ki 19:1), prayer (2Ki 19:16; Neh 4:4), building (Neh 2:17; 4:6), refusing to be afraid (Neh 6:11), blessing God for taking it up (1Sa 25:39).

15022.text: The passage. A prayer of David from deep water (69:1–2), weary with crying and waiting (69:3), hated "without cause" (69:4), and confessing "you know my folly" (69:5). The middle (69:6–12) is about reproach; the plea follows (69:13–18); then reproach again (69:19–21); and the psalm ends in praise and in "the Lord hears the needy" (69:33).

15025.text: he is cut off from his family (69:8) and made a song in the gate and among drunkards (69:11–12).

15026.text: his heart is broken, he looks for pity and comfort and finds none (69:20), and he is given poison and sour wine (69:21; John 19:28–30 is in 10.6).

15036.text: The passage. Goliath challenges the ranks of Israel (17:8–10), and Saul and Israel are "dismayed and greatly afraid" (17:11). Every morning and evening for forty days (17:16) the same words, and "All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were much afraid" (17:24). David hears (17:23), asks (17:26), is rebuked by Eliab (17:28; told in 10.15), tells Saul "Let no man's heart fail because of him" (17:32), and goes out "in the name of the Lord of hosts" (17:45).

15049.text: "For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened" (1:21). They "exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images" (1:23). Then three times "God gave them up" (1:24, 26, 28), each after an exchange (1:23, 25, and "did not see fit to acknowledge God", 1:28).

15050.text: The original (§4.6a). The English sets "honor" (1:21) against "dishonoring" and "dishonorable" (1:24, 26). The Greek does not: "honor" in 1:21 is doxazō "glorify". "Dishonoring" (1:24) is atimazō and "dishonorable passions" (1:26) is pathē atimias, literally "passions of dishonor". Atimia is the negative of timē "honour" (M71). "Shameless acts" (1:27) is aschēmosynē, "indecency", whose range runs to "nakedness, shame" (Rev 16:15).

15051.text: Romans 1 as a passage. Honour withheld from God (1:21, glorify) is followed by dishonor in the body (1:24) and passions of dishonor (1:26). The passage's own connectives say how they follow: "Therefore" (1:24), "For this reason" (1:26), "since" (1:28). That bears on the Ch 12 held item (a five-step progression). I read the passage as stating the connections itself, so the Ch 12 item can be checked against the passage's own connectives when that chapter is touched. I do not resolve it here.

15058.text: The Ch 12 Held item on Rom 1:21–32 bears on set 2. I noted it and did not resolve it.

15065.text: The stacked pairs are the paired cries of the psalms and prophets, "let them be put to shame and confounded" (for example Psa 35:4, 26; 40:14; 70:2). H2781 with H7045 is the prophetic list "a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse" (for example Jer 24:9; 42:18; 44:8, 12).

15077.text: Seen in the verses: Miriam's shame (Num 12:14), Rom 1:26 "dishonorable passions", Eph 5:12, Pro 6:33.

15081.text: The words pile up when pride is named in full. "We have heard of the pride of Moab — he is very proud — of his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart" (Jer 48:29). The next verse joins it to speech: "his boasts are false" (48:30). Isa 16:6 gives the same list and ends "in his idle boasting he is not right".

15082.text: Pride is shown as well as held: "Therefore pride is their necklace; violence covers them as a garment" (Psa 73:6). It is worn where it can be seen; The "therefore" points back to ease: "they have no pangs until death ... They are not in trouble as others are" (73:4–5); The next line is the heart: "their hearts overflow with follies" (73:7).

15084.text: Wisdom and God hate it. "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate" (Pro 8:13). Pride stands in a list with the way of evil and perverted speech.

15088.text: In these verses pride is not alone. It stands over someone weaker or someone righteous: The poor:; "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor" (Psa 10:2); Sodom's guilt was "pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy" (Eze 16:49). Pride is listed with plenty and ease, and with what was not done for others; The widow: "The Lord tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries" (Pro 15:25). Pride's house is set against the boundary of the one without defence; The righteous:; Lips "which speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt" (Psa 31:18); "The arrogant have hidden a trap for me" (Psa 140:5); "Let not the foot of arrogance come upon me" (Psa 36:11). Pride is pictured as a foot that treads; The heart closed to pity. "They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly" (Psa 17:10). A closed heart and an arrogant mouth sit side by side; The one who bears it; "Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud" (Psa 123:4); The psalm's answer is the eyes of a servant looking to the master's hand "till he has mercy upon us" (123:2); This is pride as it is felt by the one under it; Another's fall in one's mouth. "Was not your sister Sodom a byword in your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was uncovered?" (Eze 16:56–57). In the day of its pride, Jerusalem talked of Sodom's fall while its own wickedness was still covered; Taunting God's people. Moab and Ammon's lot comes "in return for their pride, because they taunted and boasted against the people of the Lord" (Zep 2:10); Repaid. "repay to the proud what they deserve" (Psa 94:2). The proud "pour out their arrogant words" and "crush your people" (94:4–5). "The Lord preserves the faithful but abundantly repays the one who acts in pride" (Psa 31:23). "let them be trapped in their pride" (Psa 59:12); Carried from M09: Isa 13:11 ("the pomp of the arrogant") and Job 22:29.

15089.text: Here the word names a thing more than a bearing: what a people stands on: Might; "the pride of your power" (Lev 26:19); Egypt's "proud might" (Eze 30:6, 18) and Israel's "proud might" (Eze 33:28), whose people "rely on the sword" (33:26); "the pride of the strong" (Eze 7:24); Splendour and pomp; Babylon, "the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans" (Isa 13:19); Tyre: "to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth" (Isa 23:9); "the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim ... the fading flower of its glorious beauty" (Isa 28:1, 3); Strongholds. "I abhor the pride of Jacob and hate his strongholds" (Amo 6:8). In the passage they lie at ease and are "not grieved over the ruin of Joseph" (6:6); What God gave, used for pride; "His beautiful ornament they used for pride, and they made their abominable images and their detestable things of it" (Eze 7:20); "Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the delight of your eyes, and the yearning of your soul" (Eze 24:21). God's own sanctuary had become what they gloried in. It sits with delight and yearning: a pride, a delight and a longing all set on one thing; Brought down; "Your pomp is brought down to Sheol" (Isa 14:11). The passage names the heart behind it: "You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven ... I will set my throne on high'" (14:13); The pride of Egypt (Eze 32:12), Assyria (Zec 10:11) and Philistia (Zec 9:6); Carried from M09 (the proud brought low): Isa 25:11, Isa 2:12, Dan 4:37, Job 40:11–12.

15091.text: The same word names a standing that God gives his people: "He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob whom he loves" (Psa 47:4); "the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel" (Isa 4:2); To a city "forsaken and hated": "I will make you majestic forever, a joy from age to age" (Isa 60:15); "the Lord is restoring the majesty of Jacob as the majesty of Israel" (Nah 2:2); The Lord is "the sword of your triumph" (Deu 33:29): Israel's "pride" is the Lord himself; "The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: 'Surely I will never forget any of their deeds'" (Amo 8:7). The oath follows the buying of "the poor for silver" (8:6). The verse does not say what "the pride of Jacob" refers to. I read: it may be Jacob's arrogance, sworn by in irony, or the honour God gave Jacob. The verse is held, not settled; God's "proudly exulting ones" are the warriors he summons to carry out his anger (Isa 13:3).

15101.text: The Son: "all were astonished at the majesty of God" at the healing of the boy. At once Jesus says: "The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men" (Luk 9:43–44). The majesty and the handing over stand side by side; "we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father" (2Pe 1:16–17). His majesty is described as received; "After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high" (Heb 1:3; also 8:1). "Majesty" is used here as a name for God; "to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority" (Jude 25).

15109.text: What the batch 1 verses state: The same words are used of God and of people. gāʾôn, gaʾăwāh, gēʾût and gāʾāh name God's majesty (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10) and human pride (Isa 9:9; Jer 48:29; Pro 16:18). So yes: these words describe a characteristic of God. In ESV English the difference shows in the choice of word ("majesty" against "pride"), not in the Hebrew; God's majesty is his own and is not taken on. He is "robed in majesty" while "you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2). Nothing in these verses shows it being acquired. It is shown in acts: the sea, the overthrow, the thunder; It is challenged, but it is not overturned. The researcher's word "undisputed" needs one qualification from the verses. God's majesty is disputed: by the enemy at the sea (Exo 15:9), by "all that is proud and lofty" (Isa 2:12), and by the one who says "I will ascend to heaven" (Isa 14:13). Each time the dispute ends with the one who rose brought down. So it is not uncontested; it is never overturned; Majesty goes with what only God can do. Job 40:10–14 makes the test plain: whoever wears majesty must abase every proud one and save by his own hand. Only God does; Human pride in these verses is mostly a standing that is taken, or kept against God; It is said in the heart against the facts: "the bricks have fallen, but we will build" (Isa 9:10); It is worn as a show (Psa 73:6); It is set over the weak (Psa 10:2; Eze 16:49; Pro 15:25); It refuses to hear (Jer 13:15–17); It stands on might and strongholds (Lev 26:19; Amo 6:8; Eze 33:26); This agrees with the researcher's "mostly assumed"; But the same word for people is not always assumed. God gives a "pride" to his people: chosen (Psa 47:4), given (Isa 4:2), made (Isa 60:15), restored (Nah 2:2). The Lord himself is their "triumph" (Deu 33:29). The verses also show a given honour turned into pride (Eze 7:20; 24:21); I read: the line the verses draw is not between God having majesty and people having none. It runs between a standing that is one's own by nature (God), a standing given by God (his people), and a standing taken, or turned against the giver (pride); The Son's majesty is described as received, and it stands beside his being handed over; "he received honor and glory from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17); "after making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty" (Heb 1:3); At the very moment of "the majesty of God", he speaks of being "delivered into the hands of men" (Luk 9:43–44); This joins 13.1 Lowering himself (M09): the one with majesty did not hold onto it in the way pride holds; I read: where Php 2:6–9 joins the two, it lies outside this batch's words; A majesty that depends on people is the contrast. Artemis's "magnificence" can be "deposed", because it rests on "she whom all Asia and the world worship" (Act 19:27). I read: this is the borrowed standing that pride is, set against God's majesty, which no one confers.

15111.text: Pride over the poor and the widow (Psa 10:2; Eze 16:49; Pro 15:25) bears on OT-105 (the poor as seen by another).

15113.text: The heart rises out of what it has been given. This is the clearest single pattern in the batch, and the verses state it each time: Strength. Uzziah "was marvelously helped, till he was strong. But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (2Ch 26:15–16); Healing and honour. Hezekiah was healed, given a sign, and "exalted in the sight of all nations". Then: "But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud" (2Ch 32:23–25). Here pride is a failure to return what was received. It was humbled the next verse (32:26, carried from M09); Greatness and majesty. "the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father kingship and greatness and glory and majesty ... But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down" (Dan 5:18–20). It lasted "until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind" (5:21); Wealth. "by your great wisdom in your trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart has become proud in your wealth" (Eze 28:5); Beauty. "You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you ... Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor" (Eze 28:15–17); Height. The cedar God made beautiful ("I made it beautiful", Eze 31:9): "its heart was proud of its height" (31:10).

15115.text: Pride deceives the one who has it: "The pride of your heart has deceived you ... who say in your heart, 'Who will bring me down to the ground?'" (Obd 3); "Though you soar aloft like the eagle ... from there I will bring you down" (Obd 4); Jer 49:16 adds a second deceiver: "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart". The fear others feel feeds the self-deception.

15117.text: It has no room for God: "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psa 10:4); "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4). Then: "an arrogant man who is never at rest. His greed is as wide as Sheol" (2:5). The swollen soul is set against faith, and joined to restlessness and greed.

15118.text: It is seen in the eyes, the walk and the house: "Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin" (Pro 21:4). It follows "the Lord weighs the heart" (21:2); "Whoever has a haughty look and an arrogant heart I will not endure" (Psa 101:5); The daughters of Zion "walk with outstretched necks, glancing wantonly with their eyes" (Isa 3:16), in the same oracle as "the spoil of the poor is in your houses" (3:14); "he who makes his door high seeks destruction" (Pro 17:19); "How sick is your heart ... the deeds of a brazen prostitute" (Eze 16:30).

15121.text: zîd and zādôn name a pride that acts where it was not sent: Speaking what God did not say. "the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him" (Deu 18:20). Such a word fails, and "You need not be afraid of him" (18:22). Presumption here borrows God's name for its own word; Going up when told not to. "Do not go up ... So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the Lord and presumptuously went up" (Deu 1:42–43). It came straight after "We have sinned ... We ourselves will go up" (1:41). After the defeat, "you returned and wept before the Lord" (1:45). I read: presumption can wear the clothes of repentance. It goes up when the moment to go up has passed; Not obeying; Not obeying the priest or judge (Deu 17:12). The rest "shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13); "they ... acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments. They ... were not mindful of the wonders that you performed" (Neh 9:16–17); "you warned them in order to turn them back ... Yet they acted presumptuously" (9:29); Joined to these are a stiff neck, a stubborn shoulder, and forgetting the wonders. Each time God's mercy answers: "But you are a God ready to forgive" (9:17); Kept from it. "Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me!" (Psa 19:13). It follows "Who can discern his errors?" (19:12). Presumption is asked to be kept from, as something that would rule; Not hearing; "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jer 13:15); "By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom" (Pro 13:10); "When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom" (Pro 11:2, carried); The opposite named for pride is hearing, taking advice, humility; The fool. "a fool is reckless and careless", against the wise who "is cautious and turns away from evil" (Pro 14:16); Scoffing. "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Pro 21:24); Intent. "if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning" (Exo 21:14). It is set against the one who "did not lie in wait for him" (21:13). Here the word names intent carried out against another; Pride named wrongly; Eliab, angry: "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart". David answers: "What have I done now? Was it not but a word?" (1Sa 17:28–29); The passage shows David asking about the one who defies "the armies of the living God" (17:26); I read: the charge of presumption here comes from an older brother's anger. The verses do not show it to be true.

15122.text: Psalm 119 gives one person's whole experience of the insolent: "The insolent utterly deride me, but I do not turn away from your law" (119:51); "The insolent smear me with lies, but with my whole heart I keep your precepts; their heart is unfeeling like fat" (119:69–70); "they have wronged me with falsehood; as for me, I will meditate on your precepts" (119:78); "The insolent have dug pitfalls for me; they do not live according to your law" (119:85); "let not the insolent oppress me" (119:122); The insolent wander from the commandments (119:21). Against them each time, the speaker holds the law, meditates, and asks for a pledge.

15123.text: Rising up, with God not set before them. "insolent men have risen up against me; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, and they do not set you before them" (Psa 86:14). The answer is "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious" (86:15).

15124.text: Trampling, and the sufferer's fear. "many attack me proudly. When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psa 56:2–3).

15125.text: Words: "They pour out their arrogant words; all the evildoers boast" (Psa 94:4); "They scoff and speak with malice; loftily they threaten oppression. They set their mouths against the heavens" (Psa 73:8–9).

15132.text: The eyes lifted against the Holy One. "Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel!" (2Ki 19:22; Isa 37:23).

15134.text: Who lifts up. "do not lift up your horn on high, or speak with haughty neck. For not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:5–7). Lifting up is God's to give.

15136.text: Ripening and fall: "the rod has blossomed; pride has budded" (Eze 7:10). Pride is pictured as a plant that has come to bud; "all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble", while "for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing" (Mal 4:1–2); The fallen cedar is made an example: "in order that no trees by the waters may grow to towering height ... For they are all given over to death" (Eze 31:14); Shebna, who "cut out a tomb on the height", is hurled away: "you shame of your master's house" (Isa 22:16–18).

15137.text: Carried from M09: Isa 2:11, 17; 5:15; 10:33; 26:5. In Isa 26:6 the lofty city is trampled by "the feet of the poor".

15139.text: A heart not lifted up. "O Lord, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me. But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother" (Psa 131:1–2). Not being lifted up is pictured as a soul at rest, against Hab 2:5's "arrogant man who is never at rest".

15141.text: "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psa 138:6, carried).

15142.text: Leviathan "sees everything that is high; he is king over all the sons of pride" (Job 41:34). This is 13.4. It comes in God's speech after "Who then is he who can stand before me?" (41:10). Leviathan rules the proud beasts, and God rules Leviathan.

15143.text: "As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable" (Pro 25:3). Height here is the measure of a heart that cannot be searched. There is no pride in it.

15146.text: The verses say outright that pride takes a place that is God's: "you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods' ... yet you are but a man, and no god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "Who will bring me down to the ground?" (Obd 3); "By the strength of my hand I have done it" (Isa 10:13); This is the researcher's "assumed position" in the verses' own words. Pride is a heart made like the heart of a god. It is not so; What was given is turned into pride; "the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar ... kingship and greatness and glory and majesty ... But when his heart was lifted up" (Dan 5:18–20). Majesty is the same word family God wears (batch 1); The pattern recurs: Uzziah's strength (2Ch 26:15–16), Hezekiah's healing (2Ch 32:24–25), the cherub's beauty (Eze 28:17), the cedar's height (Eze 31:9–10); I read: the human standing in these verses is real, and it is given. Pride begins when the heart treats it as its own. Batch 1 showed the same in Eze 7:20 and 24:21; God's height does not keep him from the low. "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psa 138:6). The high God comes near the lowly. The proud, who make themselves high, are known "from afar"; Lifting up belongs to God. "not from the east or from the west ... comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:6–7). The one who has height by nature is the one who gives height; God is known as greater through his answer to arrogance. "Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods, because ... they dealt arrogantly" (Exo 18:11). "you knew that they acted arrogantly ... And you made a name for yourself" (Neh 9:10); God knows and weighs. "Talk no more so very proudly ... for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" (1Sa 2:3). This is joined to "the Lord weighs the heart" (Pro 21:2) beside "a proud heart" (21:4). I read: pride claims a height that cannot bear being weighed. God's knowing is part of what it runs into; His mercy answers presumption. "they acted presumptuously ... But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful" (Neh 9:16–17). "insolent men have risen up against me ... But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious" (Psa 86:14–15).

15148.text: Pride and rest: Hab 2:5 ("never at rest") against Psa 131:2 ("calmed and quieted my soul"). This bears on Ch 5 Rest for the soul (M09).

15149.text: The sufferer's side (Psalm 119; Psa 56; 86; 123 in batch 1) bears on 10.12 (fear) and 10.9.

15151.text: The Greek picture is swelling, physioō, "to inflate". In Paul it is set again and again against love: Knowledge. "This 'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1Co 8:1–3). Swelling knowledge is answered not by more knowledge but by being known by God; Love is not. "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant" (1Co 13:4). Before this: "if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge ... but have not love, I am nothing" (13:2); Party; "that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:6–7); Here Paul states what the Hebrew verses showed in story: pride holds what was received "as if you did not receive it"; Talk without power. "Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you ... I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power" (1Co 4:18–20). The arrogance rests on Paul being absent; Where grief belongs. "And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?" (1Co 5:2). Pride stands where mourning should be; Without reason. "puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head" (Col 2:18–19, carried from M09); The new convert. "He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6). The verse joins conceit to the devil's condemnation. It does not say what the devil's condemnation was. I read: it is held for 13.3 (other spirits). It is not built on here; Controversy. "he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension" (1Ti 6:4). Conceit is joined to understanding nothing, and to quarrels; With pleasure. "swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power" (2Ti 3:4–5); Among the others; "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Co 12:20); "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26), after "let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (5:25); Conceit is named among the things that set people against each other.

15170.text: The given-or-taken line is stated outright. "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7): This is the plainest statement in the three batches of what the researcher suspected. Human pride holds as its own what was received; The researcher's word "assumed" fits: the standing is taken up as if it were not given; The right measure is the one God assigns. "not to think of himself more highly than he ought ... according to the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3). I read: where God has height by nature, a person has a measure by gift. Pride is thinking past the gift; Taking God's seat; "takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" (2Th 2:4); Together with Eze 28:2 and Isa 14:13 (batches 1–2), the verses show pride at its full height as a claim to God's own place; I read: God's "Most High" is the place pride reaches for. Batches 1–3 show no one holding it but God; Christ's firstness is grounded, and pleased; "that in everything he might be preeminent. For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell" (Col 1:18–19); His first place rests on what he is: before all things, the one through whom all were made, firstborn from the dead. It is not claimed against anyone; Batch 1 also has Christ's majesty as "received ... from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17), and his seat taken "after making purification for sins" (Heb 1:3); I read: in the verses the Son's height comes with his descent: firstborn from the dead, seated after purification. This bears on 13.1 Lowering himself; God's knowing is what pride meets. "God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God" (Luk 16:15). "he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts" (Luk 1:51). As in batch 2 (1Sa 2:3), God's knowledge is joined to his answer to pride; Other beings in these verses (held, not read in); A messenger of Satan is given against conceit (2Co 12:7); The conceited may fall "into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6); Angels greater in might do not blaspheme where the willful do (2Pe 2:11); These are for 13.2 and 13.3. The verses do not say that the devil fell by pride. That is not stated here and is not built on.

15178.text: Wealth, and trust in it: "those who trust in their wealth and boast of the abundance of their riches? Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life" (Psa 49:6–7). The boast is joined to trust, and both are measured against the life that wealth cannot buy; "Why do you boast of your valleys, O faithless daughter, who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?'" (Jer 49:4). This is the same "who will" as Obd 3 (batch 2).

15186.text: In idols. "All worshipers of images are put to shame, who make their boast in worthless idols", beside "you, O Lord, are most high over all the earth" (Psa 97:7, 9).

15188.text: Nothing to boast of before God: God chose "what is low and despised in the world ... so that no human being might boast in the presence of God" (1Co 1:28–29); "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship" (Eph 2:8–10); "Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded ... by the law of faith" (Rom 3:27); "if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God" (Rom 4:2); The ground of the exclusion is stated each time: a gift, a choosing of the low, faith.

15194.text: The ground for boasting: "I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me" (1Co 9:15–16); The preaching itself is no ground, because it is laid on him. The ground is that he preached "free of charge" (9:18).

15195.text: The boast is not removed. It is moved: The command. "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17). This follows Christ "who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1:30). It is joined to "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends" (2Co 10:18); What to boast in; "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24); The boast is in knowing God, and what is known is his character; The soul's boast. "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2, carried); Not in my bow. "For not in my bow do I trust ... In God we have boasted continually" (Psa 44:6–8). The psalm then turns: "But you have rejected us" (44:9). The boast in God is kept in the psalm even while the defeat is brought before him; His name. "Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!" (Psa 105:3; 1Ch 16:10); The worm. "Fear not, you worm Jacob ... you shall rejoice in the Lord; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory" (Isa 41:14–16). The one called a worm is the one who glories; Justified and glorying. "Only in the Lord, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength ... In the Lord all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory" (Isa 45:24–25); The nations. If Israel returns and swears in truth, "nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory" (Jer 4:2); Exulting; "all who swear by him shall exult" (Psa 63:11); "Let the righteous one rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!" (Psa 64:10); "that I may glory with your inheritance" (Psa 106:5); The cross. "far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Gal 6:14); Christ, not the flesh. "glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh — though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also" (Php 3:3–4). Paul has standing in the flesh, "I have more", and sets it aside; Hope, sufferings, God. ESV renders kauchaomai "rejoice" here:; "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings" (Rom 5:2–3); "we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation" (5:11); The same word that elsewhere is a proud boast is here joy in hope, in suffering, and in God; Held fast. "if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope" (Heb 3:6); The conscience. "our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12). The boast is a clear conscience, and its ground is named as grace.

15205.text: Proverbs paints the scoffer by what he will not receive: Rebuke; "A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). The verse before is "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of man!" (15:11); Hatred of correction. "Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse ... Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. "Blessed is the man who ... nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psa 1:1–2). The scoffer's seat is set against delight in the law; The warning; "do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong", then "Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23). Again the opposite of scoffing is hearing; "the scoffer cease ... who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate" (Isa 29:20–21). The scoffer works against the one who reproves. In the same passage "The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord" (29:19); Wine and company; "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" (Pro 20:1); "the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers", and "none of them calls upon me" (Hos 7:5, 7); In Job's debates; Zophar: "when you mock, shall no one shame you?" (Job 11:3); Job: "after I have spoken, mock on" (21:3); Elihu: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (36:18); I read: the charge of scoffing is thrown between the speakers. As with Eliab in batch 2, the verses do not settle that it is true of Job; "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34, carried). This is the source of Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5.

15209.text: Builders: Sanballat "was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews. And he said ... 'What are these feeble Jews doing?'" (Neh 4:1–2). Mocking comes with anger, and it belittles; The answer: "The God of heaven will make us prosper" (Neh 2:20).

15210.text: The sufferer: "My friends scorn me; my eye pours out tears to God", after "my witness is in heaven" (Job 16:19–20). Scorned by friends, he turns to God; "All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads; 'He trusts in the Lord; let him deliver him'" (Psa 22:7–8). The mockery takes the sufferer's trust as its target. The psalm answers: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9); "our enemies laugh among themselves. Restore us, O God of hosts" (Psa 80:6–7); Jeremiah: "I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me ... the word of the Lord has become for me a reproach and derision ... there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones" (Jer 20:7–9). He is mocked for the word, and he cannot hold the word in.

15211.text: The half-built tower. "all who see it begin to mock him, saying, 'This man began to build and was not able to finish'" (Luk 14:29). The fear of being mocked is used to call for counting the cost of following Jesus (14:27–28).

15224.text: Mocked as king: "kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, 'Hail, King of the Jews!'" (Mat 27:29); Herod "treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing" (Luk 23:11). Before this, "he made no answer" (23:9); "when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe ... and led him away to crucify him" (Mat 27:31; Mar 15:20).

15230.text: Wisdom: "Because I have called and you refused to listen ... I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you" (Pro 1:24–26).

15232.text: If they turn to other gods, "Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples" (1Ki 9:7; 2Ch 7:20; Deu 28:37). "a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse" (Jer 24:9). "a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror" (Eze 5:15).

15237.text: A pride word is used of God here. lāʿag "mock" and lîṣ "scorn" are said of God: "the Lord holds them in derision" (Psa 2:4); "you hold all the nations in derision" (Psa 59:8); "Toward the scorners he is scornful" (Pro 3:34); wisdom: "I will mock when terror strikes you" (Pro 1:26); The verses show how God's derision differs from human mocking; Where it comes from. It comes from the one who "sits in the heavens" (Psa 2:4), from the height that batches 1–3 found is his by nature; What it answers. It always answers a rising against him: kings set "against the Lord and against his Anointed" (Psa 2:2), those of whom it says "'Who,' they think, 'will hear us?'" (Psa 59:7), the scorners (Pro 3:34), those who "refused to listen" (Pro 1:24); Whom it never targets. In these verses it is never aimed at the weak, the poor or the sufferer. Human mocking is aimed at exactly those: the poor (Pro 17:5), a father (Pro 30:17), the sufferer (Psa 22:7), builders called "feeble" (Neh 4:2); I read: God's derision is the laughter of the undisputed height at a dispute that cannot succeed. Human mockery is a self-made height looking down on someone made low; God is not mocked. "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7). The mocking of his messengers goes on "until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16). This is the batch 1 point again: God's standing is challenged, and is not overturned; The Son is mocked, and does not answer in kind; The one with the undisputed standing is mocked on that very standing: "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Mat 27:29); "He saved others; he cannot save himself" (Mar 15:31); He "made no answer" (Luk 23:9), and he prays "Father, forgive them" (Luk 23:34); I read: in the Son, the majesty of batch 1 does not defend itself against mockery. This is the clearest instance of 13.1 Lowering himself in these words. It joins the batch 1 point that his majesty and his being "delivered into the hands of men" stand side by side (Luk 9:43–44); Mocking exposes a false height. Zion scorns Sennacherib (2Ki 19:21). Elijah mocks a god who does not answer (1Ki 18:27). Here the mocking does not come from pride. It names a claim that is empty.

15242.text: The data (135): 57 have no other M-code. These are the tabernacle and temple measurements, the pillars, Goliath, the gallows, high places and gates; 78 have another M-code, but the height word takes no part in it. For example, "the upper gate" stands beside a king, and "a high mountain" beside the Transfiguration; 25 are God, or Christ, "on high" with no other M-code joined. Examples are Psa 92:8, Psa 97:9, Heb 1:3 and Luk 24:49 ("power from on high"). They are noted in the CSV so that 13.1 can draw on them if wanted; Five are the tree and cedar figures of Eze 31:3, 31:5 and Dan 4:10, 11, 20. The pride in those passages is named in other verses (Eze 31:10; Dan 4:30, 37), and those verses are kept as P; Seven data verses are cited in the narrative: Eze 13:18, 1Sa 28:20, Job 25:2, Isa 24:18, Est 5:14, Psa 113:5 and Isa 7:11. Setting them aside here does not touch those citations. Each was cited for another word in the verse.

15257.text: Are any of the pride words indicative of God's characteristics? Yes: The gāʾôn family is used of God's majesty: "majesty", "triumphed gloriously", "robed in majesty" (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10); "Majesty" is used as a name for God (Heb 1:3; 8:1); The mocking words are used of God's derision: "He who sits in the heavens laughs" (Psa 2:4); "Toward the scorners he is scornful" (Pro 3:34); God is never the subject of a boast in these verses. He is its right object: "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (Jer 9:24).

15258.text: God's height is his own, shown in acts, and not overturned: "robed in majesty ... you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2). "In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries" (Exo 15:7); Majesty goes with what only God does: abasing every proud one and saving by his own hand (Job 40:10–14); "God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7); Human pride, in the verses' own words, is a standing taken or assumed; "you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" (2Th 2:4); "By the strength of my hand I have done it" (Isa 10:13); "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Gal 6:3); Mostly, pride holds as its own what was given; "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7); In story: Uzziah's strength, Hezekiah's healing, Nebuchadnezzar's God-given majesty, the cherub's beauty, the cedar's height (2Ch 26:15–16; 32:24–25; Dan 5:18–20; Eze 28:17; 31:9–10); This matches the researcher's "mostly assumed": the standing is real, but it is taken up as if it were not received.

15259.text: Refinement 1: "undisputed" in the sense of never overturned. God's majesty is disputed: by the enemy at the sea (Exo 15:9), by "all that is proud and lofty" (Isa 2:12), and by the kings "against the Lord and against his Anointed" (Psa 2:2). Every dispute ends with the one who rose brought down, and God's derision is his answer to it (Psa 2:4).

15261.text: The Son: His majesty is "received ... from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17); It stands beside his being "delivered into the hands of men" (Luk 9:43–44); His seat is taken "after making purification for sins" (Heb 1:3); He is preeminent because the fullness dwells in him (Col 1:18–19); He is mocked on that very standing ("Hail, King of the Jews!"), and he answers "Father, forgive them" (Luk 23:34); I read: in the Son, majesty that is undisputed does not defend itself against mockery. This bears on 13.1 Lowering himself (M09) and on the researcher's ruling that Jesus' own acts get their 13.1 face (#2148).

15262.text: Other beings, held and not read in: Leviathan, "king over all the sons of pride" (Job 41:34): 13.4; A messenger of Satan given against conceit (2Co 12:7), and "the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6): 13.3; Angels who do not blaspheme where the willful do (2Pe 2:11), and an angel mediator (Job 33:23): 13.2.

15263.text: Given, then held as one's own: 1Co 4:7, and the kings' accounts. This bears on Ch 12 claim C-209, which now has much wider support: Pride against hearing: Jer 13:15–17; Pro 13:10; the scoffer who will not be rebuked (Pro 13:1; 15:12; 9:7–8). This bears on 10.2 Humility and hearing; Presumption: acting where not sent, speaking what was not commanded (Deu 1:43; 18:20). This bears on 10.7; Pride over others: the poor, the widow, the righteous; contempt; mocking the poor (Pro 17:5). This bears on 10.10 and OT-105; The boast moved to God, and boasting in weakness (Jer 9:23–24; 1Co 1:31; 2Co 12:9). This bears on Ch 12 claim C-182 and Ch 11 §4; Pride against love (1Co 8:1; 13:4), against rest (Hab 2:5 against Psa 131:2), and in place of mourning (1Co 5:2); The other face (2Ch 17:6; Psa 138:3; Psa 47:4; Isa 60:15) goes to Ch 11 §4, as a change of character.

15275.text: The mind set on earthly things: Words: phroneō (G5426, M63); Where: 10.4; beside "Set your minds on things that are above" (Col 3:2; Ch 2 The body raised).

15277.text: E. Majesty (G3168 megaleiotēs, G3172 megalōsynē): "Majesty" in Heb 1:3 and 8:1, Jude 25, and the "majesty" of God and of Christ in Luk 9:43 and 2Pe 1:16. Under #1982 these go to God's character (13.1). The sixth verse is Act 19:27, the "magnificence" of Artemis.

15279.text: This is where the change-of-character reading (#1919) would start. No reading has been done: H1347 gāʾôn: human "pride" (25) versus God's "majesty" (9) versus "the thicket of the Jordan" (3); H1361 gābah: "proud" and "haughty" (Eze 28:2, 5; 2Ch 26:16; 32:25) versus "towered" and "higher" (physical) versus "exalted" of God (Isa 5:16) and of the servant (Isa 52:13); H1364 gābōah and H1363 gōbah: high walls and tall men versus "haughty eyes" and "a haughty spirit" (Pro 16:18); G2744 kauchaomai: "boast" versus "rejoice" (Rom 5:2–3, 11). Boasting in oneself versus "let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17); H1984H hālal: "boast" versus "glory" and "exult" (Jer 9:24, "let him who boasts boast in this"); G1702 empaizō: Jesus "mocked" in the passion accounts versus Herod "tricked" by the magi (Mat 2:16); H7292 rāhab: "insolent" (Isa 3:5) versus "plead urgently" (Pro 6:3) versus "overwhelm" (Song 6:5).

15282.text: Verses with no other M-code (96). Most are height as a measure: Exo 25 to 38, 1Ki 6 to 7, Eze 40 to 42, and Goliath in 1Sa 17:4. Others are central to the cluster: Paul's boasting: Rom 15:17, Gal 6:14, 1Co 1:31, 2Co 10:17, 2Co 12:1, Eph 2:9; Jam 3:5, the tongue that "boasts of great things"; Isa 3:16, the daughters of Zion "haughty"; the mocking of Jesus: Mat 27:31, Mat 27:41, Mar 15:20, Luk 23:36; 2Ki 2:23, the boys who jeered Elisha.

15283.text: The gāʾôn and gaʾăwāh pairs are the stacked pride sayings, for example Jer 48:29 and Isa 16:6.
