15295.text: The words for God and for people are the same. gāʾôn, gaʾăwāh, gēʾût and gāʾāh are God's majesty (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10) and human pride (Isa 9:9; Jer 48:29; Pro 16:18).

15296.text: The height words are the same. gābah and rûm are God being high (Psa 138:6; Isa 57:15) and the heart lifted up (2Ch 26:16; Dan 5:20).

15299.text: God's height is his own: "robed in majesty ... you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2); It is shown in acts: "In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries" (Exo 15:7); It is challenged (Exo 15:9; Isa 2:12; Psa 2:2), but never overturned: "God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7).

15301.text: Pride is the given held as one's own: "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7); In story, each time:; "when he was strong, he grew proud" (2Ch 26:16); "did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud" (2Ch 32:25); "when his heart was lifted up" (Dan 5:20); "your heart has become proud in your wealth" (Eze 28:5); "its heart was proud of its height" (Eze 31:10); In the law it is foreseen: "your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord your God ... Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth'" (Deu 8:14, 17); It credits its own hand. "By the strength of my hand I have done it", said by the one who was the Lord's rod: "Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it" (Isa 10:13, 15). And "which I have built by my mighty power" (Dan 4:30); I read: the line the verses draw is not between having height and having none. It is the source and the direction. Height that is one's own by nature belongs to God alone. Height that is given is held from him. Pride is the given taken as one's own, and turned against the giver or over others. This is the researcher's "assumed position", in the verses' own words.

15304.text: The same claim in other words: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isa 14:14); "you have said, 'I am a god' ... though you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "proclaiming himself to be God" (2Th 2:4).

15305.text: And it deceives: "The pride of your heart has deceived you" (Obd 3); "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jer 49:16).

15306.text: This line runs through every batch: "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jer 13:15); "if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride" (13:17); "By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom" (Pro 13:10); The scoffer: "does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12); "Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you" (9:8); "do not scoff ... Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23); Presumption acts on its own word:; the prophet "who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him" (Deu 18:20); "you would not listen; but you rebelled ... and presumptuously went up" (Deu 1:43); not obeying the decision given (Deu 17:12); The messengers mocked "until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16); God works to keep pride from a person; "he opens the ears of men ... that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17); "to keep me from becoming conceited ... a thorn was given me" (2Co 12:7); The opposite named for pride is hearing, or fear; "So do not become proud, but fear" (Rom 11:20); "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance ... I hate" (Pro 8:13).

15307.text: Pride is rarely alone in these verses. It stands over someone: the poor: "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor" (Psa 10:2); "Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker" (Pro 17:5); the widow: "tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries" (Pro 15:25); the needy left unaided: "pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy" (Eze 16:49); the righteous: "speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt" (Psa 31:18); the insolent who deride, smear and dig pits (Psa 119:51, 69, 85); with a closed heart: "They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly" (Psa 17:10); set against love, and among the things that divide: "'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up" (1Co 8:1); "love ... is not arrogant" (1Co 13:4); "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26); felt from below: "Our soul has had more than enough ... of the contempt of the proud" (Psa 123:4).

15314.text: What it is set against, God answers otherwise: "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psa 138:6); God's derision answers only those who rise against him (Psa 2:2–4; 59:7–8; Pro 1:24–26; 3:34). In these verses it is never aimed at the weak.

15316.text: The same words are not pride when the height is given, or turned toward God: "His heart was courageous [lifted up] in the ways of the Lord" (2Ch 17:6), with gābah, the word used of Uzziah's proud heart; "my strength of soul you increased" (Psa 138:3), with rāhab, elsewhere "insolent" (Isa 3:5); the honour God gives (Psa 47:4; Isa 4:2; 60:15; Nah 2:2); the boast in the Lord; "my heart is not lifted up ... I have calmed and quieted my soul" (Psa 131:1–2), set against the arrogant man "never at rest" (Hab 2:5).

15318.text: His seat comes after purification for sins. "After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high" (Heb 1:3).

15322.text: He is mocked on that very standing, as king, as prophet and as saviour (Mat 27:29; Luk 22:64; Mar 15:31). He "made no answer" (Luk 23:9), and he prays "Father, forgive them" (Luk 23:34).

15332.text: It always faces someone: "before me" (1Ki 21:29); "before the Lord" (2Ki 22:19); "before the God of his fathers" (2Ch 33:12); "before your God" (Dan 10:12); Zedekiah's failure is put as "He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the Lord" (2Ch 36:12). Humbling before the prophet is humbling before the word he carries; Most verses in this group name before whom. Of the rest, 2Ch 12:6 and 2Ch 30:11 answer a word just brought, and Lev 26:41 goes with confession (26:40). Isa 58:3–5 is a fast addressed to God.

15333.text: It answers a word heard: Rehoboam and the princes humble themselves when Shemaiah brings "You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you". What they say is "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:5–6); Josiah humbles himself "when you heard how I spoke against this place" (2Ki 22:19; 2Ch 34:27); Ahab does so "when Ahab heard those words" (1Ki 21:27); Belshazzar is charged: "you … have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this" (Dan 5:22). He had the word, in his father's story, and did not bow to it.

15336.text: What goes with it: saying "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); tearing clothes, sackcloth, fasting, going about "dejectedly" (1Ki 21:27); weeping (2Ki 22:19); entreating and praying (2Ch 33:12–13); fasting and seeking (Ezr 8:21); the condition "humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways" (2Ch 7:14); confession, and making amends for iniquity (Lev 26:40–41).

15344.text: A humbling God does not take knowledge of: Isa 58:3–5: The people ask: "Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"; The answer: "in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers", and "you fast only to quarrel and to fight"; The form is named and set aside: "Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him?"; The fast God chooses is turned to others: "to loose the bonds of wickedness … to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him" (58:6–7); Compare Ahab. His sackcloth and fasting were seen and answered (1Ki 21:27–29); I read: the outward acts are the same. What differs, by the two passages, is what goes with them. Ahab acts "when Ahab heard those words", against himself. In Isa 58 the fast is kept alongside self-pleasure and oppression. The humbling that is not taken knowledge of is one that leaves the seen poor unseen (58:7). This joins OT-105; 10.1, 10.7 and 13.1 already cite Isa 58:3, 5. The reading here is for the humbling side.

15352.text: What is brought low is named, and it is the bearing of a person, not only a rank: "The haughty looks of man … the lofty pride of men" (Isa 2:11, 17); "all that is proud and lofty … all that is lifted up" (Isa 2:12); "the eyes of the haughty" (Isa 5:15); "the pomp of the arrogant … the pompous pride of the ruthless" (Isa 13:11); Moab's "pompous pride together with the skill of his hands" (Isa 25:11); "your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down" (2Sa 22:28); "the haughty eyes you bring down" (Psa 18:27).

15355.text: Who can do it: Job is told: "look on everyone who is proud and abase him … bring him low" (Job 40:11–12). He is told this as a challenge he cannot meet: "Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you" (40:14); "not from the east or from the west … comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:6–7); "he brings low and he exalts" (1Sa 2:7); "I bring low the high tree, and make high the low tree" (Eze 17:24); "Exalt that which is low, and bring low that which is exalted" (Eze 21:26), as the crown is taken from the profane prince; God "sets over it the lowliest of men" (Dan 4:17); "The Lord lifts up the humble; he casts the wicked to the ground" (Psa 147:6); "You save a humble people" (2Sa 22:28; Psa 18:27; "humble" is H6041).

15358.text: Isa 26:5–6: "he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city … The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy." The proud city brought low is walked on by the poor. It sits beside "You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you" (26:3).

15360.text: Pro 25:6–7: "Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great, for it is better to be told, 'Come up here,' than to be put lower in the presence of a noble." This is the same teaching as Luk 14:8–11 (carried, no-other-M-code reading A). The lowering is chosen in advance, before another must do it.

15366.text: Isa 25:5 is data for M09. Its neighbour "you have been a stronghold to the poor" (25:4) belongs to OT-105.

15369.text: Data: Isa 29:4, Isa 32:19, Isa 40:4, Isa 25:12, Dan 7:24.

15370.text: OT-105 (the poor as seen by another). Isa 58:7, "when you see the naked, to cover him", as the fast God chooses. Isa 25:4 and 26:6, the poor beside the proud brought low. Psa 113:6–7, God looking low and raising the poor. To add as items when the account is approved.

15385.text: The humble hear what God did for another, and are glad: "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2). David's own deliverance follows: "I sought the Lord, and he answered me" (34:4). The superscription sets it after "he changed his behavior before Abimelech"; "When the humble see it they will be glad" (Psa 69:32). "It" is the deliverance of the speaker, who has said "I am afflicted and in pain" (69:29); I read: in both psalms, one man's boast is in the Lord, not in himself, and the humble are those who are glad at it. Their gladness is at what God did for someone else.

15386.text: The meek, beside not fretting. "Refrain from anger, and forsake wrath! Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil. For the evildoers shall be cut off, but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land … But the meek shall inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace" (Psa 37:8–11): The meek inherit what "those who wait for the Lord" inherit; Meekness stands where the psalm has just said "Refrain from anger … Fret not yourself" about the prospering wicked; Compare Num 12:3 (carried): Moses "very meek" where he is spoken against; I read: in both places meekness stands where another provokes, and the one who is meek leaves the answer to God.

15392.text: Walking humbly. "With what shall I come before the Lord, and bow myself before God on high? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings …? … He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Mic 6:6–8): The question is about what to bring. The answer is a way to walk; "humbly" (H6800A, its only use) is "with your God": a walk in company, not a gift handed over.

15393.text: Set against religious acts in three passages: the fast (Isa 58:3–7, batch 1); offerings (Mic 6:6–8); the house and the sacrifices (Isa 66:1–3, group III).

15403.text: Eze 17:14: "that the kingdom might be humble and not lift itself up, and keep his covenant that it might stand." The humble state is set by a covenant under oath. The king "rebelled … by sending his ambassadors to Egypt", and "whose oath he despised" (17:15–16). The verse names the kingdom's humbleness as the condition of its standing. The rebellion is the lifting up.

15405.text: The seven verses decided "thread" are those where the verse is about the afflicted being oppressed or crying out. They are already coded in the poor/needy split (P or G) and carried by OT-105. Two of them name the heart: "you will strengthen their heart" (Psa 10:17), and "May your hearts live forever!" (Psa 22:26).

15410.text: M08 Pride: Zep 3:11–12, Pro 11:2, Pro 18:12 and Psa 138:6 hold the pairing. It is checked against Ch 12 at the cross-check.

15411.text: M47 (#1979): Isa 57:15 (spirit, heart), Isa 66:2 (spirit), Psa 69:32 and Psa 22:26 (hearts), and Pro 18:12 (heart). Their Ch 4 and Ch 6 placements are checked at the cross-check.

15412.text: Already cited: Isa 57:15 in Ch 2, 4, 6 and 14; Isa 66:2 in Ch 6, 10.1, 10.9 and 10.12; Mic 6:8 in 10.8 and 10.13; Zep 2:3 and Psa 76:9 in 10.13 (Psa 76:9 also in 10.12); Psa 69:32 in Ch 2 and 4; Psa 37:11 in 10.1; Psa 22:26 in Ch 4 and 10.9; Psa 10:17 in 10.6; Job 24:4 in 10.11.

15414.text: Psa 138:6: God's act: "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly"; Set against: "the haughty he knows from afar".

15419.text: Job 5:11: God's act: "he sets on high those who are lowly" (Eliphaz).

15425.text: afflicted: Verses: Psa 9:12; 10:12; 10:17; 22:26; Amo 2:7; Where the verse speaks of: their cry, their oppression, God not forgetting them.

15429.text: Psa 51:17: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.": What it is set against: "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering" (51:16); What comes before: "Deliver me from bloodguiltiness" (51:14). The spirit and heart are broken over the speaker's own sin; What it is called: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit". It takes the place of the offering; The next verses: "then will you delight in right sacrifices" (51:19). The offerings are not abolished. They follow the broken heart; This is a fourth passage where what God looks to is set against a religious act. The others are Isa 58:3–7, Mic 6:6–8 and Isa 66:1–3 (batches 1 and 2). In Psa 51 the contrast is the speaker's own, and the next verses take it back up; "Contrite" here is H1794 (M10). "Broken" is H7665 (M24/T3). No M09 word is in the verse.

15431.text: Psa 34:18: "The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.": Its setting: "When the righteous cry for help, the Lord hears" (34:17), and "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers him out of them all" (34:19); Here the broken heart is the righteous man's, under affliction, not over his sin; God is "near" to it. Compare Isa 57:15, "I dwell … with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (batch 2); "Crushed" here is the M09 word H1793A.

15448.text: 3: Verse: Eze 6:9; Word: H7665; Of God: "I have been broken".

15450.text: H1793A dakkāʾ: Faces in batch 3: crushed in spirit, whom God saves (Psa 34:18) · contrite with the lowly, whom God revives (Isa 57:15); What differs: the only M09 word in the set. Both times it is God who meets it.

15456.text: Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5–6 quote Pro 3:34 (batch 2): "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.": In James it follows the passions at war within and "friendship with the world is enmity with God" (4:1–4). The humbling runs on as submitting, drawing near, cleansing, purifying hearts and mourning (4:7–10; the no-other-M-code reading); In Peter: "Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you" (1Pe 5:6–7); Humbling oneself "under the mighty hand" goes in one sentence with casting one's anxieties on him; I read: here humbling oneself is placing oneself under God's hand and letting go of what one carries, on the ground that "he cares for you"; The exalting is "at the proper time". It is God's to time.

15465.text: Where it comes from, in three verbs: Given: "the fruit of the Spirit is … gentleness" (Gal 5:22–23). In the same passage: "Let us not become conceited" (5:26); Pursued: "Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness" (1Ti 6:11). It is pursued in flight from "the love of money" (6:10); Put on: Col 3:12 (group III).

15466.text: Where it is: "let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious" (1Pe 3:4). It is in the heart, hidden, and precious "in God's sight".

15470.text: Paul, brought low and lowering himself: "I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound … I have learned … to be content" (Phili 4:11–12). Being brought low is a circumstance here, met with contentment, "through him who strengthens me" (4:13); "did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God's gospel to you free of charge?" (2Cor 11:7). A lowering taken on for others' good. I read: this has the shape of Phili 2: lowered so that another is raised; "I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented" (2Cor 12:21). Here Paul is humbled by others' unrepented sin, and the humbling is joined to mourning over them. Compare Jer 23:9 (batch 3): the prophet's heart broken over what he sees; "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2Cor 7:6). G5011 here means downcast, after "fighting without and fear within" (7:5). God's comfort came through a person's arrival.

15479.text: M47 (#1979): Mat 11:29 (heart, souls), 1Pe 3:4 and 3:8 (heart), Jam 1:21 (souls), Jam 3:14 and 4:8 (hearts), Luk 1:51 (hearts). Checked at the cross-check.

15480.text: Already cited: Jam 1:21 in Ch 14; Phili 2:8 in Ch 2; 1Pe 3:15 in 10.12; Jam 4:6 in Ch 11 and 13.1; 2Cor 7:6 in 10.6; 1Pe 3:4 in Ch 1 and Ch 9; Col 3:12 in 10.7 and Ch 11; 1Cor 4:21 in 10.10 and 10.7; Phili 3:21 in Ch 2; 2Ti 2:25 in 13.3; 1Pe 5:5 and Tit 3:2 in 10.10; Mat 11:29 in Ch 11; Jam 3:13 in 10.6.

15487.text: Eph 4:2–3: Humility named: "with all humility and gentleness"; Beside it: "with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit".

15488.text: Col 3:12–13: Humility named: "Put on … humility, meekness"; Beside it: compassionate hearts, kindness, patience, "bearing with one another … forgiving each other"; Against it: after "put … away: anger, wrath, malice" (3:8).

15494.text: Rom 10:3: "being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness." They had "a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge" (10:2). The refusal to submit is the building of one's own righteousness. Compare the Pharisee's list in Luk 18:11–12 (batch 4).

15498.text: What it is joined to inwardly: "conscience" (Rom 13:5); "mindful of God" (1Pe 2:19); "reverence for Christ" (Eph 5:21); "hoped in God", and "do not fear anything that is frightening" (1Pe 3:5–6); in 1Pe 3:1–4 the submission of a wife is set beside "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (batch 4).

15504.text: God puts all things under Christ: "God has put all things in subjection under his feet" (1Cor 15:27); "he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church" (Eph 1:22); "at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him" (1Pe 3:22); "it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come" (Heb 2:5).

15506.text: Not yet seen, and the one made lower: "putting everything in subjection under his feet … At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death" (Heb 2:8–9): The subjection of all things is not yet seen. What is seen is Jesus made lower, and crowned because of the suffering of death; This is the shape of Phili 2:8–9 (batch 4): lowered, then exalted; The word "made lower" (Heb 2:7, 9) is G1642 elattoō "to make less", filed under T3. It was not in this fan-out's pull. It is named for the OT/NT and Jesus analysis that follows.

15507.text: The boy Jesus, submissive: "he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart" (Luk 2:51): This follows "Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" (2:49); The Son who knows his Father's house goes down and is subject to Mary and Joseph; Then "Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man" (2:52); Cited in Ch 4 (for Mary's heart), not for his submission.

15510.text: From this batch: Christ under whom all things are put (1Cor 15:27; Eph 1:22; 1Pe 3:22; Heb 2:5, 8) and the Son himself subject (1Cor 15:28; Luk 2:51); Jesus "made lower" and crowned because of the suffering of death (Heb 2:7, 9). The word G1642 elattoō (T3) is outside the pull. It also stands in "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Joh 3:30). Both are to be checked in the analysis; Christ as the example of submission under wrong (1Pe 2:21); The ground given for submission is Christ ("reverence for Christ", "as to the Lord", "for the Lord's sake"); The OT words read in batches 1–3 carry no submission verb of this kind. The nearest are Gen 16:9 (Hagar told to submit), Psa 81:11 ("Israel would not submit to me") and 2Ch 30:8 ("yield yourselves to the Lord"). The OT side of the analysis is to be checked against those.

15532.text: Luk 14:11: "For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.": Setting: a parable told "when he noticed how they chose the places of honor" (14:7). The guest who sits high may be moved down "with shame". The guest who sits low may hear "Friend, move up higher" and "be honored in the presence of all" (14:9–10); Humbling here is choosing the lower place yourself, before anyone sets you there. Honour or shame is then given by the host, not taken; In the same passage Jesus turns to the host: "invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind … because they cannot repay you" (14:13–14). The humble guest and the guests who are poor stand side by side in one teaching. The guest gives up a claim to a seat. The host gives where nothing comes back; Not cited in the narrative.

15533.text: Mat 23:12: the same saying, in another setting: Setting: Jesus forbids the titles rabbi, father and instructor (23:8–10): "The greatest among you shall be your servant" (23:11). It is followed at once by the woes on the hypocrites; Here humbling oneself is refusing a title that sets you over the brothers. The saying sits between the servant and the hypocrite; 23:3–4 are cited in 10.7. 23:12 is not.

15539.text: The anointing at Bethany: Mar 14:3–9; Mat 26:6–13; Joh 12:1–8: The objection: the ointment "could have been sold … and given to the poor" (Mar 14:5; Mat 26:9; Joh 12:5); Who raises it, and how:; Mark: "some … said to themselves indignantly", and "they scolded her" (14:4–5); Matthew: "the disciples … were indignant" (26:8); John: Judas, and John gives the motive: "He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it" (12:6); Jesus' answer: "you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me" (Mar 14:7; Mat 26:11; Joh 12:8).

15542.text: Mar 12:42; Luk 21:3: "a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins". Jesus says she "has put in more than all those who are contributing … For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on" (Mar 12:43–44; Luk 21:3–4): The measure is what is left, not what is given: "out of their abundance" against "out of her poverty … all she had to live on"; In Mark the scene follows directly on the scribes "who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers" (12:40). The poor widow gives everything at the treasury, while those who devour widows pray at length for show; I read: the verses name no inner word for her. What they give is the measure Jesus sets; Mar 12:38–44 are cited in 10.5 (the long prayers and the widow; M18 group G). The M09 verse 12:42 and the Luke parallel are not.

15552.text: M64's 41 choose verses with no other M-code were parked as having "no significant additional bearing" (OT-93). The M09 set is different: 23 of the 27 carry inner-being bearing in their passage (groups A to E, less Jer 39:10); Seven of them are the plainest humility verses in the cluster (group A); The other M-codes sit in the neighbouring verses, for example M08 pride in Jam 4:6, Luk 1:51 and Luk 14:7–10, and M02 anger in Mar 14:4 and Mat 26:8.

15555.text: Eight passages have no citation at all: Luk 14:7–14, Luk 18:18–30, 2Ch 30, Joh 12:1–8, Mar 14:3–9, Pro 28:1–6, Luk 21:1–4, Jer 39:9–10.

15557.text: B: What the verses say: "The poor" spoken of by others to judge an act of devotion, and a motive hidden behind the words.; Verses: Mar 14:5, Mat 26:9, Mat 26:11, Joh 12:5, Joh 12:6, Joh 12:8 (6; one event in three Gospels).

15558.text: C: What the verses say: Giving out of poverty, measured by what is left, not by the amount.; Verses: Mar 12:42, Luk 21:3 (2; one event in two Gospels).

15561.text: F: What the verses say: The M09 word with no humility or poverty sense here (data).; Verses: Judg 11:33 "subdued", Lev 14:37 "deeper", 1Ti 3:4 "submissive" (3).

15564.text: 3. Needy as an expression to get sympathy or help: What these 27 verses show: Not in these 27, from the poor themselves. No poor person here speaks. Lazarus "desired to be fed" but says nothing. What appears is another face: others speak of the poor, and in John the words of care are a pretext (Joh 12:6). Whether "needy" said by the needy is aimed at help is a matter for the "I am poor and needy" Psalms (Psa 86:1, 70:5, 40:17, 109:22) and Pro 18:23 "The poor use entreaties"..

15569.text: The passage (5:8–16) is Eliphaz's counsel: "As for me, I would seek God" (5:8). It ends "So the poor: have hope, and injustice shuts her mouth" (5:16). The words match what the rest of Scripture says of; the lowly raised. But the book's practice with Job's friends is to name the speaker, and to note that; God's verdict stands over them: "you have not spoken of me what is right" (Job 42:7). This is done; for Bildad in Ch 2 and 10.12 (claim C-153). So if it is used at all, it must carry that frame; "those who mourn are lifted to safety" and "the poor have hope" are inner-being words: mourning; and hope.

15570.text: For OT-97.17 itself: nothing new for M09. Isa 57:15, Jam 1:9 and Eze 21:26 are already in 10.14,: and the M18 part was superseded by OT-105. The item can be closed as carried.

15571.text: Isa 57:15: M08 note: the high and holy One dwells with the contrite and lowly spirit; Also supports: M47 (done under OT-97.71).

15573.text: Eze 17:24: M08 note: I bring low the high tree and make high the low tree; Also supports: M53.

15575.text: Job 5:11: M08 note: he sets on high those who are lowly; Also supports: M22.

15576.text: Ecc 5:8: M08 note: oppression of the poor; the high official watched by a higher; Also supports: M12.

15577.text: Eze 17:24: What it adds: the reversal's purpose ("shall know that I am the Lord") and certainty ("I have spoken, and I will do it"); Where: 10.14 Only God does it (one sentence).

15578.text: Job 5:11, 16: What it adds: the lowly raised, the mourners lifted, the poor given hope, in Eliphaz's mouth; Where: only with the speaker named and Job 42:7 noted; or leave out.

15579.text: Ecc 5:8: What it adds: the onlooker told "do not be amazed" at the oppression of the poor; Where: forward to OT-105 (not woven now).

15580.text: Close as carried: What it means: close OT-97.17; forward Ecc 5:8 to OT-105.

15581.text: Add Eze 17:24 (and Job 5 with its frame), then close: What it means: one or two sentences in 10.14, with claims; Ecc 5:8 forward to OT-105; close.

15583.text: The `self` pattern catches more than it should. Only five of its ten hits are a speaker calling himself poor: 1Sa 18:23, Psa 40:17, Psa 70:5, Psa 86:1 and Psa 109:22. The other five are Luk 4:18, Isa 61:1, Luk 19:8, Job 29:16 and Job 30:25. The markers are a working aid only: they point to verses to read and decide nothing.

15587.text: Poor or needy said by the speaker as the ground of a plea: "answer me, for I am poor and needy" (Psa 86:1); "I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God!" (Psa 70:5); "As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psa 40:17).

15589.text: The poor appealing to others: "The poor use entreaties, but the rich answer roughly" (Pro 18:23); "you hear the desire of the afflicted" (Psa 10:17); "he cry to the Lord against you" (Deu 15:9).

15590.text: Note for reading. In Psa 40:17, 70:5, 86:1 and 109:22, "poor" in "poor and needy" is H6041 ʿānî, which is tagged M24, and "needy" is H0034 (M09). This was checked in `verse_lexical`. These verses therefore sit on both sides of the M09 / M24 line.

15591.text: Seeing is often named. These are quoted, not read: "Blessed is the one who considers the poor!" (Psa 41:1); "if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing" (Job 31:19); "If you see in a province the oppression of the poor" (Ecc 5:8); "Whoever has a bountiful eye … shares his bread with the poor" (Pro 22:9); "he who hides his eyes will get many a curse" (Pro 28:27); "your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother" (Deu 15:9); "His eyes stealthily watch for the helpless" (Psa 10:8).

15592.text: What the sight moves in a person, as the verses name it (G-person): "Was not my soul grieved for the needy?" (Job 30:25); "He has pity on the weak and the needy" (Psa 72:13, the king); "you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand" (Deu 15:7); "an unworthy thought in your heart" (Deu 15:9); "Whoever mocks the poor … he who is glad at calamity" (Pro 17:5); "The poor is disliked even by his neighbor" (Pro 14:20); "All a poor man's brothers hate him" (Pro 19:7); "the poor man's wisdom is despised" (Ecc 9:16); "These are only the poor; they have no sense" (Jer 5:4); "no one remembered that poor man" (Ecc 9:15); "the very thing I was eager to do" (Gal 2:10); "pleased to make some contribution for the poor" (Rom 15:26); "not because he cared about the poor" (Joh 12:6); "the master of the house became angry and said … bring in the poor" (Luk 14:21).

15593.text: What the sight moves in God (G-God): "Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, I will now arise," says the Lord (Psa 12:5); "But you do see … to you the helpless commits himself" (Psa 10:14); "he does not forget the cry of the afflicted" (Psa 9:12); "he regards the prayer of the destitute" (Psa 102:17); "I the Lord will answer them" (Isa 41:17); "He raises the poor from the dust" (Psa 113:7; 1Sa 2:8).

15596.text: Surface: humble (9), afflicted (5), poor (4), meek (4). This one word is rendered on both sides of the cluster's definition. Examples: "the meek" (Num 12:3 of Moses; Psa 37:11); "the humble" (Pro 3:34; Psa 25:9); "the afflicted" (Psa 9:12; 10:12); "the poor" (Isa 61:1; Pro 16:19).

15597.text: D. H1793A dakkāʾ "contrite": Isa 57:15 ("contrite and lowly spirit") and Psa 34:18 ("crushed in spirit"). Both are cited in the narrative.

15601.text: This is where the change-of-character reading (#1919) would start. No reading has been done: H3665 kānaʿ: "humbled himself" (kings in 2Ch, 1Ki 21:29, 2Ki 22:19) versus "subdued" (nations in Judg, 1Sa 7:13, 2Sa 8:1, 1Ch 18:1, Psa 81:14). It is the same verb for humbling oneself before God and for being brought low by another; H8217 šāphāl: "lowly" (Isa 57:15; Psa 138:6; Pro 29:23) versus "deeper than the skin" (Lev 13 and 14, leprosy, 4 verses) versus "low" of a vine and a kingdom (Eze 17; 29:14–15); G5012 tapeinophrosynē: "humility" (Phili 2:3; Col 3:12; Eph 4:2; 1Pe 5:5; Act 20:19) versus "asceticism" (Col 2:18, 23); H6035 ʿānāw: humble / afflicted / poor / meek, as in §3C; H1800 dal: poor / weak / "haggard" (2Sa 13:4, Amnon); G4434 ptōchos: poor / "worthless" (Gal 4:9, the elementary principles).

15640.text: I read: the main lines run through both testaments without a break. The NT quotes the OT on three of them. It repeats the words of two more without a formula (Psa 37:11 / Mat 5:5; and Pro 25:7 / Luk 14:10 in substance).

15650.text: The source named also changes. Gentleness is "the fruit of the Spirit" (Gal 5:22–23), and the mind of the flesh "does not submit … indeed, it cannot" (Rom 8:7). The OT verses read name God reviving the lowly (Isa 57:15) and the heart being humbled (Lev 26:41). They do not name an inner source given for it.

15652.text: What he taught happens to him. "he humbled himself … Therefore God has highly exalted him" (Phili 2:8–9). "made lower than the angels … crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death" (Heb 2:9). I read: the shape of the saying he taught (humbles himself, is exalted) is the shape told of him. Phili 2:9's "Therefore" joins his humbling to his exaltation. The tie back to the saying in Luke is mine.

15654.text: All things are put under him, and he is subject to the Father: "God has put all things in subjection under his feet" (1Cor 15:27; Eph 1:22; 1Pe 3:22; Heb 2:8); The bridge to the OT is in the text; Psa 8 says it of "man": "Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor … you have put all things under his feet" (Psa 8:5–6); Heb 2 quotes the psalm and reads it as "namely Jesus" (2:6–9). It adds: "At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him" (2:8–9); "Made lower" is H2637 in the psalm and G1642 in Hebrews, both T3; I read: the lowering said of man in Psa 8 is said of Jesus in Heb 2, and the subjection of all things to man is said of the Son. At the end, the Son "himself" is subjected to the Father (1Cor 15:28).

15657.text: OT: God "looks far down" and raises the poor (Psa 113:6–7); "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly" (Psa 138:6); he dwells with the contrite and lowly "to revive" (Isa 57:15); "your gentleness made me great" (2Sa 22:36; Psa 18:35); "I have been broken over their whoring heart" (Eze 6:9).

15666.text: Taking the lower place: OT: "better to be told, 'Come up here,' than to be put lower in the presence of a noble" (Pro 25:7); NT: "go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, 'Friend, move up higher'" (Luk 14:10).

15672.text: God lowering himself: OT: "who looks far down on the heavens and the earth? He raises the poor" (Psa 113:6–7); "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly" (Psa 138:6); "I dwell … also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isa 57:15); "your gentleness made me great" (2Sa 22:36); NT: "who, though he was in the form of God … emptied himself … humbled himself" (Phili 2:6–8); "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29).

15680.text: The verses do not name humility as a feeling. They name: an act, humbling oneself, done "before" God or before his word, with the heart named as where it happens (batch 1 group I); a standing, being humble, lowly or meek: the humble seek God, are taught and favored, and are glad at another's deliverance (batch 2 group I); a quality that is sought and walked in: "seek humility", "walk humbly with your God", "humility comes before honor", with the fear of the Lord, with wisdom and beside listening to reproof (batch 2 group II); a state of the spirit: a lowly and contrite spirit, a broken heart, which God dwells with, looks to, is near to and heals (batches 2 III and 3 I); a place taken among people: the lower seat, the servant, the title refused (Luk 14:7–11; Mat 23:8–12; Pro 25:6–7); something done to a person: God humbles to test and teach (Deu 8), and brings the proud low (batch 1 groups II and III); God's own way: he "looks far down", "your gentleness made me great", "I have been broken over their whoring heart".

15695.text: H5771 (avon) carries the same forgiveness-formula language as the other families: forgiving iniquity and transgression (Num 14:18, Exod 34:7), pardoning iniquity (Mic 7:18), and blotting out transgressions like mist (already cross-referenced in family G).

15701.text: H2342J and H2342K (chul, 9 verses combined, glossed to twist: dance and to twist: anticipate) have no bearing on moral perversion: every verse is literal, a woman dancing (2 Sam 3:29's negated wish), waiting anxiously (Ps 37:7, Mic 1:12, Judg 3:25), a dove sent out and waited for (Gen 8:10). The root's full range (dance, whirl, writhe in labor, wait) has nothing to do with corruption; it was pulled into this family only because one of its senses translates as twist. The two codes are gloss-homonym noise, not a shared concept.

15702.text: H7806 (shazar, 19 verses, the family's single largest strong) is glossed to twist, but every one of its 19 citations is literal tabernacle-construction material, fine twined linen repeated almost verbatim through Exodus 26 to 39 (curtains, the ephod, the breastpiece, the veil). It is technical textile vocabulary, not moral language at all; with the chul codes it accounts for 28 of the family's about 98 verses, a gloss-text-grouping failure of the same kind as family R and G0073.

15703.text: H5753A/B (avah) makes the metaphor's two halves visible in one root split into two codes: the physical sense (bent, bowed down in pain and anguish, Isa 21:3, Ps 38:6) and the moral sense (the confession formula we have sinned and acted perversely, 1 Kgs 8:47, 2 Chr 6:37, Dan 9:5) are literally the same Hebrew word, split only for cataloguing.

15704.text: The justice and judiciary sub-theme recurs strongly: H5557 (salaph) and H5791 (avat) are both explicitly about bribery and perverting legal judgment (a bribe subverts the cause of the righteous, Exod 23:8, Deut 16:19; does God pervert justice, Job 8:3, 34:12), and H6127 and H6140 apply the same crooked language to justice itself (justice goes forth perverted, Hab 1:4; make crooked all that is straight, Mic 3:9). This is the third family, after D and G, to converge independently on judicial and legal-fairness vocabulary: corruption of justice specifically, not wrongdoing in general.

15707.text: The same crushing verb is used destructively of enemies and redemptively of the self, with no lexical marker distinguishing the two. H1792 and H1794 (dakha, dakhah, to crush) are applied, in the same handful of verses, destructively, of enemies and oppressors crushed in judgment (you crushed Rahab like a carcass, Ps 89:10; crush the oppressor, Ps 72:4; the wicked who crush your people, Ps 94:5), and redemptively, of the self, as the state God desires and does not despise (a broken and contrite heart, Ps 51:17; him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, Isa 57:15), where crushed names the humbled disposition that draws God near. The Niphal and Pual senses of H1792 include both to be crushed and to be contrite in one entry; only the referent, an enemy or one's own heart, tells which reading applies.

15708.text: H2555 (chamas, violence, 43 verses) is the family's real anchor, structural and social and not incidental: it defines violence as a filled-world condition rather than isolated acts. The paradigm case is the pre-Flood indictment, the earth was filled with violence (Gen 6:11, 6:13); the recurring pattern afterward is social and structural: false witness (Ps 27:12, Exod 23:1), dishonest commerce and oppression of the poor (Ps 12:5, Amos 3:10), and a garment of violence worn by the wicked as a visible attribute (Ps 73:6, Ezek 7:23).

15719.text: G0073 (agōn) is not a vice at all but a positive athletic and military metaphor for perseverance. Every one of its 6 verses is Paul or Hebrews describing his own or the believer's faithful effort: fight the good fight of the faith (1 Tim 6:12), I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race (2 Tim 4:7), run with endurance the race that is set before us (Heb 12:1). Nothing in this strong's verse set describes wrongdoing, discord or a moral failure of any kind; its inclusion in the cluster looks like a gloss-text accident (the English word fight) and not a thematic match, a candidate for a cluster_strong review.

15724.text: H7379 (riv) is a distinct, formal legal and covenant-lawsuit term, not domestic quarrelling: case at law, dispute in court, and repeatedly God's own formal indictment against Israel or the nations (Mic 6:2, the LORD has an indictment against his people; Jer 25:31; Isa 41:21). This is forensic vocabulary, structurally closer to family D (crime and injustice) than to the Proverbs strife nouns it was grouped with.

15730.text: G0646 (apostasia) names departure from a founding standard (forsaking Mosaic custom, Acts 21:21; the eschatological rebellion, 2 Thess 2:3) rather than a relational breach as such.

15731.text: H5627 (sarah) adds a distinct instigation sense: it names speaking rebellion, inciting others toward covenant abandonment (Deut 13:5's false prophet who taught rebellion; Jer 28:16, 29:32, prophets who uttered or spoke rebellion against the LORD), a verbal-agency variant not present in the other members.

15735.text: H4879 (Job 19:4) is explicitly private and self-contained: my error remains with myself, offered as a defence that it harms no one else.

15742.text: H6601B (pathah) also appears in the heavenly-court scene where a spirit volunteers to entice Ahab to his death with God's own authorization (1 Kgs 22:20-22, repeated 2 Chr 18:19-21).

15745.text: Cruelty is defined by the absence of mercy, stated explicitly, not implied. Three of H0394's six verses use the near-identical formula cruel and have no mercy (Jer 6:23, 50:42) or merciless (Jer 30:14); Prov 12:10 makes the same point as a paradox, the mercy of the wicked is cruel, that is, even their gentlest disposition still qualifies as cruelty. Cruelty here is not a separate vice alongside mercilessness; the texts treat the two as the same fact stated twice.

15770.text: na'aph as a finite or infinitive-absolute verb form, narrating a specific act rather than naming a person: a narrated historical event (Jer 29:23, they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives), an infinitive-absolute generic sin-listing (Hos 4:2, Jer 23:14, Jer 7:9, adultery catalogued alongside swearing, lying, murder, stealing), and Jeremiah's extended covenant-infidelity metaphor (committing adultery with stone and tree, Jer 3:9; they have committed adultery, and blood is on their hands, Ezek 23:37).

15785.text: bagad as a finite verb form, narrating a specific act of treachery rather than labelling a class: individuals dealing treacherously with a specific party (Jer 12:6's brothers, 1 Sam 14:33's people, Judg 9:23's Shechem against Abimelech, Ps 78:57's fathers) and Israel and Judah dealing treacherously with God directly (Hos 6:7, Jer 3:20 twice, Jer 5:11 twice, Isa 48:8 twice, Jer 12:1).

15791.text: sarah (H5627, revolt) consistently as a noun naming spoken or taught rebellion against the Lord: a false prophet who taught rebellion (Deut 13:5), prophets who uttered or spoken rebellion (Jer 28:16, 29:32). The verbal-instigation register is distinct from bagad and ma'al's relational-betrayal register: this root names the act of articulating or teaching defection, not merely committing it.

15795.text: apostasia (G0646) at Acts 21:21 renders as the English verb forsake (teach to forsake Moses), but its own morph is N-ASF, a noun, not a verb. The Greek literally reads something like apostasy from Moses; the English surface restructures the noun-phrase into a verb clause, so the word's grammatical shape (an abstract-noun accusation of departure) differs from what the English sentence structure suggests (a direct verbal instruction to abandon).

15798.text: All 5 of sarah's occurrences carry noun morph (HNcfsa) yet 2 of them (Isa 1:5 rebel, Isa 31:6 revolted) render as English verbs, the same noun-rendered-as-verb pattern found for apostasia (G0646, Acts 21:21): two languages, two separately catalogued strongs, the same translation-restructuring move, an abstract Hebrew or Greek noun becoming an English finite verb. Worth checking whether this is a systematic ESV rendering habit for this whole semantic domain (apostasy and rebellion nouns) rather than two isolated cases.

15802.text: G0073 (agon) has real, coherent, human-relevant meaning: a struggle or contest, most often used in the NT as an athletic or perseverance metaphor for faithful endurance: fight the good fight of the faith (1 Tim 6:12), I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race (2 Tim 4:7), run with endurance the race that is set before us (Heb 12:1). None of its 6 occurrences describes a moral failure or an inner disposition toward wrongdoing.

15803.text: H2342J and H2342K (both chul, split by sense) have real, coherent meaning covering dancing, whirling, waiting anxiously and writhing in childbirth. Their combined 10 occurrences are literal in every case: a whirling storm-tempest (Jer 23:19, 30:23), a spindle or dance reference in a curse formula (2 Sam 3:29), the voice of the Lord making a deer give birth (Ps 29:9), a sword raging against cities (Hos 11:6), and anxious waiting (Ps 37:7, Gen 8:10, Judg 3:25, Mic 1:12). None describes moral perversion.

15804.text: H2342K's occurrences (the same root's wait or anticipate sense) are likewise all literal waiting, none moral: Ps 37:7's counsel to wait patiently, Gen 8:10's dove sent out and waited for, Judg 3:25's servants waiting outside a chamber, Mic 1:12's anxious waiting for good news.

15805.text: H7806 (shazar, to twist) has real, coherent meaning: a technical textile-craft term. All 19 occurrences are the tabernacle-construction formula fine twined linen, repeated near-verbatim through Exodus 26 to 39 (curtains, the ephod, the breastpiece, the veil, the screen). No occurrence has moral content.

15817.text: In Psalm 34:4-6 and 69:29-33 the poor man cries, and is heard: this poor man cried, and the Lord heard him and saved him out of all his troubles (34:4, 6); I am afflicted and in pain, the Lord hears the needy (69:29, 33). The poor man is the one who speaks, and his fear is among what he is delivered from (34:4).

15823.text: In Isa 57:15 and 1 Sam 16:7, both marked by the M08 strand's group B scan, the height word is not pride: it supports M47 (heart, spirit). In Isa 57:15 the height word is God's own height, set beside where he also dwells; in 1 Sam 16:7 it is the outward thing Samuel looked at, the height of his stature.

15824.text: Isa 57:15 also supports M09 (the lowly and contrite): God dwells with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly and the heart of the contrite. The main operation is God's dwelling with, and reviving, a lowly spirit and a contrite heart.

15826.text: A heart that cannot be quiet: the wicked are like the tossing sea, for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt; there is no peace, says my God, for the wicked (Isa 57:20-21). This is the figure of an inner state: restless, unable to be still, throwing up what is in it. The book already has the arrogant man never at rest (Hab 2:5) and the quieted soul of Psalm 131, but not this picture.

15827.text: 1 Sam 16:6 holds the seer's own thought, formed from what he saw: when they came, he looked on Eliab and thought, Surely the Lord's anointed is before him. The rebuke in 16:7 (man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart) answers that thought: even the prophet, sent by God to choose, made up his mind from the outside. The book quotes the principle but not the mistake it corrects.

15828.text: After the rebuke, the passage runs through seven sons (1 Sam 16:8-10), each passed over, to the youngest, out with the sheep (16:11-12): a structural point about the passage, the choice reached only after every son who looked fit has been refused.

15831.text: H2256? "cord" (filed under Grief): what it actually is in these verses: ropes, bowstring, a group of prophets, clouds (1Ki 20:31; Psa 11:2; 1Sa 10:10; Eze 31:10). [lexical: *ḥebel* = cord / pang]. Not grief here

15838.text: A stable heart means no fear [Claude reading: the text makes the heart's state the ground of fearlessness]: "His heart is steady; he will not be afraid" (Psa 112:8); "He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting" (112:7); "my heart shall not fear" (Psa 27:3); "Let not your heart faint … do not fear" (Deu 20:3; Isa 7:4; Jer 51:46); "Say to those who have an anxious heart, 'Be strong; fear not!'" (Isa 35:4); Revisit 2026-09-28: "Faint" here is *rak lēvāv*, the soft / tender heart. Read with context in Batch F §6: the heart yields to what blows on it, and fear spreads from heart to heart (Deu 20:8).; "Be strong" is *ḥāzaq*, the same verb as hardening (Batch G §3.3).; "the people in whose heart is my law; fear not the reproach of man" (Isa 51:7) — what is *in* the heart sets what the person need not fear.

15839.text: Reverent fear (of God) placed in or governing the heart: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts" (Jer 32:40); "I will give them one heart … that they may fear me forever" (Jer 32:39); "unite my heart to fear your name" (Psa 86:11); "Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me" (Deu 5:29); "my heart stands in awe of your words" (Psa 119:161); Opposite: "harden our heart, so that we fear you not" (Isa 63:17); "Blessed is the one who fears the Lord always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall" (Pro 28:14); "Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes" (Psa 36:1); [Claude reading] Hardening of heart is set against the fear of God. The fear of God is something God can put into the heart.

15850.text: Spirit as temper: "slow to anger" // "rules his spirit" (Pro 16:32) [H]; "hasty temper" (Pro 14:29) [T]; "their anger [rûaḥ] against him subsided" (Judg 8:3) [T]

15857.text: God's anger and the human spirit: "nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me" (Isa 57:16) [H].; Revisit 2026-09-28: God's restraint before the fragile human spirit, read after "revive the heart of the contrite" (57:15). See Batch F §5 and Batch G §1.2.

15865.text: Soul: "bitter in soul" (1Sa 22:2; Job 3:20); "deeply distressed [bitter of nephesh]" (1Sa 1:10); "bitterness of my soul" (Job 7:11; 10:1; Isa 38:15); "dies in bitterness of soul" (Job 21:25); "the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter" (Job 27:2); "they weep over you in bitterness of soul" (Eze 27:31).

15872.text: All three together: "sorrow in my heart … counsel in my soul" (Psa 13:2); "anguish of my spirit … bitterness of my soul" (Job 7:11); "pain of heart … breaking of spirit" (Isa 65:14).

15873.text: 3.3 Authentic vs performed grief — the heart decides: "return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning … rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joe 2:12–13); "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds" (Hos 7:14); "because your heart was tender … you have wept before me, I also have heard you" (2Ch 34:27; 2Ki 22:19); Revisit 2026-09-28: the same "tender heart" means fear before battle and lack of resolve in youth. What decides is what the heart yields to (Batch F §6).; "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning" (Ecc 7:4); "the living will lay it to heart" (Ecc 7:2)

15880.text: Revisit 2026-09-28: Pharaoh's hardening is also expressed by *ḥāzaq* "make strong" (Exo 4:21; 7:13; 14:4, 8), which is filed in M23 Strength & Courage. The same verb gives "be strong, let your heart take courage" (Psa 27:14).; In context (Exo 14:4–8), the hardening gives firmness to a change of heart Pharaoh had already made ("What is this we have done?", 14:5).; See Batch G §3.3. The data therefore hold hardening under grief (heavy), rebellion (Batch C §9.3) and strength, according to the root.

15887.text: God directly: "You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound" (Psa 4:7); "God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart" (Ecc 5:20).

15892.text: Planning peace: "those who plan peace have joy" (Pro 12:20).

15913.text: Doubt in the heart: "why do doubts arise in your hearts?" (Luk 24:38); "does not doubt in his heart" (Mar 11:23, M47 row).

15914.text: Disheartened by others: "you have disheartened the righteous falsely" (Eze 13:22, d0).

15920.text: Fainting across every component: heart: "the whole heart faint" // "the whole head is sick" (Isa 1:5); Lam 1:22; Psa 61:2; spirit [H]: Psa 142:3; 143:4; "When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints" (Psa 77:3); soul: "hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them" (Psa 107:5); flesh: "my flesh faints for you" (Psa 63:1); life: "When my life was fainting away, I remembered the Lord, and my prayer came to you" (Jon 2:7) — fainting turns into remembering and prayer; Revisit 2026-09-28: In the same book, Jonah "was faint" under the east wind and asked to die (Jon 4:8). Fainting in ch. 2 turns to prayer; fainting in ch. 4 turns to a death-wish (Batch G §6).; For spirit-fainting in meditation (Psa 77:3), memory works either way: it deepens the fainting (Psa 77) or turns it (Psa 42:6). See Batch F §9.4.; bosom: "their life is poured out on their mothers' bosom" (Lam 2:12)

15921.text: The weary soul revived: "I will satisfy the weary soul, and every languishing soul I will replenish" (Jer 31:25); "Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news" (Pro 25:25); "my soul thirsts for you like a parched land" (Psa 143:6).

15925.text: Withering — heart, spirit, and the breath of God: "My heart is struck down like grass and has withered" (Psa 102:4); "a crushed spirit dries up [withers] the bones" (Pro 17:22); "The grass withers … when the breath of the Lord blows on it; surely the people are grass" (Isa 40:7); [Claude reading] The same withering verb covers the heart, the bones under a crushed spirit, and grass under God's breath.

15932.text: Wonders set against a hardened heart: "I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders" (Exo 7:3; 4:21; 11:10).

15939.text: 1.1 The heart as the knower: "Your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others" (Ecc 7:22); "You know in your own heart all the harm that you did" (1Ki 2:44, d0); "you know in your hearts and souls … that not one word has failed" (Jos 23:14); "Know then in your heart …" (Deu 8:5); "know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the Lord is God" (Deu 4:39); "The heart knows its own bitterness" (Pro 14:10); [Claude reading] "Knowing in the heart" is inner certainty and self-knowledge, not only information.

15941.text: Given by God: "I will give them a heart to know me" (Jer 24:7); "I give you a wise and discerning mind [heart]" (1Ki 3:12); "Who has put wisdom in the inward parts or given understanding to the mind?" (Job 38:36); "God … has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge" (2Co 4:6); "having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know" (Eph 1:18)

15948.text: Desire ahead of knowledge: "Desire [nephesh] without knowledge is not good" (Pro 19:2); "The dogs have a mighty appetite; they never have enough. But they are shepherds who have no understanding" (Isa 56:11); "Before I was aware, my desire [nephesh] set me among the chariots" (Song 6:12) — the soul's desire acts before awareness

15952.text: A cool spirit = understanding: "he who has a cool spirit is a man of understanding" (Pro 17:27); "slow to anger has great understanding, but … a hasty temper exalts folly" (Pro 14:29) [T].

15963.text: 1.10 Heart and mind (nous / dianoia) side by side: "put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts" / "on their hearts … on their minds" (Heb 8:10 / 10:16); "guard your hearts and your minds" (Phili 4:7); The love command lists heart, soul, mind and strength as separate items (Mar 12:30; Mat 22:37; Luk 10:27); Revisit 2026-09-28 (context Mar 12:28–34, Batch F §2): the scribe repeats the command as "heart … understanding [*synesis*] … strength" (12:33). He replaces soul with a knowing word, and Jesus calls the answer wise (12:34). The faculty list is not fixed; what stays constant is "all".; "evil thoughts [reasonings]" come "out of the heart" (Mat 15:19; Mar 7:21); "the reasoning of their hearts" (Luk 9:47)

15965.text: 1.11 ◆ Breath, wind and thought: "When his breath departs … on that very day his plans perish" (Psa 146:4) — the brief's thought link; "he who … creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought" (Amo 4:13); "windy knowledge" (Job 15:2); "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (Ecc 1:17); "Every man is stupid and without knowledge … there is no breath in them" (Jer 10:14; 51:17)

15966.text: 2.1 "Wise of heart" = skilled ◆: "every skillful craftsman" = *wise of heart* (Exo 35:10, 25; 36:1, 2, 8; 31:6, d0); "whom I have filled with a spirit of skill" (Exo 28:3) [X]; "every craftsman in whose mind [heart] the Lord had put skill, everyone whose heart stirred him up" (Exo 36:2); "whose hearts stirred them to use their skill" (Exo 35:26); [Claude reading] Wisdom in the heart includes craft skill. God puts it there, and the stirred heart puts it to work.

15969.text: 2.4 Wisdom entering and staying: "wisdom will come into your heart" (Pro 2:10); "Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding" (Pro 14:33); Revisit 2026-09-28: *nûaḥ* "rest" has three residents: wisdom in the heart of the understanding (Pro 14:33), anger in the heart of fools (Ecc 7:9), the Spirit upon the prophet (Num 11:25; Isa 11:2). See Batch F §9.5.; "teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom" (Psa 90:12); "I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine — my heart still guiding me with wisdom" (Ecc 2:3) — the heart guiding the body's experiment

15970.text: Transmitted: "full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him" (Deu 34:9) [X].; Revisit 2026-09-28: read with Num 27:18 ("a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him") and the sequel "So the people of Israel obeyed him". The spirit is present before the hands are laid on, and it is confirmed by others' response. See Batch G §13.1, and compare 2Ki 2:15 and Num 11:25–29 (Batch F §9.5).

15974.text: 2.6 Counsel and plans: "take counsel in my soul" (Psa 13:2); "gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels" (Psa 81:12; Jer 7:24); "Many are the plans in the mind [heart] of a man, but it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand" (Pro 19:21); "The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water" (Pro 20:5); "The counsel of the Lord stands forever, the plans of his heart" (Psa 33:11) — God's heart plans

15978.text: 3.1 The ear receives, the heart keeps or understands: "all my words … receive in your heart, and hear with your ears" (Eze 3:10); "hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you" (Eze 40:4; 44:5); "making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding" (Pro 2:2); "Incline your ear … apply your heart" (Pro 22:17; 23:12); "Hear, my son … direct your heart" (Pro 23:19)

15980.text: 3.2 A hardened heart does not listen: "Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen" (Exo 7:13, 22; 8:15, 19; 9:12); "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … sent by his Spirit" (Zec 7:12) [D1]; "a hard forehead and a stubborn heart … not willing to listen" (Eze 3:7); "every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will [heart], refusing to listen to me" (Jer 16:12, d1); "did not obey or incline their ear, but … walked in the stubbornness of their evil hearts" (Jer 7:24; 11:8; 13:10); "if your heart turns away, and you will not hear" (Deu 30:17)

15983.text: Collapse: "as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man" (Jos 2:11; 5:1) [H]; "I hear the sound of the trumpet … my heart is beating wildly" (Jer 4:19); "his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him" (1Sa 25:37); Revisit 2026-09-28: the verse before has "Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk … she told him nothing … until the morning" (25:36). The news lands on a heart that was merry the night before. See the threshold pattern in Batch F §7, and Abigail's speech (25:29–31) in Batch G §9.3.; Revisit 2026-09-28: "our hearts melted … there was no spirit left in any man" (Jos 2:11) and "every heart will melt … every spirit will faint" (Eze 21:7) have their law-code counterpart in "lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own" (Deu 20:8). A heart's collapse spreads to other hearts (Batch F §6).; "Because of the news … every heart will melt … every spirit will faint" (Eze 21:7); "Let not your heart faint … at the report" (Jer 51:46)

15984.text: Revival: "when they told him all the words of Joseph … the spirit of their father Jacob revived" (Gen 45:27) — one verse after "his heart became numb, for he did not believe them" (Gen 45:26).; Revisit 2026-09-28 (context Gen 45:25–28, Batch G §2): the revival comes when the words are joined by sight: "and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent". Then: "It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die" (28).; [Claude reading] Hearing alone numbs the heart. Hearing with seeing revives the spirit. This qualifies §9.5 below ("hearing is the main channel"). Here hearing needed a second channel.

15985.text: Refreshment: "good news refreshes the bones" (Pro 15:30); "Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news" (Pro 25:25).

15988.text: Hearing as eating for the soul: "Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves [nephesh] in rich food. Incline your ear … hear, that your soul may live" (Isa 55:2–3); cf. "Your words were found, and I ate them" (Jer 15:16; Batch A)

15989.text: 3.4 God hearing the heart: "If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened" (Psa 66:18); "you hear the desire of the afflicted; you will strengthen their heart; you will incline your ear" (Psa 10:17); "you set your heart to understand … your words have been heard" (Dan 10:12); "because your heart was tender … I also have heard you" (2Ch 34:27; 2Ki 22:19); Revisit 2026-09-28: "tender heart" read across circumstances in Batch F §6.

15997.text: Revisit 2026-09-28: "uttering from the heart lying words" (Isa 59:13) uses *hāgâ* "mutter". The same verb gives "the heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Pro 15:28) and "their hearts devise violence" (Pro 24:2). The heart is an organ of rehearsal, and its content decides its moral character (Batch F §12.2).

15999.text: Telling the heart: "he told her all his heart" (Judg 16:17–18) — revealing the heart is speech.; Revisit 2026-09-28 (context Judg 16:15–30, Batch G §3.6): Delilah had framed it: "your heart is not with me … you have not told me where your great strength lies" (15).; Telling all the heart = giving away the secret of strength. The sequence runs: soul vexed (16) → heart told (17–18) → strength gone, "the Lord had left him" (19–20) → the Philistines' merry hearts (25) → strength asked for (28) → "let my soul die" (30).

16001.text: Keeping: "I kept the matter in my heart" (Dan 7:28); "he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered" (Pro 11:13) [H]; "Whoever restrains his words … a cool spirit" (Pro 17:27) [H]; "I told no one what my God had put into my heart" (Neh 2:12)

16005.text: 4.5 ◆ Word and breath/wind paired: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host" (Psa 33:6); "He sends out his word … he makes his wind blow" (Psa 147:18); "stormy wind fulfilling his word" (Psa 148:8); "My Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, shall not depart" (Isa 59:21) [D1]

16014.text: Grief makes one forget food: "My heart is struck down like grass … I forget to eat my bread" (Psa 102:4).

16021.text: God's Spirit as the true source: "the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied" (1Sa 10:10; 19:20, 23); "as soon as the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied" (Num 11:25–26); "that the Lord would put his Spirit on them!" (Num 11:29); Revisit 2026-09-28 (context Num 11:24–29, Batch F §9.5): they prophesied "but they did not continue" (25). Joshua: "stop them" (28). Moses: "Are you jealous for my sake?" (29). The resting Spirit is resisted and then defended, and it is recognised by others.; "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy" (Joe 2:28; Act 2:17–18); "carried along by the Holy Spirit" — "not by the will of man" (2Pe 1:21)

16024.text: One verb, two spirits: "a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved [*prophesied*] within his house" (1Sa 18:10) [O]; Revisit 2026-09-28 (context 1Sa 18:1–12, Batch F §1.1): this follows the day after Saul's anger at the women's song (18:8–9). In the same chapter Jonathan's soul is knit to David's. Compare the opposite order in 1Sa 11:6, where the Spirit comes first and anger follows (Batch A v3 §2.4).; "a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets" (1Ki 22:22–23) [O]

16029.text: Evil reasonings from the heart: "out of the heart come evil thoughts" (Mat 15:19; Mar 7:21); "why do doubts arise in your hearts?" (Luk 24:38); "does not doubt in his heart" (Mar 11:23).

16039.text: 0. Data notes (short): No pre-filter applies. There is no M42, M61 or M72 in this batch.; Death — v3 note (replaces the v1 note). In v1 and v2 the death words were filed outside the M-codes ("die" in T3, "death" in T10), so §1–§13 read the life side only. After #1880 both also carry M25. The death side is read in §16, and the earlier sections carry Revisit (delta) notes where it bears on them.; Tags that would mislead in the delta: "the heart of the seas" (Eze 28:8) = midst; the "flesh" of an ox (Exo 21:28) and the "meat" pots (Exo 16:3).; Not misleading, but lexically marked (kept, read in §16): *nephesh* = dead body (Lev 21:11; Num 6:6; 19:11, 13, 18); *nephesh* = "willing" (Gen 23:8); the sea's "living things" (Rev 8:9; 16:3); "heart" as the ESV surface for *nephesh* (Pro 19:18; 1Sa 2:33).; Tags that would mislead a reading (noted, and not read as the cluster's sense): "alive / living" (M25); = "raw" flesh (Lev 13:10–24; 1Sa 2:15); = "fresh [living] water" (Lev 15:13); = "wild beasts" (Psa 79:2; Hos 13:8; Eze 39:17; Lev 5:2); Generic verbs in M23: "multiply" (H7235), "be able / can" (H3201); "meet / toward / against" (H7122) in M37: ordinary encounter, not foreknowledge; M71 surfaces used in other senses: "greatness" = arrogance of heart (Isa 9:9; 10:12); "descendants" (1Sa 2:33); "proceeds" (Act 5:3); "color" (Dan 7:28); "bring / lead" (G5342, M70): Mar 9:17, 20; Act 5:16; "heart" = "midst": "the heart of the seas" (Eze 27:27); "in the heart of the oak" (2Sa 18:14)

16040.text: 1.1 "The breath of life" is shared by all flesh: "the Lord God formed the man of dust … and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature [*nephesh ḥayyâ*]" (Gen 2:7); The same phrase *nephesh ḥayyâ* is used of fish, birds and beasts: Gen 1:20, 21, 24; 2:19; 9:10, 12, 15, 16; Lev 11:10, 46; Eze 47:9.; The flood falls on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Gen 6:17; 7:15, 22).; "In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind" (Job 12:10).; [lexical; Claude reading] "Living soul" does not mark man off from the animals lexically. What Gen 2:7 adds is God's own breathing into one creature.

16050.text: Isa 57:15 (filed under "to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" [H1]): God dwelling with them

16057.text: Context Gen 45:25–28 — heart first, then spirit: "Joseph is still alive" (26); "his heart became numb, for he did not believe them" (26); "when they told him all the words of Joseph … and when he saw the wagons … the spirit of their father Jacob revived" (27); "It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die" (28); [Claude reading]

16069.text: Hardening | "I will harden [*strengthen*] his heart" (Exo 4:21); "Pharaoh's heart was hardened" (Exo 7:13, 22; 8:19; 9:12, 35; 10:20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8, 17); "to harden their hearts … that they should come against Israel" (Jos 11:20); "you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother" (Deu 15:7); Zedekiah "hardened his heart against turning to the Lord" (2Ch 36:13)

16072.text: 3.4 Might located in one's own heart fails: "he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked" (Amo 2:16); "The stouthearted were stripped … they sank into sleep" (Psa 76:5); "the valiant man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will utterly melt with fear" (2Sa 17:10); "Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth'" (Deu 8:17); "when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (2Ch 26:16) — strength → pride → ruin (M23 + M55 in one verse); "his heart shall be exalted … but he shall not prevail" (Dan 11:12); "Can your courage [*heart*] endure, or can your hands be strong, in the days that I shall deal with you?" (Eze 22:14); "guilty men, whose own might is their god" (Hab 1:11) (*wind*)

16073.text: Against these — strength given from outside: "the eyes of the Lord run to and fro … to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him" (2Ch 16:9); "The Lord is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts" (Psa 28:7); "Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion" (Psa 84:5); "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit" (Zec 4:6) [D1]; "I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the Lord" (Mic 3:8) [D1]; New Testament — Spirit and power as a fixed pair [D1/D2]: Luk 1:35; 4:14; Act 1:8; 10:38; Rom 15:13, 19; 1Co 2:4; 1Th 1:5; "God gave us a spirit … of power and love and self-control" (2Ti 1:7) [X]; "men of valor whose hearts God had touched" (1Sa 10:26); [Claude reading] The heart that holds its own might is the one that melts, flees or is stripped. The heart that has its strength "in" God is supported. In the NT the Spirit is the regular carrier of power.

16079.text: The formula: "as the Lord lives and as your soul lives" (1Sa 20:3; 25:26; 2Sa 11:11); "as the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2Ki 2:2, 4, 6; 4:30); "As your soul lives, O king, I do not know" (1Sa 17:55); "As you live, my lord" (1Sa 1:26; 2Sa 14:19); "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity" (1Ki 1:29; 2Sa 4:9); "As the Lord lives, who made our souls" (Jer 38:16); "As God lives, … who has made my soul bitter" (Job 27:2); [lexical; Claude reading] The oath sets the other person's *nephesh* beside the Lord's own life as the thing that guarantees the word. To swear by someone's soul is to stake one's word on their life. In the second form, the Lord is identified by what he has done to the soul: redeemed it, made it, made it bitter.

16083.text: 2Ki 4:27–30 | The Shunammite "caught hold of his feet … she is in bitter distress [*her soul is bitter*]" (27); "Did I not say, 'Do not deceive me?'" (28); Gehazi is sent with the staff (29) | "As the Lord lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (30) | "So he arose and followed her" (30)

16085.text: What the sequences show [Claude reading]: The oath marks adherence at a cost.; Elisha's triple oath is the price of the double spirit.; The Shunammite uses Elisha's own oath against him. Her bitterness of soul becomes a hold on the prophet that he cannot refuse.; Uriah's oath by David's soul is kept against David's wish. The wine that should have lowered his guard fails (a failed threshold — Batch F §7). He dies for keeping it.; The oath by the soul can guard a life while refusing a life. Zedekiah swears secretly by "who made our souls" to spare Jeremiah's life. He then declines the life offered to him (38:17, 20), from fear (38:19). The oath and the refusal are in one conversation.; 1Sa 17:55 stands on the threshold of 18:1. A formal oath by Saul's soul immediately precedes the knitting of Jonathan's soul to David's.; The oath misused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (Gehazi, 2Ki 5:20; §13.2).; Revisit (Batch H): God swears by his own soul: "The Lord God has sworn by himself [*his nephesh*]" (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.; The oath answers a claim of vengeance. The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf (Batch H §1.4).; Revisit (delta) — the oath with death in view: The oath formula frames the nearness of death. "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.; A life pledged for a life. Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … deliver our lives from death" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "Our life for yours even to death!" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. They pledge their own *nephesh*.; An oath on a life, broken after a spirit comes (context 1Sa 19:4–12): Jonathan: "he took his life in his hand and struck down the Philistine … Why then will you sin against innocent blood?" (5); "Saul listened … Saul swore, 'As the Lord lives, he shall not be put to death'" (6); War again; David's victory (8); "a harmful spirit from the Lord came upon Saul" (9) [O]

16087.text: 5.1 Surrender for life: "he who goes out and surrenders … shall have his life as a prize of war" (Jer 21:9; 38:2); "your life shall be spared" (Jer 38:17, 20) — see §4; Ben-hadad's servants in sackcloth and ropes: "Perhaps he will spare your life … 'Please, let me live.' And he said, 'Does he still live? He is my brother'" (1Ki 20:31–32)

16089.text: 5.3 Hunting souls: "Woe to the women who sew magic bands … in the hunt for souls! Will you hunt down souls belonging to my people and keep your own souls alive?" (Eze 13:18); "for handfuls of barley and for pieces of bread, putting to death souls who should not die and keeping alive souls who should not live" (Eze 13:19); "you have disheartened the righteous falsely … and encouraged the wicked … to save his life" (Eze 13:22)

16091.text: Context Mic 6:6–8: "With what shall I come before the Lord?" (6); "Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?" (7) (M37); "He has told you, O man, what is good … to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God" (8)

16093.text: Revisit (Batch H §2.2, §1.4) — the refusal is qualified. The law and the narratives do price a life: "The ransom of a man's life is his wealth" (Pro 13:8); "a ransom for his life … The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less" (Exo 30:12–16) — the same price for every life; "your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver" (1Ki 20:39) → the verdict drops the silver: "your life shall be for his life" (20:42); Satan: "All that a man has he will give for his life" (Job 2:4); [Claude reading] A life can be ransomed within the covenant, but a soul cannot be bought back from God. Mic 6 and Mat 16 refuse a price before God. They do not deny that the law sets one.

16097.text: 5.5 The soul's life and its failure to be satisfied: "lives many years … but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things" (Ecc 6:3); "the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the Lord" (1Sa 25:29) — see §9.3 for its sequel (25:31)

16099.text: Other texts where the soul turns against its own life: "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 10:1; 9:21)

16104.text: Revisit (delta) — Elijah under the broom tree (context 1Ki 19:1–8): Jezebel: "if I do not make your life as the life of one of them" (2); "he was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life" (3); "he asked that he might die [*asked his nephesh to die*] … 'It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers'" (4); "he lay down and slept … an angel touched him and said, 'Arise and eat'" (5); A cake and a jar of water; "he ate and drank and lay down again" (6); "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you" (7); "he went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb" (8); [Claude reading]; He runs to save his life, then asks for it to be taken. Fear for the life and weariness of the life follow each other within a day.; The death-wish is answered with food, not with argument. The questions come later, at Horeb ("What are you doing here?", 19:9).; This is the eating-and-drinking threshold of Batch F §7, reversed. There, the meal lowers the guard and something enters. Here, the meal answers an exhausted soul and becomes strength ("the strength of that food"). Compare "strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5; §3.1).; Four death-wishes, four answers (see §16.2 for the full set): Elijah (food), Jonah (a question about pity), Samson (granted, with strength), Saul (granted by another's hand, who then dies for it).

16116.text: 8.3 Faintness sent into hearts: "I will send faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies. The sound of a driven leaf shall put them to flight … they shall fall when none pursues" (Lev 26:36); "panic … fever that consume the eyes and make the heart ache" (Lev 26:16)

16117.text: Revisit: Lev 26:36 extends the Lev 26 reciprocity sequence of Batch F §4. The heart-effects of the curse run from 26:16 to 26:36.

16119.text: Listed side by side as distinct afflictions [O]: "healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits" (Luk 7:21); "healed of evil spirits and infirmities" (Luk 8:2); "those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured" (Luk 6:18); Act 5:16; 19:12; Mat 10:1
