16169.text: The death-wish is almost always the soul's, in the *nephesh* idiom ("asked his soul to die"). The anguish is placed in the spirit and the bitterness in the soul (Job 7:11), and the life "lingers" after the will to live has gone (2Sa 1:9).

16174.text: 16.3 The heart and soul measured against death: "I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets" (Ecc 7:26). The context is the searcher's own heart: "I turned my heart to know … the foolishness that is madness" (7:25).; [Claude reading] One heart searching finds another heart as the trap. A heart set with snares is worse than death.; "His greed [*nephesh*] is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough" (Hab 2:5). It follows directly on "his soul is puffed up" (2:4; §5.5).; [Claude reading] Here the soul is compared with death as appetite. Both swallow and are never satisfied.

16176.text: Context Psa 116:1–9 — cry, self-address, deliverance: "The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me" (3); "Then I called on the name of the Lord: 'O Lord, I pray, deliver my soul!'" (4); "Return, O my soul, to your rest" (7); "For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling" (8); "I will walk before the Lord in the land of the living" (9) *(missing from iba.db; read from the STEP server)*; [Claude reading] The self-address to the soul (Batch F §9.1, §15) stands between the cry (4) and the declared deliverance (8). The soul is told to rest before the deliverance is stated. What follows is walking "in the land of the living". Compare "you have delivered my soul from death … that I may walk before God in the light of life" (Psa 56:13). In both psalms, deliverance from death is for walking before God.

16177.text: Context Job 33:18–30 — the soul near the pit, and the ransom: "his life loathes bread" (20); "his flesh is so wasted away" (21); "His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death" (22); "If there be for him an angel, a mediator … 'Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom; let his flesh become fresh with youth'" (23–25); "man prays to God, and he accepts him" (26); "He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit" (28); "to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life" (30); [Claude reading] One sequence moves through three components: soul toward death; the flesh restored; the soul brought back; The turning point is a ransom found by a mediator. This is where Job's book names the price that §5.4 found refused elsewhere.

16182.text: Context Eze 18:1–4, 19–32: The proverb of sour grapes is ended: "As I live, declares the Lord God" (3); "Behold, all souls are mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine: the soul who sins shall die" (4, 20); "if a wicked person turns away … he shall surely live; he shall not die" (21); "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked … and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (23); "make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?" (31) [H1]; "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone … so turn, and live" (32); [Claude reading]

16184.text: The heart's condition as the cause of death — wisdom and sayings: "fools die for lack of sense [*heart*]" (Pro 10:21); "Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life; he who despises his ways will die" (Pro 19:16); "he who fails to find me injures himself [*his soul*]; all who hate me love death" (Pro 8:36; Batch F §3.1); "The godless in heart cherish anger … They die in youth" (Job 36:13–14); "the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead" (Ecc 9:3) → "a living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they will die" (9:4–5); "Discipline your son, for there is hope; do not set your heart on putting him to death" (Pro 19:18) [lexical: *nephesh*]; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity. They lie down alike in the dust" (Job 21:25–26). Here the soul's state at death makes no difference to the outcome. This is Job's counter to the wisdom sayings above.; "I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart" (Rev 2:23). The death is the evidence that the heart is searched.

16211.text: 16.10 Life risked "to death" for others — the OT precedent: "Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death" (Judg 5:18). This is in the same song as "March on, my soul, with might!" (5:21; §3.2).; "Our life for yours even to death!" (Jos 2:14; §4 revisit); David "took his life in his hand" against the Philistine (1Sa 19:5); The men to David: "If half of us die, they will not care [*set heart*] about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us" (2Sa 18:3). The enemy's heart is indifferent to many deaths. One life is weighed at ten thousand.; "the men who were seeking your life are dead" (Exo 4:19) → Moses returns (4:20). The death of the hunters frees the hunted life.; "Why then are you laying a trap for my life to bring about my death?" (1Sa 28:9). This is the medium to the disguised Saul.; "we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves [*our souls*]" (Jer 26:19). To put the prophet to death would harm the souls of those who kill him. It is set against Hezekiah, who "feared the Lord … and the Lord relented".; [Claude reading] Batch F §3.2 read "hating one's life" and "not loving one's life unto death" as NT discipleship. The OT already has the same shape in battle and in covenant pledges: the life risked "to the death" for a people, a household or a king. What the NT adds is the object, "for the name of the Lord Jesus" (Act 21:13), and the example, "poured out his soul to death" (Isa 53:12).

16217.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: Life is held in the breath and the soul, and it is God's to give and gather.; "Living soul" is shared with the animals. God's breathing is what marks Gen 2:7.; One decision of God's heart could gather every breath back (Job 34:14–15).; In the flood narrative God's heart changes while man's heart does not (Gen 6:5–6 → 8:21).; *rûaḥ* moves across senses within a single passage, and the passage uses the movement: Eze 37: carrying Spirit → breath → winds → "my Spirit within you"; Judg 15: rushing Spirit → one's own spirit returning; Jon 4: an appointed wind that makes the soul wish to die; Strength and hardness are one word. *ḥāzaq* is courage, hardening and the nerve to kill, according to what the heart is set toward (§3.3). This mirrors the tender heart (Batch F §6): neither softness nor strength of heart has a fixed moral value.; Revisit (Batch H §7.4): more words of this kind — *nāṣar* (keep the heart / the "guarded" wily heart), *šāmar*, vengeance, fatness of soul and of heart, *šāgâ*, kinship-flesh.; The inner components give way in order. Samson (Judg 16): the soul vexed; the heart told; the strength gone; the Lord gone; The strength returns only when asked for, and joined to the soul's consent to die.; Jacob (Gen 45): heart numb → spirit revived by words and sight.; The soul is what one swears by and what one bargains for.; Oaths "as your soul lives" mark adherence at a cost (Elisha, the Shunammite, Uriah) or protection with fear (Zedekiah).; Souls are hunted for bread (Eze 13) and "captured" by the wise (Pro 11:30).; Nothing can be given in return for a soul (Mic 6:7–8; Mat 16:26).; Eating and drinking recur at inner thresholds, now in three registers: the merry heart (Batch F §7); the heart sustained by bread before it is made merry (Judg 19:5, 8); the soul that blesses after a meal and wine (Gen 27:25); Also: the sad heart at a feast that turns to prayer (Hannah, Nehemiah), and the wine-threshold refused (Uriah).; Enticement and stirring show how other agents reach the inner seat: God stirs human spirits (Cyrus, Pul, the remnant).; God sends an other-spirit to entice through prophets' mouths (1Ki 22).; God allures and speaks to the heart (Hos 2:14).; Desire, gods and false teachers entice hearts and souls.

16219.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: It is for walking before God "in the land of the living" (Psa 116:9; 56:13).; Its turning point is a cry, a self-address to the soul, or a ransom.; "Deliver one's soul" can mean escaping bloodguilt by speaking (the watchman, Eze 3:19). The soul delivered is the speaker's, not the one who dies.; Fringe from the delta: the same consolation spoken to two dying mothers; Saul's "life still lingers"; the Amalekite executed for fulfilling a death-wish; Qohelet leaving the spirit's destination open; the oath of 1Sa 19:6 broken three verses after a harmful spirit comes; a dead king buried for his grandfather's heart; "eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" set against a call to mourn

16237.text: Answered before it is spoken: "Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came out" (Gen 24:45).

16238.text: The heart crying: "Their heart cried to the Lord" (Lam 2:18); "Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord" (Lam 2:19); "With my whole heart I cry; answer me" (Psa 119:145); "I call to you when my heart is faint" (Psa 61:2)

16245.text: 1.1 The heart prays — voiceless prayer: [Claude reading] Prayer is located in the heart, and can be complete there without voice (1Sa 1:13; Gen 24:45). Hos 7:14 is the converse: a loud cry that does not come from the heart does not count as crying to God. Cf. "said in heart" (depiction v1 §2.1c): the same organ holds private speech to oneself and silent speech to God.

16247.text: Complaint from the soul and spirit: "I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 7:11) [H1]; "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 10:1); "What shall I say? … because of the bitterness of my soul" (Isa 38:15); "Why should I not be impatient [*short of spirit*]?" (Job 21:4) [T]

16252.text: Speaking in the heart (H1696 form of the "said in heart" series; Batch B R2): "Hannah was speaking in her heart" (1Sa 1:13); "speaking in my heart" (Gen 24:45); "I said [*spoke with*] my heart … I said in my heart" (Ecc 1:16; 2:15); "speaks truth in his heart" (Psa 15:2)

16491.text: 13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

16492.text: 13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Unclean spirits recognise the Son of God (Mar 3:11) and obey him (Mar 1:27).; Spirits either confess Jesus come in the flesh or are "the spirit of the antichrist" (1Jo 4:2–3).; They must be tested (1Jo 4:1), and the spirit of error stands against the Spirit of truth (1Jo 4:6).; The Lord can dispatch a lying spirit (1Ki 22:23). Ministering spirits serve (Heb 1:14).; Flesh in relating to God: "All flesh" is humanity as it comes to God: all flesh comes in prayer (Psa 65:2), sees salvation and glory (Luk 3:6; Isa 40:5), and blesses (Psa 145:21).; Covenant is cut in the flesh, and its inner counterpart is the circumcised heart (§7.2).; Flesh vs spirit as powers: Isa 31:3; Joh 6:63; 1Co 5:5; Jer 17:5.; The "life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11) is the ground of atonement.; God is shown with his own heart and soul in these relations: his soul avenges (Jer 5:9) and he swears by it (Amo 6:8); he acts with all his heart and soul (Jer 32:41); he wishes for a heart in his people (Deu 5:29); his heart recoils in compassion (Hos 11:8); his soul delights in the servant (Isa 42:1); he gives up the beloved of his soul (Jer 12:7); the priest acts according to his heart and soul (1Sa 2:35); Speech and the heart. The heart speaks inwardly ("in the heart", §1.3), is spoken to ("to the heart" = comfort, §1.4), and its speech either matches the mouth or is betrayed by it. Hebrew prayer is an act of the heart that may or may not reach the lips.; Fringe worth keeping: *kāvôd* as the inner self (§3.2) — a possible inner-being term outside M47; the soul asked to die (§2); the double portion of another's spirit (2Ki 2:9); the dying soul naming a child and the returning spirit naming a spring (§1.8); Isaac's soul giving the blessing (§12); Qoheleth testing his own heart (Ecc 2:1); the Gentile's heart-and-conscience law-court (Rom 2:15); the flesh-then-breath sequence of the dry bones (Eze 37:6–8); "gain the whole world and forfeit his soul" (Mat 16:26); "transgression speaks [as an oracle] deep in his heart" (Psa 36:1); the heart with "highways to Zion" (Psa 84:5); "absent in body … present in spirit" (Col 2:5)

16493.text: 0. Data notes: "Holy" inside "Holy Spirit" (M61) — pre-filter.; 93 pairs in 92 verses are G0040G / H6944G "holy" at d1 from *pneuma / rûaḥ*. In these, M61 is carried by the name of the Spirit, not by a statement about purity.; They are not dropped. They are summarised as a group in §7.1 for what they say about the Spirit and the inner seat.; The other 90 M61 verses are read in §7.2–7.5.; The other pre-filters do not apply here. Neither "declares the Lord" (M42) nor "Lord of hosts" (M72) falls in Batch D clusters.; "Arise" (H6965B) accounts for 30 of the 101 M08 verses. None is about pride. They are noted and not used in §9. → Ruling R1.; "Brothers" (G0080) accounts for 32 of the 126 M14 verses. None is about deceit. They are noted and not used in §4. → Ruling R2.; Sin-root verbs used for purification [lexical]. H2398 *ḥāṭāʾ* in the piel means "to de-sin", i.e. purify: "does not cleanse himself" (Num 19:13, 20); "purify yourselves" (Num 31:19); The qal can mean "miss": "misses his way" (Pro 19:2); "fails to find me" (Pro 8:36); These are kept only where the sin sense is present (Pro 8:36, §3.2).; Justice / "rules" (H4941 *mišpāṭ*).; Most M12 *mišpāṭ* pairs are "rules / judgments" = statutes (Lev 26:15; Psa 119:20; Deu 26:16). They are kept in §1.5, because the soul's and heart's relation to God's rules is a real theme.; H4941J "custom" (1Sa 2:13 "the custom of the priests … while the meat was boiling") and Num 27:11 "a statute and rule" (with *šĕʾēr* "kinsman") are noted and not used.; H4941G/H also carries an active FLAG row in cluster_strong (old).; Misfiled tags, noted and not used: Gen 41:3, 4, 19: "ugly and thin" cows — *bāśār* "flesh" + *raʿ* "bad" (M58).; Exo 36:8: "craftsmen [*wise of heart*] … fine twined linen" (H7806 "twist", M57).; Heb 13:9 "heart … strengthened [*confirmed*]" (G0950, M62) — confirmation, not truth. Phili 1:7 "confirmation of the gospel" (G0951) likewise.; Eze 42:20 "on the four sides" (H7307I *rûaḥ* = side / quarter) + "holy" (M61).; Job 26:13 "By his wind the heavens were made fair" (H8235, M61).; Pro 19:15 "idle person" (H7423B, M14); Isa 3:20 "perfume boxes … amulets" (*nephesh* "perfume box" + H3908, M14).; Psa 109:24 "my body has become gaunt" (H3584, M14).; Judg 19:5, 8, 9; 2Sa 19:7; Judg 19:3 "heart" beside "arise / delay" (M08, M09) — idioms: "strengthen your heart" = eat; "speak to the heart" = speak kindly.

16726.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch D [Claude reading]: Moral condition is predicated above all of the heart. The heart is: upright, whole, pure, clean or blameless (§1); evil, crooked, perverse, twisted, false or double (§2, §4, §5); proud / high or humbled / tender (§9, §10); It is also where sin is stored, engraved or hidden (§3.3). God tests and weighs it (Psa 7:9; Pro 21:2; Luk 16:15; Act 15:8). The heart is the organ that is morally evaluated.; The soul (*nephesh*) is the accountable person and the life at stake.; It sins, realises guilt, bears iniquity and is cut off (§3.1). It is the unfaithful party (§5).; It is the life that righteousness delivers (§1.7) and that sin injures (§3.2).; It is the innocent blood that is shed (§1.7). It is afflicted on holy days (§7.5).; At the limit it is the corpse that defiles (§8.2).; The soul is less often *evaluated* (righteous soul: 2Pe 2:8; puffed-up soul: Hab 2:4) than *answerable*.; The human spirit is evaluated chiefly on the pride–humility axis (§9.2, §10.2): haughty, proud, hardened, lowly, poor, contrite. Otherwise it is: without deceit (Psa 32:2); right / clean (Psa 51:10); faithful in marriage (Mal 2:15–16); trustworthy (Pro 11:13); holy or defiled with the body (1Co 7:34; 2Co 7:1); sanctified with soul and body (1Th 5:23); perfected in the righteous dead (Heb 12:23); weighed (Pro 16:2); broken by a perverse tongue (Pro 15:4); [observation, not a count]; Other spirits carry the negative moral adjectives. They are evil / harmful (§2.1, 15 verses), unclean (§8.1, 23 verses) and lying / deceitful (§4.1, 6 verses). They are the moral clusters' names turned into kinds of spirit.; In the OT some are sent by God (1Sa 16; Judg 9:23; 1Ki 22:22–23).; In the NT they indwell and are cast out.; The Holy Spirit is the positive counterpart, and the one against whom human sin is directed: blasphemed, lied to, grieved, resisted, outraged (§2.4, §4.2, §7.1).; Inner vs outer purity.; Ritual clean / unclean / holy vocabulary attaches to flesh, body and *nephesh*-as-person or corpse.; Moral purity attaches to heart, spirit, soul and conscience.; Several texts deliberately contrast the two: Psa 24:4; 2Ch 30:19; Mar 7:19–21; Heb 9:13–14; 10:22; Jam 4:8.

16727.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch D [Claude reading]: Conscience is the NT's named moral-awareness faculty. It can be clear, pure, good, evil, defiled, seared, weak or wounded. It testifies (2Co 1:12; Rom 9:1) and is purified by Christ's blood (Heb 9:14). It is frequently paired with the heart (1Ti 1:5; Heb 10:22).; The OT does this work with the heart: "David's heart struck him" (2Sa 24:10); "my heart does not reproach me" (Job 27:6).; The Levitical "realizes his guilt" (Lev 5) describes the same moment without naming an organ.; The heart deceives itself and is the source of evil.; It deceives its owner: Jer 17:9; Obd 3; Isa 44:20.; Evil comes from it: Gen 6:5; Mat 15:19; Luk 6:45.; Its evil hides behind speech: Psa 28:3; 41:6; Pro 26:23–25.; Pride deceives the heart that holds it (Obd 3), linking M08 and M14.; Flesh carries on from Batch C (§11.5).; OT: flesh is the ritual body and meat — clean or unclean, holy or tainted.; NT Pauline: flesh is the seat of sin (Rom 7–8; Gal 5:19) and the ground of false boasting (Phili 3:3).; Positive NT uses remain: "holy … in his body of flesh" (Col 1:22); "bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).; Wind and breath are the image of moral emptiness: iniquity takes us away like wind (Isa 64:6); the wicked are chaff (Psa 1:4); "wind and lies" (Mic 2:11); idols with no breath (Jer 10:14); the *hevel* + *rûaḥ* refrain (Ecc); Only the messianic "breath of his lips" (Isa 11:4) and the breath that conveys the Holy Spirit (Joh 20:22) are active and effective.; Fringe worth keeping: *nephesh* = corpse as the defiling body (§8.2); the "high heart" that is pride or courage depending on direction (2Ch 17:6 vs 2Ch 32:25); the heart that strikes or does not reproach — pre-conscience (§3.3, §9.5); sin against one's own soul (§3.2); the servant's soul as guilt offering (§3.6); lies that kill and keep alive souls (Eze 13:19); the spirit of jealousy that comes whether or not the defilement is real (Num 5:14); false humility of the flesh (Col 2:18, 23); the thorn in the flesh against conceit (2Co 12:7); Eliab misreading David's heart (1Sa 17:28); "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" (2Ki 10:15)

16728.text: 0. Data notes (short): Pre-filter — "Lord of hosts" (H6635B, M72): 28 pairs in 22 verses. This is a divine title, not dominion as a relation. The group is reported in §1.9, not dropped.; Misleading tags (noted, and not read as the cluster's sense): "choirmaster" (H5329 "to conduct", M76): 10 psalm superscriptions (Psa 9:1, 11:1, 14:1, 36:1, 42:1, 45:1, 53:1, 57:1, 62:1, 69:1). The M47 word belongs to the psalm body. The heading has no bearing on it.; "hand: power" (H3027H, M72): 49 verses. Mostly the idiom "into the hand of" (Jeremiah's "into the hand of those who seek their life"; Joshua's conquest lists). It is read as agency, and only where the hand acts on an inner component (§1.1, §1.4).; Quantity words in M46: "abundance / greatness / multitude" of iniquity or idols (Jer 13:22; Hos 9:7; Eze 14:4), "numerous" (Deu 10:22), "to no avail" (Dan 11:27), "good for nothing" (Jer 13:10), "retinue" (1Ki 10:2). None of these is about wealth.; Words in M76 and M26 used in other senses: "pity" (Psa 69:20) — *nûd*, a sympathetic shaking of the head; "intoxicated" (Pro 5:20) — *šāgâ*, see §4.2; "appointed" (Jon 4:8) and "count on" (2Co 10:2); "heart" = "midst": "the heart of the seas" (Eze 27:27).; "spokes" (Eze 10:12) is tagged hand.; The death words are outside the M-codes (see the handoff §3), as in Batch G.

16729.text: Held and turned: "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord; he turns it wherever he will" (Pro 21:1); "the Lord … had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them" (Ezr 6:22); "who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king" (Ezr 7:27); "God has put it into their hearts … handing over their royal power to the beast" (Rev 17:17); "his wisdom, which God had put into his mind" (2Ch 9:23)

16734.text: [Claude reading] In the text the king's heart is the heart with the most power over others. It is also the heart shown most often as acted upon: God turns it, puts things into it, stirs it, hardens it, and cuts it off. The unsearchable heart of Pro 25:3 is unsearchable to subjects. To God it is a stream in his hand.

16735.text: 1.2 The heart that claims a throne: "You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven … I will set my throne on high'" (Isa 14:13); "in his own mind he shall become great … he shall even rise up against the Prince of princes" (Dan 8:25); "in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow'" (Rev 18:7); "the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria" (Isa 10:12); "Your heart was proud because of your beauty … I exposed you before kings" (Eze 28:17); "when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened … he was brought down from his kingly throne" (Dan 5:20). Then "his mind was made like that of a beast … until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind" (5:21). See Batch G §14.10.

16736.text: The remedy in the law of the king: he is to write out the law and "read in it all the days of his life … that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers" (Deu 17:19–20).

16747.text: What the sequence shows [Claude reading]: Allegiance is a heart-matter, and it moves by attention. Absalom wins hearts by standing where the king is absent (15:2–4) and by the kiss the king himself gave him (14:33 → 15:5). The heart follows whoever hears the cause.; The king's own heart drives the plot. The heart that "went out to Absalom" (14:1) opens the way for the son who steals every other heart. After the victory the same heart grieves, and nearly loses the army (19:6–7).; Flesh as a claim on the heart. David recovers Judah's heart with "bone and flesh" — kinship offered as grounds for allegiance.; The same claim in the opposite direction: Abimelech — "Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh" (Judg 9:2) → "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (9:3) → he kills his seventy brothers "on one stone" (9:5).; One appeal to kinship-flesh wins hearts for restoration in one case and for fratricide in the other. [Claude reading]

16750.text: Esther — the soul reversed. Context read: Est 4:12–16; 5:6–14; 7:3–8.; Mordecai: "Do not think to yourself [*in your nephesh*] that in the king's palace you will escape" (4:13) → "if I perish, I perish" (4:16).; Then, at the wine: "let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request" (7:3).; The king "arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking … Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther" (7:7).; [Claude reading] Within one banquet the *nephesh* asked for passes from Esther to Haman. Esther's inner reckoning ("do not think in your soul") is corrected first. Only then does she stake her life. See §7.6 for the wine-threshold.

16751.text: Ben-hadad and the prophet's parable. Context read: 1Ki 20:31–43.; "Perhaps he will spare your life" (31) → "Please, let me live" → "Does he still live? He is my brother" (32); The disguised prophet: "Guard this man; if … he is missing, your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver" (39); "your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people" (42) → Ahab "went to his house vexed and sullen" (43; the same phrase as 21:4 — Batch F §7); [Claude reading] A life has a price in silver in the parable, but not in the verdict. Ahab spares one life by calling him "brother", and forfeits his own life for it. This bears on Batch G §5.4 (§R-V).

16776.text: 1.10 ◆ Fringe (M72): "Let her lie in your arms [*bosom*], that my lord the king may be warm" (1Ki 1:2) — the king's failing body (G §8); "everyone who was in distress … and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him. And he became commander over them" (1Sa 22:2) — bitterness of soul as the recruiting ground of a future king; "With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the Lord … And the people took confidence" (2Ch 32:8), spoken "encouragingly [*to their heart*]" (32:6); "fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate the king's food" (Dan 1:15) → §7.6; "the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh" (Dan 2:11); "Our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers … yet we are forcing our sons … to be slaves … it is not in our power to help it" (Neh 5:5) → §3; "the kings … their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them" (Jos 5:1) [H2]; "the souls of those who had been beheaded … came to life and reigned with Christ" (Rev 20:4); "the king … had sackcloth beneath on his body" (2Ki 6:30) — hidden grief under royal clothes

16780.text: Wealth does not satisfy a heart set on a grievance. Context read: Est 5:9–14.; Haman goes out "joyful and glad of heart", sees Mordecai, and is "filled with wrath" (5:9).; He "recounted … the splendor of his riches, the number of his sons, all the promotions" (5:11). Then: "Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai" (5:13).; The gallows follow (5:14).

16782.text: 2.2 The price of a life, again: "The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat" (Pro 13:8); "each shall give a ransom for his life … The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less … to make atonement for your lives" (Exo 30:12–16; context read) → Batch D; Batch E; "your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver" (1Ki 20:39) → §1.4; Satan: "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life" (Job 2:4) → "only spare [*guard*] his life" (2:6). Context read: Job 2:3–7.; "they have devoured human lives; they have taken treasure" (Eze 22:25); [Claude reading] Batch G §5.4 read Mic 6:7 and Mat 16:26 as a refusal to set any price on the soul. This batch shows the law and the narratives do set a price, and state it: a ransom in wealth (Pro 13:8); a half-shekel that is equal for every life (Exo 30:15); a talent of silver in a parable that turns into "life for life" (1Ki 20:39–42); Satan's axiom (Job 2:4) is that a man will give everything for his *nephesh*. The difference from G §5.4 is the direction of the transaction: a life can be ransomed within the covenant, but a soul cannot be bought back from God (Mat 16:26). See §R-V.

16789.text: 2.5 ◆ Fringe (M46): "my heart moans for Moab like a flute … Therefore the riches they gained have perished" (Jer 48:36) — grief of heart over an enemy's lost wealth; "The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing" (Pro 13:4); "his eyes are never satisfied with riches … 'For whom am I toiling and depriving myself [*my soul*] of pleasure?'" (Ecc 4:8); "When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul" (Psa 94:19) — abundance of cares answered by consolation; "Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease" (Psa 123:4)

16794.text: 3.2 The servant's inner sentence: "if that servant says to himself [*in his heart*], 'My master is delayed,' and begins to beat the … servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk" (Luk 12:45; Mat 24:48–49). Context read: Luk 12:42–46; Mat 24:49–51.; The faithful manager feeds the household "at the proper time" (Luk 12:42).; The unfaithful servant says in his heart that the master is delayed → beats → eats and drinks with drunkards → the master "will come on a day when he does not expect him" (46).; → Batch D §10 (inner speech). New here: the inner sentence is followed at once by eating and drinking, then the sudden arrival (§7.6).

16796.text: Moses' burden, then the Spirit shared. Context read: Num 11:10–17.; "why … you lay the burden of all this people on me?" (11); "Did I conceive all this people? … Carry them in your bosom" (12); "kill me at once … that I may not see my wretchedness" (15); "I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden … with you" (17) [D2]; [Claude reading] Despair under a burden (like Batch G §6) is answered by distributing the Spirit, not by removing the burden.

16801.text: The way follows the heart: "he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart" (Isa 57:17); "Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes. But know that … God will bring you into judgment" (Ecc 11:9) → Batch F §7.4; "if … my heart has gone after my eyes" (Job 31:7)

16802.text: Heart and way given together: "I will give them one heart and one way" (Jer 32:39); "I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart" (Psa 119:32); "Teach me your way … unite my heart to fear your name" (Psa 86:11)

16808.text: 4.2 Going astray — five agents: The heart itself: "a people who go astray in their heart" (Psa 95:10); The spirit, with a way back: "those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding" (Isa 29:24) [H1]; A foreign spirit: "a spirit of whoredom has led them astray" (Hos 4:12) [X]; "The Lord has mingled within her a spirit of confusion … as a drunken man staggers" (Isa 19:14) [X]; God: "O Lord, why do you make us wander from your ways and harden our heart?" (Isa 63:17). Context 63:1–6, 15–17: this complaint follows the divine warrior's "day of vengeance was in my heart" (63:4) and a plea that "the stirring of your inner parts and your compassion are held back" (63:15). → §6.1; The loss of understanding: "He takes away understanding [*heart*] from the chiefs … and makes them wander in a trackless waste" (Job 12:24)

16815.text: 4.4 ◆ Fringe (M76): "Reproaches have broken my heart … I looked for pity [*someone to shake the head*], but there was none" (Psa 69:20); "you have disheartened the righteous falsely" (Eze 13:22) → G §5.3; "they have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isa 66:3); "Your ways and your deeds … it has reached your very heart" (Jer 4:18) — the consequence of the way arrives at the heart; "The dogs have a mighty appetite [*nephesh*] … they have all turned to their own way" (Isa 56:11); "Ephraim feeds on the wind" (Hos 12:1)

16824.text: The prophet-watchman | Context read: Eze 33:6–9. If he does not warn, "his blood I will require at the watchman's hand" (6, 8). If he warns, "you will have delivered your soul" (9). The watchman keeps his own soul by guarding others'.

16830.text: 5.5 ◆ Fringe (M74): "guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms [*bosom*]" (Mic 7:5) — the closest intimacy as the place for guarding; The Gerasene: "He was kept under guard and bound with chains … but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon" (Luk 8:29) [O] — human guarding fails against the spirit; the word of Jesus succeeds (8:29a); "who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places [*nāṣar*] … eat pig's flesh" (Isa 65:4); "they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh" (Gal 6:13); "guard the good deposit … by the Holy Spirit who dwells within us" (2Ti 1:14) [D1]; "maintain the unity of the Spirit" (Eph 4:3) [D2]; "I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes and be careful to obey" (Eze 36:27) [D1] — the carefulness is caused by the Spirit

16836.text: A stirred human spirit, as instrument | "The Lord has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes … that is the vengeance of the Lord" (Jer 51:11) [H1]

16837.text: Jeremiah's sequence — context read, Jer 20:7–14: "you have deceived me" (7); "there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones … I cannot [hold it in]" (9); "my close friends, watching for my fall … 'take our revenge on him'" (10); → "let me see your vengeance … to you have I committed my cause" (12); → "Sing to the Lord; praise the Lord! For he has delivered the life of the needy" (13); → "Cursed be the day on which I was born!" (14); Jer 11:18–21 has the same prayer, and names "the men of Anathoth, who seek your life" (21).; [Claude reading]; Vengeance changes value with the heart that holds it. In the Philistines' soul it is malice. In God's heart it stands in one line with redemption (Isa 63:4). To the anxious heart it is rescue (Isa 35:4).; The prophet's heart does not take vengeance; it hands vengeance over. The friends want "our revenge" (20:10). Jeremiah asks to *see* God's (20:12). The handing over ("to you have I committed my cause") is what makes the praise of 20:13 possible. Two verses later the heart falls to cursing its birth (20:14). The inner seat swings from fire, to entrusting, to praise, to despair in five verses (cf. the despairing soul, Batch G §6).; What follows the divine heart's vengeance is complaint (Isa 63:15–17): the people ask where God's compassion has gone and why he makes them wander (§4.2).

16846.text: 6.5 ◆ Fringe (M26): "my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. 16847.text: 7. Cross-cutting observations for Batch H [Claude reading]: The most powerful heart is shown as the least its own. The king's heart is turned, filled, stirred, hardened and cut off by God (§1.1). When it claims a throne for itself, it falls (§1.2). Deu 17:20's daily reading is the one preventive.; Allegiance is a heart-matter, and it moves by attention and kinship. Absalom steals hearts by hearing their causes. David sways them back by "bone and flesh". Abimelech uses the same flesh-claim to incline hearts toward fratricide (§1.3).; The social relations of this batch supply the vocabulary for the self's relation to itself: rule: one rules one's spirit; peace rules the heart (§1.5); service: one serves from the heart, or serves sin with the flesh (§3.1); guarding: one keeps one's heart, soul and spirit (§5.1); judgment: the heart condemns or justifies the self (§6.2); Setting-words turned inward describe the inner seat as governed. This is the batch's main contribution.; More words with opposite value by circumstance (for synthesis item 3): *nāṣar*: keep the heart (Pro 4:23) / the "guarded" wily heart (Pro 7:10) (§5.1); *šāmar*: keep the law / God keeps the soul / enemies watch for the life (§5.2); vengeance: malice in the soul / redemption in God's heart / comfort to the anxious heart (§6.1); fatness: a satisfied soul / a dull heart (§2.3); *šāgâ*: unwitting error / self-accusation / intoxication (§4.2); the heart "lifted up": courage in the Lord's ways / pride (2Ch 17:6; already in Batch D); kinship-flesh: restoration (David) / fratricide (Abimelech) (§1.3); A life has a price in law and in narrative, but not before God (§2.2; §1.4). This qualifies Batch G §5.4.; The eating-and-drinking threshold, extended (Batch F §7): Esther's wine-banquets: Haman leaves "joyful and glad of heart" → wrath → gallows (Est 5:6–14). At the second banquet the king rises "from the wine-drinking" in wrath, and Haman begs for his life (7:7–8). The same banquet is the threshold for Esther's petition and for Haman's fall.; The threshold refused at the heart: "Daniel resolved [*set on his heart*] that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine" (Dan 1:8) → "fatter in flesh" than those who ate it (1:15). Compare Uriah (Batch F §7.5).; The inner sentence before the feast: "My master is delayed" → eat, drink, get drunk → the master arrives (Luk 12:45–46; §3.2).

16932.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The merry heart is a threshold state. In every narrative it comes after eating and drinking and immediately before a decisive event, which others usually initiate. The good heart lowers guard. What enters at that moment decides the outcome: murder (Amnon); exposure and anger (Vashti, Ahasuerus); mockery turned to catastrophe (Samson); outrage (Gibeah); approach and redemption (Ruth); a dead heart the next morning (Nabal); God's claim on the soul (the rich fool); The heart's condition swings overnight. Nabal: merry heart → dead heart (1Sa 25:36–37). Ahasuerus: merry heart → burning anger (Est 1:10–12). The heart's state is not stable; wine sets it high, and news or refusal drops it.; 1Ki 21 joins spirit and heart. Ahab's spirit is vexed and he stops eating. Jezebel prescribes food and a good heart, secured by injustice. A spirit-state is "cured" by manufacturing a heart-state — the only place in the batch where one is treated through the other.; Positive merriment exists outside the narratives: "they … went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown" (1Ki 8:66); "A joyful heart is good medicine" (Pro 17:22); "A glad heart makes a cheerful face" (Pro 15:13); "let your heart cheer you … But know that … God will bring you into judgment" (Ecc 11:9); When the heart is good because of God, no threshold event follows. When it is good from wine, one does.; Revisit (Batch G) — the threshold pattern extended: The step before the merry heart: "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5, 8). The father-in-law alternates *strengthen* (5, 8) and *merry* (6, 9). Each round delays departure (G §3.1).; The threshold engineered and refused: David "made him drunk" (2Sa 11:13). Uriah, who had sworn "as your soul lives, I will not do this thing" (11:11), still does not go home. The next morning: the death letter (11:14–15) (G §4).; The soul's version: "prepare for me delicious food … that my soul may bless you" (Gen 27:4). "He ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank" (27:25) → the irreversible blessing of the false firstborn → Esau's hatred "in his heart" (27:41; §8.2 below) (G §13.3).; The Samson sequence in full (Judg 16:15–30): soul vexed (16); heart told (17); strength and the Lord gone (19–20); the Philistines' merry hearts (25); strength asked for (28)

16933.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: "let my soul die" (30); The merry-heart threshold is the penultimate step (G §3.6).; The counter-case: the sad heart at a feast.; Hannah "would not eat … why is your heart sad?" → prays "after they had eaten and drunk" → is taken for drunk → "troubled in spirit … pouring out my soul" → face no longer sad (1Sa 1:7–18).; Nehemiah: "when wine was before him … Why is your face sad? … sadness of the heart" → prayer → request granted (Neh 2:1–5).; The sad heart at the feast is also a threshold, but what enters is prayer, and the outcome is a gift (G §8.2).; Revisit (Batch H §7.6) — the threshold pattern extended again: Esther's wine-banquets (Est 5:6–14; 7:3–8): "as they were drinking wine after the feast" (5:6) → Haman goes out "joyful and glad of heart" (5:9) → sees Mordecai → wrath → "all this is worth nothing to me" (5:13) → the gallows (5:14).; At the second banquet Esther asks for her life (7:3). The king "arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking" (7:7), and Haman begs for his life (7:7–8).; One banquet is the threshold for two outcomes: Esther's petition is granted; Haman falls.; The threshold refused at the heart: "Daniel resolved [*set on his heart*] that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank" (Dan 1:8) → "fatter in flesh" than those who ate it (1:15). Compare Uriah (point 5).; The inner sentence comes first: "if that servant says to himself, 'My master is delayed,' and begins … to eat and drink and get drunk" → the master comes "on a day when he does not expect him" (Luk 12:45–46; Mat 24:48–51).; The warning: "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34).; The counter-statement: "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17).; Revisit (Batch G v3 §16) — the threshold and death: Nabal's sequel: the heart dies in the morning (1Sa 25:37), and "about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (25:38). The dead heart comes before the dead man.

16934.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The threshold entered with death in view: the Lord "called for weeping and mourning … and behold, joy and gladness … eating flesh and drinking wine. 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.'" → "this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die" (Isa 22:12–14). The feast is held against a call to mourn.; The threshold reversed: Elijah asks to die (1Ki 19:4) → "Arise and eat" (19:5, 7) → "in the strength of that food" to Horeb (19:8). Here the meal does not lower the guard. It carries an exhausted soul across from wanting to die to going on.

17042.text: 1.11 The desires of the flesh (NT): "walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh" (Gal 5:16) [D3]; "the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh … to keep you from doing the things you want to do" (Gal 5:17) [D3] — the Spirit also desires; "those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires" (Gal 5:24); "carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind" (Eph 2:3); "the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes" (1Jo 2:16); "make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires" (Rom 13:14); "the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul" (1Pe 2:11) — flesh against soul; "no longer for human passions but for the will of God" (1Pe 4:2); "the lust of defiling passion" (2Pe 2:10, d0); "sensual passions of the flesh" (2Pe 2:18); "born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God" (Joh 1:13)

And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom" (Dan 6:3) [H2+X] — a quality of spirit prompts another's plan.; "in whose spirit there is no deceit" beside "the Lord counts no iniquity" (Psa 32:2) [H1].; "his mind was made like that of a beast … until he knew that the Most High … sets over it whom he will" (Dan 5:21).

(1Co 9:11); "spiritual blessings … material blessings" (Rom 15:27) — neutral; "not by earthly [*fleshly*] wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12) — with "the testimony of our conscience"

(Psa 22:26); "For I will not contend forever … for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (Isa 57:16) [H2] — God limits his contending for the sake of the human spirit; "who inhabits eternity … I dwell … also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isa 57:15) [H1]; "Do not deliver the soul of your dove to the wild beasts" (Psa 74:19)

17107.text: Setting the heart to seek (cf. Batch B §0.1): "set your mind and heart [*heart and soul*] to seek the Lord" (1Ch 22:19); "those who had set their hearts to seek the Lord" (2Ch 11:16); "you … have set your heart to seek God" (2Ch 19:3); "who sets his heart to seek God … even though not according to the sanctuary's rules" (2Ch 30:19); "Ezra had set his heart to study [*seek*] the Law" (Ezr 7:10); Failure: "he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (2Ch 12:14)

Return to the Lord your God" (Joe 2:13); "lest they … understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed" (Isa 6:10; Joh 12:40); "the intent of your heart may be forgiven you" (Act 8:22)

17135.text: 8.2 The heart turning away: "lest his heart turn away" (Deu 17:17); "that his heart may not be lifted up … that he may not turn aside" (Deu 17:20); "Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside" (Deu 11:16); "Cursed is the man who … makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the Lord" (Jer 17:5) — heart turning and trusting flesh are the same act; "this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside" (Jer 5:23); "Let not your heart turn aside to her ways" (Pro 7:25); "his wives turned away his heart after other gods" (1Ki 11:4); "their whoring heart that has departed from me" (Eze 6:9); "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jer 32:40) — God guards the heart against turning; "keep your soul diligently … lest they depart from your heart" (Deu 4:9); "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds … they rebel against me" (Hos 7:14).

17136.text: 8.3 God removes and replaces — heart, spirit and flesh in one act: "I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh" (Eze 11:19; 36:26) [H1]; "remove the foreskin of your hearts" (Jer 4:4)

17139.text: 8.3 God removes and replaces — heart, spirit and flesh in one act: [Claude reading] In Eze 11:19 / 36:26, heart, spirit and flesh are all tagged "remove" within four positions. Flesh is the good material here (a "heart of flesh") and stone is the bad, the reverse of NT flesh-desire (§1.11). Compare 2Co 3:3 (§3.3).

17140.text: 8.4 The contrite spirit and heart (§0.7): "The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit" (Psa 34:18) [H1]; "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psa 51:17) [H1] (M30 tag); "to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isa 57:15) [H1]; [Claude reading] In each verse the spirit and the heart are paired as the crushed, and God is the one who draws near, accepts or revives.

17141.text: Revisit 2026-09-28: Read in context, Psa 51:17 ends a sequence of four spirits: right (v10), Holy (v11), willing (v12), broken (v17).; Isa 57:15 continues: "I will not contend forever … for the spirit would grow faint before me" (57:16).; See Batch F §5 for the full crushing vocabulary by agent.

17142.text: 8.5 God's regret and relenting: "the Lord regretted that he had made man … and it grieved him to his heart" (Gen 6:6); "rend your hearts … he relents over disaster" (Joe 2:13); "did not the Lord relent … But we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves [*our souls*]" (Jer 26:19)
