18875.text: *Ṭāman*, "to hide, bury". A thing is put into or under something. Achan's plunder is "hidden in the earth inside my tent" (Joshua 7:21). Moses "hid him in the sand" (Exodus 2:12). An enemy's net is hidden in the path (Psalm 140:5). It is also the word for the sluggard who "buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it back to his mouth" (Proverbs 19:24).

18878.text: Hiding from people: Much of the hiding in Scripture is from people who could do harm, and in these verses it is the weaker side that hides. "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). "The poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). When Israel hid in the caves, "all the people followed him trembling" (1 Samuel 13:7).; Often the verse records not the feeling of the one who hides but someone else's counsel to hide.; Jonathan: "Saul my father seeks to kill you … Stay in a secret place and hide yourself" (1 Samuel 19:2).; God to Elijah: "hide yourself by the brook Cherith" (1 Kings 17:3).; Where the feeling is named, it is fear.; Jacob fled from Laban "secretly", and he said why: "Because I was afraid" (Genesis 31:27, 31).; Joseph of Arimathea was "a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews". The same verse ends with him going to Pilate and taking away the body (John 19:38).; Hiding can be good sense: "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it" (Proverbs 22:3). It ends when the news changes. The men who had hidden in the hills "heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle" (1 Samuel 14:22).; And sometimes hiding is refused, or impossible.; The servant chooses not to hide: "I gave my back to those who strike … I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6).; No one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend" (Psalm 55:12–13).

18879.text: Rahab hid the spies, and gave her reason: "as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted … for the Lord your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath" (Joshua 2:11). All Jericho's hearts melted. It was her confession that turned her to hide them.

18882.text: Hiding another: God hides people too, and those he hides ask for it.; "Hide me in the shadow of your wings" (Psalm 17:8).; "You hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues" (Psalm 31:20).; The servant is hidden to be used later: "in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away" (Isaiah 49:2).; At the last, a life is hidden in someone: "your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3).; There is a false shelter too: "we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter" (Isaiah 28:15).

18883.text: Hiding what I hold: A person can hide what he has done. Achan tells it in order: "when I saw … then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent" (Joshua 7:21). Joshua had to ask him first: "do not hide it from me" (7:19).; What happens next differs.

18886.text: It can be kept because it is enjoyed. "Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue, though he is loath to let it go" (Job 20:12–13).

18889.text: The hidden trap: In the Psalms a purpose is hidden in order to catch someone. "They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, 'Who can see them?'" (Psalm 64:5). The next verse says where the purpose was hidden first: "For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (64:6).; The one it is set for prays out of his weakness. "When my spirit faints within me, you know my way! In the path where I walk they have hidden a trap for me" (Psalm 142:3). "No one cares for my soul" (142:4). It is worse when it comes from those he had prayed for: "Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them" (Jeremiah 18:20).; And the trap turns. "In the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught" (Psalm 9:15). The soul the pit was dug for (Psalm 35:7) is the soul that rejoices: "Then my soul will rejoice in the Lord" (35:9). The one taken "out of the net they have hidden for me" says, "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:4–5).

18891.text: Who hides whom. God hiding a person is safety. God hiding his face from a person is dismay. The two are four verses apart in one psalm (Psalm 27:5, 9; 10.9).

18904.text: What it is. Knowing that cannot close: a mind held open before something it cannot interpret. The bearers are all human: Herod (Mar 6:20; Luk 9:7), the disciples (Joh 13:22), the women at the tomb (Luk 24:4), the Pentecost crowd (Act 2:12), the temple captain and chief priests (Act 5:24), Peter (Act 10:17), Paul (2Cor 4:8; Gal 4:20), Festus (Act 25:20), and Belshazzar's lords (Dan 5:9).

18905.text: What carries it instead of a seat: the question spoken aloud: "What does this mean?" (Act 2:12); "who is this about whom I hear such things?" (Luk 9:9, context); the gaze: "The disciples looked at one another" (Joh 13:22); a reflexive pronoun: Act 10:17 "inwardly perplexed" is *en heautō*, "in himself". The inner location is there, but through a pronoun, not a seat word.; the body of the other party: in Dan 5:6 the king's "color changed … his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together". The body tells the alarm while his lords are perplexed.

18906.text: Before and after. Perplexity is a waiting state that something from outside ends: Luk 24:4, "While they were perplexed … behold, two men stood by them"; Act 10:17–19: the men arrive at the gate, and the Spirit speaks; Act 2:12–14: "But Peter, standing … lifted up his voice"; Dan 5:10–12: the queen names Daniel; The operation rarely resolves from within. An interpreter arrives.

18908.text: How the sense shifts. In Mar 6:20, Herod "feared John, knowing … greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly". Four inner operations sit on one bearer with no seat word, each named by a word from a different cluster (fear M01, knowing M15, gladness M04). The operations name themselves. In Gal 4:20 the perplexity is love's: it comes straight after "my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth" (4:19).

18912.text: Compare the one seated resurrection doubt: in Luk 24:38 (an M63 word, so outside this set), "why do doubts arise in your hearts?". Doubt gets its seat when Jesus names it from outside. When the narrator records it, it has none.

18925.text: *satar* H5641, hide (75 no-seat) | Psa 143:7 "my spirit fails! Hide not your face"; Psa 88:14 soul; Psa 104:29 "they are dismayed … breath"; Psa 10:11 heart | God hiding his face. The seat is the human recipient's: Psa 13:1 (13:2 "sorrow in my heart"); Psa 30:7 "you hid your face; I was dismayed"; Psa 44:24; 69:17; 102:2; Isa 8:17 ("I will wait … and I will hope in him"); Isa 54:8; 59:2; 64:7; Mic 3:4; Deu 31:17 | Physical hiding (David 1Sa 20, 23, 26; Jeremiah and Baruch Jer 36): outward, with inner being behind the act at most. God concealing (Pro 25:2; Deu 29:29): divine subject

The body carries it. The sense shifts in Psa 38:18, "I am sorry for my sin": anxiety turned to repentance

18933.text: 3. What carries the inner being when there is no seat (M20): The operation word names itself. *Perplexed, doubted, anxious, discouraged* need no seat. The seat is added when someone diagnoses (Luk 24:38) or sets the frame of a discourse (Mat 6:25; Luk 12:22).; The act carries it. Hiding for fear; the sluggard's buried hand (§1.5; §2 *taman*).; The body carries it. Peter sinking; Belshazzar's knees; bread eaten with trembling (§1.2; §1.1; §2).; Speech carries it. The grumblers' quoted words; "What does this mean?"; the father's "What shall I do about my son?" (§1.6; §1.1; §2).; The seat is inside the word. *Dipsuchos*, *athumeō*, *alupos*, and brokenhearted *ka'ah* (§1.3).; Inner places named outside M47: "bosom" H2243 T2 (Job 31:33: ESV "heart" is *chob*); "chambers of the belly" (Pro 18:8); "in himself" (Act 10:17); These are seats the M47 list does not hold.; The passage carries it. The seat is stated once and inherited (Luk 12; Mat 6), stated as the cause in the next clause (Deu 1:28), or given as the passage's frame (Jer 17:5–10; 2Cor 4:6, 16).; Another party's seat. Jesus troubled in spirit while the disciples are perplexed (Joh 13:21–22); the oppressor's heart and the victim's crushing (Psa 10:10–11); God hides his face and the human is dismayed (Psa 30:7).; No inner operation at all. Physical concealment of objects and people, and "cut off". This is the largest single group, and the tag does not describe it.

18935.text: Books: Isaiah is high because of H8213 "bring low" (Isa 2, 5, 25, 26) and the Sennacherib account (Isa 37). Mark is the mute spirit and the silencing words.

18959.text: 8. Earlier work: There is no pre-reset M53 study in _analytics/Clusters/archive/stale-20260907/, and the M53 folder was empty before this pull.; Group B was read in M09 (#2148) and M08 (#2156).; Group A: Sennacherib (2Ki 19:22–23; Isa 37:23–24), Judg 5:18, Zep 2:10 and Pro 17:5 were decided in M08; batch 1 of #2171 has now read 18 group A verses in their passages (1Sa 17, 2Ki 19, Isa 37, 2Ch 32, Neh 6:13, Judg 5:18, Judg 8:15, 2Sa 21:21, 23:9, 1Ch 20:7), and the trial read Psa 69:9 and Rom 15:3.

Verb and noun share 4 verses and come within three verses of each other in 9: Goliath (1Sa 17:25–26), Psa 44:13–16, Psa 69:6–10, Psa 79:12, Psa 89:50–51, Psa 119:39–42, Zep 2:8–10. Rom 15:3 quotes Psa 69:9 with both Greek words: "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me."

18962.text: Reading A apart from M07 would split one passage across two strands. Sennacherib's mocking (2Ki 19:23; Isa 37:24) ends in its inhabitants "dismayed and confounded" (2Ki 19:26; Isa 37:27), which are among M07's 8 M72 forwards.

Rom 1:27 "shameless acts" is one sentence of a passage that also has "the dishonoring of their bodies" (1:24) and "dishonorable passions" (1:26), both M07 (read in the trial). 18971.text: a. "In the Spirit / in spirit" — visionary or prayer state: Rev 1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10; 1Co 14:2; Act 19:21; 20:22.; Could be the person's own spirit (cf. 1Co 14:14 "my spirit prays") or God's Spirit.

18972.text: b. The flesh–Spirit antithesis — D3: Gal 5:5, 16–18, 22, 25; 6:8; Rom 8:4–6, 13; Gal 3:3; 4:29; Rom 7:6; Joh 3:5.; The ESV reads these as divine. The verses alone don't decide it, although the paragraphs contain explicit D1 verses (Gal 4:6; Rom 8:9).

19000.text: Already carried: Lev 25:43 and Neh 5:15 (10.10 *The fear of God and the weak*); Isa 14:6 (10.10 *Anger between people*)

19019.text: The passage. Vashti refused to come (1:12; cited in 10.1, 10.13 and Ch 11). The counsel was that the noble women *"will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be contempt and wrath in plenty"* (1:18). The decree was to have this result: *"all women will give honor to their husbands"* (1:20). *"This advice pleased the king"* (1:21).

19020.text: Reading: The rule of each house is made a matter of royal law.; The motive given is fear of contempt and wrath (1:18), and the aim is honour (1:20). Honour, an inner act, is commanded by decree.

19028.text: The inner ground of harsh rule: feeding oneself (Eze 34:2), a lack of understanding and love of gain (Pro 28:16), anger (Isa 14:6).

19031.text: Already carried: Luk 4:6, the devil's offer of all authority (13.3); Dan 11:3–4, *"rule with great dominion and do as he wills"* (10.7 *Willing*); 2Pe 2:10, *"despise authority"* (Ch 7)

19034.text: What follows at once: He asks for the earrings of the spoil (8:24).; *"Gideon made an ephod of it … And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family"* (8:27).

19035.text: The passage. *"their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'"* (9:3). He hired *"worthless and reckless fellows"* with silver from the house of Baal-berith (9:4). He *"killed his brothers … seventy men, on one stone"* (9:5).

19046.text: Joh 19:10–11. The trial read these, and its reading stands. Pilate claims his authority out of fear (19:8). Jesus names its source, *"given you from above"*.

19048.text: Home: Ch 11 §7, face *where authority comes from*, beside Joh 19:11. Pointers to Ch 8 (13:5) and 10.12 (13:3).

19057.text: The verses: *"Am I not free?"* (9:1); *"Do we not have the right to eat and drink? … to take along a believing wife … to refrain from working for a living?"* (9:4–6); *"Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ"* (9:12); *"I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting"* (9:15); *"For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward"* (9:17); *"present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel"* (9:18); *"For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them"* (9:19)

19061.text: The verses: *"our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you"* (10:8). *"I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters"* (10:9).; *"that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down"* (13:10). The verses before: *"we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for"* (13:9).

19062.text: What the group shows (the face *a right held and not used*): Each verse holds the right as real, and names its source: the Lord gave it.; The reason for not using it is always another person: the gospel and those it might win (1Cor 9); an example to imitate (2Th 3:9); the weak brother (1Cor 8:9); building up, not tearing down (2Cor 13:10)

19082.text: Psa 8:4–6. *"what is man that you are mindful of him … Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor. You have given him dominion over the works of your hands"*.: The psalm opens and closes with *"O Lord, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!"* (8:9).

19101.text: Spirits and nature (16).: 13.3: the dragon's authority given to the beast (Rev 13), *"the power of darkness"* (Luk 22:53), and the evil spirit that *"mastered"* the sons of Sceva (Act 19:16).; 13.2: the angels with authority (Rev 14:18; 18:1).; 13.4: the lights *"to rule the day"* (Gen 1:16; Psa 136:8–9).

19102.text: Face: Dominion given; From: Gen 1:26–28; Psa 8:4–6; Dan 2:37–38; Where the detail lives: 13.1, 13.4, 10.9

19146.text: Luk 10:19–20. *"Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven."*

19198.text: (f) Hiding as prudence. Pro 22:3 = 27:12, "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it." The sequence is seeing leads to judging leads to hiding. The failure is the simple one's: seeing without acting.

19200.text: How it co-exists across the strands. Trembling (1Sa 13:7; Dan 10:7), fear (Gen 31:31; Joh 19:38), and seeing danger (Pro 22:3; 1Ch 21:20). Its opposite is the prudent/simple pair (f).

19201.text: Seat.; In the verse: 2Ch 22:9 "heart". The word has a genuine inner-being sense, but the heart is Jehoshaphat's, the dead grandfather's: "who sought the Lord with all his heart". Ahaziah, the one hiding, has no seat. Spurious for this phenomenon (v1 §0). Batch C v3 §7.1 read it as seeking the Lord with the heart. Batch G v3 §16.11 read it as "a dead man honoured for his grandfather's heart". Both readings stand. Neither concerns hiding.; Whose seat: none of the 40 hiders has one. In strand (a) the inner operation belongs to the counsellor, and it is shown by what the counsellor says, not by a seat word (v2, kept above).; Outside the verse — new in v3. In strand (a), the nearest seat word is *nephesh* in its life sense: the life being hunted. David, in the psalm headed by the Ziphites' report that he is "hiding among us" (Psa 54:1), says "the Lord is the upholder of my life" (54:4). The seat word names what is at stake in the hiding, not where the hider feels it. This fits Batch G v3 §5 ("Life spared, life hunted — the *nephesh* as a prize"), which it does not change.; Strand (f), prudence — new in v3: Pro 22:3 ("The prudent sees danger and hides himself") → 22:5 "Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them". The prudent one's hiding is a guarding of the soul. *Nephesh* here is the self that is kept from harm, and it passes the check in that sense. Strand (f) is the only strand of §2 where the one who hides has a seat, and the seat is the thing the hiding protects.

19202.text: The human who hides another: Rahab (Jos 2:6; 6:17, 25). The reason she gives: "as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted … for the Lord your God, he is God" (2:11). The hiding comes out of a confession.; Obadiah hid a hundred prophets "by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water" (1Ki 18:4, 13). He recalls it himself when he fears for his life (18:13).; Jehosheba hid Joash (2Ki 11:2–3; 2Ch 22:11–12). The text's reason: "because she was a sister of Ahaziah" (2Ch 22:11).; Moses's parents (Heb 11:23): "By faith … hidden … by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king's edict". The one who hides another acts without fear, the reverse of §2.; The mother in the famine (2Ki 6:29): "she has hidden her son". This is the one protective act in a scene where two women agreed to eat their children (6:28). Her inner movement is not stated; the act alone shows it.; The command: "shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive" (Isa 16:3).

19203.text: God hiding the person: "hide me in the shadow of your wings" (Psa 17:8); "he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble" (Psa 27:5); "you hide them from the plots of men; you store them … from the strife of tongues" (Psa 31:20); "Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked" (Psa 64:2); "You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue" (Job 5:21); "the Lord hid them" (Jer 36:26); "in the shadow of his hand he hid me … in his quiver he hid me away" (Isa 49:2): hidden for later use, not only for safety; "enter your chambers … hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by" (Isa 26:20): God's own people hidden from God's own fury; "perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3): conditional, after "seek humility"; "your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Col 3:3), after "Set your minds on things that are above" (3:2)

19204.text: What it does. For the sheltered it answers a petition (Psa 17:8; 64:2) and grounds trust. In the hider it shows confession (Rahab), fearlessness (Heb 11:23), or kinship (2Ch 22:11).

19205.text: Where it comes from. A threat to life. Notably, in three verses the threat is speech: "the strife of tongues" (Psa 31:20), "the lash of the tongue" (Job 5:21), "secret plots" (Psa 64:2).

19207.text: Seat.; In the verse: none of the 23 names a seat.; Outside the verse — new in v3. For Rahab, the one human hider who explains herself, the seat arrives in her own confession: "our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the Lord your God, he is God" (Jos 2:11). The seat is the hider's own, and genuine. It is the collective heart of Jericho that melted. [Claude reading] What turns Rahab to shelter the spies is not the melting itself, which all Jericho shares, but the confession she draws from it. The seat is where the fear sits. The act of hiding comes from the confession.; Isa 26:20 → 26:18 "wind" ("we have given birth to wind") is *ruach* as wind. Spurious.; Psa 17:8 → 17:9 "my deadly enemies who surround me". The seat word is inside the English "deadly": *nephesh*, the life the enemies are against. Life-sense only. It names what is at stake in the petition "hide me", as in §2 (Psa 54:4).; Whose seat, God as hider: none is named. The sheltered person's inner state is carried by the petition ("hide me") and the trust, not by a seat word.

19212.text: What it does in the human: Dismay: "you hid your face; I was dismayed" (Psa 30:7); "When you hide your face, they are dismayed; when you take away their breath, they die" (Psa 104:29); The spirit failing: "My spirit fails! Hide not your face from me, lest I be like those who go down to the pit" (Psa 143:7); Being cast away: "why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face" (Psa 88:14); Feeling forgotten: "Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psa 13:1). The seat follows at once: "How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day?" (13:2); The body pressed down: "Why do you hide your face? … For our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly clings to the ground" (Psa 44:24–25); Melting: "you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities" (Isa 64:7). The previous verse: "We all fade like a leaf" (64:6); Being counted an enemy: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24); "Will you frighten a driven leaf?" (13:25); A collective conclusion: "Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?" (Deu 31:17); Complaint: "My way is hidden from the Lord, and my right is disregarded by my God" (Isa 40:27). The answer: "He does not faint or grow weary … He gives power to the faint" (40:28–29); Banishment and the fear that follows it: Cain, "from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive … whoever finds me will kill me" (Gen 4:14), after "My punishment is greater than I can bear" (4:13). Being hidden from God's face is followed at once by fear of man.

19217.text: Psa 51:9 → 51:10 "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me". New in v3: when God is asked to hide his face *from the sin*, the next request places the remedy in the heart and spirit. The seat is where the cleansing is to happen. The requests go on: "Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me" (51:11), then "uphold me with a willing spirit" (51:12). The face hidden from the sin (51:9) is set against the presence not withdrawn from the person (51:11). Between them stand two spirits: God's, which is not to be taken away, and the human's, which is to be renewed and made willing.; New in v3: Psa 102:2 ("Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress") → 102:4 "My heart is struck down like grass and has withered; I forget to eat my bread". The distress of 102:2 is a withered heart, and it reaches the body: the sufferer forgets to eat. It is the same movement as Psa 44:25 ("our belly clings to the ground").; New in v3: Psa 27:9 ← 27:8 "You have said, 'Seek my face.' My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek.'" The heart seeks the face one verse before it asks that the face not be hidden. The petition "Hide not your face" (27:9) is the voice of a heart already turned toward the face. What hiddenness would cut off is the heart's own seeking.; New in v3: Psa 69:17 → 69:20 "Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none". The "distress" of 69:17 is named three verses later as a broken heart that finds no comforter. The hidden face of 69:17 and the absent human pity of 69:20 are the same lack, felt from God and from people. In between, the petition names the soul: "Draw near to my soul, redeem me" (69:18). The opposite of the hidden face is God drawing near to the soul.; New in v3, the resolution in the heart: Psa 22:24 ("he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard") → 22:26 "The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the Lord! May your hearts live forever!" When the face is not hidden, the outcome lands in hearts that live. It is the reverse of the withered heart that forgets to eat (Psa 102:4): here the afflicted eat, and the hearts live.

19218.text: Life-sense, in the passage: Psa 89:46 ("How long, O Lord? Will you hide yourself forever?") → 89:48 "What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" *Nephesh* here is the life facing death. The hidden face is set against human mortality. This is a pointer to Batch G v3 §16.4 ("The soul delivered from death"), not read further here.; New in v3: Isa 54:8 ← 54:6 "the Lord has called you like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit, like a wife of youth when she is cast off". The momentary hiding of 54:8 is borne in a grieved spirit (the bearer's own, Zion's). The image is marital: the hidden face is felt as desertion.; Spurious context links: Isa 64:7 ← 64:6 "our iniquities, like the wind, take us away" (*ruach* as wind); Mic 3:4 ← 3:2–3 "flesh" (the flesh torn from the people). Neither is an inner seat.; What the map shows. Every genuine seat in this phenomenon falls on the human side. Three forms: The sufferer's spirit, soul or heart is where the hiddenness is felt: failing, cast away, sorrowing, bowed down, broken, grieved.; The offender's heart is where it is misread or ignored: "God has forgotten" (Psa 10:11); "the way of his own heart" (Isa 57:17).; God's Spirit is where it ends: poured out (Eze 39:29).

19224.text: (a) Concealing one's own wrong. Each case has its own sequence: Achan: "when I saw … then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent" (Jos 7:21); Joshua: "tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me" (7:19); Achan: "Truly I have sinned" (7:20); "behold, it was hidden in his tent" (7:22); Seeing, coveting, taking, hiding, being demanded to disclose, confessing, being found.; Moses: "He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand" (Exo 2:12). When the deed surfaces: "Moses was afraid, and thought, 'Surely the thing is known'" (2:14). Concealment fails, and fear follows.; The hidden adultery: "it is hidden from the eyes of her husband" (Num 5:13). The next verse: "the spirit of jealousy comes over him" (5:14). Where a deed is hidden, suspicion grows in the other person.; Job's denial: "if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart [*chob*, bosom], because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence" (Job 31:33–34). The verse names the motive for concealing sin: fear of social contempt. Job denies he acted on it.; The lepers: they hid the plunder (2Ki 7:8), then "said to one another, 'We are not doing right … If we are silent … punishment will overtake us'" (7:9). Conscience reverses concealment into telling.; Concealment as savouring: "Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue, though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth" (Job 20:12–13). The hidden sin is kept because it is enjoyed.; Not hiding at all: "the look on their faces bears witness against them; they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it" (Isa 3:9). The face discloses: shamelessness.

19230.text: How it co-exists. Fear is the most frequent companion, on both sides: fear drives concealment (Job 31:34; Mat 25:25), or follows its failure (Exo 2:14); fear blocks disclosure until it is overcome (1Sa 3:15–18); Joy (Mat 13:44), enjoyment of sin (Job 20:12–13) and conscience (2Ki 7:9) are the other companions.

19231.text: Seat.; In the verse, the bearer's own (genuine): Psa 40:10 "I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart". Batch A v3 §6 ("The heart can conceal or not"). The heart is the place where a word could be kept back, and the verse says it was not.; In the verse, the offender's own self: Isa 3:9 "they have brought evil on themselves [*their nephesh*]". Batch D v2 §2.3 ("Evil against one's own soul"). Seat-sense: *nephesh* is here the self, reflexively, and it passes the check in that sense. New in v3: the verse holds the phenomenon and its outcome together. The face does *not* conceal ("they do not hide it"), and the evil disclosed comes back on the self that disclosed it. Shamelessness is not a safe disclosure.; In the next verse, the other party's (genuine): Num 5:13 → 5:14 "the spirit of jealousy comes over him". The deed is hidden in the wife; the seat that registers it is the husband's spirit (v2).; A seat outside M47: Job 31:33 *chob*, "bosom", where the iniquity would be hidden (v1 §3 item 6; not an M47 word).; In the passage, the bearer's own — new in v3: Job 6:10 ("This would be my comfort … for I have not denied the words of the Holy One") is flanked by two uses of *nephesh*: "My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me" (6:7). *Nephesh* is appetite here. The sense passes the check only as bodily desire, and it has turned to loathing.; "What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient?" (6:11). *Nephesh* is inside the English "be patient", literally "lengthen my soul". It is genuine, and the soul cannot endure.; Job's one comfort, that he has not concealed God's words, stands between an appetite that loathes and a soul that can no longer wait. Not concealing is the one thing left intact.; Spurious context link: 2Sa 14:18 → 14:19 "As surely as you live [*nephesh*]" is an oath formula. Batch G v3 §4 read the formula as "the soul as what one swears by". It says nothing of the disclosure.; Whose seat, strand (b) and (e): none. The disclosures of Samuel, the kings' demands, the treasure-finder's joy and the servant's fear are all carried by speech and act, not by a seat word.

19235.text: Seat.; In the verse: none of the 13 names a seat.; In the passage — new in v3: in six passages the seat arrives close by. Each time it is genuine, but it belongs to a different party or plays a different role: The other party names it. Luk 9:45–46 → 9:47 "But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child". The disciples' blocked perception, their fear of asking and their rivalry have no seat word. The seat appears only when Jesus reads it: their hearts, known by another. This matches what v1 §3 item 1 found for doubt (Luk 24:38): the seat is named when someone diagnoses.; The offender's heart as the cause. Isa 29:14 ← 29:13 "their hearts are far from me" (v2; Batch G v3 §12.3). Hidden discernment is the consequence of a heart that has gone elsewhere.; The bearer's own heart as the prayer's end. Psa 19:12 (hidden faults) → 19:14 "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight". The one who cannot see his own hidden faults hands the heart's meditation over to God's sight. What is hidden from the self is entrusted to the one from whom nothing is hidden (§6).; The bearer's own soul as the source of the plea. Psa 119:19 ("hide not your commandments from me!") → 119:20 "My soul is consumed with longing for your rules at all times". The plea not to have the commandments hidden comes from a soul consumed with longing for them. Here the not-knowing is feared, and the fear comes from desire, the reverse of Luk 9:45, where the disciples are afraid to ask.; Heart and soul in the response to what is revealed. Deu 29:29 → 30:2 "return to the Lord your God … and obey his voice … with all your heart and with all your soul". The revealed things (29:29) are to be done, and the next verses place that doing in the whole heart and soul.; The sufferer's soul. Job 3:23 ("a man whose way is hidden") sits in the passage opened by "life to the bitter in soul" (3:20; see §4). The hemmed-in man is the bitter soul.

19236.text: Who bears it: Herod (Mar 6:20; Luk 9:7); the disciples (Joh 13:22); the women at the tomb (Luk 24:4); the Pentecost crowd (Act 2:12); the temple captain and chief priests (Act 5:24); Peter (Act 10:17); Festus (Act 25:20); Paul (2Cor 4:8; Gal 4:20); Belshazzar's lords (Dan 5:9).

19237.text: Where it comes from. Something heard or seen that exceeds the categories at hand: "it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead" (Luk 9:7); "we hear them telling in our own tongues" (Act 2:11–12); "what the vision … might mean" (Act 10:17); an empty tomb (Luk 24:3–4); Jesus's "one of you will betray me" (Joh 13:21–22); writing on a wall no one could read (Dan 5:8–9)

19238.text: What it does. It asks aloud: "What does this mean?" (Act 2:12); "who is this about whom I hear such things?" (Luk 9:9). It looks at others: "The disciples looked at one another" (Joh 13:22). It turns inward: "Peter was inwardly [*en heautō*, in himself] perplexed" (Act 10:17). Festus hands the question on: "Being at a loss how to investigate … I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem" (Act 25:20).

19239.text: How it co-exists.; Herod: "Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man … When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly" (Mar 6:20). Fear, knowledge, perplexity and gladness are all present in one man towards one prophet, and the perplexity keeps him listening.; Amazement: "all were amazed and perplexed" (Act 2:12).; The body of another man: Belshazzar's "color changed … his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Dan 5:6) while his lords were perplexed (5:9).; Anguish of love: "I am perplexed about you" (Gal 4:20), after "my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth" (4:19).; A limit held: "perplexed, but not driven to despair" (2Cor 4:8). The perplexity is bounded, and the neighbouring verses set it inside "God … has shone in our hearts" (4:6) and "this treasure in jars of clay" (4:7).

19240.text: What it leads to. Mostly, something from outside ends it: "While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them" (Luk 24:4); "the men … stood at the gate" and "the Spirit said to him" (Act 10:17, 19); "Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice" (Act 2:14); the queen names Daniel (Dan 5:10–12); Herod "sought to see him" (Luk 9:9); Perplexity ends when an interpreter or a meeting arrives.

19241.text: Seat.; In the verse: none of the 11 names a seat. The operation word names itself (v1 §1.1, §3 item 1). Act 10:17 locates it with a reflexive pronoun, *en heautō*, "in himself", which is not an M47 word (v1 §3 item 6).; In the passage, the other party's (genuine): Joh 13:22 ← 13:21 "Jesus was troubled in his spirit". The seat is Jesus's, and the perplexity is the disciples' (v1 §1.1).; In the passage, the bearer's own (genuine): 2Cor 4:8 ← 4:6 "God … has shone in our hearts" (v1 §1.1). The bounded perplexity sits inside hearts already lit.; In the passage, the interpreter's — new in v3: Dan 5:9 → 5:12 "an excellent spirit, knowledge, and understanding to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve problems were found in this Daniel". The lords are perplexed and have no seat. The seat that arrives belongs to the interpreter, and it is named as the very capacity the perplexed lack. This gives v2's finding a seat. Perplexity ends when an interpreter arrives, and in Daniel's case the text locates the interpreter's gift in his spirit.; Divine Spirit: Act 10:17 → 10:19 "the Spirit said to him". That is the other party, and divine. It ends the perplexity from outside.

19245.text: Seat.; In the verse, the bearer's own (genuine): Jam 4:8 "purify your hearts, you double-minded". Batch A v3 §6 ("Double-mindedness"); v1 §1.3.; Inside the word: *dipsuchos* (Jam 1:8; 4:8) carries *psychē* in its own form (v1 §1.3). The seat is present in both Jam verses, once by compound and once by a separate word.; No seat: Mat 14:31 and 28:17. The doubt is carried by the sinking body and the divided company (v1 §1.2). Mat 28:17 → 28:19 "the Holy Spirit" is divine and does not bear on the doubt.; Outside M20, for comparison only: "why do doubts arise in your hearts?" (Luk 24:38) and "does not doubt in his heart" (Mar 11:23) are Batch A v3 §6 ("Doubt in the heart"). They are other words and other clusters. They agree with v1 §1.2: doubt gets a seat when someone names it from outside (Jesus, twice), and has none when the narrator records it.; New in v3, what the map shows: in the four M20 doubt verses, the seat appears only in the remedy, "purify your hearts" (Jam 4:8). The doubt itself is shown in a wave, a sinking and a divided company, and the heart is named as the place to be cleansed.

19250.text: (e) Cares that choke. The sower parable: "the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word" (Mat 13:22); "the cares of the world … enter in and choke the word" (Mar 4:19); "as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life" (Luk 8:14); "lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life" (Luk 21:34).; Where from: outside ("enter in").; What it does: it acts on the word already received. It chokes it and weighs down the heart.; Co-exists with riches, pleasures and drunkenness.; Leads to: "it proves unfruitful"; "that day come upon you suddenly like a trap".

19256.text: Strand (b), a divine Spirit replaces the anxious speaker's own seat. Mat 10:19 → 10:20 "it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you". Batch E v2 §1.6 ("The Spirit speaks through the person"). The anxiety about what to say is answered by another's Spirit in the speaker's place. The Luke parallel runs the same way: Luk 12:11 → 12:12 "for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say". Luke gives the answer as teaching: the Spirit supplies the knowing that the anxiety lacked.; Strand (e), the choked hearer is set between two hearts — new in v3. Luk 8:14 (the thorns) stands between "the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts" (8:12) and "hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience" (8:15). The cares act on a heart where the word has been sown, and the contrast the passage draws is with a good heart that holds the word fast. Mat 13:22 ← 13:19 "snatches away what has been sown in his heart" is the same frame (v1 §2 *merimna* row).; The man who is not anxious. Jer 17:8 is framed by "whose heart turns away from the Lord" (17:5), and by "The heart is deceitful … I the Lord search the heart and test the mind" (17:9–10) (v1 §2 *de'agah* row). The unanxious tree stands between two statements about the heart.; Strand (g), a neighbouring oracle's heart. Jer 49:23 (Hamath and Arpad "melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea") follows 49:22, the end of the oracle against Edom: "the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains". The party is different: Edom in 49:22, the cities of Damascus in 49:23. So the seat does not belong to the anxious ones of 49:23. What the two oracles share is the same collapse under bad news. It is stated as a heart in labour for Edom's warriors, and as melting and a troubled sea for Hamath. It is recorded as a parallel, not as the seat of 49:23.; Spurious context link: Jer 38:19 → 38:17 "your life shall be spared". *Nephesh* is bodily life here: the life Zedekiah fears to lose. It names what the dread is about, not a seat.

19257.text: Where it comes from. In all five verses, from another party: a father's provoking: "Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); false prophets' lies: "you have disheartened the righteous falsely, although I have not grieved him" (Eze 13:22). God did not do the grieving; the lie did.; an oppressor: "The helpless are crushed, sink down, and fall by his might" (Psa 10:10), while "He says in his heart, 'God has forgotten'" (10:11); a persecutor who "pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death" (Psa 109:16), who "loved to curse" (109:17); military defeat: "ships of Kittim shall come against him" (Dan 11:30)

19259.text: Seat.; Inside the word or phrase, the victim's own (genuine): Eze 13:22 "you have disheartened the righteous". The Hebrew includes *lev*, the heart, in the phrase. Batch A v3 §6 ("Disheartened by others").; Psa 109:16 "the brokenhearted" (*nikh'eh levav*). Batch G v3 §16.1 ("A broken heart is the prey of the pursuer"); Batch D v2 §10.3 and R6 (poverty and lowliness entangled).; Col 3:21 *athumeō*, "without *thumos*" (v1 §1.3). Not an M47 word, but the inner place is inside the verb.; New in v3, what the map shows: in all three cases the seat named is the victim's, and the cause is another person's act. Losing heart is the one M20 phenomenon where the seat word always sits with the one acted upon.; In the passage, the aggressor's heart (genuine): Psa 10:10 → 10:11 "He says in his heart" (v1 §1.3; the same verse is FH §5, Batch A v3 §6 ). The oppressor's heart speaks while the victim is seen only from outside.; New in v3: Dan 11:30 ← 11:27 "as for the two kings, their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table". The king who is disheartened in 11:30 is one of the two whose heart was already bent on evil three verses earlier. The losing of heart feeds an aggression that was already in the heart. The rage of 11:30 has a prior seat. The next step names that seat's object: "he shall return to his land with great wealth, but his heart shall be set against the holy covenant" (11:28). The act of 11:30, "take action against the holy covenant", is the act of a heart set on it two verses earlier. Losing heart does not create the target. It releases a hostility the heart already held.; Different party, next verse: Col 3:21 → 3:22 "with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord" is addressed to bondservants, the next household group. It does not bear on the children's discouragement (v1 §1.3).

19272.text: What it does to the one it is set for. "When my spirit faints within me, you know my way! In the path where I walk they have hidden a trap for me" (Psa 142:3). The next verse: "no one cares for my soul" (142:4). The trap is aimed at "my life" (35:7).

19275.text: Seat.; In the verse, the victim's own (genuine): Psa 142:3 "When my spirit faints within me … they have hidden a trap for me". Batch A v3 §7 (Faintness & Despair, M24). → 142:4 "no one cares for my soul" (v2).; In the verse, the victim's life (life-sense): Psa 35:7 "without cause they dug a pit for my life". *Nephesh* here is the life aimed at, in its life sense. It passes the check as life, not as an inner faculty. New in v3: this verse was not read in the M47 batches. It is the same use as Batch G v3 §5.3 ("Hunting souls").; In the next verse, the trapper's (genuine): Psa 64:5 → 64:6 "the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (v2). The heart is where the trap is first hidden, before the net is hidden in the path. New in v3, a second instance: Psa 140:5 ("The arrogant have hidden a trap for me") follows "who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually" (140:2). The trappers' heart is again where the plan starts.; Life-sense, in the passage: Jer 18:22 ("they have dug a pit to take me") comes two verses after "Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them" (18:20). *Nephesh* is the life aimed at, as in Psa 35:7. New in v3: the verse adds what makes the hidden trap bitter. It is set by those the victim once interceded for. Good repaid with evil, as in Psa 55:12–13 (§2 g), where the betrayer is the familiar friend.; In the next verse, the victim's soul after the reversal — new in v3: Psa 35:8 ("let the net that he hid ensnare him") → 35:9 "Then my soul will rejoice in the Lord, exulting in his salvation". The soul the pit was dug for (35:7) is the soul that rejoices when the trap turns on its maker (35:9). The seat is the same in the threat and in the rescue.; In the next verses, the victim's own — new in v3: Psa 31:4 → 31:5 "Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O Lord, faithful God", and → 31:7 "you have seen my affliction; you have known the distress of my soul". The one taken out of the hidden net commits his spirit into God's hand. The next verses then say that the soul's distress has been known by God. Being known (§6) answers the concealment of the trap. Batch E v2 §1.7 reads Psa 31:5 as the spirit committed at death. Here the committal comes in the middle of danger, not at death.

19276.text: What the map shows. This phenomenon has three seats in three hands: the trapper's heart (the hiding place of the intent), the victim's spirit (fainting, then committed), and God's knowing of the victim's soul.

19279.text: Objects hidden or laid up: Gen 35:4; Deu 33:19; Job 20:26; Jer 43:9, 10

19286.text: Seat.; Spurious: Zec 11:9 and 11:16 "flesh": flesh as food, "devour the flesh of one another"; "devours the flesh of the fat ones" (v1 §2 *kachad* row; Batch A v3 R6).; Rev 2:17 "Spirit": the divine Spirit speaking to the churches (v1 §0). Batch E v2 §11 read the verse for its "new name", not the seat.; Genuine, but not the M20 word's: Zec 11:8 "I" and "they" are *nephesh* twice: "my soul was short with them, and their soul loathed me". Batch F v4 §4 ("Mutual detestation between shepherd and flock"). The inner-being content is real and belongs to both parties. The M20 word in the verse (*kachad*, "destroyed") is the cut-off sense and carries none of it. The verse is kept in NO. The seat is recorded against the verse, not the phenomenon.; New in v3, a seat arriving in the interpretation of a sign-act: the loincloth verses (Jer 13:4–7) are a sign-act with no inner state. Its interpretation names one: "This evil people, who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own heart … shall be like this loincloth, which is good for nothing" (Jer 13:10). The hidden, spoiled loincloth stands for a people whose heart goes its own way. The seat is the people's, and genuine, but it belongs to the sign's meaning, not to the hiding. No ledger change. The four verses stay NO, because the M20 word describes the prophet's act with the cloth. The interpretation is recorded here as a pointer to M30 (stubbornness of heart; Batch C v3 §9.1).

19288.text: Jos 7:19–22: seeing → coveting → taking → hiding → demand to disclose → confession → found

19290.text: Luk 9:45–47: perception blocked from outside → fear to ask → rivalry → Jesus knows the reasoning of their hearts (v3)

19294.text: Psa 27:8–9: the heart seeks the face → "Hide not your face" (v3)

19301.text: Dan 11:27–30: hearts bent on evil (v3) → disheartened → withdraw → enraged → action against the covenant

19302.text: Dan 5:9–12: lords perplexed → the queen names Daniel → an excellent spirit … to interpret (v3)

19303.text: Two phenomena face each other in one psalm: "he will hide me in his shelter" (Psa 27:5) and "Hide not your face from me" (27:9). The same verb gives safety (§3) and dread (§5), depending on whether God hides the person or hides himself from the person. v3 adds that the heart between them, "My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek'" (27:8), is seeking the face.

19317.text: Psa 142:3 | "spirit" *ruach* (H7307G) | TR §15 | the victim's | genuine | A v3 §7

19324.text: Eze 13:22 | "disheartened" *lev* (H3820A) | LH §12 | the victim's | genuine, inside the phrase | A v3 §6

19328.text: Zec 11:16 | "flesh" *basar* (H1320) | NO §17 | none | spurious: flesh as food | v1 §2

19335.text: Totals (30 verses).: Within the 16 bearer's-own seats: three are the object of the anxiety, not its location (Mat 6:25; Luk 12:22; 1Cor 7:34); two carry the seat inside the M20 word's own phrase (Psa 109:16; Eze 13:22)

19341.text: Spurious for the phenomenon | Gen 3:8; Exo 16:8; 2Ch 22:9; Zec 11:9; Zec 11:16; Rev 2:17 | 6

19342.text: What the map shows across the phenomena.: Where the genuine seats fall: on the one who suffers the phenomenon (FH, AX, TR, LH); on the one who causes or misreads it (FH, CD, and in context TR and LH); on an interpreter or diagnoser (PX Dan 5:12, UC Luk 9:47, both in context); The concealment phenomena that are outward acts (HG, HS, SH) have no genuine seat in-verse at all. In context, their nearest seat word is the life that is hunted (Psa 54:4) or the heart that melted into confession (Jos 2:11).; The seat word does four jobs in M20, and only one is "where the phenomenon sits": the location (Pro 12:25; Psa 143:7); the object (Mat 6:25; 1Cor 7:34); the landing place of the answer (Psa 94:19; Phili 4:7); the site of the remedy (Jam 4:8; Psa 51:10); The seat often comes one verse away, and the direction matters: before the phenomenon, as its cause or ground (Psa 27:8; Deu 1:28; Isa 29:13; Isa 54:6; Dan 11:27); after it, as its experience, its diagnosis, or its answer (Psa 13:2; 69:20; 102:4; Luk 9:47; Phili 4:7; Psa 31:5–7; 35:9; 22:26); The seat of the one who does *not* undergo the phenomenon sometimes stands beside it: Caleb's "different spirit" among the grumblers (Num 14:24); the prudent one who "guards his soul" (Pro 22:5); Daniel's "excellent spirit" among the perplexed (Dan 5:12). The seat is named in the contrast figure, not in the crowd.; Concealment of the heart behind speech or act recurs outside §7: the trapper's heart (Psa 64:6; 140:2), the whisperer's glazed lips over an evil heart (Pro 26:23, 25), the aggressor's heart set before the act (Dan 11:28). In these phenomena the hidden thing is the heart itself.

19343.text: Psa 17:8 (SH) | Psa 17:9 "deadly enemies" | the sheltered one's · life-sense | §3 Seat

19348.text: Psa 102:2 (FH) | Psa 102:4 "My heart is struck down … withered" | bearer's own · genuine | §5 Seat

19356.text: Pro 22:3 (HS) | Pro 22:5 "whoever guards his soul" | the prudent one's self · genuine | §2 Seat

19367.text: Candidate for the synthesis theme "the inner seat as governed" (v1 §R-V): v3 adds the interpreter's seat (Dan 5:12) and the diagnoser's reading of another's heart (Luk 9:47). Both are forms of "the seat of the other party". This is noted, not proposed.

19369.text: Co-existence in one psalm, Psa 27: "he will hide me in his shelter" (27:5) and "Hide not your face from me" (27:9). Being hidden by God and God hiding from me are asked for side by side (see §5).

19398.text: H2803G is mostly craft: skillfully, skilled, designer, skillful men. 11 of its 18 verses are the tabernacle work in Exodus. The other 7 include Haman's plot (Est 8:3, 9:25) and God's devising (2Sa 14:14).

19401.text: Overlap with the other sets: Heb 6:17 is also in the will set and Rom 9:11 is also in the choose set. Every other verse is new to this strand.

19402.text: 10 of the 29 marked M64 × M47 verses (m64-m47-marked-verses-v1-20261006) are in this set: Lev 7:18, 1Ki 12:33, Neh 6:8, Psa 17:3, Psa 35:4, Dan 6:3, Jon 1:4, Act 11:23, 1Co 4:5 and 2Co 1:17.

19403.text: Joshua 24:15 — "choose this day whom you will serve": Joshua does not open with the choice. He opens with eleven verses in which the Lord speaks of what *he* did: *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"*; *"I brought you out"*; *"I gave them into your hand"*; *"it was not by your sword or by your bow"* (v3–12); The recital starts where the people's story started: *"your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates … and they served other gods"* (v2). Before Israel ever chose, the Lord had already taken Abraham out from among those gods. The choice put to the people at Shechem comes at the end of that history, not at the start of it.; The choice is not whether to serve. Serving is taken for granted: the fathers served gods beyond the River, and the Amorites serve the gods of the land. The only question is *whom*. So the choosing is a choice of master.; It begins in the eyes: *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day"*. Joshua treats the people's own view of what is good and evil as where the choice starts, and he leaves it open to them. He even names the alternatives for them. Then he makes his own choice in front of them, before they answer: *"as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord."*; The people choose from memory: *"it is the Lord our God who brought us … up from the land of Egypt, … and who did those great signs in our sight"* (v17). Their choosing rests on what they saw.; Joshua's reply is not what a speaker would say if he only wanted agreement: *"You are not able to serve the Lord, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God"* (v19). Choosing and being able to carry the choice out are not the same thing, and Joshua says so plainly. The people insist, *"No, but we will serve the Lord"* (v21).; At that point the choice turns back on the one who made it: *"You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord"* (v22). Once spoken, a choice becomes a testimony the chooser will be held to.; It also exposes what is still in the house: *"Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the Lord"* (v23). The people have just chosen the Lord, yet the foreign gods are still among them. So the choice spoken with the mouth has to be followed by two things: putting something away; an inner turning, the heart inclined (H5186, "to stretch, bend")

19405.text: Psalm 119:30 — "I have chosen the way of faithfulness": This verse sits in the stanza that begins *"My soul clings to the dust; give me life according to your word!"* (v25). Two verses before it the psalmist says *"My soul melts away for sorrow; strengthen me according to your word!"* (v28). The person who chooses here is low and spent, not standing strong over the options.; Around the choosing the psalmist is mostly asking: *"teach me"*; *"Make me understand"*; *"strengthen me"*; *"Put false ways far from me"* (v26–29); The false way is not refused by his own strength alone. He asks God to put it at a distance. Then he states the choice: *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me"* (v30). The choosing is joined at once to keeping something in view: he puts the rules in front of himself, where he can see them.; The next verse uses the same word as the first verse of the stanza: v25: *"My soul clings to the dust"* (H1692); v31: *"I cling to your testimonies, O Lord"* (H1692); The verb is the same, and what it holds on to has changed. I read the choice in v30 as the turn between the two: the soul that was clinging to the dust now clings to the testimonies. The stanza places the verbs in this order; it does not name the change.; The stanza ends forward-looking, with a condition: *"I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!"* (v32). The choice has been made, but running in the chosen way waits on something God does to the heart.

19406.text: Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in": This is an oracle. It opens with God, not with the people: *"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me … I said, “Here I am, here I am,”"* (v1); *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices"* (v2); The wrong choosing in v12 is made in front of a God who is calling and holding out his hands.; The oracle shows what they turned to instead: sacrifices *"in gardens"*, sitting *"in tombs"*, eating *"pig’s flesh"* (v3–4); a pride that says *"do not come near me, for I am too holy for you"* (v5); they *"forget my holy mountain"* and *"set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny"* (v11); They put their trust in luck and fate.; The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.; The verse then gives the reason, and the reason is in the inner being: *"because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."* The choosing does not stand alone. It is the far end of not answering and not listening. When they turned away from the voice calling them, that was already a choice, and choosing what God does not delight in is where it ends.; There is a phrase to set beside Joshua 24. There, the choice turned on what was *"evil in your eyes"*. Here they *"did what was evil in my eyes"*. The measure has moved from their eyes to God's, and his delight is the standard their choice is judged by.; In the same oracle the word "chosen" is used of the others: *"my chosen shall possess it"* (v9); *"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse"* (v15); So in one passage there are those who chose what God did not delight in, and those God calls *"my chosen"*. The outcome sets the two side by side and reaches the inner being on both sides: *"my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (v14). The choice ends in the heart and spirit of the one who made it.

19409.text: 1.1 He forms a plan and makes it known: *"Therefore hear the plan that the Lord has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman"* (Jer 49:20). The same words are used against Babylon in Jer 50:45.; In both passages the plan follows his question *"For who is like me? Who will summon me?"* (49:19; 50:44).; *"the Lord has both planned and done what he spoke concerning the inhabitants of Babylon"* (Jer 51:12).; The verse before gives the purpose and how it moves: *"The Lord has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it"* (51:11).; His purpose goes forward through the stirred spirit of other people.; *"for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God"* (Act 20:27). His counsel is something to be declared in full, and Paul counts it a matter of his own innocence (20:26).

19410.text: 1.2 His devising answers human devising: Micah 2 opens with those *"who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds"* (2:1), who *"covet fields and seize them"* (2:2). Then: *"Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, against this family I am devising disaster"* (2:3).; The same verb is used for both. The "therefore" ties his devising to theirs.; In Jeremiah 18 he says *"I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return"* (18:11). They answer: *"We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart"* (18:12).; His plan and their plans stand in one exchange.

19412.text: 1.4 He also purposes and does not turn back: *"for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back"* (Jer 4:28). The verse before sets a limit within it: *"yet I will not make a full end"* (4:27).; *"As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent … so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not"* (Zec 8:14–15).; The fixed purpose is set beside a fixed purpose for good.; *"the unchangeable character of his purpose"* (Heb 6:17). He guaranteed it with an oath, *"so that … we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us. We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul"* (6:18–19).

19413.text: Both are stated. The verses say he relents (Jer 18:8, 10; 26:3; 36:3) and that he does not relent or turn back (Jer 4:28; Zec 8:14; Heb 6:17). No verse in this set explains how the two stand together, and this account does not.

19414.text: 1.5 It is carried out, and people see afterward that it was his: *"The Lord has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago"* (Lam 2:17).; *"The Lord determined to lay in ruins the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out the measuring line; he did not restrain his hand"* (Lam 2:8).; Straight after 2:17: *"Their heart cried to the Lord … Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord!"* (2:18–19). The fulfilled purpose is met with the heart poured out to the one who purposed it.; *"So they repented and said, 'As the Lord of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us'"* (Zec 1:6).; The fathers recognised his purpose in what had happened to them, and they repented.

19415.text: 1.6 Plans for welfare, and thought for the one in need: *"For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope"* (Jer 29:11).; The verse looks ahead to *"When seventy years are completed"* (29:10).; It is followed by *"You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart"* (29:13).; *"As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me"* (Psa 40:17).; *"But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (2Sa 14:14). The wise woman says it against the fact that *"We must all die"*.

19416.text: 1.7 It takes in what people do against him, without excusing them: *"this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men"* (Act 2:23). The plan and the guilt are stated in one sentence.; The church prays Psalm 2, *"Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain?"* (Act 4:25). They say those gathered against Jesus came *"to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place"* (4:28).; Their next words are a request for themselves: *"grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness"* (4:29).; Pointer, from outside the 31: *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Gen 50:20). The same verb is used for both.

19420.text: Turning: in Jer 18:8, 11; 26:3 and 36:3, the plan is spoken so that a person may hear and turn.

19424.text: The heart poured out after his purpose is carried out (Lam 2:18–19).

19427.text: Fear not: *"so again have I purposed … to bring good … fear not"* (Zec 8:15), with commands that follow (8:16–17), including *"do not devise evil in your hearts against one another"*. The verb is the one used for his own purposing in 8:14–15.
