19835.text: H0977, "choose". This is the ordinary verb, and it carries most of these verses. The ESV renders it in several ways: *"choose"*; *"desire"*: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38); *"to be chosen"* in the sense of preferred: *"To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16); The same verb is used of the Lord choosing the place for his name (Deu 12:5, 14), and of the Lord's answering choice: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them"* (Isa 66:4).

19838.text: G0830, "of one's own accord". One word, literally "self-chosen" (2Cor 8:3, 17).

19841.text: Being taught. *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (Psa 25:12). The teaching comes from who the Lord is: *"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way"* (25:8). The psalmist asks for it: *"Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths"* (25:4). In Psalm 119 he asks *"graciously teach me your law"*, and asks God to do the refusing with him: *"Put false ways far from me"* (119:29).

19855.text: Choosing before a God who has already acted: In these verses the human choice is never the first move.; At Shechem it comes after eleven verses of what the Lord did, beginning with *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"* (Jos 24:3).; In Isaiah 65 the wrong choice is made in front of a God who says *"Here I am, here I am"* and *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people"* (65:1–2).; At the Jerusalem council the church's choosing follows Peter's word that *"God made a choice among you"* (Act 15:7), in the same verb.

19856.text: Own accord, and God at work: Two things are named side by side and not set against each other: *"thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you"*; *"being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (2Cor 8:16–17); The Macedonians gave *"of their own accord"*, and the order of their giving is set out: *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (8:3, 5). The church's choice is joined to the Spirit's in the same verb: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (Act 15:28). The psalmist chooses, and asks God to give the room to carry it out: *"I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!"* (Psa 119:32). I read these verses as saying that what God puts into the heart becomes the person's own. The verses name both and do not explain how they fit.

19858.text: A choice that is honoured: Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and Scripture gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you … in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deu 23:16). The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38).; The phrase *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same wording as *"the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (Deu 12:5, 14). I read this as the law giving the slave a small share of the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw this comparison (open item).

19861.text: It exposes what is still there, and calls for the heart. *"Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the Lord"* (Jos 24:23).

19913.text: Isa 42:1 | 13.1 v9 *Choosing*, through Mat 12:18 "quoting Isaiah 42:1", with the servant's bearing (Mat 12:19–20 = Isa 42:2–3) | You ruled that Mat 12:18 points to Jesus, part of the divine. So the servant's quiet and gentle bearing belongs to 13.1, where it already stands. I recommend no 10.7 *Being chosen* placement.

19920.text: 3.2 Job 7:15, in Ch 2 *Wanting to die*: Extend the Job bullet: > … (7:11). The wish comes out of his nights: *"When I say, 'My bed will comfort me' … then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions"* (7:13–14). He says it to God, *"Leave me alone"* (7:16), and he does not act on it.; (The section's opening already says that Job's "I" is *nephesh*.)

19924.text: 3.6 Exo 36:2, in 10.7 *Willing*, *The willing heart*: Add a bullet after the Exo 35:21–22 bullet: > - Of the craftsmen, the skill given and the heart that moves are named together: *"every craftsman in whose mind the Lord had put skill, everyone whose heart stirred him up to come to do the work"* (Exodus 36:2).

19929.text: 3.11 Pro 1:29, in 10.12, the *It strikes* bullet: After the Pro 1:26–27 quote, add: > The same speech says they *"did not choose the fear of the Lord"* (1:29). I read the passage as setting the fear of the Lord, not chosen, beside the terror that comes.; (Pro 1:22, *"How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple?"*, is not proposed. 10.7 *Willing* already carries the refusals of this passage.)

19931.text: 2Sa 14:13–14, in 10.7 *Planning*. This is a citation fix of the #1990 kind: the same Joab issue in a place the #1987 reading did not list. Replace the paragraph that begins *"A plan can also be held against someone's good"* with: > A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).

19935.text: Carefulness, against presumption. When a case is *"too difficult for you"* (17:8), the decision is sought at the place. What is asked of the person then is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:10), and not to turn *"to the right hand or to the left"* (17:11). Presumption is the opposite, and the man who acts presumptuously dies. The end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage gives the limit (*"too difficult for you"*) and the carefulness. It does not describe the inner struggle.

19937.text: Given room away from the place. Ordinary meat need not be eaten at the chosen place. *"If the place that the Lord your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill … and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire"* (Deu 12:21). "Whenever you desire" is the soul's desire (*ʾawwāh*, desire, with *nepeš*, soul). It is spoken of plainly and allowed, with one limit: *"the blood is the life"* (12:23).

19939.text: Turned toward it from far off: For those far from the chosen city, the city is the direction of prayer. Solomon's prayer gives the hardest case, the people in captivity because they sinned: *"for there is no one who does not sin"* (1Ki 8:46). The inner turning comes in steps: *"yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive"* (8:47); *"and repent and plead with you … saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly'"* (8:47); *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies … and pray to you toward their land, … the city that you have chosen"* (8:48); "Turn" and "repent" are the one verb, *šûb*. The turning happens in the enemy's land. The whole heart and the whole soul are in it. The prayer is turned toward what God chose. Solomon prays it before the one who knows hearts: *"for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind"* (8:39). He also asks God to do the turning: *"that he may incline our hearts to him"* (8:58).; Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb. He asks God to remember his word to Moses: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Neh 1:9). Here the return is to God himself, and the place is where he brings those who return. Nehemiah's own part comes first: he *"sat down and wept and mourned for days"* (1:4), and confessed *"Even I and my father's house have sinned"* (1:6).

19943.text: Despising and abhorring. The servant is addressed as *"one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation"* (Isa 49:7). "Despised" is the same verb as Michal's. The verse turns it round by God's faithfulness and choosing: *"Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the Lord, who is faithful, … who has chosen you"*.

19956.text: Seeking, and not obtaining. *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Rom 11:7). The rest were seeking. They were given *"eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear"* (11:8). Paul at once refuses the conclusion that this is the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11). The remnant is chosen *"by grace"*, not works (11:5–6). The passage says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

19958.text: Desire.; The soul's desire for food is given room away from the chosen place (Deu 12:21).; The soul's whole desire draws a Levite to the chosen place (Deu 18:6).; The soul delights in its own abominations, beside a wrong choice (Isa 66:3, §2a).; *Why:* what the desire is turned toward. The same words for the soul's desire are used for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming. The verses allow both. What the soul delights in decides the third.

19959.text: Despising.; Michal despises the chosen man *"in her heart"*, by the eyes of people (2Sa 6:16, 20).; The servant is *"deeply despised"* by others, and kings will bow (Isa 49:7). Same verb, *bāzâ*.; The chosen people themselves *"despised the pleasant land"* (Psa 106:24, §2b; *māʾas*).; Others *"despised my people"*, concluding that God had rejected them (Jer 33:24; *nāʾaṣ*).; *Why:* who despises what. It is aimed at the chosen by others, and by the chosen at what they were given. Each verse names its own ground: honour before people, the chosen people's ruin, no faith in the promise.

19963.text: The held phrase (Deu 23:16 beside Deu 12:5, 14) stays held. The forms of words differ (*"out of all your tribes"*, *"in one of your tribes"*, *"within one of your towns"*).

19967.text: Deu 12:21 | desire (given room away from the place); what changes the character (desire) | batch 1

19985.text: Isa 49:7 | set against (despised and abhorred; turned round by God's faithfulness and choosing); what changes the character (despising) | batch 2

19997.text: Where it is placed. The verses place this in the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way"* (Pro 16:9); *"who plan evil things in their heart"* (Psa 140:2); *"the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1Ki 12:33); *"the purposes of the heart"* (1Co 4:5); *"every intention of the thoughts of his heart"* (Gen 6:5)

20002.text: 3.1 It happens in the heart, and it is hidden until it acts: *"Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass"* (Pro 16:30). The planning shows only in small signs.; *"I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jer 11:19). Jeremiah did not see the plan aimed at him.; *"they intended to do me harm"* (Neh 6:2). The intent sat behind the friendly invitation, *"Come and let us meet together"*.; *"But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy"* (Isa 10:7). Of Assyria, what is in the heart differs from the role God gives it. I read this as the intention belonging to the one who holds it, whatever use another makes of the act.; *"thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme"* (Eze 38:10). Here the thought arrives first and the devising follows. This is the one verse in the set that states such a sequence; no other verse is joined to it here.; *"you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Neh 6:8). The same capacity can produce what is false.

20003.text: 3.2 It works in time: the night before, the morning after: *"Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand."* (Mic 2:1); *"He plots trouble while on his bed"* (Psa 36:4).; *"For I know what they are inclined to do even today, before I have brought them into the land"* (Deu 31:21). The inclination is already there before the occasion comes.; I read Mic 2:1 as the clearest picture in the set of looking ahead as such. The scheme is held overnight and carried out at dawn, when the hand has the power to do it. The verse itself names the power of the hand as the reason it is done.

20008.text: Others in the group: Dan 6:3 (the king plans to set Daniel over the kingdom, *"because an excellent spirit was in him"*) and Act 15:37 (Barnabas wanted to take Mark).

20009.text: 3.4 Devising a design: skill given: *"He has filled them with skill to do every sort of work done by an engraver or by a designer"* (Exo 35:35). Also *"to devise artistic designs"* (Exo 31:4, 35:32).; In Exodus the capacity to devise a design is something God fills people with (route A and B).; Elsewhere the same word is used for human invention: Uzziah's machines *"invented by skillful men"* (2Ch 26:15), and in a woe, those who *"like David invent for themselves instruments of music"* (Amo 6:5).

20010.text: The forms: plotting (*"as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life"*, Psa 31:13); imagining (*"they imagine the worst for me"*, Psa 41:7); using the tongue (*"Your tongue plots destruction"*, Psa 52:2; *"let us strike him with the tongue"*, Jer 18:18); group plans (*"Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!"*, Jer 48:2; *"they made plans to put him to death"*, Joh 11:53); against God himself (*"What do you plot against the Lord?"*, Nah 1:9)

20011.text: What is commanded: *"let none of you devise evil against another in your heart"* (Zec 7:10, and again 8:17).

20012.text: What comes back on the planner: *"you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother"* (Deu 19:19); Haman's plan should *"return on his own head"* (Est 9:25); *"Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer"* (Pro 24:8)

20018.text: 3.8 The plan and its outcome: *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Pro 16:9).; *"Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing"* (Isa 8:10).; *"if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail"* (Act 5:38). Gamaliel's counsel.; *"I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented)"* (Rom 1:13).; *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Gen 50:20). The same word, H2803I, is used for both meanings.; *"they will not succeed"* (Psa 21:11), and *"but only for a time"* (Dan 11:24).

20024.text: H2803I: God shaping disaster that he may relent from (Jer 18:8, 11); God's plans for welfare (Jer 29:11); people devising evil (Psa 35:4); Saul's plot (1Sa 18:25); a ship "threatened" (Jon 1:4)

20025.text: H2161: God's fixed purpose, *"I have purposed; I have not relented"* (Jer 4:28); the psalmist's resolve (Psa 17:3); the wise woman considering a field (Pro 31:16); the wicked plotting (Psa 37:12)

20026.text: H2803G: craft skill given by God (Exo 35:35); Haman's plot (Est 8:3); God's means for the banished (2Sa 14:14)

20028.text: God's intentions in Jeremiah are conditional: *"if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended"* (Jer 18:8; also 26:3, 36:3). His plan is stated so that people may *"Return, every one from his evil way"* (Jer 18:11). These 31 verses on God's purposing are routed A for 13.1; the 15 that invite or bear on a human response are also B.

20029.text: 10.7 Choosing and setting direction, new section *Planning* | The account of looking ahead. Planning carries a choice ahead (Gen 11:6; Pro 16:9). It covers: weighing first (Luk 14:28–33; Pro 31:15–16; Judg 19:30); planning without knowing (Act 27:10–14, 39–41; Rom 1:13; Jam 4:15); a plan carrying a person's word (2Co 1:17–18); planning together and parting (Act 15:37–39; Luk 23:51–52); planning for another's good (Dan 6:3–4), with the king's planning measured against God's (2Sa 14:13–14); a purpose held (Psa 17:3, 5; Act 11:23; 2Ti 3:10; 1Ch 29:18; Rom 8:6–7; Isa 26:3); devised from one's own heart (1Ki 12:32–33; Neh 6:8); the plan and its outcome (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38–39; Psa 21:11; Dan 11:24; Gen 50:20); seen and disclosed (1Ch 28:9; 1Co 4:3–5) | New section

20031.text: 10.10 Relating to others, new section *Plotting against another* | Planned in the heart (Psa 140:2; Zec 7:10; 8:17). Done together (Psa 31:13; Jer 48:2; Joh 11:53; 12:10–11; Eze 11:2; Dan 11:25, 27; Jer 49:30). Aimed at the quiet and the weak (Psa 10:2; 35:20; 37:12; Eze 38:10–11). Hidden behind something friendly (Neh 6:2–3; 1Sa 18:25). Accusing the other of a plan (Neh 6:6, 8–9). The one plotted against: not knowing (Jer 11:19–20); praying to be guarded (Psa 140:4, 8; 35:4); trusting (Psa 31:14–15); another pleading (Est 8:3; 9:24); another stopping it (Act 27:42–43). Named and checked (Pro 24:8–9; 30:32–33; Deu 19:19–20) | New section

20032.text: 10.4 Thinking | *Where thoughts come from*: Eze 38:10 (the thought arrives, then the devising). *It designs*: Huram-abi (2Ch 2:14). *It reckons*: Gen 31:15; Lam 4:2; Isa 33:8; 13:17–18; being reckoned (Psa 44:22; 88:3–4; Num 23:9; Neh 13:13). *What is devised comes back*: Deu 19:19. Connections: planning (10.7) and plotting (10.10) | Widened

20033.text: 10.9 Relating to God | Plotting turned against him (Hos 7:14–15; Nah 1:9, 11). His word reckoned strange, and his name esteemed (Hos 8:12; Mal 3:16). A pointer to 13.1 *Purposing* | Widened

20034.text: 10.11 Hiding and disclosing, *The hidden trap* | The friendly word as cover (Neh 6:2), not knowing (Jer 11:19), the trap hidden (Psa 140:5) | Widened

20035.text: 10.13 Anger, *What it does next* | The plot with gnashing teeth (Psa 37:12); rage that wants to kill at once, which is not a plan (Act 5:33–35) | Widened

20036.text: Ch 11 §4 One word, opposite values | New faces: "Purposing" (*zāmam*: Psa 17:3; 37:12; Pro 31:16; Jer 4:28) and "Planning ahead" (Luk 14:31; Act 27:12; 2Ti 3:10; Joh 11:53; Pro 16:9). The reading of what changes them is marked "I read" | New faces

20037.text: 2. The count question: In the scan I asked whether the "count, regard, esteem" verses belong with looking ahead. Your instruction counted all 77, so the 13 count verses are woven too. They went where reckoning already lives, in 10.4 *It reckons* (and 10.9 for Hos 8:12), not into *Planning*. This keeps the two apart, as the verses do.

20118.text: The will steers. *"they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs"* (Jam 3:4). The will is pictured as what sets a ship's direction. In its passage (3:3–5) the picture is used of the tongue.

20121.text: An intention carried ahead. Herod put Peter in prison, *"intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people"* (Act 12:4).

20126.text: God's will (route A, for 13.1): *"Of his own will he brought us forth"* (Jam 1:18); *"not wishing that any should perish"* (2Pe 3:9); *"when God desired to show more convincingly … the unchangeable character of his purpose"* (Heb 6:17), where will and purpose stand in one sentence; *"who can resist his will?"* (Rom 9:19); the Spirit *"apportions to each one individually as he wills"* (1Co 12:11)

20128.text: The epistle openings and requests (*"I want you to know"*, Phi 1:12; Tit 3:8; Jude 5; 1Ti 2:8; 5:14; 2Jo 12; Phm 13; 3Jo 10) mostly use the word as a stated wish in teaching. Their bearing on setting direction is slight, but each still needs to be read.

20138.text: The willing heart (*nāḏîḇ*, H5081G, 5 verses) is the will freely given: *"Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the Lord's contribution"* (Exo 35:5); *"All who were of a willing heart brought"* (Exo 35:22; also 2Ch 29:31; 1Ch 28:21); It is asked of God: *"uphold me with a willing spirit"* (Psa 51:12).; 10.7 *Setting the heart* already cites Exo 35:21, *"everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"*, the verse just before 35:22.

20143.text: 5. If you want this woven: Read the 99 verses in their passages, the method used for the plan set.; Route them under rule 72. By scan, God's or the Spirit's will (route A) is 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Luk 22:42 (with B); Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9. Job 39:9 is the wild ox (13.4 Nature).; A home in 10.7 would be a section on willing, next to *Planning* and *Holding a choice*. The working note already reserves "Will and resolve" for there.; Placed already (in the narrative for another reason, #1987): Deu 1:26; 2:30; 1Sa 31:4; Psa 51:12; Pro 6:35; Dan 5:19; Act 25:20; 1Ti 2:8. Each still needs reading for its will word.

20151.text: A gift: water from Bethlehem, brought at the risk of three men's lives (2Sa 23:16–17; 1Ch 11:18–19).

20167.text: Moved from inside: *"they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"* (Exo 35:21), then *"All who were of a willing heart brought"* (35:22). Moses had said *"Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring"* (35:5).

20180.text: Herod. *"when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter … intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church"* (Act 12:3–5). His intention is set beside the church's prayer, and the intention was not carried out (12:6–11).

20183.text: The pilot's will. *"they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs"* (Jam 3:4). In its passage the picture belongs to the tongue: *"we guide their whole bodies"* (3:3), *"So also the tongue is a small member"* (3:5). The will directs a whole ship; the tongue sets on fire *"the entire course of life"* (3:6).

20186.text: Paul's wishes for the churches are mostly stated wishes in teaching. Their passages give each one a reason: *"I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling"* (1Ti 2:8); *"I would have younger widows marry … for some have already strayed after Satan"* (1Ti 5:14–15); *"I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works"* (Tit 3:8); *"I want you to know … what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel"* (Phi 1:12); *"I would rather not use paper and ink … talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete"* (2Jo 12); *"I want to remind you"* (Jude 5)

20199.text: Against the self-blessing stubborn heart: of the one who *"blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'"* (Deu 29:19), *"The Lord will not be willing to forgive him"* (29:20).

20201.text: His will, positively: *"he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills"* (Rom 9:18). *"So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy"* (9:16). Then the objection, *"who can resist his will?"* (9:19), and the potter: *"Will what is molded say to its molder, 'Why have you made me like this?'"* (9:20).; *"Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth"* (Jam 1:18). Just before: *"desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin"* (1:15), and the Father of lights *"with whom there is no variation"* (1:17).; *"not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance"* (2Pe 3:9), said against those who *"count slowness"*.; *"when God desired to show more convincingly … the unchangeable character of his purpose"* (Heb 6:17). This verse is in both the will set and the plan set.

20206.text: Toward God | plotting against him (Hos 7:15; Nah 1:9) | refusing him: his land, rest, filling and counsel

20207.text: 2.2 Passages where Scripture itself puts them together: Pro 1:29–31. Did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel, are filled with their own devices: choosing, willing and devising in one sentence. Earlier in the same chapter, *"if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood'"* (1:10–11) puts the will's "no" right against a group plot. That is plotting as written in 10.10.; Psa 81:11–12. Would not submit, given over to stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.; Isa 30:1, 9, 15–16. A plan *"but not mine"*; unwilling to hear; unwilling, and *"No! We will flee upon horses."* The refusal and the people's own plan are in their own mouth together.; 1Ch 28:19–21. The plan from the hand of the Lord, and *"every willing man who has skill"*. This is the positive pairing: a plan given, and the willing who carry it out.; Gen 24:5–8. Planning ahead allows for another person's will (*"Perhaps the woman may not be willing"*).; 2Sa 13:24–28. A planner presses another's will until it gives way, and the plan goes on to murder.; Mat 1:19–20. Unwilling, then resolved, while still considering, then redirected by God.; Act 12:3–5. Herod's intending is set beside the church's prayer.; 2Co 1:15–17. Wanting, then plans, then the question of a divided word.; Act 27:42–43. One man's wish against a group's plan.; Dan 4:27–35. Counsel offered and not taken; the human will made absolute; the Most High *"does according to his will"*; reason returned.

20210.text: Heb 6:17 is in both sets. God *"desired"* (will) to show the unchangeable character of *"his purpose"* (plan).

20211.text: The heart and spirit named with the act.; Planning: *"The heart of man plans his way"* (Pro 16:9); *"plan evil things in their heart"* (Psa 140:2).; Willing: the heart or spirit hardened, stubborn or lifted up (Exo 10:27; Deu 2:30; Eze 3:7; Psa 81:12; Deu 29:19; Dan 5:20); the willing heart and spirit (Exo 35:21–22; 2Ch 29:31; Psa 51:12).; So the will verses name the state of the heart and spirit more often than the plan verses do. Chapters 4 (the heart) and 6 (the spirit) should take this.

20224.text: A (other beings) — 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9; Luk 22:42.; Also B: Deu 10:10 (Moses' intercession), Deu 29:20 (the self-blessing heart), Dan 4:25 and 4:32 (the king's learning), Dan 5:21, Luk 22:42.

20228.text: Colossians 3:12: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones … compassionate hearts": The chapter begins with where the chosen now stand: *"If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above"* (v1); *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (v2); *"your life is hidden with Christ in God"* (v3).; Then it tells them what to put away: *"Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry"* (v5); *"But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth"* (v8); They have *"put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator"* (v10).; The verse comes next: *"Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience"* (v12). "Compassionate hearts" is literally the inward parts (G4698) of compassion. The verse gives being chosen as the ground ("as God's chosen ones"), and then gives a command. The qualities are not described as already there. They are to be put on, as clothing is.; The chosen are called *"holy and beloved"*. The holiness that is the purpose of the choosing in Ephesians 1:4 is here a name the chosen already carry, and the inner qualities are still to be put on. I set the two letters side by side; neither refers to the other.; What the chosen put on is turned toward one another: *"bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive"* (v13); *"And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony"* (v14); *"And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful"* (v15); The forgiving is measured by being forgiven. The peace is to rule in the heart.

20229.text: 2 Thessalonians 2:13: "God chose you … through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth": The chapter is about deception. Paul asks them *"not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed"* (v2), and warns *"Let no one deceive you in any way"* (v3). The lawless one comes *"with all wicked deception for those who are perishing"* (v10).; Before the choosing verse, the passage names the inner state of those who perish: *"because they refused to love the truth and so be saved"* (v10); *"Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false"* (v11); *"in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness"* (v12); Then: *"But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth"* (v13). "Belief" in v13 and "believe" in v12 are the same root (G4102, G4100), and "truth" is the same word in v10, v12 and v13 (G0225). The chosen are set against the perishing in the passage's own words. The perishing did not believe the truth. The chosen are saved *"through … belief in the truth"*. The perishing had pleasure in unrighteousness. The chosen are sanctified *"by the Spirit"*.; In the verse, God's choosing and the person's belief stand in one sentence. The verse does not say which comes first, or how they fit.; The passage then gives the chosen two things to do, and asks for one thing to be done in them: *"To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ"* (v14); *"So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us"* (v15); *"comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word"* (v17), asked of the Lord Jesus Christ and of God the Father, *"who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace"* (v16)

20230.text: Titus 1:1: "for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness": Paul opens by saying what his own service is for: *"for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began"* (v1–2). Faith, knowledge of the truth, godliness and hope are named as belonging to the elect, and his work serves them.; The rest of the chapter is about who may lead them. The overseer's inner life is set out in full: *"He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain"* (v7); *"but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined"* (v8); *"He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught"* (v9); Against the elect's knowledge of the truth, the chapter sets those who teach otherwise: *"not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth"* (v14); *"to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled"* (v15); *"They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works"* (v16); The elect's knowledge of the truth *"accords with godliness"*. The others say they know God and deny him by what they do. The chapter sets the two side by side.

20231.text: James 2:5: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith": The setting is an assembly that chooses where people sit: *"if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, 'You sit here in a good place,' while you say to the poor man, 'You stand over there'"* (v3). James names what that shows of them inside: *"have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?"* (v4).; He answers their way of choosing with God's: *"Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him?"* (v5). The poor man they sent to stand is the kind of man God chose. The assembly went by clothing. God's choice goes by something else, and its aim is that the poor be *"rich in faith"*.; The promise is to *"those who love him"*. The love here is the chosen people's love for God.; Then: *"But you have dishonored the poor man"* (v6). Choosing against God's choice is a sin: *"if you show partiality, you are committing sin"* (v9).; The faith of the chosen poor is then tested by what it does: *"What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works?"* (v14); *"So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead"* (v17); Abraham: *"faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works … and he was called a friend of God"* (v22–23)

20234.text: Revelation 17:14: "those with him are called and chosen and faithful": The chapter is a vision of judgment on *"the great prostitute"*, with whom *"the dwellers on earth have become drunk"* (v2). The seer himself is moved: *"When I saw her, I marveled greatly"* (v6). He is asked *"Why do you marvel?"* (v7). Those who marvel at the beast are *"the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world"* (v8). The vision *"calls for a mind with wisdom"* (v9).; The kings who serve the beast are of one mind: *"These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast"* (v13). Then: *"They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful"* (v14).; The chosen are named by three words, and the third is about them: *"faithful"*. They are *"with him"*. The verse says nothing more of their inner life.; The chapter says this of the kings: *"for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled"* (v17). "Mind" in v13 and "purpose" in v17 are the same word (G1106): the kings' one mind is God's purpose carried out. This is God acting on the hearts of others, not on the chosen. It belongs with 13.1 more than here.

20236.text: The chosen are told to act. Being chosen is given as the ground of commands: put on compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, patience and love (Col 3:12–14); stand firm and hold on (2Th 2:15); be diligent to confirm your calling and election, adding quality to quality (2Pe 1:5–10); This sits with batch 1: *"be strong and do it"* (1Ch 28:10).

20237.text: What they put on is turned toward others. Bearing with, forgiving as they were forgiven, and love that binds (Col 3:13–14). The assembly in James is told not to dishonour the poor God chose (Jam 2:6).

20240.text: Knowing and remembering.: The chosen are prayed for, that the eyes of their hearts be enlightened to know their hope (Eph 1:18).; Their knowledge of the truth accords with godliness (Tit 1:1).; Forgetting one's cleansing is blindness, and another works to keep them remembering (2Pe 1:9, 12–15).; Batch 1 had the chosen called to remember (Psa 105:5; Isa 44:21).

20241.text: God giving over the perishing (2Th 2:11, *"a strong delusion"*), and God putting a purpose into the kings' hearts (Rev 17:17). These are God acting on the hearts of others. They are for 13.1, not §2b.

20258.text: Deuteronomy 18:6: "and he may come when he desires": Two choosings stand in the passage. First the tribe: *"For the Lord your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand and minister in the name of the Lord, him and his sons for all time"* (v5). Then the place: a Levite living in any town *"may come when he desires—to the place that the Lord will choose, and ministers in the name of the Lord his God, like all his fellow Levites"* (v6–7).; "When he desires" is literally "with all the desire of his soul": *kol* (all; H3605) with *ʾawwāh* (desire; H0185) and *nepeš* (*soul: appetite*; H5315L). It is the same desire of the soul that is given room for meat in Deu 12:20–21. Here it is turned toward the chosen place.; The Levite has no land: *"They shall have no inheritance among their brothers; the Lord is their inheritance, as he promised them"* (v2). The law secures his share when he comes: *"then he may have equal portions to eat"* (v8).

20259.text: 1 Kings 8:48 (and 2 Chronicles 6:38): "if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul … and pray to you toward … the city that you have chosen": Solomon dedicates the house. Before the prayer he recalls two choosings: *"I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house … But I chose David to be over my people Israel"* (v16). He also recalls David's heart: *"you did well that it was in your heart"* (v18). David was not allowed to build (v19).; The prayer that follows is a run of cases. In each, someone far from the house prays toward it, and Solomon asks God to hear in heaven. The heart is named throughout: *"each knowing the affliction of his own heart and stretching out his hands toward this house"* (v38); *"render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways (for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind)"* (v39); *"that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land"* (v40); The case of v48 is the hardest one, captivity: *"If they sin against you—for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy"* (v46). Then the inner turning, in steps: *"yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive"* (v47). Literally, "bring it back to their heart" (*šûb*, H7725N, with the heart).; *"and repent and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly'"* (v47); *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies … and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name"* (v48); "Repent" in v47 and v48 is *šûb* (*to return: repent*; H7725O), the same verb as "turn their heart". The turning happens in the enemy's land, far from the city. The whole heart and the whole soul are in it. The prayer is directed toward the chosen city.

20260.text: 2 Chronicles 6:38 gives the same words, with *"the land of their captivity"*. Chronicles closes the prayer differently: *"let your saints rejoice in your goodness"* (6:41).

20264.text: At the place: rejoicing before the Lord, shared with the household, the servants, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow (Deu 12:7, 12, 18; 16:11, 14, 15); learning to fear the Lord, at a meal where the soul's appetite is satisfied (Deu 14:23, 26); remembering, at Passover and beside the rejoicing (Deu 16:3, 12); carefulness to do what is declared there, when a matter is too hard, against presumption (Deu 17:8–13)

20266.text: Away from the place: the soul's desire for food, given room because the place is far (Deu 12:20–21)

20270.text: Corrections to the HIB/qualifier file: Deu 12:21 is "away from the chosen place", not "setting" (see above).

20271.text: The held phrasing in 10.7. The working note in 10.7 holds the shared phrasing of Deuteronomy 23:16 (*"in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him"*) and Deuteronomy 12:5, 14. Batch 1 read Deuteronomy 12 in full. The forms of words differ: 12:5 has *"out of all your tribes"*, 12:14 *"in one of your tribes"*, and 23:16 *"within one of your towns"*. In 23:16 the chooser is the escaped slave. The reading does not settle whether the shared phrase is more than a form of words. It stays held.

20274.text: *"If the place that the Lord your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill any of your herd or your flock … and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire"* (v21)

20281.text: What Solomon asks of God in return: *"forgive your people … and grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive"* (v50). At the end he prays for the heart once more: *"that he may incline our hearts to him"* (v58), and *"Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the Lord our God"* (v61). The day ends with the people going home *"joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown"* (v66).

20282.text: John 15:19: "but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you": Jesus speaks to his disciples on the night before his death. The passage begins with love among the chosen: *"This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you"* (v12). The choosing is said twice: *"You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit"* (v16); *"If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"* (v19); The world's two inner acts are set side by side. "Love" is *phileō* (G5368): the world loves *"its own"*. "Hates" is *miseō* (G3404). The verse says the hatred is *because* of the choosing: *"I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"*.; The passage says the hatred was first aimed at Jesus: *"If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you"* (v18). It gives a reason in the haters: *"because they do not know him who sent me"* (v21). It says they have *"seen and hated both me and my Father"* (v24), and *"They hated me without a cause"* (v25).; Beside the world's hatred stands the command given twice to the chosen: *"love one another"* (v12, v17).

20283.text: Acts 15:7: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe": The chapter is the dispute over circumcision: *"no small dissension and debate"* (v2), then *"much debate"* among the apostles and elders (v7). Peter stands up and appeals to what they already know: *"Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (v7).; "Know" is *epistamai* (G1987). Their knowing of a past choice by God is the ground Peter argues from. The purpose of that choice lies in others: *"that … the Gentiles should hear … and believe"* (*pisteuō*, G4100).; Peter goes on to the Gentiles' hearts: *"God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us"* (v8); *"he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith"* (v9); *"why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?"* (v10); The debate ends: *"And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened"* (v12). The assembly's own choosing follows later in the chapter: *"it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men"* (v25). That was read for §2a.

20284.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: God's choosing of one man has its purpose in others: that the Gentiles hear and believe.; Knowing that God has chosen is the ground on which a dispute is settled.; The Gentiles' hearts are known by God and cleansed by faith (v8–9). God's knowing is rule 72, A. The cleansing of their hearts is in the human inner being.; The debate gives way to silence and listening (v12).

20285.text: Romans 11:7: "Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened": Paul asks whether God has rejected his people and answers: *"By no means!"* (v1). *"God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew"* (v2). He gives Elijah, who thought he was alone, and God's reply: *"I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal"* (v4). *"So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works"* (v5–6).; Then v7: *"What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"*.; The others are *"the rest"*. Two things are said of them: They were seeking (*epizēteō*, G1934) and did not obtain.; They were hardened (*pōroō*, G4456).; The hardening is described from Scripture: *"God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day"* (v8). The giving is God's act (rule 72, A). The eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear are in the human inner being.; Paul does not leave it there: *"So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11). He goes on: *"how much more will their full inclusion mean!"* (v12).

20286.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: Those who are not among the chosen are described as seeking and not obtaining.; They were hardened: eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear (v8).; The hardening is not the end. Their stumbling is not *"in order that they might fall"* (v11).; Jealousy is named as an aim: *"so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11).; The remnant is chosen *"by grace"*, not by works (v5–6). The verse says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

20287.text: 1 Thessalonians 1:4: "For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you": Paul writes of what he remembers of them: *"your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ"* (v3). Then: *"For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (v4–5).; "Know" is *oida* (G6063). Here another person knows that someone has been chosen. The ESV joins v4 to v5 with "because": the knowing rests on how the gospel came to them. The passage goes on to what was seen in them: *"you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit"* (v6); *"you became an example to all the believers"* (v7); *"your faith in God has gone forth everywhere"* (v8); *"you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven"* (v9–10)

20288.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: Another person can know that someone is chosen.; In this verse the knowing rests on what was seen when the gospel came: power, the Holy Spirit and full conviction.; What is seen in the chosen is faith, love and hope (v3), joy in affliction (v6), and turning from idols (v9).; The one who knows it gives thanks and prays for them (v2).

20289.text: 2 Timothy 2:10: "Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect": Paul writes from chains: *"my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!"* (v8–9). Then: *"Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory"* (v10).; "Endure" is *hupomenō* (G5278). The same word comes in the saying that follows: *"if we endure, we will also reign with him"* (v12). The endurance is Paul's. It is for others, the elect, and for their salvation.; The same passage calls Timothy to it: *"Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus"* (v3). It gives the ground: *"if we are faithless, he remains faithful—for he cannot deny himself"* (v13).

20290.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: A person endures suffering for the sake of the chosen.; The aim is their salvation: *"that they also may obtain"*.; The same endurance is promised its outcome: *"if we endure, we will also reign with him"* (v12).

20291.text: 1 Peter 2:4: "a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious": The chapter opens with what the readers are to put away and to long for: *"So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk"* (v1–2).; Then: *"As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious"* (v4).; Two measures stand in one verse: *"rejected by men"* and *"in the sight of God chosen"*. "Rejected" is *apodokimazō* (G0593), to reject after testing. The quotation in v7 uses the same word: *"The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone"*.; The readers share the same name: *"you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation"* (v9). They will be spoken against in turn: *"when they speak against you as evildoers"* (v12).

20292.text: 1 Peter 2:6: "a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame": *"For it stands in Scripture: 'Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame'"* (v6).; The other's inner act here is believing (*pisteuō*, G4100), toward the chosen stone. The outcome is stated: *"will not be put to shame"*.; The next verses divide people by it: *"So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,' and 'A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense.' They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do"* (v7–8).

20293.text: 2 John 1: "The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth": *"The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth, and not only I, but also all who know the truth, because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever"* (v1–2).; The love is the elder's, and it is shared by *"all who know the truth"*. "Love" is *agapaō* (G0025). "Know" is *ginōskō* (G1097). Both are toward the one called elect. The verse grounds the love *"in truth"* and *"because of the truth that abides in us"*. It does not ground it in the choosing.; The letter goes on: *"I rejoiced greatly to find some of your children walking in the truth"* (v4), and *"this is love, that we walk according to his commandments"* (v6).; The HIB/qualifier file has the relation as "none". The reading agrees that the love is not bound to the choosing. "Elect" names the reader.

20304.text: Job 15:5 — Eliphaz: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty": Eliphaz weighs Job by his words. He opens with *"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge"* (v2), and charges *"you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God"* (v4). Then he names the choice: *"For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty"* (v5). He reads it this way: something inside, iniquity, teaches the mouth; the mouth then chooses a crafty tongue; From that he gives the verdict: *"Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you"* (v6).; He takes his evaluation further inside. He moves from the mouth to the heart, eyes and spirit: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?"* (v12–13). For Eliphaz, the words show what the heart has chosen.; His grounds for judging are age and tradition: *"Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father"* (v10); *"what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers"* (v18); His picture of the outcome is the wicked man's end (v20–35).; Set against the book's frame, his charge *"you are doing away with the fear of God"* (v4) runs against the narrator's and the Lord's *"one who feared God"* (1:1, 8). The Lord's verdict in 42:7 is on how Eliphaz spoke of God, not directly on this charge. Still, the man Eliphaz says has chosen the tongue of the crafty is the one the Lord twice calls *"my servant Job"* (42:7–8).

20305.text: Job 34:4 — Elihu: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good": Elihu is angry with both sides. He *"burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God"*, and at the friends *"because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong"* (32:2–3).; He calls the listeners to weigh Job's case together, and calls that weighing a choosing: *"Hear my words, you wise men"* … *"for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food"*; *"Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good"* (v2–4). The choosing here is not of a course of life. It is a judgement: picking out what is right in the case before them.; The picture is tasting. The ear tests (H0974) as the palate tastes (H2938). Then *"let us know among ourselves what is good"* uses the same words as Barzillai's *"Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not"* (2Sa 19:35): know (H3045), between (H0996), good (H2896). Barzillai said the palate's knowing had gone with age. Elihu uses the palate as the picture for weighing words.; What they are to weigh is Job's own claim. Elihu quotes it: *"I am in the right, and God has taken away my right"* (v5). He judges it at once: *"What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water"*, *"who travels in company with evildoers"* (v7–8). His ground is God's justice: *"far be it from God that he should do wickedness"* (v10); *"his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps"* (v21).

20306.text: What this verse shows of choosing, as weighed by another: Weighing another person's choices is itself a choosing, *"what is right"*.; It is made together (*"let us … among ourselves"*), by testing words as the palate tests food.; It is a judgement on a case, not a course of life.; The one who calls for it has already decided (v7–8).

20309.text: Job 34:33 — Elihu: "For you must choose, and not I": Elihu's verdict follows anyway: *"Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight"*; *"Would that Job were tried to the end"* (v35–36).; The book records what Job did choose, and when. It is not after Elihu, but after the Lord speaks (38–41): *"I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me"* (42:3); *"I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes"* (42:5–6); *"I despise"* is the same verb, H3988A, as Elihu's *"you reject"*. In the record the verb stands without its own tagged object; the ESV supplies *"myself"*. I read this as Elihu having named the right kind of choice, a refusing, but the choice being made when Job's eye saw the Lord, not under Elihu's argument. The text gives the order (*"now my eye sees you; therefore"*). It does not comment on Elihu.

20313.text: The refusing verb returns at the end. Elihu's *"you reject"* and Job's *"I despise … and repent"* are the same verb (34:33; 42:6), the verb of *"refuse the evil"* (Isa 7:15). In Job the choice is made when *"now my eye sees you"* (42:5). This stands beside the test reading of Jos 24, where the people chose from what they had seen.
